News.title: Martin Lewis Wednesday alert over key document 'change and check today'
News.content:
Martin Lewis Wednesday alert over key document 'change and check today'

The personal finance expert told ITV This Morning viewers '“The one thing I would warn people, this is really important'

View Image Martin Lewis gave a chilling warning over the potential problems with pensions and wills (Image: ITV)

Martin Lewis has given a warning to anyone with a pension and explained ‘you need to check one thing’. The personal finance expert appeared on This Morning to discuss money - and told people they need to make sure their pension has been set up correctly - or it could go to the wrong person in the event of their sad death.

‌



He said people need to check their pension - because when it was set up decades ago it could be going to the wrong person. He said: “The one thing I would warn people, this is really important. You cannot leave your pension in your will. It is not something you leave in your will. What happens is you need to fill in an expression of wishes form, also known as a nomination form. Now, most people when they set up a pension will have done this,

‌



“But again, that could be 20 years ago. And I get people who find out, you know, their pension, their mother’s pension’s not gone to them, it’s gone to their ex partner, and this type of thing. So you want to check your nomination or expressions and wishes form has been done and you want to check it’s up to date. Now I should note all that does is tell the trustees of the pension scheme where you would like it to go. They are not bound by it but it is generally a very good idea. So that’s worth knowing too and that’s totally separate to your will. You need to do that as well.”

‌



He has previously explained the importance of having an up-to-date will on his Martin Lewis Money Show Live ITV show, saying if they’re not married and one of them dies and there’s no will - the partner will potentially get nothing.

He spoke out in Will Aid month starting, in which solicitors offer their services pro bono in return for charitable donations - in 2026 this takes place in November. Mr Lewis pointed out the urgency of drafting a will for those wanting control over the distribution of their assets post-mortem.

‌



He said: “If you have assets, do a will, then you get to decide where they go. If not, what’s called the intestacy laws will decide where your assets go. It depends on which UK nation you’re in. Go on to Gov.uk and have a look at what the situation would be in your case, especially if you’ve got dependent children.”

He even highlighted the complicated dynamics that come with marriage and re-marriage: “In most cases, if you’re not married, nothing will go to your partner. If you don’t have a will or you have a blended family, you want to give money to your children from your first marriage. But it might all go to your current partner.”

“Wills are important in all those cases. Plus, dying intestate can also slow down and complicate dealing with your estate.”

‌



Intestate means dying without a will and an example was explained to the show. In it, a viewer said: “My uncle died Intestate in 2022. It took 13 months for letters of administration to be granted. My parents left Wales last year, and probate took eight weeks.”

Mr Lewis explained: “People say I’m not doing a will because it will all go to my wife or partner anyway. But it actually speeds up the process when they’re already dealing with the grease. In many cases, if you’ve already got a will, check if it is up to date, especially if you’re recently married because in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, getting married can often invalidate a will. Fascinating. Getting married can. Getting divorced doesn’t. But hey, that’s how it works. So you’ll need to do a new will.”

AJ Bell warns on £3,000 gifting rule for giving money to family READ MORE :

Money Saving Expert founder Martin Lewis highlighted the benefits of Will Aid month, where solicitors recommend a donation of £100 for a single will or £180 for a mirror will – a bargain compared to standard rates. He urged: “If you can’t afford it, you can give less. But please don’t game it because it is set up to give money to charity.”

‌



On the topic of pensions, he warned: “Pensions don’t go in your will, so you need to make sure you have an up-to-date expression of wishes or nomination form with your pension provider.

“I hear too many cases where people haven’t updated it. They pass away. They haven’t changed it since they got divorced. It still says I want it to go to my ex-partner and that causes some real problems. While these expressions of wishing forms aren’t binding, they are what pension firms look at.

“So make sure your expression of wishing on your pension is up to date because they don’t go in your will.”

Article continues below

To book a Will Aid appointment in November 2026, you can:

Visit the Will Aid website from September onwards to find a participating solicitor in your area

Call the Will Aid hotline on 0300 0309 558

Visit https://www.willaid.org.uk/ for more details.

News.title: At least 11 dead including pregnant woman after mass shooting at South Africa house party
News.content:
At least 11 dead including pregnant woman after mass shooting at South Africa house party

A manhunt is underway for three suspects after at least 11 people were killed and three others were injured in a mass shooting at a house party in South Africa

View 2 Images Police said they cannot rule out a 'feud between rival groupings' (Image: SAPS)

At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting at a house party in South Africa, with a manhunt underway for three suspects.

‌



One of the victims was a woman who was believed to be pregnant, while three others were wounded, police said in a statement.

‌



Ten people, including the woman, died at the scene while four were taken to hospital where one of them died from their injuries.

‌



The horror unfolded on Tuesday night in the KwaMakhutha township around 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of the city of Durban on the east coast.

The group had gathered at the house for a party when the gunmen entered and opened fire, police said. No arrests have been made as officers continue searching for the suspects.

View 2 Images A manhunt is underway for three suspects (Image: @encanews/Youtube)

‌



Police said some of the victims were known to them in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".

The statement added that while a motive has not yet been confirmed, police cannot rule out a "feud between rival groupings".

"Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the statement reads.

‌



"Ten victims, including the woman, died at the scene and four were taken to hospital were one of them succumbed to gunshot injuries.

"Preliminary investigations have revealed that some of the victims were on Crime Intelligence' radar in connection with illegal activities which police cannot divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched.

"Although the motive of the shooting cannot be confirmed yet, feud between rival groupings cannot be ruled out. "

News.title: M20 traffic - live: Westbound closed after crash as drivers face 60 minute delays
News.content:
There are long queues on the M20

Traffic has ground to a halt during rush hour, with National Highways warning motorists to expect delays of 60 minutes on the M20 in Kent following an accident

Drivers are facing massive queues on the M20 in Kent this morning following a crash.

Traffic has ground to a halt during the busy rush hour period, with National Highways warning motorists to expect delays of 60 minutes on the westbound lane between J5 and J4 near Maidstone.

Lanes 3 and 4 were closed at around 6:30am before re-opening an hour later, but queues in the area are ongoing, according to live traffic cameras.

A second collision and car fire has sparked a closure eastbound between J8 Hollingbourne Interchange and J9 Drovers Interchange.

"Delays of 10 minutes approaching the incident," National Highways said. "Please allow extra time if you're travelling in the area."

News.title: AJ Bell warns on £3,000 gifting rule for giving money to family
News.content:
AJ Bell warns on £3,000 gifting rule for giving money to family

Many people choose to help their children or grandchildren with the cost of living, but this generosity could be included in tax calculations, Martin Lewis warned

View 2 Images Grandparents and parents often need to help their children and grandchildren pay for life's expenses (Image: Getty Images)

Financial experts have highlighted a '£3,000 rule' for anyone offering financial support to family members. Numerous relatives, especially those in later life with extra disposable income, often opt to assist their children or grandchildren with the escalating expenses of contemporary living.

‌



Yet this generosity could be included in inheritance tax assessments. Finance specialists at AJ Bell stated in September: "Some gifts do not have IHT consequences. There is an annual exemption of £3,000 per person making the gift - so Mum could give one child £3,000 annually, whilst Dad gives the other child the same; these would always be outside the estate. Any unused portion of the £3,000 can be carried forward for one year.

‌



"Small gifts of up to £250 per recipient are also exempt - although this cannot be to the same person as any of the annual exempt gift. Gifts can take the form of either cash or assets, so out of the £250 would come things like Christmas and birthday presents.

‌



"Wedding gifts of £5,000 to a child, £2,500 to a grandchild, and £1,000 to anyone else are also exempt. You can combine this allowance with the annual allowance for gifts, but not the small exemption."

Renowned personal finance specialist Martin Lewis has previously delivered a crucial warning to those providing financial assistance to relatives. On his BBC Podcast, the money-saving expert tackled the topic of inheritance tax.

Currently, people can typically pass on up to £325,000 (referred to as the nil-rate band) without taxation at death, increasing to £500,000 when bequeathing a main residence to direct descendants. An unlimited value of assets can be transferred to a spouse, civil partner or charity completely free from Inheritance Tax (IHT), with any unused allowances being transferable.

‌



A married couple can pass on up to £1 million tax-free - comprising two £325,000 tax-free allowances and two £175,000 main residence allowances. To qualify for this arrangement, the couple must be legally married.

Above this threshold, the inheritance tax liability can be reduced through gifting. However, stringent rules govern this process and its operation.

There is also a time restriction in place, meaning any gifts made seven years or more before death are not subject to tax. Martin asked Lucie Spencer from Evelyn Partners to explain all the available gift allowances.

‌



He said: "There's a £3,000 rule isn't there?" Lucie explained: "So there's the large gift allowance, which is £3,000 per individual per tax year. And what that means is I can give £3,000, my large gift allowance, either to one person or split between multiple people and also I could reclaim a tax year as well, so if you haven't given that £3,000 in the last tax year, you can effectively give £6,000 today."

View 2 Images Martin Lewis has told people about 'gifting' rules (Image: ITV)

Martin enquired: "So this is so people understand. This is outside of the 7-year rule. Outside of the giving money from surplus income rule. You, as an individual, can give up to £3,000 per tax year without paying inheritance tax. How do you denote that you're using this large gift allowance? Do you have to note down that's what your intention was or is it just back count?".

‌



Lucy recommended: "I recommend with all gifts and that's the small gift allowance of the £250, the large gift allowance of the £3,000 or any gifts are written down on a piece of paper or a spreadsheet and held with your will because when someone passes away and you come to complete their inheritance tax form there's actually a whole list where you have to detail all of the gifts which you've made leading up to your death.

"So definitely make a note of it and put it in one column and put 'large gifts allowance for this tax year.'".

To summarise, Martin stated: "I can give money from surplus income, I can give money away as long as I last 7 years as a gift without restriction. I can give £3,000 to as many people. The maximum I can give is £3,000, but I could share that between different people. What's the £250 rule?" Lucy explained: "So the £250 rule effectively I could stand on a street corner and give £250 to as many people as I wish. What I can't do is give a person £1 more. So Martin, if I were to give you £250 in this tax year, what I can't do is come back to you and say 'have another £50 on top of that'."

‌



When Martin enquired how this interacted with the £3,000 allowance, Lucy clarified: "The person who has been given the £3,000 you can't then give them £250. The way I look at it is you give your daughter £3,000 and your grandchildren £250."

Martin then posed the question: "At what age would you say it is sensible for people to start keeping notes on all this type of stuff?" To which tax barrister Harriet Brown responded: "Early 40s."

Lucy offered her own perspective: "I would say in your 50s. Maybe when you've received an inheritance so your wealth is more."

Article continues below

There are also special occasion exemptions available when gifting money, permitting family members to make financial contributions towards weddings without facing any tax consequences.

Harriet outlined the details: "You've got gifts in relation to marriages or civil partnerships, where a parent of either party to the union can give £5,000, so if all four parents gave the maximum, that would be £20,000. Other people who are relations, such as grandparents, could give £2,500, and anyone else could give £1,000 on the occasion of marriage. grandparents, could give £2,500, and anyone else could give £1,000 on the occasion of marriage."

To listen to the full podcast click here. For the Martin Lewis Money Saving Expert advice on inheritance tax click here.

News.title: Seven vital items you need to stockpile after 'Russia threat' - full list
News.content:
Seven vital items you need to stockpile after 'Russia threat' - full list

A soldier has explained the basic kit we should all keep at home, from food and water to a simple plastic bottle

View 3 Images You need to keep a plastic bottle at home

A former British Army soldier has urged households to prepare for a potential emergency by keeping seven everyday items in their homes, including a plastic bottle that can be useful in a power cut. The warning comes after defence expert Professor Michael Clarke revealed three ways Russia could attack Britain, including a cyberattack that could leave part of the country without electricity.

‌



Paul Evans, a former British Army soldier from private investigation firm I-Spy Detectives, says that one thing drilled into soldiers is the importance of being prepared for emergencies before they happen. According to the expert, having a few common items, including an ordinary plastic bottle, could make a huge difference.

‌



Paul said: "It's better to be prepared than to act as the situation is happening. I'm not suggesting that people should panic and spend hundreds on survival equipment, but there are a few items every household should have."

‌



View 3 Images Keep food that doesn't need to be cooked

One mistake people make is relying on their mobile phone's torch in an emergency, this can drain the battery quickly and often doesn't give off enough light to keep the whole room illuminated.

Paul said: "Keep your phone for contacting relatives or calling for help. Instead of draining the battery when using it as a torch, get a cheap torch from the supermarket, along with a plastic bottle.

‌



"From here, you can fill the bottle with water and then place your torch underneath it. The water will help to spread the light around the room, which can stop you from falling over, and it can be useful if you have small children who are frightened of the dark."

According to the expert, you should also have:

Enough drinking water to last three days.

Food that doesn't need cooking.

A fully charged power bank.

A battery-powered radio.

A small first aid kit.

£20-£30 in cash.

‌



View 3 Images You may need cash

Paul said: "You don't have to be a prepper to survive an emergency incident, having the above will see you through for a few days if the worst were to happen."

For a family of four, you should have around 36 litres of water so that each person can have around 3 litres of water a day. You should also think about storing more water for cooking and hygiene too. Food that doesn't require cooking is also useful, as in an extended power cut you may not be able to use your oven or microwave. Tinned fruits, crackers, and cereal bars can all be eaten safely when there is no power.

Article continues below

A power bank can be useful if the grid goes down, as it can be used to power essentials in the home. Paul said: "You should check your power bank every month to make sure it has a charge. There is no point having one in the drawer if it's flat when you need it."

A battery-powered or wind-up radio can be useful in an emergency, so you can access important information that you may not otherwise be able to get. Finally, the expert says that keeping a small amount of cash available can help if electricity or internet services are disrupted. If this were to happen, card machines and cashpoints could stop working, which would make it difficult for you to get food or anything else that you need.

Paul said: "Spend half an hour over the next few days to see which of these items you have at home, you probably have more of them than you would expect."

News.title: Santander contacts customers directly with UK branch closure update
News.content:
Santander contacts customers directly with UK branch closure update

It has explained the latest situation to its customers

View 3 Images Santander has updated customers (Image: tupungato via Getty Images)

Santander has contacted customers directly to update them on its plans in relation to branches across the UK.

‌



In an email received by some customers on Tuesday, it said: "We’re investing in our branches to give you more than just banking. From Work Cafés to face-to-face support, we want to keep providing greater convenience and choice in how you bank. That's why we won't make any further branch closures before 2028. And for those times you don’t need to visit in person, our online help and support services are here to save you time."

‌



It pointed customers to further advice on its website, which explained that the pledge applied to Santander and TSB branches, with the latter being owned by the Spanish banking giant.

‌



It added: "There may be situations we can't control that mean we have to close or relocate a branch. We'll only do so if there's no other option."

View 3 Images Santander owns TSB (Image: VV Shots via Getty Images)

Explaining further, the bank said: "Banking is changing, and so are we. In July 2026, we opened our newly refurbished Canary Wharf branch, featuring the UK's first Santander Work Cafe with a coffee machine. With 6 more planned this year, we're delivering even better customer service and community-friendly banking.

‌



"By the end of 2026, around 80% of our branches will be refurbished with digital self-service spaces and advanced ATM technology, helping us better support customers today and in the future.

"More than a place to bank, our Work Cafes are vibrant community spaces where banking, co-working and the local community come together. Following the opening of our largest UK Work Cafe in Oxford, we're continuing to invest across the UK, creating more free workspaces, expert support and events."

In July, Santander's new boss Mahesh Aditya said he saw branches as an “important part of our strategy” as he unveiled the commitment, which will see it maintain 305 Santander and 175 TSB branches across the UK for nearly another 18 months at least. But the promise comes after Spanish-owned Santander UK announced another wave of branch closures at the start of the year, with 44 sites earmarked to be axed, putting 291 jobs at risk.

‌



The lending giant also continues to cut costs across the business as it ramps up the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and automation and is targeting at least £400 million of savings by the end of 2028 following the £2.65 billion TSB acquisition, which was completed in May.

View 3 Images Santander has set out its plans (Image: Shootdiem via Getty Images)

Mr Aditya, who took over from former chief executive Mike Regnier on March 1, said at the time: “As we integrate TSB with Santander UK, our ambition for customers is to combine leading digital services with the personal support they value, helping us to create the best bank for customers in the UK.

Article continues below

"I see branches as an important part of our strategy and do not intend to close any additional Santander or TSB branches before 2028 at the earliest, alongside our continued commitment to invest in modernising our network and to introduce new Work Cafes.”

News.title: New NHS message as law change 'makes it illegal' for people born from 2009
News.content:
New NHS message as law change 'makes it illegal' for people born from 2009

An historic law change comes into effect in 100 days

View 3 Images A big change is coming (Image: Alexander Shapovalov via Getty Images)

Smokers are being urged to reflect on the moments that matter most in their lives, as a major campaign gets under way to help more people kick the habit for good.

‌



Central to the campaign, being launched in the South West of England, is a straightforward question aimed at the 500,000 people who still smoke across the region: "What will you miss?". The campaign launches with 100 days to go until January 1, 2027, when the UK's smokefree generation law comes into force, meaning anyone born on or after January 1, 2009, will never legally be sold tobacco.

‌



The legislation is designed to prevent the next generation from ever taking up smoking. It does not alter anything for adults who currently smoke, and the NHS confirmed that was precisely who this campaign was targeting.

‌



Smoking remains the biggest preventable cause of illness and early death across the South West, according to the NHS. Each year, approximately 6,600 people in the region lose their lives to smoking-related illnesses — the equivalent of around 18 deaths every single day.

View 3 Images The aim is to stamp out smoking (Image: Jason Finn via Getty Images)

Now, Smokefree South West — a partnership of 15 local authorities working in conjunction with the NHS — is launching the "What Will You Miss?" campaign ahead of Stoptober, encouraging smokers to take their first steps towards quitting and access free local support. The campaign is modelled on a proven approach developed by Greater Manchester's Make Smoking History programme, created alongside people who smoke.

‌



The campaign will reach smokers across through television, radio and social media, supplemented by local s. At its heart is a film following a bride on her wedding day, surrounded by family but missing the one person she most wanted present. It delivers a straightforward message: smoking doesn't just take years from your life, it takes you away from the moments that matter most.

People 'want to quit'

A recent survey of over 1,600 smokers throughout the South West revealed many already wish to quit, but find it difficult to turn that desire into action. While health worries are amongst the strongest motivators for considering stopping smoking, the survey discovered that approximately two in three smokers did not have any current intentions to quit.

The research also showed that most smokers have already attempted to quit at least once, yet confidence remains low, with many doubting their ability to stop successfully. The NHS stated the campaign sought to make smoking's dangers more real to smokers, encourage quit attempts across the region, and swiftly link people to effective support.

‌



Hein le Roux, deputy medical director for NHS England South West, said: "More than 6,500 people in the South West die from smoking-related illness every year. Behind every statistic is a person, a family and moments that matter.

"That's why partners across the South West are united in our ambition to become a smoke-free region by 2030. By helping more people quit now, we can improve lives today and protect the health of future generations.

"This campaign isn't about judging people or telling them something they don't already know. It's about helping people think about the moments, milestones and people that matter most to them, while reminding them that effective support is available.

‌



"There is no better time to quit. Even if someone has tried before, support can make a huge difference and every quit attempt is a step closer to success."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Smoking law change on January 1, 2027

Matt Lenny, director of public health for North Somerset Council and senior programme sponsor for Smokefree South West, said: "In 100 days' time, a child born today will grow up in a country where they can never legally be sold a cigarette. That is a genuine landmark. But it changes nothing for the 500,000 people across the South West who smoke right now, many of whom have been trying to stop for years. This campaign is for them.

‌



"Smoking remains one of the biggest causes of poor health and health inequalities across the South West, but it doesn't have to be this way. The good news is that people are three times more likely to quit successfully when they have the right support, and free help is available locally in every part of the South West.

"We're building on a proven campaign that has already been used successfully in Greater Manchester and in other regions. By bringing that evidence-based approach to the South West and connecting people with local stop smoking services, we have a real opportunity to help more people quit and live longer, healthier lives. Through our partnership with the NHS we'll reach more people, raise awareness of the support available and help create a healthier, smoke-free future for our region."

View 3 Images People born on or after January 1, 2009, will never legally be able to buy tobacco (Image: Alamy/PA)

‌



Hazel Cheeseman, chief executive officer at the charity Action on Smoking and Health, said: "Most people who smoke want to quit, but it can be tough. Campaigns like this are necessary to help turn intention into action. Tobacco is lethal and from next year we will start phasing out the sale of tobacco to the next generation, but it is just as important to help those who currently smoke, moving us even closer to making smoking obsolete.

"It is particularly encouraging to see local areas come together to support this campaign alongside renewed investment in local authorities' stop smoking support. This South West campaign is a strong example of what can be delivered through collaboration."

Jessica Holloway, strategic lead for population health at NHS Greater Manchester, said: "'What Will You Miss?' was co-designed with people who smoke in Greater Manchester. The feedback was clear: people wanted a campaign that reflected the realities of what smoking takes away from their lives, but in a way that felt supportive and non-judgemental. That insight helped shape a campaign that is honest, relatable and rooted in lived experience.

Article continues below

"We're delighted to see the campaign adapted for the South West. By sharing proven approaches and building on what works, more investment can be directed towards reaching people who smoke with effective support, helping more people take a step towards a smokefree future."

The NHS stated that smokers stand a far greater chance of quitting successfully with support rather than relying solely on willpower alone. Free nicotine replacement therapy and vaping starter kits are on offer at every local stop smoking service across the South West, alongside tailored guidance on a variety of evidence-based quitting methods from trained advisors.

For help giving up smoking, visit smokefreesouthwest.co.uk.

News.title: TV doctor verdict on government advice to stockpile 9 items - list
News.content:
TV doctor verdict on government advice to stockpile 9 items - list

Dr Amir Khan spoke out after UK residents warned by Defence Secretary to make plans for serious problems

View Image Dr Amir Khan gave his advice after the government launched a 'resilience' initiative (Image: doctoramirkhan/instagram)

A TV doctor has given his verdict on a government campaign which is urging people to stockpile 9 items in case of serious problems hitting the UK. Later this year officials will start efforts to encourage people to make sure they have key items including things like tinned food, batteries, first aid and bottled water.

‌



The nation has faced serious issues in recent months including droughts and heatwaves, with other likely problems including power issues such as blackouts, and even potentially even hybrid attacks from foreign states.

‌



There are also serious issues with oil currently as the Saudi main company halts some deliveries to Europe after attacks on key pipelines, and with the Middle East conflict severely hampering tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz potentially causing supply issues this winter.

‌



Dr Amir Khan, who is an NHS GP and regularly appears on ITV shows Lorraine and This Morning said he was ‘tired’ of the news. He said in a video on Instagram: “I’m getting really tired of being told that we all need to get ready for war. Like, get your emergency food in, get your supplies, become more resilient, prepare yourself mentally for war.

“What the hell? Why aren’t we putting this much energy in getting ready for peace? Of course, I know our governments have to prepare for things we hope will never happen, right? But I really don’t like this idea that war is somehow inevitable and the ordinary person’s job is simply to prepare themselves for it by getting a can of chickpeas in.

“Have you met ordinary people recently? We are exhausted. Like food costs so much, housing costs so much, energy costs so much, people are working incredibly hard and still struggling and now apparently we need to become resilient enough for war as well.”

‌



Instead Dr Khan has a different plan: “I don’t want to be war ready. I want to be peace-ready. I’m a lover, not a fighter. And perhaps that starts with doing the exact opposite of what so much of modern life encourages us to do, right? We need to stop retreating into smaller and smaller tribes. We need to get to know our neighbours. Talk to somebody who doesn’t look like You join something locally, help somebody, bake a cake and take half of it next door, feed some wildlife, plant something, stroke a cat or a dog if you prefer, check on the person down the street who lives alone. Because I don’t think resilience should mean I’ve got enough of these things in my cupboard to look after myself.

“Real resilience is knowing that if something terrible happens, we will all look after each other.”

Last week Defence Secretary Wes Streeting issued an urgent warning urging people to stockpile 9 essential items, cautioning that emergencies can strike at any moment. The UK Government this summer said it will soon publish a key plan over resilience and how the country will cope with major problems.

‌



Here’s everything else you might require:

A battery or wind-up torch - torches are safer than candles. A portable power bank for charging your mobile phone.

A battery or wind-up radio to receive updates during a power outage - a car radio can be utilised, however, in severe weather it might be safer to stay indoors.

Spare batteries for torches and radios and a backup battery for any medical equipment you depend on.

A first aid kit (or some first aid supplies) including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.

Hand sanitiser and wet wipes for hygiene purposes when the water supply is disrupted.

Bottled water - there is no standard quantity for this as emergencies can vary in duration and people consume different amounts. The World Health Organisation recommends a minimum of 2.5-3 litres of drinking water per person per day for survival. 10 litres per person per day will make you more comfortable by also providing for basic cooking and hygiene needs. Additional water might be required for preparing baby formula, for medical devices, and for pets.

Non-perishable food that doesn’t require cooking, like ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, the quantity you need will depend on your personal circumstances.

Don’t overlook food for pets.

Baby essentials such as nappies and baby formula - ready made or ready-to-feed formula is ideal as you may not have the ability to boil water or sterilise bottles.

In a statement earlier this year Darren Jones Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister, Chancellor of Duchy of Lancaster and Minister for Intergovernmental Relations announced the key Resilience Action Plan sayin it was needed as: “Conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s war in Ukraine have exposed the vulnerabilities in global energy supply chains and driven up energy prices, and the increasing sophistication and proliferation of artificial intelligence not only brings huge opportunities, but threats too if it is weaponised by criminals against us. This could include novel ways of developing or carrying out hostile cyber-attacks against businesses and our critical infrastructure.

“As we saw with temperatures across the UK breaking records in May, only to be exceeded again in June, the risks we face from climate change cannot be underestimated, from our infrastructure, food and water systems or people’s immediate health. Climate change is also exacerbating the spread of high-consequence infectious diseases, alongside the changing boundaries of the human-animal interface.”

Article continues below

The government is set to launch a national resilience public awareness campaign later this year, in order to inform the public of the small but important steps they can take to be prepared in case of emergencies and disruption – ‘be that severe weather or a cyber attack which can impact access to power, water, phone signal or local shops to get food’.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said last week: “I think we do need to have a national conversation about our resilience as a country and our preparedness. And before we turn to that scenario you described of an event where this country is under attack, I would actually say let’s think about resilience today. We’ve just had a summer of wildfires across the country.

“Lots of communities across the UK will be looking to winter with trepidation about extremely cold weather or flood. And I’d ask people watching actually on a really practical level, in the event you have a power cut, would you know where you keep a torch? Have you even got matches or candles?”

News.title: UK to step up fight against Russian disinformation and push global AI standards, PM says
News.content:
The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation, including from Russia, and lead efforts to establish global safety standards for artificial intelligence, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

In his first major international speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, Burnham warned Russian agencies are using "every means at their disposal", including bots and fake websites, to "spread lies and disinformation".

The prime minister noted AI will "multiply" existing threats, and pitched the UK as an "honest broker" on the technology.

Fears about AI have grown after industry insiders recently warned it could threaten humanity.

In Burnham's speech, he accused Russia of running a disinformation campaign.

"The Kremlin spends around Â£1.3bn each year on manipulating information," Burnham told the UN General Assembly.

"They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC.

"We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community â creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.

"On top of that we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. And we know that AI will multiply the threat."'

He also referenced the 2019 UK general election, in which the government previously said Russia almost certainly sought to interfere.

To counter this, Burnham announced a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt AI-enabled disinformation campaigns by hostile states.

The centre will work alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, law enforcement and social media to bring together expertise to combat "information warfare".

There was no immediate comment from Russia, a representative of which was sitting in the room listening to Burnham.

When the UK government put out a report in 2020 about Russian activity in the UK, including in elections, Moscow described the allegations as "Russophobia".

Addressing a forum about disinformation in Moscow on Tuesday, before the prime minister's speech, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Western media of embracing "anti-Russian cliches and fantasies".

News.title: Chris Mason: From inside the room, how Burnham survived first Trump meeting
News.content:
As I crouched between the cameras, determined to catch Donald Trump's eye and ask a question, I listened to a president seeking to be magnanimous.

Remember, Trump can and does do warmth when he wants to, as well as acerbic.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a mayor a matter of months ago, sat next to the most powerful man in the world.

Put like that, it sounds believable when he said in advance he was looking forward to the meeting, but there must have been a jab of nerves too.

Burnham did look a little nervous as us reporters trooped into the room, but then, for the most part, the compliments flowed from the president.

The original plan was for journalists to be invited in at the beginning of the meeting, perhaps just minutes after the men had first met.

Instead, we were kept waiting while the private talks took place, which came with the upside that they had more to say about each other and what they had discussed than would otherwise have been the case.

Burnham knew, the world knows, how explosive these rolling, free wheeling, live on camera encounters with Trump can go.

It is rollercoaster without a harness stuff.

News.title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal after Trump's latest criticism
News.content:
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of Â£101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.

In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".

"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where we can support it."

News.title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
News.content:
They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.

Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.

As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight.

UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad.

Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than â¬4,000 (Â£3,400).

Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for â¬750 (Â£650).

She described its clinic in DÃ¼sseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".

The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.

It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.

The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.

Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.

She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before.

"I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."

News.title: 'My eyelids became infected - I was scared to sleep'
News.content:
Doctors specialising in surgery around the eyes say a concerning number of patients are reporting problems from having had cheap so-called "bleph" surgery on their eyelids, typically abroad.

Women have told us they have sought medical help back in the UK, because scarring has not healed properly and they have been in pain.

News.title: Rare look at the remote engine rooms powering China's AI ambitions
News.content:
The BBC's Laura Bicker is in Inner Mongolia where dozens of Chinese data centres are being built, as the country aims to lead the world in artificial intelligence.

She explains how attitudes differ between people in China and the US when it comes to the data centre industry, ahead of leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump's meeting in Washington later this week.

Read more on this story here.

News.title: Man who sold toxic chemicals should rot in hell, says mother of woman who killed herself
News.content:
A Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals to people who went on to kill themselves should "rot in hell", the mother of a British woman who took her own life has said.

Imogen Nunn, known as Immy, died in January 2023 aged 25 after buying drugs online from Kenneth Law.

Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in online suicide forums. But almost 80 deaths in the UK have also been linked to him.

However, as part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.

Imogen's mother, Louise Nunn, told the BBC she was angry he would not face justice here. "I think we've been let down as families. Our children have been let down," she told the BBC.

It comes as the impact statements of UK families will be read in court in Ontario this week.

News.title: Migrants taken to Dover after more than 30 hours at sea
News.content:
A total of 51 migrants arrived in Dover on a small boat after spending more than 30 hours at sea.

The arrival at 00:30 BST came after protesters gathered in the Hampshire town of Gosport on Tuesday evening as it was initially believed this is where they would be brought ashore.

The boat left the Normandy coast on Monday morning and the French coastguard, which shadowed it, said the migrants were in "precarious conditions" and refused help as they were "determined to take all risks to reach" the UK.

British rescue boats were sent to collect those on board, who were then transferred to Border Security Command.

A government spokesperson said Border Security Command worked "around the clock to protect our border and will continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival".

The French coastguard said the migrants had been on the small boat for more than 33 hours.

The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) said it was tasked by HM Coastguard with assisting those on board "out of concern for their safety and deteriorating health".

Migrants could later be seen disembarking in Dover wearing orange life jackets and carrying personal belongings.

About a dozen protesters were spotted in the area, with local police having blocked off a nearby road.

News.title: Investigations continue into fatal house fire
News.content:
Investigations are continuing after a mother and three children died in a house fire on Merseyside.

Another casualty who was outside the property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, when fire crews arrived during the early hours of Tuesday was taken to hospital.

The Bishop of Liverpool the Rt Rev Ruth Worsley and Bishop of Warrington the Rt Rev Simon Robinson said they are "deeply saddened to hear of the devastating incident".

"Our thoughts and prayers are with their families and loved ones at this unimaginably difficult time," they added.

Six fire engines were called out at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property.

Firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom who were showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

A joint investigation involving Merseyside Police and Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service is expected to continue into this afternoon.

News.title: Child ketamine users getting bladder damage describe 'peeing a jellyfish'
News.content:
Ketamine abuse in children and young people is on the rise in the UK.

The Alder Hey doctors, external saw one young patient in 2023, nine in 2024, and then "a rapid escalation" in 2025, which led them to open the bespoke clinic in May.

They get about one referral every week from GPs or emergency departments in Cheshire, Merseyside and other nearby regions.

Of the first 60 they saw, 43 were girls.

Despite its name, "ketamine bladder" can affect the entire urinary tract, including the kidneys and ureters.

Symptoms include an urgent and frequent need to urinate. This can be very painful and the pee can be blood-stained.

Although stopping using ketamine can help, sometimes the damage can be so serious that the bladder needs surgical repair or even removal.

Some users experience abdominal pain and spasms, or "K cramps" too.

There are reports that heavy users are getting liver damage, but it is difficult to separate harms from other things people may also be taking, including other street drugs and alcohol.

Isba says cannabis and alcohol are still more popular, but ketamine is "probably up into third place".

Children at the clinic often say they have also tried other drugs, drank alcohol, and vaped.

About three out of every 10 people who frequently use ketamine get bladder issues, says the British Association of Urological Surgeons, external.

Sometimes it is reversible, if the drug use stops.

Given the risks, there have been calls to reclassify it as a Class A drug - like cocaine and heroin - but the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs has recommended to government that ketamine should remain a Class B controlled substance, like amphetamines and cannabis.

Isba says children are disadvantaged when it comes to accessing services.

"There are definitely some children out there who are under the age of 16 who if they were 18 would be offered an inpatient detox stay. But because we don't have those facilities in the UK, they are not able to access that and that feels unfair. Particularly for the ones who are ready to stop."

News.title: Frost, wind and rain forecast as autumn warmth fades for many
News.content:
Temperatures are set to drop across many parts of the UK as summerlike September warmth gives way to more autumnal conditions.

A weather front delivering outbreaks of heavy rain for some places on Wednesday will move eastwards, leaving cooler air in its wake.

Daytime highs will be close to the late September average in most regions but some cold nights are expected with frost possible in a few locations on Thursday morning.

Higher temperatures will stage a partial comeback at the end of the week, however, with south-east England likely to return to the mid-20s Celsius.

News.title: Council leaders wary of radical plan to redraw Scotland's local government map
News.content:
Council leaders have been voicing their concerns about proposals for the biggest shake up of local government in 30 years.

Some have warned Scottish government plans to potentially streamline the number of authorities from 32 to six will not save money.

Others have questioned the potential impact on rural parts and the "absurd" timeline.

Under proposals for a new two-tier system, external, the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth.

Between 120 and 160 community authorities would also be created, contributing to local issues such as licensing and town centre improvements.

News.title: Plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community disrupted, say police
News.content:
Two men have been arrested over a suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester, police have said.

The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on Sunday on the eve of Yom Kippur - considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar - when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues already guarded with a heavy security and police presence.

The men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, according to the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation.

Sources have told the BBC the suspected plot was "fairly imminent" and in the later stages of planning.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the government would "continue to do all in our power to address threats against our Jewish community".

She added: "We cannot expect our Jewish community to live behind higher walls.

"We must also tackle antisemitism at its source and root it out wherever it rears its head."

News.title: Man's body found in river sparks IOPC inquiry
News.content:
The death of a man who was being chased by police before he was found in the River Lea, is being investigated by an independent watchdog.

Emergency services were called to the High Street and towpath in Stanstead Abbotts, Hertfordshire, on 14 September at about 13:20 BST.

Officers said they pursued the man on foot after identifying him as being wanted in connection with two robberies. He was no longer in their line of sight when he entered the water.

Hertfordshire Constabulary said it had referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which subsequently decided to launch an investigation.

"We are assisting the IOPC with its enquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further at this time", a police spokesperson said.

An IOPC spokesperson said officers had attempted to stop the man on the High Street. The man was later found in the river and pronounced dead at the scene.

The spokesperson added the investigation was in its "early stages" and that the man's family would be kept updated on its progress.

News.title: 'All anger has been taken away' - says daughter of solicitor murdered by IRA, as report published
News.content:
The daughter of a solicitor who was murdered by the IRA in 1977, has said a meeting where she and her brother learned the details of their father's death moved them into a "space of serenity and light, all anger taken away".

It comes as the legacy body set up to investigate Troubles cases published its first report, examining the shooting of 59-year-old Rory O'Kelly, who was targeted because he worked for the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).

The murder, which happened in Coalisland, County Tyrone, was examined by the Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery (ICRIR).

The investigation into his death was requested by O'Kelly's now deceased son, Roger, who met ICRIR staff last year alongside his sister Anne Frances O'Kelly and Roger's wife.

The meeting, which included ICRIR chief commissioner Sir Declan Morgan, happened just before Roger died from cancer in a hospice in England in October 2025 and was set up to share the investigation's findings.

In a statement, Anne Frances O'Kelly described the meeting as "sacred and transformative".

She added: "Everyone present was transported 50 years back to the hour and place of our father's death."

She said she "would never have expected to know this sort of release," by the end of the meeting.

"I can never thank members of the ICRIR enough for working so hard to piece together the facts of the death of our father."

News.title: RAF base prepares for threats at home and abroad
News.content:
A front-line RAF base has expanded training for all personnel to reflect evolving threats at home and abroad.

RAF Coningsby, in Lincolnshire, is one of two quick reaction alert stations that protect UK airspace with combat-ready squadrons of Typhoon jets.

Military leaders have raised the level of force protection training, which includes combat first aid, additional firearms drills and awareness of chemical, nuclear and biological hazards.

Wing Cdr Ian Hart, who commands 29 Squadron, said the change in posture was "a recognition that the threat can come to us very, very easily in today's world".

He added: "We need to be ready here and we need to refresh those drills and be ready to act on them should any of those threats actually become a reality for us."

Mikel Arteta has committed his future to Arsenal by agreeing a new contract with the Premier League champions.

The extension of Arteta’s tenure as head coach – which had been up for renewal at the end of the season – was seen as something of a formality.

Though the terms of a new deal have now been struck, it is not anticipated that confirmation of the 44-year-old’s stay will be announced imminently.

Arteta began his Arsenal reign in 2019 and has overseen their rise back to the forefront of English football, with the Gunners last season securing their first league title in 22 years.

Arteta’s side had started their title defence with a perfect record until their shock 3-0 defeat at Brighton prior to the international break.

Asked about his next contract ahead of the clash with the Seagulls, Arteta said: “I think we are all very much aligned; whenever the time is right, we’ll get that done. There is nothing to be concerned about.”

As well as ending Arsenal’s wait for a league title, Arteta also steered Arsenal to their first Champions League final in two decades.

Arsenal lost to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties but in the days leading up to the final in Budapest, Arsenal co-owner Josh Kroenke said: “Keeping Mikel around is (an) utmost priority and I think the good news for Arsenal fans worldwide is he’s enjoying the project, he’s enjoying being here and from his time as a player all the way up until now, he’s an Arsenal man through and through.”

Following their surprise defeat at the Amex Stadium on Saturday, Arsenal will next be in action with a home match against Leeds on October 10.

Away from the grandstanding and his first face-to-face encounter with Donald Trump, Andy Burnham has taken a significant step further towards engaging in a direct conflict in the Gulf.

The prime minister has agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia for military assistance to combat the rebel Houthi guerrillas who are in the process of taking control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

The rebels are in effective control of the vital Strait of Bab al-Mandab, after a rapid advance against Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Saudi Arabian air power, as has often been the pattern during the decades-long on-off civil war in Yemen.

Reawakened by the Israeli-US attacks on Iran, the Houthi rebels have now secured a veto over shipping in and out of the Red Sea, and thus all that economically vital traffic to and from Europe, the Gulf and the rest of Asia via the Suez Canal. As the western counterpart to the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf itself, this means that Tehran has now further tightened its grip on the world’s energy supplies and the global economy: Iran, through its proxies, has thus taken another strategic supply route “hostage”.

Mr Burnham has taken the decision to provide airborne refuelling facilities to Saudi air force planes. It is expressly limited and “defensive”, as was the permission granted by Sir Keir Starmer earlier for the US to use its air bases on British territory. However, that obviously isn’t how the Houthis or the Iranians view it, and such force commitments tend to stretch over time through “mission creep”.

It is a curious move from Mr Burnham, given that President Trump, already embroiled in the Iran war, has turned down the request from such a cherished ally as Saudi Arabia for assistance, which would seem to be entirely in the United States’s interests. Yet, it is precisely because Mr Trump is so badly trapped in this unwinnable war now that he cannot open up a new front in the conflict, even at the Saudis’ request. He may also be running a little low on money and munitions; and above all, he must be acutely conscious of just how unpopular his war is with American voters, who’ll be off to the polls in a few weeks in the Congressional elections to register their displeasure.

In return for Mr Trump’s uncharacteristic restraint, Houthi leaders have graciously agreed not to target US or other Western shipping moving in the Red Sea, reserving their attacks for Saudi-identified tankers. This is hardly reassuring. So, rather than watch as the Houthis take over the whole of Yemen and potentially escalate the war further into Saudi Arabia, the British have decided to take the risk and support Saudi Arabia. After all, there were suggestions a few weeks ago that the Houthis were planning a strike against Mecca, with all the particular suffering, distress and chaos that would entail for that holy site.

Despite its appalling human rights record and a poor record of success in its merciless proxy war with Iran in Yemen, Mr Burnham judges this a risk worth taking. So do the French, simultaneously bolstering the air defences around Saudi infrastructure that the US has neglected. The UK and France are looking to their own interests, principally domestic energy bills and the risk of a domestic recession. But there are even bigger stakes in play.

The worst-case scenario is simply too horrible to contemplate: the entire Gulf region collapsing into internecine war and eventually coming to be dominated by Iran. The dire consequences for the people of the region and for the world can hardly be overstated. It would thrust the traditional Shia-Sunni schism, which lies underneath most of the violence and the Iran-Saudi rivalry, even more into geopolitics, and neither Israel nor the West could ignore such a conflagration.

These are some of the “dark clouds of global instability” directly affecting people’s lives all over the world that Mr Burnham has referred to, and he is entirely right. He knows who it is that has landed us in this mess; but there is only so much a middle-sized power edging towards a fiscal crisis can do, both in the Middle East and on AI and climate change, to influence the Trump administration.

If the modest assistance being afforded to the Royal Saudi Air Force helps to halt the rise of the Houthis, and thus the Iranians, and hasten the end to the Gulf war, then Mr Burnham will rightly take some credit. If not, then he will soon discover just how Sir Keir Starmer felt when his handling of the Iran conflict angered the increasingly emboldened parliamentary Labour Party – accomplished rebels themselves.

For years, artificial intelligence researchers have warned of ways the technology could wipe out humanity: AI bots could design an unstoppable disease, unleash a nuclear war, or transform all of Earth into paper clip factories, as one thought experiment goes.

Debates inside the AI industry and beyond over the plausibility of these doomsday scenarios have heated up since several executives endorsed slowing the technology's development for safety reasons.

Despite warnings of the potential for humans to lose their grip on the technology, some suspect the worst-case scenarios described by the AI companies themselves have more to do with validating the importance of their work than reality.

“These arguments just don’t really hold water. I think they’re sci-fi and they’re enticing to a certain childish style of thinking and it’s very tempting for the frontier labs because it helps them recruit certain types of folks,” said Juan Andrés Guerrero-Saade, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne and a member of OpenAI’s Frontier Risk Council.

Still, more people are beginning to worry about the risks of the technology that has dazzled the world with its astounding capabilities.

Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic researcher who resigned from the company over concerns that it and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development, said on X recently that he needs to “work on” communicating to people more effectively exactly how AI would end humanity. “Unfortunately it is very difficult to convey specific scenarios,” he wrote earlier this month.

Here are some of the more widely discussed doomsday scenarios.

Nuclear winter

Researchers have long speculated that AI systems could trigger a nuclear war by getting countries to fire warhead-tipped missiles at each other. The nuclear blasts, and ensuing lingering radioactive atmospheric fallout resulting in a “nuclear winter,” could devastate life on Earth.

In a report last year, RAND Corp. researchers concluded that “at present” it wouldn’t be possible for AI to cause the use of nuclear weapons “because of strict safeguards built into the command and control systems.” However, the report said this could change if AI models are integrated into the nuclear weapon “decision chain” or gain unauthorized access to these systems.

For many AI researchers, that’s where the danger lies — not in AI agents suddenly deciding to end humanity, but people, nations or groups using it to wipe out their adversaries.

Bioweapons

One of AI's greatest promises is that it could help humans develop treatments and cures for diseases.

The flip side of curing diseases is creating or advancing them to harm humanity. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI for a host of malicious activities such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.

In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for assistance from its Claude tool for a research proposal seeking to enhance mutations to make the mosquito-borne chikungunya virus progressively more harmful. While such research could be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”

Along the same lines, the RAND report noted recent progress in AI development “has the potential to transform the design of synthetic pathogens.”

Outlining a bioweapon doomsday scenario, the report said novel pathogens could be created in a lab, delivered to target locations, and spread to infect large populations of people in multiple places. But it still envisioned humans — and not autonomous AI — as overseeing and carrying out such an attack.

Runaway AI

Some AI researchers fear a human extinction event could result from “misalignment” — that is, when AI models act without human authorization, coordinate with other models or evade oversight. It would develop not from malicious intent — AI is not human, nor is it good or evil, after all — but simply because humans might get in the way of the model accomplishing its goal.

Take the decades-old “paper clip maximizer” thought experiment by the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom, which states that if advanced AI was told to produce as many paper clips as possible, it could eventually transform all of Earth, and then increasing portions of space, into paper clip factories.

This is to illustrate how superintelligent AI — often referred to as artificial general intelligence, or AGI — could advance a goal humans may see as desirable but “which in fact turns out to be a false utopia, in which things essential to human flourishing have been irreversibly lost,” Bostrom wrote in 2003.

“We need to be careful about what we wish for from a superintelligence, because we might get it,” he wrote.

AI internet takeover

Given the rate of AI’s development, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned this month that within months a swarm of AI agents could be capable of “taking over” the internet with a botnet (a network of bots linked together with malware), potentially causing billions of dollars in damage. This could mean hacks into electrical grids, water or transportation systems and financial institutions — attacks that might not spell the end of humanity but could cause chaos and lives lost.

Disruptions from software glitches in the past have highlighted the fragility of a digitized world dependent on just a few providers for key computing services, and more powerful AI models have raised concerns about vulnerabilities to cyber attacks. But some experts say the notion of bots overtaking the entire extremely bifurcated internet is far-fetched.

Dolly Parton’s estate has accused the country music legend’s nephew of threatening violence and trying to destroy his late aunt’s legacy and business empire, according to court filings submitted Tuesday.

Bryan Seaver, who ran a company that provided Parton’s security and was handpicked by the singer to announce her death from cancer last month, allegedly invoked his experience working for private military contractors during the Iraq War as part of his threats, the filings claim.

Parton’s estate is now asking a Nashville judge to keep Seaver away from its employees and business dealings.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton’s estate has accused the country music icon’s nephew of threatening violence ( PA Archive )

The allegations provide the first signs of turmoil in what had been a carefully managed process surrounding the estate of one of country music’s most celebrated stars.

Seaver has not yet commented on the allegations.

The claims were made in a request for a temporary restraining order filed by She’s Alive, the entity responsible for managing and protecting Parton’s professional property and business interests. Danny Nozell, Parton’s longtime manager, runs the organization.

She’s Alive terminated Seaver and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, last week, saying his alleged “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable,” according to court documents.

open image in gallery Bryan Seaver announced his aunt Dolly Parton's death ( YouTube/Dolly Parton )

The filings include a series of text messages and emails that She’s Alive alleges Seaver sent beginning shortly before Parton’s death. They claim the messages initially contained threats to damage the singer’s brand before Seaver began reveling in his newfound attention following her death and describing himself as an “international arms dealer.”

In a Sept. 1 message included in the filings, Seaver allegedly threatened to launch a podcast devoted to damaging Parton’s brand partnerships unless he was paid.

The complaint alleges Seaver also cited his work with private military contractors overseas during the Iraq War in connection with his threats.

open image in gallery The shake-up over Dolly Parton's property security comes nearly a month after her death ( AFP/Getty )

The messages have prompted Parton’s trusts and estates attorney to leave and several She’s Alive employees to resign, according to the filings. The organization also said it has hired private security to protect employees, including at their homes.

The proposed restraining order would bar Seaver from contacting or coming within 1,000 feet of She’s Alive employees, attorneys and business partners. It would also prohibit him from interfering with the organization’s business relationships.

Parton wrote hundreds of songs during her career, including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You.” Her music generated more than 100 million sales worldwide and more than 1 billion online streams.

The UK is set to launch an RAF squadron to disrupt, degrade, and deny hostile threats in space.

The dedicated military unit will protect satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the Ministry of Defence said.

The No III Space Effects Squadron will be announced by Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth at the UK’s Space Power Conference on Wednesday, where Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will warn the UK must “keep pace in the new space race”.

Mr Streeting is expected to say: “Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th century deterrence.

“That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world-class air force to protect us.

“This century will depend on control of space. Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. That threat is growing in scale, speed, and sophistication. And challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will give a keynote address at the Space Conference ( PA )

“My job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as it is on Earth, and to modernise our armed forces so that they are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat any adversary, in any domain.”

The announcement comes weeks after the release of a new government strategy designed to strengthen defences against threats from space.

SaxaVord Spaceport, on the island of Unst, Shetland, at the northernmost point of the UK, is set to receive a further £30 million in support through the UK Space Strategy.

The strategy sets out funding of £7.8 billion across the space sector up to 2030.

Included in the funding is £2.8 billion for the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and Skynet defence communications programme.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds previously said the government wanted to strengthen the UK’s ability to launch satellites.

Mr Reynolds said: “As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.”

A number of companies plan to use SaxaVord Spaceport as a hub for commercial rockets, hoping to tap into global demand for satellite launches.

German company Rocket Factory Augsburg is working towards the first vertical orbital test flight from UK soil, while HyImpulse is preparing for a sub-orbital launch campaign.
