“The season has started well individually and as a team. England’s got unbelievable talent and players all over the pitch. I believe I am good enough to be in the England squad so hopefully I can show that.”

Sports.title: Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card
Sports.content:
Anti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led by Reform UK ended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card.

Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader of Sunderland city council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”.

Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding.

The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”.

Bennett, who became only the second black player in Sunderland’s history when he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996.

View image in fullscreen Gary Bennett in Sunderland’s stripes in 1994. Photograph: PA/Alamy

The former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years.

Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces.

He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing. For something like this to happen now, we just want to know the reasons why.”

Bennett said the racist riots across many English cities including Sunderland in 2024 showed there was “still lots of work to be done”.

While Britain had come a long way since the 1980s, he said, there remained issues to confront around attitudes towards asylum seekers and migrants.

“You’ve got all different issues going on now. It keeps moving, it’s always something else which causes some form of racism,” he said. “It’s something that is challenging every single day and we’ve got to keep the fight. There’s still lots of work to be done and we can’t just ignore it and think it’s going to go away because it’s not.”

Eynon, whose party gained control of the council in May, said the authority was not “stepping back from its opposition to racism or discrimination” and that “racism has no place in Sunderland”.

He took issue with Ged Grebby, the chief executive of Show Racism the Red Card, describing Reform as a “very dangerous organisation”.

Grebby defended his right to express personal views and said the charity had support across the political spectrum.

Separately, Reform UK has been accused of “vice signalling” after its councillors in Bradford proposed to pull out of the Local Authority of Sanctuary scheme, which is intended to show a city is a safe place for migrant communities.

The Reform group that runs the council said it would be putting forward a motion at the next meeting in October to end the status, which it said has meant the council had “led Refugee Week engagement and utilised local libraries to celebrate all new arrivals into Bradford”, adding that “public services should instead be prioritised for Bradford residents”.

The Reform councillor Jayne Morgan said the move “may upset oversensitive political opponents” but was firmly in the public interest.

In response, Imran Khan, the leader of Bradford’s Labour group, said: “Reform failed to deliver on various promises they made to Bradford residents this summer, so instead they fall back on their usual toxic recipe of hate, victimhood and division.”

He said pulling out of the scheme would “do nothing to help a single person” in Bradford. “This is vice signalling from Reform and all it does is damage integration and promote division and resentment, which helps no one,” he said.

Sports.title: ‘It’s bordering on exploitation’: how pseudoscience is duping football
Sports.content:
Dr Claire-Marie Roberts was working at Coventry City when she received a call from someone asking whether she knew how much oxygen was in the atmosphere. As the performance director, responsible for optimising players’ potential, she was accustomed to being pitched the latest gimmick promising miraculous gains. At times, she could receive up to 50 LinkedIn messages a week offering a device, supplement or technology that claimed to produce magical results.

“It is only 21%,” the caller told her. That’s GCSE chemistry, she thought. Then came the sales pitch: “So what we’ve done is put oxygen in a can and we think you might want to use it.”

“Right … oxygen in a can,” Roberts says, laughing at the memory. Suffice to say, she did not take the caller up on his offer to buy oxygen in a can for Coventry’s players.

Roberts has spent decades working in elite athlete performance and professional football, including nine years at the Premier League and two at Coventry, where she played a key role in their promotion as Championship champions before joining the Formula One team McLaren as director of human performance in the summer. She is shocked by how professional football is being duped by pseudoscience: from coaches and performance staff misled by snake-oil sellers, to players desperate for a shortcut and with money to burn.

“It’s the science-practice gap, which is widening in my experience,” Roberts says. “I think it’s getting much worse. There’s so much sparkly marketing behind all these things. It’s bordering on exploitation.

“They’re taking a population that is very susceptible to: ‘How can I hack my performance advantage? How can I shortcut my preparation and recovery?’ Which I don’t think is a great starting point.”

Roberts says some of the practices commonplace in elite football have little evidence behind them. She includes cryotherapy chambers – a common feature at elite training grounds. If unavailable, ice baths are a fallback. Players enjoy them so much that Harry Kane was photographed standing in a wheelie bin full of ice after a Bayern Munich match at last year’s Club World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Claire-Marie Roberts was part of Frank Lampard’s staff during Coventry’s Championship-winning season. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

“Most clubs have got cryotherapy chambers – most people cannot articulate to you why they use them, because there’s no evidence for them apart from a very slim piece of work that says it might help prevent dementia,” Roberts says. “There’s very sketchy evidence on cryotherapy.”

They could even be detrimental to recovery, Roberts says. “There’s a recent suggestion that cryotherapy might blunt muscular adaptation. When are you using it and why are you using it? If you’re using it for recovery, sleep and nutrition are your best recovery modalities. No amount of putting anybody in a whole-body cryotherapy chamber is going to help them recover more if those two things aren’t taken care of.”

But players are constantly attempting to shortcut nutrition, too. Supplements are a multibillion-pound industry that has its claws in the game. But beyond vitamin D, in which it is “evidence-based” that people in the northern hemisphere are commonly deficient owing to a lack of sunlight, and vitamin C, which is usually short in our diets, supplementation should, Roberts says, be targeted to deficiencies.

“You’ve got people popping pills not really asking what they’re for. It should always be needs-based. If you don’t eat fish and fish oil is important to you, you might supplement it. It should all be based on need.

“Your athletic performance and recovery is based on sleep quality and nutritional quality and amounts. No amount of supplementation will improve a bad diet, but people think it will. We don’t do enough of the basics and think we can shortcut and hack everything.”

View image in fullscreen Claire-Marie Roberts: ‘Most clubs have got cryotherapy chambers – most people cannot articulate to you why they use them.’ Photograph: Eddie Keogh for The FA/Rex/Shutterstock

Roberts says she used an evidence-based, scientific approach to support Frank Lampard’s squad and that many clubs follow practices from the top of the game when often they are flawed.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“People passively suck these things up,” she says. “Because England or Manchester City or Chelsea who have all the resources under the sun have got this, there’s a misappropriation of confidence and understanding of the scientific basis or evidence. It’s powerful in driving behaviour, but it’s driving the wrong behaviour.”

Roberts, a former swimmer who missed the 1996 Atlanta Olympics owing to injury, says: “Football is more susceptible to it than any other sport I’ve experienced first-hand. I think because the stakes are higher.”

Kinesiology tape – or k-tape, as it is commonly known – is another trend that baffles Roberts. Players from Cristiano Ronaldo to Gareth Bale and David Beckham have been spotted wearing it over the years, often resembling strips of gaffer tape stuck to limbs.

“There’s no evidence kinesiology tape has any impact on injury prevention or performance-related outcomes. It gives you a bit of proprioception – maybe you feel like someone has done something – but in any environment I’ve worked in you’d never see anyone wearing k-tape. It’s a big white elephant.

“If an athlete has dislocated their shoulder, you should strap it – strapping is different. It provides an element of external support that can provide minimal protection to the joint and reminds the person they’ve got a problem. It’s a risk-mitigation strategy. It’s not hugely successful, but you’d do it rather than not do it. K-tape is a placebo.”

Often, managers who have been in the game for decades insist on practices they have adopted for years, or because another coach, with no scientific background, has heard about a revolutionary new product. Roberts believes that until football puts science at the centre of decision-making and employs qualified staff to scrutinise claims, the problem will worsen.

“We think we can accelerate to an outcome without putting the hard yards in – the basic things: diet and sleep and the quality of your training,” she says.

“Football in general is very anti-intellectual and it has been for a long time. There are a few clubs that do it well, but the majority don’t. The game is definitely anti-science. There’s a reason for that. There isn’t a critical mass of people that are applying critical thought to situations.”

Sports.title: 'I went limp, slid to the floor... and stopped breathing': Former Millwall captain MATT LAWRENCE on his crippling drug addiction, the bad batch that 'killed' him (twice) and how he's rebuilding his life in New York
Sports.content:
Matt Lawrence died twice in March 2021.

Only nine years after bringing his career as a professional footballer to an end, 17 years after he walked out beside Manchester United's Roy Keane as Millwall captain in the FA Cup final, he lay lifeless in a New York street.

Lawrence was in the grip of a drink and drug habit and the cocaine he had bought turned out to be laced with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid deadly in anything but the most miniscule quantities.

The first time was on St Patrick's Day, and his good fortune was that he was – as so often during the height of his addictions – out in Manhattan with people around to raise the alarm. He was resuscitated by the emergency services and taken to hospital.

Three New Yorkers died the same day, taking drugs cut with fentanyl and sold from the same batch. The dealer responsible, who ran a door-to-door delivery service, was sentenced in 2023 to 30 years in prison for selling drugs resulting in death.

Text messages from Lawrence to his dealer warning that the cocaine he had sold him could be lethal were used in court.

Matt Lawrence, the former Millwall captain, has battled a crippling drink and drug habit

CCTV footage shows Lawrence 'dead' on the floor of a Manhattan bar after he took drugs laced with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid deadly in anything but the most miniscule quantities

Four days later, on March 21, having discarded the remnants of a small bag of cocaine he took that night, Lawrence picked up another small bag bought at the same time. He went out, took the drugs and died again when the fentanyl kicked in. This time inside a bar. The outlook was so bleak a priest issued the last rites.

'It's scary how I came to normalise everything,' Lawrence tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Normalised buying drugs, which is illegal. Normalised being an angry person because that's what drugs do. They make you snappy and argumentative.

'I managed to normalise dying because I came out of hospital and didn't stop. I normalised dying twice in the space of four days.'

His recall of those incidents is incomplete. 'The first time, I remember going to the bathroom, doing the drugs and feeling a bit weird,' he says. 'I walked back to the bar past the person I was with and said I was going to get some air.

'Everything else I know is from the accounts I've read, and that's that I walked halfway across Bleecker Street and passed out, stopped breathing and a Good Samaritan stopped the traffic. I didn't breathe again until the emergency services gave me a Narcan shot in the middle of the road.'

Narcan is the brand name for naloxone, an emergency antidote which instantly reverses the effects of opioids.

'Apparently, I didn't want to go to hospital and was fighting off the paramedics, so they sedated me and I woke up in hospital. Four days later, it happened again. In a bar, I remember sitting down in a chair, three or four of us around a table, and I don't remember any more. My friend said I just went limp and slid onto the floor.

'My muscles stopped working. I stopped breathing. I was given the last rites, it was that close. There is CCTV footage but I haven't been able to watch it. Again, luckily, this is the middle of Manhattan and the emergency services were there very quickly.

'This time I do remember waking up with a needle in my arm. I assume that was the Narcan. None of this sounds particularly good out loud. I'm talking because I need the catharsis. This is me purging my soul in a way. I need the reality to hit. I need other people to read it.'

'I managed to normalise dying because I came out of hospital and didn't stop. I normalised dying twice in the space of four days'

Lawrence (pictured playing for Millwall) did not, he insists, ever take drugs during a 16-year professional playing career which peaked in the Championship

Lawrence is 52 years old, more than a year clean and sober and talking publicly for the first time about what happened. He looks in good shape. Lean and healthy, recently recovered from an achilles tendon torn playing football. His eyes are bright, he smiles and laughs easily and fires out one-liners, almost all of them at his own expense.

He is apprehensive about telling his story but determined and once he starts, the words flow freely.

Lawrence did not, he insists, ever take drugs during a 16-year playing career which peaked in the Championship and blended minor successes in with the inevitable disappointments.

Relatively late into the professional game, he was 21 when he first signed for Wycombe Wanderers, having completed a football scholarship at Hartwick College in New York and played a handful of games in non-League for Grays Athletic. From Wycombe he went to Fulham and back, fighting a feeling that he did not really belong.

'I'd been unwanted by John Gregory at Wycombe and unwanted at Fulham by Kevin Keegan, who was a hero of mine,' says Lawrence. 'Every second of my professional football career was amazing, but I just didn't believe in it or believe in me to start off with.'

These insecurities continued even when he was a proven Championship player at Millwall. 'I probably came across as arrogant because we'd go into children's hospitals at Christmas and I'd hide away,' he says. 'I'd be like, "These kids don't want to see me dressed as Santa". It wasn't because I thought I was too good, it was because I didn't think I was good enough.'

Six years at Millwall included a glorious run to the club's first FA Cup final in 2004 and their first European campaign, albeit brief.

'The FA Cup final is a blur,' says Lawrence. 'I remember the semi-final vividly against Sunderland. The final though, I remember we lost 3-0, I remember Cristiano Ronaldo was very good and I remember Ruud van Nistelrooy kicked me in the testicles.

Lawrence (right) in action for Millwall in the 2004 FA Cup final against Ruud van Nistelrooy and Manchester United

Lawrence also played for Crystal Palace but struggled with issues around his self-confidence

'I trod on Van Nistelrooy's achilles when he was in a wall and he obviously clocked me doing that. Then they had a corner and I was facing him, sort of on the half-turn and looking at the ball, and he straight-up sprinted towards me and volleyed me in the testicles. He apologised after the game.'

Lawrence crossed the divide in south London to spend four years at Crystal Palace and counts the relegation escape of 2010 among his fondest football memories, along with a similar last-gasp relegation escape with Wycombe in 1999.

'Roy Keane will probably shout out loud and say that's not success and I agree but I didn't win many league titles or trophies and the adrenaline rush when you push above the line on the last day is amazing.'

The Palace move, though, felt like a mistake at first. 'The dressing room was at odds with itself, worse than anything I'd known, and it took Neil Warnock to come in and put his stamp on it,' he says. 'Neil came in on the first day, told the players to put their shinpads on and meet him on the pitch.

'He condensed the pitch, moved the goals about 30 yards apart, threw in a ball and basically told us to kick the s*** out of each other. I imagine he thought he'd find out in 10 minutes who he needed to get rid of. And that's the genius of the man.'

Lawrence's playing career closed with two years at Gillingham in League Two and a spell at Whitehawk, winning the Isthmian League and promotion to what was then the Conference South.

'I thrived on being told what to do and staying fit and healthy,' says Lawrence. 'Things deteriorated when I stopped playing for Whitehawk. I was 40 and no longer paid to play football, so I didn't consider myself a footballer anymore.

'When it stops, it stops very rapidly. The same as death happens very quickly at the end. There is no recreating the adrenaline rush of a matchday so I numbed the loss.'

His domestic life unravelled and he fell deeper into drink and drugs. 'I was happy to be controlled by something. By anything. Cocaine and alcohol are pretty good at that.'

'I was happy to be controlled by something. By anything. Cocaine and alcohol are pretty good at that'

Lawrence has lived in the United States since 2016, working as TV analyst in Major League Soccer and living in Jersey City with a wonderful view of the Manhattan skyline across the Hudson River from his apartment.

'I'd be doing a disservice to New York if I said that was a catalyst for my problems,' he says. 'New York was not my downfall. I was my downfall. I'd have found trouble in any far-flung island.

'It was my own fault. A sad sort of demise. Through drink and drugs, I created my own little bubble where I didn't have to think about anything, didn't have to think about life or work or money.

'Not because I had so much money. I had a great football career, but I didn't have limitless money to spiral out of control buying mansions and Ferraris.'

Lawrence stayed clear of drugs for a while after his second brush with death in March 2021 but carried on drinking and eventually slipped back into the habit of taking cocaine again.

'I fell back into it within six months, and fell back even deeper,' he says. 'I didn't die again but my drug intake and frequency got worse.

'I regret all of that. What it did to me financially, what it did to me domestically and what it did to me professionally. I thought I was living my life and getting away with it, but I was out of control.

'I was incredibly depressed. Spending days in tears doing drugs and days in tears not doing drugs. Miserable and upset. My girlfriend and I sat across the dinner table last August, and she just said: "You have to stop, you can't do this anymore."'

'Every second of my professional football career was amazing, but I just didn't believe in it or believe in me'

August 10 last year, by coincidence the opening weekend of the Championship season 2025-26, was his first day of true sobriety.

In the time since he has been learning to enjoy his life again. Learning to appreciate his family and his work again. Learning to love football again, reconnecting with his former clubs and team-mates and finding a warm embrace. Maybe even learning to respect himself again and value his playing career and achievements.

And, alive to tell the tale, he is writing an autobiography and writing it himself, without the help of a ghostwriter, finally finding a use for a degree in American literature more than 30 years after graduating.

'Sobriety is the finality,' says Lawrence. 'There is no five years. No 10 years. No finish line. It's the only thing.

'I am sober as we speak today, I'll be sober for the rest of today and tomorrow. I won't preach to anybody else about how to live their lives, but I know I am an infinitely better human being sober.'

Sports.title: Olympic gymnast Simone Biles reveals three masked men broke into Chicago home and stole her six-figure Porsche
Sports.content:
Olympic gymnast Simone Biles reveals three masked men broke into Chicago home and stole her six-figure Porsche

Simone Biles has revealed three masked intruders broke into her Chicago home and stole her luxurious Porsche.

The legendary Team USA gymnast dropped the bombshell news during a TikTok video this week. It remains unclear when the burglary happened or if the police have made any arrests but Biles confirmed the car was recovered.

'Feel like I need a new car because during our last few months in Chicago, three men in masks came to our house and stole my Porsche,' she said.

'Stole the GTS. But that's another story. If you guys want to know, I'll do a story time on that.'

Biles shared the property in Chicago with her NFL husband Jonathan Owens, who now plays for the Indianapolis Colts but did play for the Bears in 2024 and 2025.

'I feel like I need a reality TV show,' Biles added. 'The things that happen to me are absolute insanity, and so it would be really easy for producers to just film regularly.'

Simone Biles revealed three masked men broke into her Chicago home and stole her Porsche

The legendary Team USA gymnast dropped the bombshell news during a TikTok video

In another TikTok posted soon after, Biles could be seen uncovering an expensive new Lamborghini at a dealership in Houston.

Biles, who said the burglary was one of the reasons why her and Owens got their new Doberman, joins a growing list of superstar athletes who have been the victims of burglaries in recent years.

In May, Argentine police arrested two Chilean citizens suspected of being part of a transnational gang that orchestrated burglaries at the homes of well-known athletes, including stars from the NBA and NFL.

According to local police, the two were part of a crime ring that targeted the homes of prominent athletes in the US and Argentina, including NFL stars Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce and former tennis player Juan Martín del Potro.

Targets also included the homes of NBA players Luka Doncic and Mike Conley Jr.

In 2024, the NFL issued a security alert to teams and the players´ union following the burglaries involving the homes of Mahomes and Kelce.

According to the FBI, organized crime groups from South America used publicly available information and social media to track athletes´ habits and travel.

The groups used technology allowing them to bypass alarm systems, block wireless internet connections and disable devices, cover security cameras and hide their identities.

Jewelry, millions of dollars in cash, trophies and medals were among items stolen from residences while the athletes were out of town.

In another TikTok posted soon after, Biles could be seen uncovering a new Lamborghini

Biles shared the Chicago property with husband Jonathan Owens, who now plays for the Colts

In July, there was also a break-in at the home of Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley.

Earlier this month, Biles was seen on the sidelines supporting her man for his first NFL game of the season.

Biles stepped onto the turf at Lucas Oil Stadium to watch Owens make his debut for the Colts against the Baltimore Ravens after arriving in Indianapolis in free agency.

She continued her tradition of dressing up in custom gear with Owens' name and number on it. This time, she arrived in a royal blue dress made out of Owens' brand-new jerseys. His name and number were seen down the left side of the garment as well as on her chest.

Sports.title: Man City flop Tijjani Reijnders brazenly admits he went to Saudi Arabia for the money - insisting he doesn't want to work after retiring from football
Sports.content:
Man City flop Tijjani Reijnders brazenly admits he went to Saudi Arabia for the money - insisting he doesn't want to work after retiring from football

Manchester City reject Tijjani Reijnders has admitted that he moved to Saudi Arabia for the vast financial benefits.

The 28-year-old midfielder left Man City over the summer for the relatively unknown Saudi outfit Al-Qadsiah in a £52million deal.

He spent just a season at the Etihad and, despite a hugely impressive debut after joining them from AC Milan for £46.5m, he struggled to make a consistent impact across his 50 appearances.

Reijnders is on a five-year contract with Al-Qadsiah, who are managed by Brendan Rodgers, and is reportedly set to earn around £86million over the half-decade.

Now a month into his time there, he said: 'Once my playing career is over, I don’t want to have to work anymore.

'Of course, I probably wouldn’t have needed to work anymore after my contract at Manchester City either, but this move allows me to secure the future of the next generations of my family.

Former Manchester City midfielder Tijjani Reijnders has admitted he moved to Saudi Arabia for the money

He says he wants to secure generational wealth, thinking ahead to his future grandchildren

'I’m not going to lie about that. By signing this contract, I can make sure even my grandchildren are financially secure, so why wouldn’t I do it?'

He currently has one son, Xavien, with his wife Marina. Speaking about what attracted him to the club in August, Reijnders was not so quick to mention cash.

He said at the time: 'Especially the ambition of the club (is what attracted me).

'The club wants to be the biggest in Asia and what they did already in the past and what we can do now in the future, it triggered me a lot.

'And, yeah, I want to help the club to bring it to the highest level.

'I came here to try and win trophies with my teammates - we're playing for four trophies, if I'm right.

'We want to win as many as possible and we are all very eager to do that. And, personally, I hope I can help the team as much as possible with goals and assists.'

The Netherlands international has scored three goals in five Saudi Pro League outings for Al-Qadsiah, who also feature in the AFC Champions League.

They are currently fourth in the Saudi Pro League, where they have finished for the last two seasons.

The club is owned by the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, the majority state-owned petroleum and natural gas firm.

They do not have as many big names as some of their Middle Eastern counterparts but do have some respected faces from around Europe, such as former Spain and Italy defender Nacho Fernandez and Italy striker Mario Retegui.

Reijnders played three matches for the Netherlands at the World Cup.

Sports.title: Furious Real Madrid turn on 'intolerable' LaLiga president Javier Tebas with explosive statement calling for him to resign after mocking their 'conspiracy' complaints over refereeing
Sports.content:
Furious Real Madrid turn on 'intolerable' LaLiga president Javier Tebas with explosive statement calling for him to resign after mocking their 'conspiracy' complaints over refereeing

Real Madrid have called for 'intolerable' LaLiga president Javier Tebas to resign - after he mocked their complaints about refereeing.

The Spanish giants were furious with the officiating in the Madrid derby, which they lost 2-1 to city rivals Atletico.

It prompted Jose Mourinho to rant about the 'poor' referee Ortiz Arias, who he suggested was unqualified, and led to the club releasing an official statement condemning the 'very terrible refereeing'.

They felt that Cristian Romero and Lee Kang-In should have been sent off - the former for a stamp on Jude Bellingham and the latter for a challenge on Federico Valverde.

In the aftermath, LaLiga boss Tebas responded to an article which claimed there was a 'conspiracy' against Madrid, saying that 'claiming that referees are directed against Real Madrid is living in another galaxy.'

But now Madrid have hit back, writing: 'Our club considers it intolerable that the president of LaLiga uses his institutional position to continue discrediting and attacking Real Madrid.

Real Madrid have called for LaLiga president Javier Tebas (above) to resign after he mocked their complaints over refereeing in the capital city derby

Jose Mourinho was furious at the refereeing performance of Ortiz Arias (right) on Sunday

Mourinho was so livid at the refereeing performance that he printed out fouls he felt were missed, calling for two red cards

'Given this inappropriate and persistent behaviour, we believe that the professional football competition in Spain urgently needs a leader capable of ​managing it and realising ​its full potential ⁠with the fundamental duty of neutrality.

'His latest intervention is particularly serious and incomprehensible - unbecoming of a responsible administrator - as it involves commenting on an article by an independent journalist in a digital media outlet.

'Yet, he reacts against our club by taking the liberty of critiquing our sporting strategy - an utterly absurd and irresponsible move.'

Tebas' comment in full had read: 'Claiming that referees are directed against Real Madrid is living in another galaxy.

'That narrative serves as an excuse to cover up other shortcomings that are plain to see in these first matches of the season.

'It's more comfortable to point to a conspiracy than to explain what's happening on the pitch.'

Real Madrid were reduced to 10 men in the derby after Dean Huijsen dragged down Giuliano Simeone in the penalty box.

That allowed Alejandro Grimaldo to convert from the spot, before Jonathan David doubled Atletico's lead. Madrid got a late goal back via Antonio Rudiger.

Mourinho was in disbelief at a referee he is adamant will never make it to the highest level

Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham was furious at officials after Cristian Romero was not sent off

The result leaves Madrid fourth in the table, six points behind league leaders Barcelona, who have a perfect record. They also trail Atletico and Real Betis.

Manager Mourinho was seething in his press conference and arrived with printed out photos which showed, in his opinion, a series of major calls missed by the referee.

'We could save ourselves the press conference,' an irritated Mourinho began.

'Here they are [shows photos of the possible red cards], two clear reds. It would have been 50 minutes of 11 against nine. All I can do is hug my players, who gave everything, who produced a first half full of class and personality. I prepared the match so we could win it in the second half.'

'The one who should be happy is the Refereeing Appointments Committee because the whole thing was very strange,' Mourinho's rant continued.

'A week in advance, they already knew who the referee would be, when it used to be 24 hours before. A 41-year-old referee, who has never been an international, that won't be top level.

'The poor guy came here and couldn't handle the pressure.

'The pressure here is like something out of the 1980s. Trujillo, the VAR official, called him over for the first red and didn't call him over for the second, which was even clearer. This Trujillo has a history with Real Madrid: last year in the Copa final, Osasuna, Girona...

🚨🫵🏽 Jude Bellingham against the referee at full time: “Two red cards! Two!”.@postunited — oscarolleroo on IG 📸 pic.twitter.com/1qkCTlsMUO — Fabrizio Romano (@FabrizioRomano) September 20, 2026

'If the poor referee has no experience, no stature for a derby, then this man is either under no pressure, or under a kind of pressure we know nothing about.

'I would have liked to leave here with the win or without having to speak. I arrived here three months ago and you know I'm not usually one to go in this direction.

'Two reds against Elche and we won. Two reds today, that's already more difficult. It's a referee with only small matches behind him and a VAR official who has a history.

'Congratulations to the Refereeing Appointments Committee.'

In an official club statement, Real Madrid said: 'Real Madrid lose the derby at the Metropolitano in a match marked by Ortiz Arias' VERY TERRIBLE REFEREEING.

'He failed to send off Cuti Romero in the first half for stepping on Bellingham's knee (despite going to the monitor to review the incident), nor did he send off Lee Kang-In for stepping on Valverde's left ankle.

'Both decisions had an impact on the match, which was ultimately decided in Atlético's favor in the second half.'

Sports.title: Alan Shearer accuses Tottenham of overspending on £330m summer makeover and claims splurging an 'absolute fortune' has only piled on pressure - as he questions the 'ability' of Sandro Tonali, Savio and Co
Sports.content:
Alan Shearer has accused Tottenham of overspending as their £330million summer splurge has left them bottom of the Premier League.

Spurs splashed huge money on Sandro Tonali (£100m), Mateus Fernandes (£85m), Savio (£85m), Jan Paul van Hecke (£52m), and Tosin Adarabioyo (£7m) but have picked up just two points in five games.

Shearer has questioned the 'ability' of Tottenham's new signings, with pressure mounting on Roberto De Zerbi to get a tune out of them.

He told Betfair: 'I guess De Zerbi went into this summer with a list of players that he wanted and they have spent a fortune perhaps on all those players.

'I'm not sure the fees warrant the ability, but no one would have expected them to be bottom of the league.'

He added: 'I've said many times, that they brought the players in this summer, but they spent an absolute fortune on them. On everyone, I think.

Alan Shearer has accused Tottenham over overspending and questioned the 'ability' of their signings

The club have endured a nightmare start to the season under Roberto De Zerbi and are bottom of the Premier League

'Van Hecke was a lot of money, Tonali was incredible money, Savio, and Marmoush (on loan) are others as well. It is a long, long three weeks for Tottenham and they simply have to start winning football games when they are back from the international break.

'All the bigger questions will start to be asked, if not already, if they don’t start winning football games very, very soon.

'I still think they'll have enough to stay up. They'll use the Aston Villa situation and what happened to them at the start of last season when I don't think they won in their first five games and they then managed to climb the league and qualify for Europe again.

'They will look at that and think there's still loads of football to be played, which there is, but there's a massive amount of work to be done at Spurs.

'I had them to finish in the top six this season and I am not sure that that will happen now.'

Tottenham did manage to register their first Premier League goals of the season late on in the 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa.

But that was only late on, when the game was lost and many of the fans had already left the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

De Zerbi tore into his men after an abysmal performance in that defeat, saying: 'I am very disappointed, sad and frustrated with the performance.

Spurs spent £329million over the summer, including £85m on Savio from Manchester City

New man Jan Paul van Hecke was at fault for one of Aston Villa's goals over the weekend - but did score later

'We can’t lose the game in this way, we can’t concede the second goal (a simple ball over the top), we can’t lose balance just because we are losing.

'I spoke with our four attackers in minute 51, I asked them to use their head, all second half I was telling people to be calm. But the second goal was incredible.'

Van Hecke fluffed his lines when Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki punted it long, allowing Nicolas Jackson to race through for the opposition's second goal.

De Zerbi added: 'We knew this season Aston Villa are playing 86 per cent more long balls than last season and we spoke in many meetings about it. Now we have to explain another game like (Newcastle) where we played the first half well, got to 60 minutes OK, and then we lose.'

The only match Spurs have won this campaign was a 5-1 thrashing of Championship side Charlton in the second round of the Carabao Cup.

This is the first time they have been bottom of the Premier League since January 2009.

They are second-bottom of the league goalscoring charts, just one goal ahead of Coventry, but have had the ninth-most shots, suggesting that finishing is an issue.

Steven Gerrard pointed to their striking issues on TNT Sports, saying: 'I think Spurs have improved in certain areas, but they've not got a poacher.

'They've not got a goalscorer. They've got some exciting players in the front line, but who is going to get you 20 goals?'

Their only natural striker is Dominic Solanke - with Richarlison exiled - and he has scored 12 goals across two full Premier League seasons with Spurs.

In the summer they sold young English striker Will Lankshear to Middlesbrough for £10m, potentially rising to £20m, and he has scored eight goals in 10 games there.

Tottenham will be looking to make amends quickly after the international break, with their first fixture back coming at Manchester United on October 10.

Sports.title: Liverpool's new Virgil van Dijk, three Chelsea stars and a Spurs summer signing make the cut as stats boffins reveal their Premier League team of the season so far - but there's NO room for Arsenal's David Raya in goal
Sports.content:
It's advantage Manchester City as the Premier League pauses for the first international break of the season after Arsenal suffered a shock 3-0 loss at Brighton.

After five matches, a revamped Tottenham have hit rock bottom while unbeaten Leeds United (fifth) sit above a reviving Liverpool (sixth), an inconsistent Chelsea (tenth) and a struggling Manchester United (12th).

Enzo Maresca has big shoes to fill but he could not have asked for a better start to his reign at City while Alexander Isak could well be the one to challenge Erling Haaland for the Golden Boot... finally.

Newly promoted Hull are enjoying their return to the big time while fellow promoted side Coventry secured their first win of the season in matchweek five.

But which players have stood out and done enough to earn a place in Sofascore's team of the season so far?

Daily Mail Sport takes a look at the Premier League's best XI – and there are a few surprise names...

GK: Emiliano Martinez (Chelsea) – 7.70/10

Sold to Chelsea for a throwaway price of £7.5million by Aston Villa, Emiliano Martínez had every chance to start the new season as the bargain buy of the summer. But the 2026 World Cup finalist has not fully lived up to his billing under new manager Xabi Alonso.

Martinez replaced Robert Sanchez immediately in goal but has struggled to become a fan favourite so far this season. So, how did Martinez make the cut for this team?

In his first game against Brighton, Martinez made four saves in the 4-3 win at home; the visitors had six shots on goal with four big chances. In the London derby against the defending champions, the Chelsea goalkeeper produced eight saves – the most on the Premier League matchday.

With zero clean sheets, Chelsea's defence averages 2.4 goals per game in the top flight. Martinez averages 4.5 saves per game.

His average rating of 7.70 is the highest by any goalkeeper so far this season with his saves per game the highest. Arsenal's impressive No1 David Raya averages 1.8 saves per game.

Emiliano Martinez tops Sofascore's rankings of Premier League goalkeepers with an impressive number of saves among the goals Chelsea have conceded so far

CB: Jeremy Jacquet (Liverpool) – 7.72/10

Signed by Liverpool for £60million in July, Jacquet has already won his first senior call-up to Zinedine Zidane's French national side for their respective international matches.

With Liverpool losing Ibrahima Konate to Real Madrid and Giovanni Leoni to an anterior cruciate ligament injury, the 21-year-old has stepped up seamlessly to team up with captain Virgil van Dijk at the back.

The former Rennes centre back is also showing Liverpool fans what life after the Dutch veteran could look like at Anfield.

Though Isak grabbed the headlines after Liverpool's 1-0 away win at Bournemouth, Jacquet was equally impressive, settling quickly into defence and providing much-needed composure at the back.

The Jacquet-Van Dijk pairing has also earned Liverpool three consecutive clean sheets for the first time in two years. Jacquet has won 76 per cent of his duels this season.

CB: Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham) – 7.62/10

For the first time since the 2008-09 season, Tottenham are bottom of the Premier League after five games. At a time when Spurs are struggling badly under Roberto De Zerbi following heavy summer spending, a consistent presence in central defence is a genuine boost.

Jan Paul van Hecke has played every minute of Tottenham's forgettable Premier League campaign so far this season.

Playing all 450 minutes matters early in a season when many new signings are still rotating. With a consolation goal to his name in the 3-2 defeat against Aston Villa, the Dutch centre-back has two clean sheets despite Spurs' winless run.

CB: Lewis Dunk (Brighton) – 7.70/10

Fresh from smashing a showstopper against Frank Lampard's Coventry, Brighton defender Lewis Dunk has played 360 minutes for Fabian Hurzeler's men.

His second Premier League goal from outside the box was also his first since his clever free-kick against Liverpool in 2019.

Averaging four clearances per game, Dunk has enjoyed two clean sheets in four starts.

Nursing a knee injury, Dunk was replaced by Olivier Boscagli for Brighton's crucial league clash with Arsenal.

Despite missing the services of the 34-year-old, Hurzeler's men stunned holders Arsenal 3-0 to secure third place in the table.

CDM: Granit Xhaka (Sunderland) – 7.66/10

Losing his place in the Switzerland squad over a fake vaccine certificate, Granit Xhaka is the only central defensive midfielder named in the team of the season after five rounds.

Xhaka has created five big chances for Sunderland and the 33-year-old is averaging 1.2 interceptions and 1.8 tackles per game across the first five matches.

The Sunderland captain has also impressed with his ball recoveries (6.6 per game) this season.

With a 67 per cent dribble success rate, he has won 60 per cent of his duels across 450 minutes for Regis Le Bris's men.

Xhaka's sublime delivery paved the way for hat-trick hero Brian Brobbey to complete a historic treble against Manchester City, although the Sunderland midfielder is still waiting for his first assist of the new season.

Granit Xhaka has impressed both defensively and as an a creative force for Sunderland

CAM: Martin Odegaard (Arsenal) – 7.60/10

Leading the Gunners from the front, Martin Odegaard delivered when it mattered the most – the London derby.

The Arsenal captain earned a 9.2 rating after he netted the winner against Chelsea. He also made four key passes and created two big chances against Alonso's men.

Odegaard enjoys 1.4 shots per game and has a goal conversion of 29 per cent after five matches.

Arsenal's captain has found the net with either foot for his side. With a passing accuracy of 91 per cent, the 27-year-old is also drawing 1.2 fouls per game.

A calm and smooth operator on the field, Odegaard averages 2.4 balls recovered per game.

He has made the team of the week twice and has looked back to his best so far this season.

CAM: Morgan Rogers (Chelsea) – 7.68/10

Before Odegaard flourished, Morgan Rogers announced his arrival in the London derby with a volley to beat Arsenal's Raya.

The £117million signing registered an assist in Chelsea's high-scoring Stamford Bridge draw with Brighton and found the net against Hull City, only for the Blues to then turn in a toothless performance at Brentford.

With three goals and one assist under his belt, Rogers averages 88 minutes per game for the Blues so far this season.

He is expected to draw at least one foul from the opposition and his passing accuracy ranges from 75 to 80 per cent. The former Villa star is also defensively strong averaging 4.6 balls recovered per game.

RW: Bukayo Saka (Arsenal) – 7.56/10

Besides being a constant threat on the right wing and threading defence-splitting passes, Bukayo Saka has been pivotal for Mikel Arteta's Arsenal so far this season, and like Odegaard is in fine form.

It only took 23 minutes for Saka to open his Premier League account in Arsenal's 3-0 win over Coventry City on matchday one at the Emirates Stadium last month.

When the Gunners travelled to Birmingham to face Unai Emery's Aston Villa, Saka scored the only goal of the match to give the defending champions all three points.

The England international then converted his penalty late in the 97th minute against Sunderland to further enhance his goal tally. He has an XG of 3.21 goals.

LW: Marcus Tavernier (Bournemouth) – 7.62/10

Marcus Tavernier slotted home Bournemouth's only goal in their 2-1 loss at Manchester City on matchday one, before the Cherries shared the spoils in a 1-1 draw with Everton.

With his side developing a trend of conceding late goals, the 27-year-old opened the scoring again at Newcastle – only to witness a Jacob Ramsey equaliser in the 88th minute.

The scoreline remained identical against Brentford for the hosts when Tavernier scored in the 52nd minute, before the visitors found the equaliser four minutes later.

Tavernier has three goals to his name, has featured in team of the week twice and averages 1.6 shots on target per game.

Marcus Tavernier has already bagged three goals for Bournemouth this season

ST: Joao Pedro (Chelsea) – 7.63/10

Fernando Torres, Radamel Falcao, Alvaro Morata, Gonzalo Higuain, Romelu Lukaku and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang all failed to live up to expectations after taking the No 9 shirt. Joao Pedro has flipped the script at Stamford Bridge.

Scoring in the first minute, Pedro assisted Cole Palmer, who decided Chelsea's five-goal thriller against Fulham at Craven Cottage. A goal and an assist – the same story followed against Brighton.

Following a quiet outing against Arsenal where he only managed a solitary shot on goal, the 24-year-old returned with his 'assist, goal and repeat' drill against Hull City.

Three goals and three assists. A strong start. Chelsea lost 3-0 at Brentford last week with the Brazilian forward out injured.

ST: Erling Haaland (Manchester City) – 7.60/10

No surprise here. With Haaland leading the Premier League goalscoring charts, Maresca's City have opened the season with five straight league wins for the first time since 2017.

Haaland added Sunderland to the 25-team strong list of different clubs against which the Manchester City forward has found the back of the net in the Premier League.

The Man City striker needed three meetings to score his first goal against Sunderland, after failing to do so in both outings last season.

After ending his goalless run against Sunderland, Haaland is now averaging one goal per game in the English top flight.

Averaging two shots on goal per game, the 26-year-old has an XG of 4.43 goals.

Haaland has taken his goal tally to 117 in 137 league appearances. Will anyone be able to stop him this season?

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Thomas Tuchel is indulging in some elite-level gaslighting by blaming Argentina defeat on his players. No, it was the England manager's first big test - and he blew it spectacularly
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel wants to forget about the recent past. Argentina in the semi-finals of the World Cup just over two months ago? Our best chance to get to the final for 60 years?

Let’s move on, eh? In fact, let’s have a bit of a laugh about it. Tactics? Nobody wants to talk about tactics, Tuchel says.

Only the pesky press want to talk about tactics, Tuchel says, as if that is something the media should be ashamed of. Heaven forfend that some England fans still feel bitter about why the dream died. The real people, Tuchel says, just want to remember Mexico and the glory of the Azteca.

I want to remember Mexico, too. I’ll never forget it. It was one of the greatest football occasions I’ve ever witnessed. I’ll always be grateful to Tuchel for the fact he masterminded that beautiful victory. It was one of England’s greatest performances at a tournament. It was also a last-16 game.

Unfortunately, I’ll never forget the Argentina tie, either. I’ll never forget the missed opportunity. Tuchel and the FA might want to move on to the Nations League campaign stretching ahead of us over the next few weeks and the tie against Spain at Wembley on Saturday but I can’t do it. Not yet.

Tuchel seems flatly unable to accept that he got anything wrong against Argentina. He and those around him are trying to style it out. It’s not him, it’s us. And by ‘us’, I mean English football. We are petty for still dissecting it, apparently.

Thomas Tuchel wants us all to move on from the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina. Well, I'm sorry, I can't do that yet

Tuchel seems flatly unable now and in the immediate aftermath to accept that he got anything wrong in that match

It’s not his fault we blew it against Argentina, he is saying. The fault is in ourselves that we are underlings, he continues to tell us. It’s in our DNA, you see. There’s really absolutely nothing he can do about it.

There is some elite-level gaslighting going on here. Most of us can see through it so let’s be honest about what happened in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta on July 15: Tuchel faced his first big test as England manager and he blew it. He blew it spectacularly.

He was not hired to get us to the World Cup semi-finals. Gareth Southgate did that. Tuchel was hired to get us beyond the semi-finals. He was hired to coach a talented group of England players to win the World Cup. He was hired, famously, because he would have the ability to get us ‘over the line’.

But when the test came, he wasn’t up to it. That’s the truth. I’ve heard all his excuses and all his deflections. But when the test came, he blew a 1-0 lead against an ordinary Argentina side. He was comprehensively out-coached by Argentina’s Lionel Scaloni. When the heat was on, Tuchel folded.

England always find a way to lose the big games at World Cups and lo and behold we had done it again. Tuchel was being paid the big bucks to fix that glitch in our psyche but he couldn’t do it. When it mattered most, England froze. And he froze with them.

In a weird way, I admire his front. There is something awfully bold about blaming his players and saying there was nothing he could do about their inability to keep the ball. ‘I should be coaching them to keep the ball?’ Tuchel asked on Friday, as if it were an utterly alien idea. ‘That’s my job? I’m not sure that I have the time.’

That’s why many England fans are finding it hard to let the mistakes of the Argentina game go. Because if Tuchel can’t accept that mistakes were made, then how can England move forward? How can we have any confidence at all that the next time we face a critical match, Tuchel does not blow it again?

If I were one of his players, I’d still be thinking about what he said in the aftermath of that Argentina tie. I’d still be thinking about the way he ducked responsibility. I’d still be thinking about what he said about English players and their DNA.

Enzo Fernandez celebrates his goal against England in the World Cup semi-finals

If I were one of Tuchel's players, I’d still be thinking about what he said in the aftermath of that Argentina tie

Put it this way, it wasn’t a surprise to me when the news came through on Monday morning that Cole Palmer had pulled out of the squad for the games against Spain, Czech Republic and Croatia with a ‘small muscle injury’. A few hours later the FA announced that Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford, Declan Rice and Tino Livramento would also be absent due to 'respective injury issues'.

Palmer didn’t make the World Cup squad, of course. Tuchel discarded him. Mainoo went but he didn’t play a single minute in the USA and Mexico. Tuchel humiliated him. Palmer and Mainoo are two of England’s best players. They are brilliant technical athletes. Of all England’s players, they are two of the best at keeping the ball.

Tuchel chose not to use them at the World Cup. He ignored Trent Alexander-Arnold, too, another of England’s best technical players. And now he has the gall to suggest our players are like neanderthals who can’t keep possession. If you want to keep possession in a World Cup semi-final against Argentina, maybe pick players in the squad who are the best at keeping possession.

It is surely not too great a stretch to suggest that Tuchel’s disdain for the ball-retention abilities of England’s players is not conducive to future harmony in the squad as the country turns its eyes towards a home European Championship in the summer of 2028.

If Tuchel could admit the errors he made in Atlanta, if he could take responsibility for the failure against Argentina, then maybe England could move forward with confidence. But he can’t. The delusion of infallibility has been his downfall before. And so doubt remains.

LIGHT SHONE ON UNITED'S ABSURD RECRUITMENT POLICY

Watching Fulham play Manchester United at Craven Cottage on Sunday afternoon, it was hard not to be reminded once more of the absurdity of United’s stated plan of fixing their team section by section in successive summer transfer windows.

The rationale, apparently, is that they fixed the attack in the summer of 2025, they fixed the midfield this summer and they will turn their attention to the defence next summer.

It is, frankly, bizarre. Football doesn’t work like that. Maybe Matheus Cunha, for example, will want out by next summer. Andrey Santos can’t get a kick at the moment. Football teams are like whack-a-mole: problems crop up everywhere.

And in the meantime, the creaking defence is a liability and another season’s hope of winning the Premier League is over already.

Manchester United's policy of fixing the team section by section is frankly odd. What if Matheus Cunha decides he wants out next summer?

And what of the newly-acquired £50m signing Andrey Santos who cannot get a kick at the moment?

CALLING IT 'THE DOCKERS' DERBY' IS JUST WRONG!

A point of order: a West Ham-supporting friend of mine wishes to advise that the habit of referring to the Championship match between his side and Millwall at the weekend as ‘The Dockers’ Derby’ ground the gears of him and many of his fellow Hammers.

‘West Ham were born from an ironworks yard, not a dockyard,’ he writes. ‘Prior to the advent of people needing to place some corny moniker on every football match, it was never, ever included in the vocabulary of sensible people growing up on the terraces of Upton Park and The Den.’

A fair point, I think. As an adjunct, reports from the aforementioned derby on Saturday, which ended in a 2-2 draw, suggest it was played in a fiercely wonderful atmosphere.

Sports.title: Celtic chief offers full backing to under-pressure boss Martin O'Neill
Sports.content:
Celtic chief executive Michael Nicholson insists the club remain fully supportive of Martin O'Neill despite the veteran manager being under mounting pressure.

O'Neill stated after the 1-0 defeat to Rangers at Parkhead last Sunday that he would take time to consider his future during the international break and whether it might be time to 'wrap it up'.

The 74-year-old, who agreed a one-year deal back in the summer to remain at the helm, has presided over three damaging defeats to Rangers and Ferencvaros over the past week.

Although Celtic do still remain top of the league by two points, a large section of the support had called for a change to be made in recent days.

But, as Celtic released their latest annual accounts showing a post-tax loss of £4.8million as well as cash reserves of £66.4m, Nicholson was adamant the club remain fully behind O'Neill.

'We were delighted to end season 2025/26 on a high, winning the Scottish Premiership on the final day of the season and adding the Scottish Cup and Women's Scottish Cup in the weeks following,' said Nicholson.

Martin O'Neill says he's considering his future as Celtic boss after three defeats on the bounce

Celtic chief Michael Nicholson has offered his support to the under-fire manager

'But last season was a challenging one for the club, both on and off the pitch. Following a period of stability, which has borne fruit in terms of success and growth over recent years, we experienced turmoil which affected the club's performance.

'We will address and learn from the challenges faced and mistakes made.

'The final weeks of the Premiership season; the final match at Celtic Park; the Scottish Cup final; these will live long in the memory for Celtic fans, whose support was a decisive factor.

'I thank Callum McGregor and all of the players and staff for their hard work and determination throughout the season that made the success possible.

'As the Chairman has noted, the environment was unstable, following Brendan Rodgers' resignation and our decision to move on from Wilfried Nancy.

'We owe a debt of gratitude to Martin O'Neill and his management team, who stepped up for Celtic, twice, and who guided the team to success.

'We were therefore delighted that Martin agreed to lead the Club again this season and we have worked with Martin and his team over the summer transfer window to invest in the squad.

'Having started well in the Premiership this season, we experienced disappointment in the UEFA Champions League play-off.

'Reaching the league phase of the Champions League is an objective for us all, and we are sorry not to have achieved it.

'On top of that, the losses in the last week have been painful for us all. We will now come together and support Martin and the players, as we focus our efforts on achieving success domestically and in the Europa League.'

In his own address to supporters, Celtic chairman Brian Wilson claimed that the disastrous appointment of Nancy last season could have worked had it not happened mid-season.

Nancy lasted only a month in the job after presiding over a shambolic run of form and eventually left as statistically the worst – and shortest-serving – manager in the club's history.

The Celtic hierarchy at full-time in Sunday's 1-0 home defeat to Old Firm rivals Rangers

'The events of the past 12 months have been dramatic, sometimes joyful and at other points deeply frustrating,' said Wilson.

'The departure of Brendan Rodgers was an unanticipated event which initiated a period of instability.

'In other circumstances, the appointment of Wilfried Nancy might have worked but his arrival in mid-season and the changes which followed clearly did not.

'Parting ways with Wilfried was hugely disappointing but decisive action had to be taken.

'The return of the great Martin O'Neill, supported by his backroom team as well as a fine squad of players, then proved to be a triumphant success.

'The early stages of the 2026/27 season have brought mixed fortunes.

'Our league campaign started strongly and the first leg tie in the Champions League qualifier gave cause for optimism.

'The second leg defeat to LASK was, accordingly, all the more deeply disappointing for every supporter of the Club.

'This has been followed by our exit from the League Cup. We now move into the Europa League as well as pursuing our defence of the Scottish Premiership and Scottish Cup, with renewed commitment to success.'

In terms of their annual accounts for the year ending June 30, 2026, Celtic's revenue decreased by 22.7 per cent to £111.0million (2025: £143.6million).

Operating expenses including labour increased by 4.3 per cent to £122.1million (2025: £117.1million).

Gain on sale of player registrations of £16.0million (2025: £31.5million). Acquisition of player registrations of £15.6million (2025: £38.6million)

Loss before tax of £6.6million (2025: profit of £45.7million). Loss after tax of £4.8million (2025: profit of £33.9million).Year-end cash of £66.4million (2025: £77.3million).

Sports.title: Daniel Levy's £27m Tottenham exit package explained after huge pay-off and exit
Sports.content:
Daniel Levy's £27m Tottenham exit package explained after huge pay-off and exit

Daniel Levy left Tottenham a year ago and was handed a significant pay-off fee

View 2 Images Daniel Levy left Tottenham last year (Image: David Rogers/Getty Images)

Tottenham Hotspur reportedly paid £27million to their former executive Daniel Levy following his exit from the club last year. Levy saw his 24-year tenure with Spurs come to an end in September last year.

‌



It has been reported by The Athletic that the payout from Spurs to Levy factored in his salary, as well as any bonuses and the long-term incentive plan in place at the club. It is thought that the £27m given to Levy is one of the largest amounts given to a football executive.

‌



Non-executive chairman Peter Charrington wrote an open letter to Tottenham fans at the end of last season following a major overhaul of the club’s hierarchy.

‌



He wrote: "Last September, we recognised that something seismic had to change at Spurs.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"The Lewis family stepped in and authorised a full reset. That decision was not taken lightly, and it came later than it should have."

Since taking the reins, the Lewis family have pumped a staggering £320million into the club over the past year, most recently injecting £120million in working capital as they continue to steadily grow their shareholding.

Levy still holds around 24% of Tottenham, though his stake was diluted earlier in the summer. He was offered the opportunity to participate in a £100million equity investment but did not respond before the August deadline, seeing his share drop from 26%.

‌



Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi has also been generously backed in the transfer market, with the club signing 10 new players over the summer for a combined outlay of nearly £400million.

View 2 Images Tottenham Hotspur are yet to win a Premier League match this season (Image: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Offside via Getty Images)

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Savio, Jan Paul van Hecke and Tosin Adarabioyo were amongst the high-profile arrivals at the club.

The substantial outlay on playing staff is aimed at steering clear of a repeat of last season's struggles, when the club spent the vast majority of the campaign battling to preserve their Premier League status. Spurs required a final day victory over Everton to secure their survival.

Yet heading into the first international break of the season, Tottenham find themselves at the bottom of the Premier League table. Of their five top-flight fixtures so far this term, Spurs have lost three and drawn two.

Article continues below

De Zerbi's side return to action on Saturday, October 10 when they make the trip to face Manchester United at Old Trafford.

Sports.title: Arsenal news: Mikel Arteta 'agrees new deal' as manager dealt fresh injury blow
Sports.content:
Arsenal news: Mikel Arteta 'agrees new deal' as manager dealt fresh injury blow

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta reportedly looks set to extend his time in charge of the Gunners

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta has been in charge of Arsenal since December 2019 (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

The international break has prevented Arsenal from immediately responding to their recent Premier League setback. The Gunners suffered an emphatic 3-0 defeat to Brighton, which saw the champions fall from top spot.

Mikel Arteta will have plenty of time to mull over any mistakes he may have made on the south coast as Arsenal are not back in action until October 10. The manager can also use this period to focus on off-field matters, with the Spanish coach reportedly agreeing to a new contract.

Arteta has been in charge of Arsenal since 2019 and is aiming to build on last season’s title triumph. The Gunners boss will hope the players away with their national teams can remain fit for when club football resumes.

Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice has withdrawn from the England squad and will not feature for Thomas Tuchel’s side at the start of their Nations League campaign. While Rice’s decision is reportedly due to load management, Arsenal prospect Marli Salmon has picked up an injury ahead of international duty. Here, Mirror Football looks at some of the biggest stories surrounding the Gunners.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Mikel Arteta ‘agrees new deal’

Arteta has reportedly been rewarded with a pay increase after ending Arsenal’s 22-year wait for the Premier League title. The 44-year-old will be eager to continue his recent success, having also led the club to the Champions League final last term.

BBC Sport reports that Arteta has agreed on an improved contract with the Gunners, which will see him paid more than his current £10million annual salary and £5m in bonuses. The precise length of his new deal is unknown, but it is claimed that it will take him into his 10th year in charge, meaning the contract will run until at least 2029.

The Spaniard has entered the final year of his current contract. However, Arteta was quick to dismiss any worries about his future last week.

He said: “They [the fans] don't have to worry about any of that because I want to be here. I'm extremely happy and I feel very grateful to work with the people I work with.”

View 2 Images Marli Salmon has withdrawn from international duty (Image: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Offside via Getty Images)

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Arsenal dealt injury blow

Arsenal starlet Marli Salmon has withdrawn from international duty due to an unspecified injury. The 17-year-old defender was named in the England U18 squad for their upcoming games against Colombia, Egypt and South Korea as part of the UEFA Friendship Cup in Switzerland.

The England squad lists state that Salmon has withdrawn through injury and been replaced by Chelsea's Gabriel Sambou in Will Antwi’s side. Salmon has yet to play for England U18s but was involved in last year's U17 World Cup.

He started Arsenal’s Carabao Cup victory over Ipswich Town earlier this month and was in the Champions League matchday squad against Napoli, while also featuring three times for the club’s U21 side this term. The teenager has played five first team games under Arteta since making his debut in December 2025.

Sports.title: Willie Mullins tribute to legendary dual champion hurdler Hurricane Fly after death aged 22
Sports.content:
Willie Mullins tribute to legendary dual champion hurdler Hurricane Fly after death aged 22

The star jumper scored at the Cheltenham Festival in 2011 and 2013 under Ruby Walsh and won the Irish Champion Hurdle a remarkable five times

View 3 Images Ruby Walsh and Willie Mullins with Hurricane Fly (Image: PA)

Willie Mullins’s legendary dual champion hurdler Hurricane Fly has died aged 22.

‌



The star jumper triumphed at the Cheltenham Festival in 2011 and 2013 under Ruby Walsh and also won the Irish Champion Hurdle a remarkable five times from 2011 to 2015. His nine-year career came to an end in August 2015 when he was retired from racing to spend the rest of his days at the Irish National Stud in Kildare.

‌



Announcing the sad news to the Sporting Life, Mullins said: “He won a record-breaking 22 Grade 1 races, which was remarkable. He’s one of the greatest horses to ever come through our stable.

‌



Value Scope Extra: Saffie Osborne could have more reason for tears at Ascot READ MORE :

Jockeys to wear black armbands on Tuesday after death of popular ex-rider READ MORE :

“He was a horse who loved a battle and was so brave. Ruby was able to stand back anywhere on him and he’d answer. He just put his rivals into trouble. He was such a proper horse. He was awesome, one of the biggest legends ever to come through Closutton.

“I want to say my personal thanks to Leona Harman at the National Stud who does such a wonderful job looking after the Living Legends who are retired there. My thoughts are with Gail Carlisle who was Hurricane Fly’s groom throughout his days with us at Closutton and had such a wonderful relationship with him.

“I was lucky enough to visit him today just before the end and met Gail who had popped over to see him as well as she’d heard the news. It was very poignant and we were able to say our goodbyes.

‌



View 3 Images Hurricane Fly: won the Champion Hurdle twice (Image: PA)

"It's especially poignant following so shortly after the passing of his co-owner Frank Boyd and I'm thinking of his family and George Creighton's family too at this time. Hurricane Fly provided us all with so many wonderful days and memories."

The owners released a statement which read: "The Boyd and Creighton families are deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Hurricane Fly. He provided us with so many great days and long lasting memories. We would like to thank Willie Mullins, Gail Carlisle, Harold Kirk and all the staff at Closutton, as well as the National Stud who provided him with such a happy retirement."

Article continues below

View 3 Images Hurricane Fly: won five successive Irish Champion Hurdles (Image: PA)

Walsh said: “Hurricane Fly was a brilliant racehorse but was without doubt the best jumper of a hurdle I ever rode. He was incredible, his accuracy, his bravery, the speed at which he could move his feet. He was bombproof, you could ride him down to hurdles like they weren’t there because he was going to do the right thing every time.

“He had the engine to go with it. He had speed, class, he stayed and was in my eyes, for a little horse, the perfect horse.”

Sports.title: Andrew Robertson ‘feels sorry’ for Trent Alexander-Arnold amid Real Madrid issues
Sports.content:
Andrew Robertson ‘feels sorry’ for Trent Alexander-Arnold amid Real Madrid issues

Former Liverpool star Trent Alexander-Arnold has endured a tricky time since joining Real Madrid last summer and his former teammate Andrew Robertson has now spoken out

View 2 Images Andrew Robertson has leapt to Trent Alexander-Arnold's defence (Image: Getty Images)

Ex-Liverpool star Andrew Robertson has admitted he feels sorry for former teammate Trent Alexander-Arnold due to the increased level of criticism he receives. The pair struck up a brilliant partnership during their respective spells at Anfield.

‌



They were key to Liverpool claiming two Premier League titles under Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot, while they also played a role in the club’s Champions League success. Despite their glittering spell at Anfield, Alexander-Arnold faced severe criticism for defensive errors, while he has never quite managed to establish himself in the England side.

‌



And Robertson says he sympathised with his former teammate. Speaking on The Overlap, the Scottish defender said: "It's very different when you are English, compared to another nationality.

‌



“I always said to Trent, 'I will never get as much high praise as you, but I'll never get as much criticism as you.'"

‌



He added: "The way I defended at Liverpool compared to Trent was very different. I had Sadio helping me out and he was a bit more aggressive so if I missed [a tackle], he'd usually be there.

“With Mo [Salah], we didn't want him coming back towards our box. A lot of times, Trent was waiting on someone like [Jordan Henderson] to come over, so, sometimes, I started to feel sorry for him."

Alexander-Arnold has since departed Liverpool, having joined Spanish giants Real Madrid on a free transfer last summer. He has endured an inconsistent spell in La Liga so far, having started just 14 league games during his debut campaign.

‌



View 2 Images Trent Alexander-Arnold has not hit the heights expected of him at Real Madrid (Image: Getty Images)

That has continued this season, with new manager Jose Mourinho preferring Denzel Dumfries at right-back. But Robertson remains sure that Alexander-Arnold has the talent to be a success at the Bernabeu.

"I've seen him lock out [Kylian] Mbappe at PSG. In the Champions League finals, he was unbelievable," he said. "Trent is a very, very good defender… [in his] best games, he was an unbelievable one-v-one defender.

Article continues below

"Now, at times, he maybe makes mistakes. But we all do. But it's if [Trent] had this stigma around him, that he can't defend. And he's had that from a very early age. It's as if he can't shift it."

Like Alexander-Arnold, Robertson left Liverpool this summer as he joined Premier League rivals Tottenham. The 32-year-old has started all but one of his new club’s league games this season, with Roberto De Zerbi’s men currently without a win and bottom of the table.
