The very resource being mobilized to save the school is, in the meantime, occupying and potentially damaging the space that school needs to function. Residents watching this unfold are left with a daily, physical reminder of the gap between their aspirations for their children and the economic reality constraining them — a school building slowly becoming indistinguishable from a warehouse, its educational purpose paused indefinitely while it earns its keep as storage space instead.

A Town That Has Already Buried Too Much

Kpolokplah’s current struggles do not exist in isolation from its past. This is a town that carries the weight of Liberia’s civil war within its history, having been the site where several residents were killed during the 1994 massacre — one of many dark chapters etched into Bong County’s collective memory. For a community that has already endured such loss, the slow erosion of its children’s access to education represents not just a present-day crisis, but another entry in a long history of hardship that seems to have outlasted the war itself.

Residents, understandably, see the school closure as part of a broader pattern — one in which promises of post-conflict rebuilding and development have been slow to reach communities like theirs, leaving basic services like education perpetually just out of reach.

A Lawmaker’s Balancing Act

The predicament in Kpolokplah has not gone entirely unnoticed at the political level. Hon. James M. Kolleh, Representative for Bong County Electoral District 2, has publicly acknowledged the education and water challenges facing communities under his watch, responding to reports that span not just Kpolokplah but other struggling schools such as Barsee Kpangbai Public School in Blemeyea, which reportedly operates with just two teachers for its entire student body.

In Kpolokplah, there was no fallback plan, because there was no government presence to fall back on. The PTA was not merely supplementing the school’s teaching staff — it was the entire staffing infrastructure, quietly substituting for a state responsibility that never arrived. When that substitute system broke down, there was nothing behind it to catch the fall.

Rep. Kolleh’s response has focused heavily on Barsee Kpangbai, where he has pledged to work toward deploying two additional teachers, while more broadly promising to assess the needs of other schools across the district — a commitment that, for now, leaves Kpolokplah’s specific staffing vacuum without a direct answer.

He pointed to past efforts, including last year’s distribution of 5,000 armchairs to area schools, and indicated plans to expand on that furniture initiative this year. Whether

such efforts will translate into the one thing Kpolokplah actually needs — salaried government teachers — remains an open question.

On water access, another pressing concern in the district, Rep. Kolleh was more specific about Kpolokplah itself, confirming that the town is slated to benefit from ongoing water projects and promising, in the interim, to repair the community’s existing hand pump. He framed his broader approach as one of continued responsiveness to constituent needs, describing service to the district as central to his mandate as its elected representative.

Waiting for a Callback

What remains missing from this story is an official accounting from the very body responsible for staffing and overseeing public education in the county. FrontPage Africa contacted County Education Officer David Boakai, who answered the call and indicated he would follow up with a fuller response. That callback never came before publication.

In its absence, silence from the Ministry of Education’s local representative stands in stark contrast to the noise Kpolokplah’s crisis has already generated — a community publicly airing its struggle, a lawmaker publicly responding to it, and, at the center of it all, a county education office that has, for now, said nothing at all. For the children of Kpolokplah, still waiting for a return to their classrooms, that silence may prove just as costly as the unpaid wages that emptied them in the first place.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Prepares to Take Cybercrime Law Fight to Supreme Court After Wrato Release
World.content:
Monrovia-The release of political commentator Jerry Nyantee Wrato from police custody has opened a new and potentially consequential legal battle over Liberia’s recently enacted Cybercrime Law, with the Congress for Democratic Change(CDC) announcing plans to ask the Supreme Court to determine whether portions of the law are consistent with the Constitution.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Lenn Eugene Nagbe, Chief of Office Staff to former President George Manneh Weah said Tuesday, September 22 that the CDC’s Executive Committee had instructed its lawyers to institute proceedings before the Supreme Court challenging the constitutionality of the law.

Nagbe said the party’s decision goes beyond Wrato’s individual case, arguing that the controversy raises broader questions about the limits of political expression, criticism of public officials and the government’s authority to prosecute speech disseminated through digital platforms.

“It is not just about Jerry Wrato; it is about a threat to our democracy,” Nagbe said, announcing the party’s intention to challenge the law.

He said the CDC’s legal team would seek to have the Cybercrime Law declared unconstitutional, describing it as legislation that, in the party’s view, could be used to suppress political expression.

The announcement came hours after Criminal Court “B” of the First Judicial Circuit ordered Wrato released from police custody following a habeas corpus petition filed by his lawyer, Cllr. Garrison Doldeh Yealue Jr.

Judge Pape Suah issued the writ Tuesday, September 22, directing that Wrato be released from further police custody and turned over to the Sheriff of the court.

The order followed a challenge to Wrato’s continued detention after police announced that they had completed their investigation and intended to prosecute him on four alleged violations of Liberia’s Cybercrime Act of 2025.

Wrato’s detention followed the circulation of artificial intelligence-generated images and videos appearing to portray Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung in a derogatory manner.

The material surfaced amid controversy over reports concerning Koung’s security screening at Brussels Airport, reports the Vice President has denied. Police subsequently investigated the circulation of the manipulated content under the Cybercrime Act.

But the case took a different turn after Koung publicly appealed for Wrato’s release, indicating that he did not wish to pursue criminal action against him over the material. Police Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman nevertheless maintained that the matter could not be resolved solely based on the Vice President’s wishes.

In a September 21 communication to Vice President Koung, Coleman said the Liberia National Police had a statutory obligation to investigate suspected criminal conduct and had resolved to proceed against Wrato.

Police identified four alleged offenses, misuse of devices, cyberstalking, distribution of data messages that incite damage to property or violence, and distribution of harmful data messages.

The offenses were cited under Sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Cybercrime Act. Coleman stressed that forwarding Wrato to court would not amount to a finding of guilt and that the accused would retain the presumption of innocence and other constitutional protections.

CDC Challenges the Law

Nagbe, however, said the CDC considers the detention a violation of Wrato’s constitutional rights. He said the party assembled a team of lawyers to defend what it described as the right to political expression and fair treatment under the law.

“The CDC hired a team of lawyers that advocate for fair play, for freedom of political expression,” Nagbe said. According to him, the lawyers viewed Wrato’s detention from Thursday, September 17, through Tuesday, September 22, as unlawful and moved quickly to challenge it through habeas corpus proceedings. The petition relied on Article 21(f) of the 1986 Constitution and provisions of Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law governing habeas corpus.

The court subsequently ordered Wrato’s release. The case is expected to return to court on Thursday, September 24, when further proceedings are scheduled.

Where Does Political Speech End, and Cybercrime Begin?

At the heart of the emerging legal dispute is a difficult concern on how far the state can go in regulating political expression when that expression is delivered through digital platforms. Nagbe argued that Liberians have a constitutional right to criticize and even make fun of politicians, particularly those who voluntarily enter public life.

“If you do not want anyone to talk about you, don’t get in the political space,” he said.

But the police position presents a different legal question as to whether digital material that allegedly crosses into cyberstalking, incitement, harmful communications or other conduct specifically prohibited by law can be treated simply as political speech.

That question has not been finally determined in Wrato’s case. The police have maintained that their investigation is based on alleged criminal conduct rather than the political identity of the person involved. Wrato, meanwhile, remains presumed innocent unless and until a court of competent jurisdiction determines otherwise.

The habeas corpus ruling itself addresses Wrato’s detention; it does not, on its face, constitute a final judicial determination that the Cybercrime Act is unconstitutional or that the underlying allegations against him are without legal merit.

A Bigger Legal Test Ahead

The CDC’s planned Supreme Court action could therefore move the controversy beyond Wrato’s individual detention and into a broader constitutional examination of Liberia’s cybercrime framework.

Such proceedings could require the Supreme Court to examine the relationship between statutory restrictions on digital communications and constitutional guarantees relating to freedom of speech, expression and political participation.

For the CDC, Nagbe said, the objective is clear, to challenge what the party considers an unconstitutional restriction on political expression.

“We will render the Cyber Crime Law unconstitutional,” he declared. Whether the Supreme Court ultimately accepts that argument, and, if so, how it interprets the contested provisions, will depend on the legal challenge, the provisions placed before the Court and the constitutional questions the justices are asked to determine.

For now, Wrato is out of police custody, the police say prosecution remains warranted, and the CDC is preparing to take the broader constitutional fight to Liberia’s highest court. The next courtroom appearance on September 24 could provide the first indication of how the dispute over Wrato’s detention will proceed, even as a separate constitutional battle over Liberia’s Cybercrime Law begins to take shape.

World.title: Liberia: Chinese Nationals “Brutalize” Liberian Employee as Victim Alarms Over Selective Justice, Illegal Dismissal
World.content:
The accused and the victim

MONROVIA – The Ministry of Labour has launched a probe into reports of an alleged assault on a Liberian worker by two Chinese nationals in Congo Town, outside Monrovia.

By Obediah Johnson

Victim Francis Flomo was allegedly assaulted by his bosses, one Mr. Liu and another unidentified Chinese national at a local Chinese restaurant O’Cake located adjacent the Giant Gym in Congo Town, outside Monrovia.

In a detailed report submitted to the Ministry of Labour, a copy which is in the possession of Frontpage Africa, victim Francis was physically attacked and assaulted by his bosses for allegedly playing with his phone during working hours.

The report claimed that the alleged perpetrators used steel and stick to physically assault defenseless victim Francis.

Police Intervention

Following the alleged assault, police officers riding a motorbike while on their regular patrol were requested by other aggrieved employees to arrest the situation. According to the report, the LNP officers later took the victim and the accused to the Palace Police Station in Swankamore Community, Oldest Congo Town, around the SKD Boulevard Junction, outside Monrovia.

It added that while at the police station, several unidentified Chinese nationals stormed the area with another police officer. “Shortly after, the officer at the Charge of Quarters who was investigating the case allegedly changed his approach. Instead of treating Francis Flomo as a victim of assault, he charged all three persons — the two Chinese nationals AND the young Liberian Francis Flomo — for “Disorderly Conduct” and effectively threw the case out.”

The report maintained that victim Francis suffered a swollened hand as a result of the assault. It disclosed that the victim was immediately sacked by his Chinese bosses immediately after the case was threw out by the police.

It noted that the victim bosses also refused to pay his one month salary. “The central question this incident leaves is: How can two men jump on a defenseless young boy, beat him with objects, and then the victim himself is charged for disorderly conduct by the police?,” it stated.

The report divulged that the incident points to the abuse and exploitation of a Liberian employee by his foreign bosses in Liberia

It added that the situation also denies the victim the payment of his fair wage and a compromised justice system in the Liberian society.

Meanwhile, the victim is calling on government to investigate the alleged use of influence at the police station to turn a clear assault case into a disorderly conduct charge, thereby denying the victim justice.

“The family and community are now calling for a proper investigation into the matter by the Liberia National Police Professional Standards Division and the Ministry of Labour.”

Labour Inspector General Mr. John O. F. Kangbah reportedly led a team of LNP officers at the restaurant late Tuesday afternoon and requested the management to produce the accused Chinese nationals.

But the management reportedly failed to produce the accused. However, the Labour Inspector promised to shutdown the Chinese restaurant if management fails to produce the accused today Wednesday, September 23.

World.title: Liberian Contractors Urge Boakai to Expand Access to Public Works
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE— The Association of Liberian Construction Contractors is calling on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to intervene in what it describes as the growing exclusion of qualified Liberian-owned construction firms from public infrastructure projects.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

In an open letter dated September 21 and signed by its President, Kimberly K. Toure, the Association said Liberian contractors continue to face difficulties securing government contracts, despite investing heavily in registration, certification, equipment, personnel, and other requirements to remain eligible.

The Association expressed concern that public infrastructure opportunities are frequently awarded to foreign-owned companies, leaving qualified local firms with limited access to projects they have the experience and capacity to execute.

“Our members have raised concerns that opportunities are frequently awarded to foreign-owned companies, leaving capable Liberian firms with limited access to the public investment that should also contribute to the growth of domestic enterprises,” the letter stated.

The ALCC clarified that it does not oppose foreign contractors, acknowledging their capital and expertise. However, it argued that Liberia’s infrastructure development agenda should also provide meaningful opportunities for domestic companies to grow, create jobs and retain wealth within the local economy.

US$2,202.50 Just to Stay Compliant

The ALCC highlighted the financial burden Liberian contractors face to maintain legal and regulatory compliance, even when they have no active government contracts.

Citing documentation dated September 18, 2026, from a locally owned construction firm, the Association said a company must spend at least US$2,202.50 in direct registration and certification fees alone.

The breakdown includes US$50 for a Liberia Business Registry business certificate, US$150 for Articles of Incorporation, US$1,400 for Ministry of Public Works CCCS certificates, US$102.50 for a NASSCORP certificate, and US$500 for Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) vendor registration.

The Association noted that these expenses exclude transportation, office maintenance, staff salaries, equipment acquisition and maintenance, bid preparation, and site visits.

Such costs, it said, place a significant burden on small and medium-sized Liberian firms that must maintain compliance while waiting for contract opportunities.

“These investments are made by Liberian entrepreneurs before they can benefit from any government contract. Yet compliance alone does not guarantee access to work,” the letter stated.

Wider Economic Impact

The ALCC warned that limiting local contractors’ access to public infrastructure projects could have consequences extending beyond individual businesses.

Construction companies, the Association noted, support a broad network of professionals and workers, including engineers, architects, surveyors, masons, carpenters, electricians, plumbers and equipment operators.

They also generate business for building-material suppliers, transport operators, workshops, food vendors and other small enterprises.

“When local contractors collapse, workers lose income, suppliers lose customers, families struggle to pay school fees and rent, and government loses revenue from reduced formal employment,” the letter warned.

The Association further cautioned that without reasonable access to contracts, experienced local companies could lose skilled employees and equipment, creating a cycle in which they are considered too small for major projects while being denied the opportunities needed to expand.

ALCC Outlines Requests to Boakai

To address the concerns, the Association outlined several measures it wants the Boakai administration to consider, including full implementation of domestic preference and reservation measures when Liberian companies submit competitive bids, transparent review of Liberian firms’ participation and success rates in public procurement, procurement requirements proportionate to project size, including dividing large projects into manageable lots, and greater transparency through accessible procurement plans, evaluation criteria and contract award notices.

The Association called for access to financing and timely payment for certified work, including through engagement with commercial banks, properly structured joint ventures with clearly defined responsibilities and genuine skills transfer to Liberian partners.

The ALCC also requested a high-level meeting involving the Office of the President, the Ministry of Public Works, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, the PPCC and the Association to develop a practical action plan.

“The nationality of a company should neither substitute for evidence of competence nor become a barrier to a qualified Liberian company’s participation,” Toure emphasized.

“Our central appeal is that Liberian firms with proven ability should have a fair and meaningful place in building their own country.”

The Association reaffirmed its commitment to high standards, competitive procurement, quality construction and accountability, expressing readiness to work with the government to improve performance and transparency in Liberia’s construction sector.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Launches Third Women, Peace and Security Plan, Pledges Greater Role for Women in Peacebuilding
World.content:
New York, USA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has launched Liberia’s Third National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security (NAP III), reaffirming his administration’s commitment to expanding women’s participation in peacebuilding, governance and national security.

By J.H. Webster Clayeh, [email protected]

President Boakai made the declaration Monday, September 21, at a High-Level Event on Women, Peace and Security held at the United Nations Headquarters in New York.

Speaking before diplomats, international partners and representatives of women’s organizations, President Boakai said Liberia’s experience demonstrates that women are not simply participants in peace processes but key architects of peace.

“We have a saying in Liberia, that, ‘Men make the big decisions while women make the small decisions. But it is the women who decide which decisions are big and which decisions are small,’” President Boakai said.

He also extended greetings to women participating in the event from Monrovia, including women gathered at the Peace Hut in Fish Market. The President said the history of Liberia’s civil war cannot be told without recognizing the courage and determination of Liberian women, who played a critical role in bringing an end to the conflict.

“The story of the end of Liberia’s civil war cannot be told without recognizing the courage and determination of Liberian women,” he said.

According to President Boakai, Liberia’s peace was not achieved solely through negotiations at the peace table in Accra, but was also driven by women who mobilized in markets, churches, mosques, streets and communities across Monrovia.

“Our war did not end only at the negotiating table in Accra. Peace was driven from the markets, churches, mosques, streets, and communities of Monrovia, where women refused to be silent and refused to leave until leaders listened,” he said.

He cited the contributions of the Women in Peacebuilding Network, the Liberian Mass Action for Peace, market women, and Muslim and Christian women who mobilized across religious, ethnic and political divisions.

“They were not invited to the peace processes; they made themselves impossible to exclude,” Boakai declared.

NAP III Builds on Previous Plans

President Boakai recalled that Liberia became the first post-conflict country in the world to adopt a National Action Plan for the implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 on Women, Peace and Security.

He said Liberia subsequently implemented a second National Action Plan and has now introduced its third iteration.

“Since then, we have implemented a second NAP, and today we present the third iteration of that commitment: NAP III,” he said.

The President acknowledged that Liberia encountered challenges and made mistakes during the implementation of previous plans, saying those experiences informed the development of the new action plan.

“Because of those experiences, NAP III is our answer not only to what worked but also to what did not,” he said.

The new plan, according to President Boakai, is organized around five areas of action and aligned with his administration’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development.

The five areas are prevention; protection and access to justice; participation; relief, recovery and resilience; and coordination, accountability and financing.

Focus on Prevention and Justice

On prevention, President Boakai said Liberia would focus on addressing the underlying causes of conflict rather than merely responding to its consequences.

“Prevention means investing in social cohesion, addressing inequality, challenging harmful norms, strengthening early-warning mechanisms, and ensuring that women are at the center of efforts to prevent violence before it escalates,” he said.

On protection and access to justice, President Boakai pointed to Executive Order 131 of 2024, which established the Office to operationalize the War and Economic Crimes Court.

He said transitional justice remains essential for women who survived conflict-related violence. “For women who survived conflict-related violence, transitional justice is essential to accountability and closure,” he said.

President Boakai also credited women advocates and civil society organizations for their role in advancing statutes that prioritize gender-sensitive justice through the establishment of the Office of the War and Economic Crimes Court.

He said the framework addresses conflict-related sexual violence and gender-based atrocities committed during Liberia’s civil wars. Boakai Seeks Greater Female Representation in Armed Forces

On participation, President Boakai said sustainable peace cannot be achieved if women remain victims of conflict while being excluded from decision-making.

“Peace cannot be sustainable when women are present as victims but absent from decision-making,” he said.

The President said his administration is committed to increasing women’s representation in elected and appointed positions and ensuring their meaningful participation in peace and security decision-making.

He also highlighted efforts to increase female participation in the Armed Forces of Liberia.

In February 2026, the AFL, in partnership with UN Women Liberia, launched a two-year Elsie Initiative Fund project aimed at removing institutional barriers, strengthening the recruitment and retention of women, and expanding opportunities for women to serve in leadership and United Nations peacekeeping roles, where applicable.

“Our immediate ambition is to reach 15 percent female representation in the Armed Forces by 2028, while contributing to our broader national goal of 40 percent by 2030,” Boakai said.

He added that Liberia, as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, must demonstrate domestically the same commitment it advocates internationally. “Now, we must ensure they have the opportunity, authority, and institutional support to lead,” he said.

New Threats to Peace

President Boakai said NAP III also recognizes that threats to peace and security extend beyond Liberia’s past civil wars.

He cited climate pressures, democratic reversals, violent extremism, transnational crime, displacement, economic insecurity and other forms of violence as emerging challenges with significant implications for women and girls.

“For women and girls, these challenges can further deepen existing vulnerabilities and inequalities,” he said.

Boakai said the new action plan is therefore designed not only to address the legacy of Liberia’s civil war but also present and future threats.

“Our approach to recovery must go beyond rebuilding infrastructure. It must also rebuild livelihoods, restore dignity, strengthen institutions, and ensure that women and girls are not left behind,” he said.

Liberia’s Security Council Presidency

The President said Liberia’s current position on the United Nations Security Council presents an opportunity for the country to make Women, Peace and Security a signature priority.

Liberia, he noted, spent fourteen years on the UN Security Council agenda before becoming a member of the Council and preparing to assume its presidency in December.

“This moment is significant for another reason. Liberia’s journey from being on the UN Security Council agenda for fourteen years to now sitting at the Council table and assuming its Presidency in December presents an important opportunity for the country to make Women, Peace and Security a signature priority,” he said.

Boakai said Liberia intends to draw on its own peacebuilding experience, particularly the Peace Hut model, as part of its contribution to the global Women, Peace and Security agenda.

“Drawing on Liberia’s peacebuilding experience and women’s leadership through initiatives such as Peace Huts, Liberia offers evidence of localization, with the Peace Hut model as our contribution to the global Women, Peace and Security toolkit,” he said.

He also pointed to challenges facing the West African sub-region, including democratic reversals, transnational crime, insecurity and contested borders.

Liberia, he said, will advocate for preventive diplomacy and locally led solutions before crises escalate into conflicts requiring reactive intervention.

‘A Seat Is an Opportunity, Not an Achievement’

President Boakai recalled Liberia’s commitment, when seeking a seat on the Security Council, to bring the voices of women and young people into

the chamber, particularly those involved in peacebuilding within their communities.

“As a member of the Security Council, we intend to arrive at the annual Women, Peace and Security Open Debate having done at home what we ask of others internationally,” he said.

He stressed that Liberia’s presence on the Council should be measured by what the country does with the opportunity.

“A seat is an opportunity, not an achievement. What we do with it is the achievement,” Boakai declared.

According to the President, NAP III represents the domestic component of that commitment at a time when financing for peacebuilding is declining globally.

He said Liberia recognizes that it cannot implement the plan alone and will seek support from international partners, while emphasizing that the country must demonstrate political ownership. “We have learned an important lesson that a plan that depends entirely on the priorities of others is not truly a national plan,” he said.

“While we recognize that Liberia cannot do this alone, and seek support to implement the NAP III, we are committed to demonstrating the highest level of political will to own it,” he added.

‘Women Changed the Course of Our Nation’

President Boakai said Liberia’s ultimate responsibility is to ensure that future generations inherit not only the memory of the peace fought for by women but also the institutions, opportunities and freedoms needed to sustain that peace.

“Our task now is to ensure that the next generation inherits not only the memory of the peace women fought for, but also the institutions, opportunities, and freedoms that make that peace enduring,” he said.

He thanked Liberia’s international partners for supporting the country and recognizing the role of Liberian women in building and sustaining peace.

Addressing women gathered at the Fish Market Peace Hut, President Boakai said their contribution had permanently shaped Liberia’s history. “To the mothers at the Fish Market who joined us today, your courage changed the course of our nation. Today, we carry that courage forward,” he said.

He said NAP III represents a commitment to creating a Liberia where women and girls can live safely, participate fully in national affairs and exercise leadership. “That is the promise of this Third National Action Plan—to build a Liberia where every woman and girl can live safely, participate fully, lead with dignity, and help shape our country’s future,” President Boakai said.

He subsequently formally launched Liberia’s Third National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security.

World.title: Liberia: Court-Ordered Eviction Forces More Than Me Students Out of Class Amid Heavy Rain
World.content:
MONROVIA — Rain and tears marked a chaotic morning at More Than Me Academy on Tuesday as a court-ordered eviction forced hundreds of students out of their classrooms at the all-girls school on Ashmun Street in central Monrovia.

By J.H. Webster Clayeh, [email protected]

The eviction came amid a heavy downpour, disrupting classes as students were reportedly ordered to gather their books and leave the premises shortly after arriving for the school day.

Teachers had not yet begun classes, while students had little time to collect their belongings before being forced to vacate the building. The development is the latest turn in a long-running legal dispute over ownership of the property, which has been occupied by More Than Me Academy for years.

A court sheriff reportedly arrived at the school with an order directing the institution to vacate the premises. Police subsequently barricaded the entrance, preventing students from re-entering the building as the eviction exercise unfolded.

The property is claimed by the Montgomery family, which says it has been denied access to the premises for more than 15 years.

Speaking on behalf of the family, Erica Davis said the family recently obtained a favorable ruling from the Supreme Court, which it believes paved the way for enforcement of the court’s decision.

Davis described the eviction as the culmination of a legal battle that the family had pursued for more than a decade.

“I told them that they suppose to move. I got my documentation. It has been 15 years on this case. They got to go today and we are not going to be nice to them and say let’s talk about it later, no, we gave them time, we gave them 15 years to talk but they called me crazy woman, she is not the property owner. And so, we are not sorry for them l, they need to go,” the Montgomery family spokesperson says.

Davis further questioned why students were present at the property despite the ongoing legal dispute.

“Let the children go home, they can’t use the children of Liberia. Why they had the children out here when they know they are going through court issues.”

School Blames Government

The school’s administration, however, said it does not blame the Montgomery family for the eviction, instead accusing the Liberian government of failing to adequately communicate the status and outcome of the legal proceedings.

According to officials of the school, More Than Me Academy had been occupying the premises under government instruction and expected government officials to keep the institution informed as the legal case progressed.

School authorities said they received no subsequent information about the status of the case, describing the sudden eviction as a betrayal and arguing that the government’s responsibility should have included protecting the interests of students whose education has now been disrupted.

“We do not blame the Montgomery family, but the government failed us,” an official of the school said.

The school said it was particularly disappointed that it was not informed whether the government had prevailed or lost the case, arguing that either outcome should have been communicated to the institution before enforcement of the ruling reached its doors.

With the academic year already underway, the eviction has left hundreds of students without access to their classrooms.

School administrators are now reportedly exploring alternative arrangements to ensure that students can continue their education.

The institution is also said to be attempting to negotiate with the private property owners in the hope of finding a temporary or long-term arrangement that would allow classes to continue and prevent students from losing additional instructional time.

World.title: Congolese Traditional Leader Mfumu Nkusu Nangola Calls for Greater African Unity, Heritage, Cultural Identity During Liberia Outreach Mission
World.content:
R2 Community, Paynesville City-R2 Community, Paynesville City Congolese traditional spiritual leader Mfumu Nkusu Kiambu Nzalampanda Nangola has called for greater African unity, cultural awareness, and self-reliance, saying Africans must reconnect with their ancestral roots and take a leading role in shaping the continent’s future.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

Nangola serves as the Spiritual Chief of the traditional African religious movement known as Vuvamu (full name: Vutuka Vana Mpambu Uvidila), which roughly translates to “returning to the roots” or “the original path”.

The Vuvamu, unlike Western-style churches, this movement aims to preserve traditional African customs, ancestral worship, and indigenous knowledge, where they operate as a strict traditional revivalist movement.

The Vuvamu movement is rooted in the spiritual legacy of Simon Kimbangu, who is revered by its followers as the ultimate prophet and spiritual savior of Africa.

Kimbangu was arrested by Belgian colonial authorities in 1921 and later died in prison in 1951. Leadership of the core Kimbanguist movement passed directly to his immediate family before Nangola, who is leading a 13-member delegation from the DR. Congo on a two-week outreach mission in Liberia to assume the leadership.

The delegation was invited by the Liberia Independent Elders Council for Peace and Reconciliation to engage government institutions, youth organizations, academics, women’s groups, and community stakeholders on issues affecting Africa’s development.

Speaking through his interpreter, Liongo Sanza, Nangola said the primary purpose of the visit is to rebuild the connection between Africans and their traditional heritage.

“So, how to explain his mission here in Liberia is first of all to recreate the connection with the people of Liberia and the African religion,” Sanza said on behalf of Nangola. “So as we have two weeks here, this whole time will be dedicated to this mission, to the reconnection.”

The Congolese leader said the mission seeks to encourage Africans, particularly young people, to take responsibility for their future and rediscover their identity and purpose.

“The objective of this mission, of these two weeks, is that at the end of this mission, black people have to understand that in the period that we are in, black people have to work, to use themselves, to use their brain, to use their hands, to come back, to be the people that they are supposed to be,” he said.

Nangola said Africans must gain a deeper understanding of their history, culture, and place in the world to become active participants in Africa’s transformation.

“Black people have to understand how the world works, actually, the creation of the world. You have to know it, to understand it, so he can no longer be just a passenger, but an actor inside of the evolution of the world, inside of the evolution of Africa,” he said.

According to the delegation leader, the message being shared in Liberia centers on self-determination, self-sufficiency, and independence in key sectors needed for Africa’s advancement.

“What Liberian youth could get from this message is actually self-determination, self-sufficiency, and spiritual, economic, and technological independence,” he said.

Nangola said Africa stands at a critical moment in its history because of the continent’s natural wealth and strategic importance. He urged young Africans to position themselves as leaders capable of managing the continent’s future.

“Africa is at a turning point, because Africa is the continent that all the races are actually fighting for,” he said. “If we, as young black people, don’t fight to become the leaders of Africa, we are risking coming again and being slaves.”

The traditional leader also spoke about African identity, arguing that colonial-era boundaries should not prevent Africans from recognizing their common heritage and shared destiny.

“If we call ourselves Liberian, Congolese, or all of the names that we can have, it’s because of the Berlin Conference,” he said. “Before that, there was no country, actually, in Africa.”

While promoting traditional African beliefs, Nangola said his message is not intended to exclude people based on religion and that the delegation is open to engagement with people of different faiths.

“We don’t care of you are Christian, you are Muslim, or what, because we want to talk to the black people,” he said. “Christians say that they believe in God. Muslims say that they believe in God. We too, we believe in God, so why not unite him?”

Responding to questions about why the mission focuses primarily on Black communities, Nangola used the example of repairing a vehicle engine to explain what he described as the need to address the most pressing challenges first.

“If you look at a car engine, and you want to repair it, and maybe you have four inductors, and one inductor is not working properly, you will not try to repair the three inductors that are working properly,” he said. “You will try to repair the inductor that is not working properly.”

He added: “In this time, in this era that we are in, black people are the inductor, the one that is not working properly. So if you want to repair the world, you have to start with the inductor that is not working properly.”

The delegation’s visit received the backing of the Liberia Independent Elders Council for Peace and Reconciliation, which said it reviewed the group’s objectives before extending an invitation to Liberia.

Chairman Elder Samuel O. Philips said the council found that the delegation’s message focuses on African unity, peace, and cooperation.

“I went and checked his profile, you know, what he can do, who are they?” Philips said. “The whole topic, the whole thing is black unity.”

Philips said Africa’s abundant natural resources make unity among Africans increasingly important, arguing that divisions on the continent often benefit outside interests.

“Because we have all the minerals, all the resources in Africa,” he said. “They don’t want us to be united, because if we are united, we’ll be controlling our own resources.”

The council chairman also stressed that the delegation’s outreach was not aimed at creating religious division but rather encouraging dialogue and peaceful coexistence.

“I think you heard him; he did not talk anything about separation in religion,” Philips said. “If he had said, ‘I don’t trust God, I don’t love God, I don’t believe in peace,’ the council was not going to invite them.”

Philips said the delegation will spend about two weeks meeting students, educators, women’s groups, youth organizations, traditional leaders, and other stakeholders across Liberia as part of efforts to promote discussions on African culture, identity, education, and development. “So they are here with us for 15 days,” he said.

According to the delegation, planned activities during the visit include meetings with Ministry of Education officials, university professors, students, youth groups, and women’s organizations.

A panel discussion will also be held to explore issues relating to African unity, traditional education, cultural preservation, youth participation, women’s empowerment, and the future development of the continent.

The delegation says it hopes the visit will encourage more Africans to embrace their cultural heritage while promoting dialogue on how traditional knowledge and values can contribute to the development of modern African societies.

World.title: Mushimba Warns Against Removing Presidential Term Limits
World.content:
Organised People’s Party (OPP) president Dr Brian Mushimba has opposed calls to remove presidential term limits. He warned that such a constitutional change would weaken democratic safeguards and undermine peaceful succession. In a statement, he said the party was concerned about remarks from individuals aligned to those in power who are advocating the removal of the limits.

He said term limits guard against political power gathering in the hands of one individual, one party or one generation. “Presidential term limits are not an obstacle to democracy. They are one of democracy’s most important safeguards,” Dr Mushimba said.

The OPP leader said the presidency carries wide powers and commands vast resources, which is why it must remain subject to accountability and regular succession. He cautioned against any attempt to amend the Constitution to suit the interests of those holding public office. “Constitutions are not written for individuals; they are written to protect future generations,” he said.

He also answered leaders who say they need more time to complete their programmes. Such leaders should strengthen institutions and raise a new generation able to carry national programmes forward, he said. “If two terms are not enough to deliver your vision for Zambia, the answer is not to abolish the limits.”

The party also rejects proposals to extend presidential terms or scrap the 50-plus-one electoral threshold. “We therefore say ‘no’ to any selfish proposals on constitutional amendments,” Dr Mushimba said. He urged Zambians to resist any unconstitutional attempt to remove the safeguards, which he said protect the country’s democracy, peace and unity.

“These constitutional safeguards must not be removed at all,” he said. The statement did not name the individuals behind the calls, nor did it say where or when the proposals were made.

The warning arrives in the opening weeks of the 2026 to 2031 term. President Hakainde Hichilema was re-elected in August, and his Government has made economic growth the core of its second-term agenda. The Constitution has already been amended once in this cycle. The 2025 amendment, known as Bill 7, created 40 proportional representation seats for women, youth and persons with disabilities, and those members took their seats in the National Assembly this week.

Christopher Mundia, State House Special Assistant to the President for Legal Affairs, said the start of the new legislative sitting and Executive tenures marked an important chapter in the country’s democratic life. “The legacy of Bill 7 will forever be entrenched in our rich history as a country,” Mr Mundia said.

The two-term limit and the 50-plus-one threshold both remain in the Constitution. The OPP has put on record that it will oppose any attempt to change either.

World.title: Prison Gate Shut On Visitors To Mundubile, Makebi Zulu
World.content:
Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility in Kabwe has barred visitors from seeing detained opposition leaders Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others. Prison officers now require written clearance from Zambia Correctional Service (ZCS) headquarters in Lusaka before anyone is let through the gate.

The new rule turned back a delegation led by former local government minister Dr Charles Banda. He arrived with former minister Moses Mawere and found opposition leader Cosmo Mumba and other prominent figures already waiting outside. The detained leaders face treason and sedition charges.

Dr Banda said he was stopped after handing over his identification.

“After presenting my ID, they asked if I had gotten written permission from HQ. I was shocked,” he said.

“I was referred to an assistant superintendent who confirmed the fresh instructions, saying anyone intending to visit the treason and sedition charged leaders must first get authorisation from Lusaka.”

The former Kapoche member of Parliament said the requirement was new. He had recently visited Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu without any letter of authorisation from Lusaka.

Most of the people turned away were women who had travelled long distances. Dr Banda said they raised their voices in anger at the gate and he stepped in to calm the situation.

“I’m very hurt. It was embarrassing in front of many people at the prison gate,” he said.

“The law allows senior citizens to visit inmates to check how they are coping, encourage and pray with them. I shouldn’t be treated like this in my own country.”

Dr Banda called the charges against the opposition leaders unfair and appealed for political tolerance.

Sakwiba Sikota, the lawyer representing the detainees, condemned the restriction as discriminatory and unconstitutional. He said no other inmates at the facility faced the condition.

“This is terribly unfair. All other inmates are visited without restrictions. The Constitution allows all inmates to be visited by relatives and friends without any form of discrimination,” Mr Sikota said.

He connected the order to concerns the European Union had already raised about the detentions. He said the new rule placed an unreasonable burden on families and supporters travelling from other provinces.

“These are concerns raised by the EU in its resolutions, but instead of addressing them they are coming up with more draconian issues,” he said.

“So, if someone is coming from Luapula, they must bypass Kabwe, come to Lusaka, book a hotel whilst waiting for permission and then travel back to Kabwe. It is absolutely ridiculous.”

Mr Sikota accused the State of stalling the court proceedings for lack of evidence. He said the Director of Public Prosecutions was on record saying investigations were still going on.

“This is wrong and is why the EU and international law bodies have raised the flag,” he said.He asked the State to reconsider the restriction and allow justice to prevail.

ZCS head of public relations Cornelius Mwanza said the service would comment after a meeting.

Mr Zulu’s detention is also being tested in a separate courtroom. There, the question is whether a jailed advocate can go on defending a client.

Chisanga Chanda was aide-de-camp to the late former President Edgar Lungu, and his defence has asked the court to let Mr Zulu keep representing him and cross-examining a prosecution witness. The defence argues that imprisonment does not end Mr Zulu’s professional obligations as counsel. Mr Zulu is being held at Mukobeko in connection with a separate matter.

The application was made in chambers after the trial could not go ahead. State witness Maxwell Timba, commissioner of police in charge of the Criminal Investigations Department, was unavailable, and State advocate Frank Sikazwe applied for an adjournment.

Defence lawyer Charles Changano asked Judge Ruth Chibbabbuka to order the State to let Mr Zulu keep appearing for Mr Chanda and cross-examine the witness now on the stand.

Mr Changano argued that Mr Zulu was still a lawyer and that detention did not automatically strip him of his professional responsibilities. He said Mr Zulu, who was Mr Mundubile’s running mate in the August election, remained innocent until proven guilty.

The defence relied on the Supreme Court decision in Shamwana and 7 Others v The People (1985). It argued the case showed that an accused person could take part in proceedings and cross-examine prosecution witnesses, so criminal proceedings did not necessarily stop an advocate from carrying out professional duties.

The State opposed the application. It argued the Shamwana case was different because Mr Shamwana was an accused person in the same proceedings he was taking part in, which is not Mr Zulu’s position in the Chanda trial.

Judge Chibbabbuka reserved her ruling on the application to October. The main case has been adjourned to 23 November for the trial to continue.

World.title: “Our Diplomacy Must Help To Grow Zambia,” Haimbe Tells New York
World.content:
Foreign Affairs and International Co-operation Minister Mulambo Haimbe signed joint communiqués establishing diplomatic relations with Uruguay and Vanuatu in New York. The signings opened Zambia’s campaign at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81), where the delegation is working to turn foreign relations into new markets, investment and partnerships under the Grow Zambia agenda.

Mr Haimbe is representing President Hakainde Hichilema at the Assembly. His delegation includes Health Minister Roma Chilengi and Permanent Secretary for International Relations and Co-operation Etambuyu Gundersen. This year’s proceedings opened under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.”

The minister said Zambia’s diplomacy had to serve the country’s development priorities.

“Our diplomacy must help to grow Zambia,” Mr Haimbe said. “New diplomatic relationships mean new markets for our farmers, new partners for our investment drive and new friends for Zambia in the institutions that shape the global economy.”

New York is the first major diplomatic outing since the Head of State’s re-election in August. Government has made economic growth the core of its second-term programme. Namatama Njekwa, first secretary for press and public relations at Zambia’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations, said in a statement that the delegation’s work was focused on financing for development, investment, trade and partnerships that support economic growth.

Under the communiqué signed on Monday, Zambia and Uruguay will explore co-operation in agriculture and livestock, trade and investment. The two countries will also pursue economic, social, cultural and people-to-people exchanges.

The agreement with Vanuatu covers climate change adaptation, agriculture, eco-tourism and people-to-people exchanges. It gives Lusaka its first formal diplomatic link with the Pacific island state.

Mr Haimbe also held talks with Malawi’s Foreign Affairs Minister George Chaponda. The two sides agreed to explore closer co-operation in trade, investment, infrastructure, energy and connectivity.

Malawi’s interest in the Lobito Development Corridor came up in the discussions. The neighbours agreed to convene their Joint Permanent Commission of Co-operation in Malawi. Zambia also thanked Lilongwe for leading the SADC Election Observation Mission that monitored the August polls.

In a separate meeting, Mr Haimbe and Cuba’s Foreign Affairs Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla reaffirmed the long-standing friendship and solidarity between Lusaka and Havana. The Foreign Affairs Minister thanked Cuba for its support to Zambia’s health and education sectors. Both sides committed to keep co-ordinating at the United Nations and on other multilateral platforms.

Zambia used its meetings with Uruguay, Vanuatu, Malawi and Cuba to seek support for its bid for a seat on the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027 to 2029 term.

Lusaka and Havana also exchanged support for each other’s candidatures for the 2028 to 2030 period and for the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions.

Zambia’s top diplomat paid a courtesy call on UN Under-Secretary-General and Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide Professor Chaloka Beyani. They discussed the rule of law, human rights, misinformation and the importance of regional early warning mechanisms.

He then met Assistant Secretary-General for Development Coordination Oscar Fernández-Taranco. Their talks covered Zambia’s co-operation with the UN development system and the strengthening of the resident coordinator system.

On the margins of the Assembly, Mr Haimbe joined Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey at the 74th Extraordinary Meeting of the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group.

Professor Chilengi worked on the human capital side of the growth agenda. At a high-level World Food Programme (WFP) meeting titled School Meals for Future Leaders: Accelerating Progress, he presented Zambia’s school feeding programme as an investment in the workforce the economy will need.

“School meals are the bedrock of this human capital development,” Professor Chilengi said.

“By ensuring adequate nutrition, improving cognitive development, and keeping children, especially girls, in the classroom, we are actively shaping a highly capable workforce ready to drive Zambia’s future economic transformation.”

The programme now reaches more than 4.6 million learners in over 8,000 schools across the country. Government aims to extend it to 5.6 million learners by the end of 2026, with an ultimate target of 6.6 million children.

Zambia kept and expanded the programme through the severe El Niño-induced drought. The National Drought Response Plan made school meals a core intervention, and an additional 2.2 million children were reached across 36 drought-stricken districts.

The minister said Government had tied the programme to local economic development by decentralising procurement and buying directly from farmer co-operatives. He said the approach had given smallholder farmers stable markets and regular incomes while putting capital into rural communities.

Professor Chilengi also attended the launch of the report of the Accra Reset High-Level Panel on Reform of the Global Health Architecture and Governance. The report proposes reforms that strengthen countries’ own priorities and capabilities rather than requiring them to organise around separate institutions and funding streams.

Beyond bilateral talks, the delegation met United Nations officials on development co-ordination and the strengthening of regional early warning systems.

Zambia was due to co-host a follow-up meeting on the Sevilla Commitment on Wednesday. Further bilateral engagements on investment, energy and infrastructure are lined up for the rest of the week. Mr Haimbe will deliver Zambia’s national statement to the General Assembly on Monday, 28 September, setting out the country’s priorities and its position on the key issues before the international community.

World.title: Kawambwa bar owners warned against under age patrons
World.content:
Kawambwa Town Council has issued a final warning to bar and nightclub owners against admitting persons under the age of 18 into their premises.

Council Secretary, George Biemba emphasised that allowing underage patrons into bars and nightclubs is prohibited under the Liquor Licensing Act No. 20 of 2011.

Mr Biemba noted that despite an earlier warning issued in February this year, some establishments in the district have continued to entertain minors.

“We are reminding all licensed premises that the law forbids admitting persons below 18 years, selling or supplying them with liquor, or permitting them to consume alcohol on the premises. This is a final warning and all should comply,” MrBiemba said.

Mr Biemba said bar and nightclub owners found violating the law risk facing fines, prosecution, and closure of their businesses.

He urged all operators to strictly comply with the law, stressing that the stated penalties will be enforced without further delay by the local authority.

The Council has since called on liquor-licensed premises to cooperate with the local authority and ensure that underage persons are not allowed to access or consume alcohol.

The warning by the local authority comes in the wake of a surge in the number of underage persons patronizing bars and nightclubs in the district.

World.title: ZRA calls integrity in tax administration
World.content:
The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) has called for collective responsibility from stakeholders in Nakonde District in Muchinga Province in ensuring integrity in tax administration within the trading ecosystem.

Nakonde ZRA Station Manager, David Mungela, said integrity is tested when financial interests and pressure come into play.

Mr Mungela was speaking during an ethics engagement meeting with the business community held at Izukanji Lodge in Nakonde district.

The meeting was held in collaboration with the Anti-Corruption Commission.

Mr Mungela stated that ZRA has adopted an outward looking approach to its integrity agenda by engaging beyond its officers to include taxpayers and other players.

“Corruption, smuggling and fraud do not only affect ZRA, they increase the cost of doing business and undermine resources meant for national development,” he said.

Meanwhile, Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Corruption Prevention Officer, Chindika Mtonga, said corruption disproportionately affects the vulnerable in society.

Mr Mtonga noted that while institutions such as ZRA, the Drug Enforcement Commission and Zambia Police support the Commission in fighting the vice, citizen participation remains critical.

“Citizens must join the fight against corruption because without your involvement our efforts will be in vain,” he said.

And speaking during the same meeting, Nakonde Chamber of Commerce and Industry President, Thomas Botha called for enhanced collaboration between ZRA and the ACC to curb corrupt practices.

Mr Botha further commended ZRA for simplifying the process of acquiring a Taxpayer Identification Number (TPIN).

“We need to collaborate more to reduce corrupt practices and we commend ZRA for automating the issuance of TPINs,” Mr Botha said.

World.title: Hichilema underscores the importance of diplomatic ties
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says diplomacy is a critical tool in achieving the Grow Zambia Agenda, as it nurtures mutually beneficial relations for countries.

President Hichilema has underscored Zambia’s focus on growth in his second term, noting that diplomatic relationships are critical for mutually beneficial economic development.

The Head of State said this in a speech read for him by Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe at the United Nations General Assembly, in New York.

“Diplomatic relations mean new markets for our farmers, new partners for our investment drive and new friends for Zambia in the institutions that shape the global economy,’’ he stressed.

This is contained a statement issued to the media in Lusaka by First Secretary for Press at the Permanent Mission of Zambia to the UN, Namatama Njekwa, Zambia signed Joint Communiqués with Uruguay and Vanuatu.

Ms Njekwa revealed that the agreements open avenues for cooperation in agriculture, livestock, climate change adaptation, eco-tourism, trade, and investment.

She stated that Zambia also held talks with Malawi, agreeing to enhance collaboration in trade, energy, infrastructure, and connectivity, including Malawi’s interest in the Lobito Development Corridor.

Ms Njekwa further indicated that Zambia also held talks with Cuba where the two countries reaffirmed their longstanding friendship and solidarity, pledging continued cooperation in health, education, and multilateral coordination.

She added that Zambia also exchanged support with Cuba for respective candidatures to the UN Human Rights Council and other committees.

Ms Njekwa revealed that the Zambian delegates further engaged UN officials, focusing on rule of law, human rights, misinformation, and the country’s cooperation with the UN development system.

She however stated that Minister of Health, Roma Chilengi participated in the launch of the Accra Reset High-Level Panel report on reforming global health governance, which aligns with Zambia’s principle of strengthening national priorities through international cooperation.

Ms Njekwa further disclosed that Zambia will co-host the follow-up meeting on the Sevilla Commitment on Wednesday, with additional bilateral engagements on investment, energy, and infrastructure scheduled throughout the week.

The Assembly is convened under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”

World.title: Masebo cautions the public against fake social media messages
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) Senior Management Committee Member and Former Minister of Lands , Sylvia Masebo has urged Zambians to ignore social media messages allegedly aimed at promoting hatred and division by individuals who want to destroy the good name of the country.

Ms Masebo has cautioned the public that social media is heavily laden with falsehoods, disinformation, and manipulated content targeting the UPND members especially former cabinet Ministers.

She has noted that all online content or insinuations tagging her name are all fake, adding that she has never given an interview to any media platform, individual journalist or blogger since the August 13 , 2026 general elections.

Ms Masebo who is an entrepreneur and politician who has served in various portfolios said this during a media engagement in Lusaka today.

“All they want is to create division between the President and his former Ministers like myself and others which will never work.

Masebo has pledged deep loyalty to President Hichilema, stating that she will remain committed to the UPND regardless of electoral losses or results of her petition in court.

“President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration has stabilised Zambia’s macroeconomic environment and all the constitutional laws that have been made by this government. I was part of them so I am still in the government, I am in the senior management committee of the party;” she said.

“Zambia must remain under the leadership of President Hichilema as the country is on a stable path of economic recovery and democratic governance, the country is in safe hands under President Hichilema,” she said.

She further denied social media reports claiming that she called the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) a corrupt institution, saying that she fully respects the constitutional mandate of the commission as an independent body managing national elections.

Ms Masebo stressed that taking a petition to court is her constitutional right and not undermining the ECZ.

“I took the matter to court because I was aggrieved by how I was maligned by my competitor, how I was defamed by one competitor which is my constitutional right and I have no issues with the ECZ,” she stated.

She further revealed that attempts to divide UPND party members by enemies of the government should be ignored.

Ms Masebo stressed that following the August 2026 general elections, quite a number of parliamentary election petitions have been lodged at the high court by various losing candidates, saying that she is not the only one who has petitioned her opponent.

World.title: Govt. launches of Transformative Sustainable Food Systems programme
World.content:
Government has called for stronger coordination among sectors and institutions in addressing Zambia’s food security and nutrition challenges.

Permanent Secretary for Administration in the Office of the Vice President, Lillian Kapusana, says the challenges affecting food systems are interconnected and require a coordinated, systems-based approach rather than isolated interventions by individual institutions.

Ms Kapusana was speaking today at the official launch of the US$500,000 two year Technical Cooperation Programme, on Catalysing Transformative and Sustainable Food Systems in Zambia, supported by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations.

She said the programme provides an opportunity to bring institutions together around a common food systems agenda and shared results, saying the initiative would also support the review of nutrition coordination guidelines and Zambia’s food systems pathways developed in 2021.

Ms Kapusana said the two year programme will support government and FAO in catalysing practical and institutional changes aimed at improving nutrition outcomes and strengthening the resilience of Zambia’s food systems.

She further said the project will focus on strengthening food systems coordination and governance, as well as promoting sustainable production, markets and consumption, surveillance and compliance mechanisms.

Ms Kapusana said the project will be implemented in Solwezi and Zambezi districts of North-Western Province, targeting vulnerable farming households and building the capacity of agriculture and nutrition extension workers.

She said combining targeted local implementation with national systems strengthening would allow lessons from the pilot activities to inform policy, guide future investments and support scaling up of successful interventions.

Ms Kapusana observed that Zambia has made progress in agricultural production and nutrition, with stunting levels declining from 35 percent in 2019 to 32 percent in 2024, but the progress remains insufficient to achieve Sustainable Development Goal number Two, of ending hunger by 2030.

She however, said Zambia continues to experience production and consumption patterns heavily centred on maize, while diversification into nutrient-dense crops, livestock, fisheries and other nutritious foods remains low.

“The situation contributes to low dietary diversity, while smallholder farmers continue to face climate variability, post-harvest losses, market access constraints and limited integration of crop and livestock systems,” added Ms Kapusana.

Ms Kapusana has since assured stakeholders that the Office of the Vice President would support government ownership, inter-sectoral coordination and strategic partnerships throughout the project cycle.

Meanwhile, FAO Representative in Zambia, Suze Filippini, said the project will support the government in strengthening coordination across sectors while promoting nutrition-sensitive and climate-smart agriculture, improving food safety systems and market linkages, operationalising the animal identification and traceability system.

Ms Filippini explained that the project is intended to catalyse lasting transformation by strengthening national institutions, partnerships, approaches and investments beyond the lifespan of the programme.

She said food systems affect production, household food choices, nutrition and health, environmental sustainability, employment, markets and the resilience of communities to climate and economic shocks.

Ms Filippini pointed out that Zambia continues to face interconnected challenges, including limited production diversity, market barriers, post-harvest losses, climate vulnerability, food safety risks and persistent malnutrition which need coordinated action.

She further said improved food safety and traceability systems will help protect consumers, strengthen livestock disease surveillance and create opportunities for producers to access domestic, regional and international markets.

Ms Filippini said the success of the project will ultimately be measured by improvements in the livelihoods of Zambians, stating that the project will support efforts to make rural communities more resilient to climate-related and economic shocks.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 22, 2026
World.content:
Monrovia — South Africa Pushes for Permanent African Seat on UN Security Council

South Africa is leveraging ongoing intergovernmental negotiations on UN reform to advance the African Union's demand for permanent representation. Speaking at the 81st UN General Assembly, South Africa's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Mxolisi Sizo Nkosi, highlighted Security Council reform as a core priority for Pretoria as it rallies support across member states.

The Security Council currently comprises 15 members: five permanent and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. South Africa maintains that the body must expand to reflect contemporary global realities, specifically addressing Africa's historic absence from the permanent category.

UN Voices Deep Concern Over Escalating Security Crisis in Ethiopia

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The UN has expressed strong concern over a deteriorating security situation in Ethiopia, pointing to the formation of a new coalition of armed groups, widespread instability, and repeated drone strikes.

Speaking at a press briefing on September 21, UN Secretary-General Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was "deeply concerned" by the ongoing escalation. The warning comes amid heightened tensions across the country, including fresh clashes between federal forces and regional troops in northern Tigray.

South West Somalia Steps Up Flood Preparations Ahead of El Niño Rains

South West State President Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe convened a high-level ministerial committee and the Somalia Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) to review emergency preparations ahead of expected El Niño rains.

Officials outlined risk mitigation plans aimed at preventing flood damage, safeguarding communities, and enhancing disaster response capabilities across the state. President Madobe urged government agencies and humanitarian partners to streamline coordination and ensure emergency equipment is pre-positioned in high-risk zones.

South African Women Need Protection, Not Warnings, Says Human Rights Watch

The discovery of several women's bodies on the outskirts of South Africa's commercial capital, Johannesburg, has caused fear, anxiety and outrage across the country. All the women were found naked or partially clothed, according to police. Some of the bodies had bruising. At least three suspects are already in custody as authorities continue to examine possible links between the killings

Writing for Human Rights Watch, researcher Stacey-Leigh Manuel emphasized that these horrific killings are not isolated incidents, but rather symptom of South Africa's ongoing national emergency regarding gender-based violence.

World.title: Niger: Junta Strips 5 More Exiled Critics of Nationality
World.content:
press release

Nairobi — Latest Crackdown Heightens Rights Concerns Amid Renewed Political Tensions

Niger's junta has provisionally stripped five more exiled opposition figures of their nationality, extending a controversial policy increasingly used against critics of the military authorities, Human Rights Watch said today.

On September 17, 2026, Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani, who has led Niger's junta since the July 2023 coup, signed a decree removing the nationality of five prominent Nigeriens living in exile. The decree derives authority from a 2024 order creating a national terrorism database with overbroad inclusion criteria and inadequate due process requirements and safeguards for redress. The order jeopardizes privacy and data protection rights and increases the risk of statelessness.



"The Niger junta's use of a terrorism database to deprive people of their nationality without any meaningful legal safeguards raises serious human rights concerns," said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Nationality is a fundamental legal status, not a privilege that governments can take from people for political reasons."

The five affected are former Prime Minister Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou; Amadou dit Ange Barou Chekaraou, Oumarou Moussa Ibrahim, and Ousmane Abdoul Moumouni, all former advisers to President Mohamed Bazoum, who was ousted in 2023 and remains arbitrarily detained; and Boubacar Seyni Souley, a social media activist critical of the junta.

The September 17 decree accuses the men of various offenses, including disseminating information capable of disturbing public order, providing intelligence to foreign powers, electronic defamation, demoralizing the armed forces, and threatening state security.

The decree raises questions about compliance with Niger's existing legal framework. The 1984 Nationality Code does not provide for "provisional loss" of nationality. Where deprivation of nationality is permitted, the law requires the authorities to notify the person concerned and give them one month to submit a written defense before the measure is published in the official journal.

"Nothing of the sort is happening here," the Alliance of Sahel Democrats, a coalition of Nigerien, Malian, and Burkinabè diaspora political opposition groups advocating a return to constitutional rule, said in a statement on September 18. The alliance also noted that the September 17 decree is depriving individuals of their nationality while they are still being prosecuted, in contravention of the 2024 order, which states that deprivation of nationality can only be imposed after a conviction.

According to Niger's press agency, the junta's latest action brings the number of people provisionally deprived of Nigerien nationality under the 2024 order to 25. In October 2024, the junta provisionally stripped nine people linked to former President Bazoum of their nationality. In June, authorities revoked the citizenship of Mariama Djibrine, an opposition figure living in exile.

In a September 19 statement, the G25-Niger, an opposition coalition of civil society groups and media organizations formed in 2025, said the 2024 order "is being used as a tool of political repression ... to crack down on opponents and other dissenting voices."

Since taking power in 2023, Niger's military junta has entrenched authoritarian rule and consolidated sweeping and unchecked powers, systematically weakening institutions capable of holding the military authorities to account.

In the past year alone, the military authorities have dissolved all political parties and several independent unions, suspended dozens of civil society groups, detained journalists under a broad cybercrime law, criminalized consensual same-sex relations, announced Niger's withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, and prolonged the country's political transition without any roadmap toward democratic elections. In addition to Bazoum, the junta continues to arbitrarily detain Moussa Tchangari, a prominent human rights defender.

The authorities have also taken steps to curb criticism from abroad. In June, Niger's foreign affairs minister instructed diplomatic missions to monitor online criticism of the military authorities, signaling growing scrutiny of the diaspora's discussions of the country's political and human rights situation.

The political climate in Niger has become increasingly tense in recent weeks, Human Rights Watch said. On August 28, mutinous soldiers attacked a military base at the international airport in Niamey, Niger's capital, and the presidential palace, with hours of gunfire. The mutineers also briefly seized the headquarters of the state-run national television, disrupting broadcasts. General Tiani called in Russia's government-controlled Africa Corps, whose intervention, including the use of armed drones, helped loyalist forces suppress the mutiny.

Close 

Niger is a party to the United Nations Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which restricts states from depriving people of their nationality when doing so would leave them stateless. Colleagues of the five affected by the September 17 decree said that at least four of them only possess a Nigerien passport.

Those who are without a nationality as well as their families risk being deprived of legal and social protection abroad. It could prevent them from returning to Niger, which is their right under international human rights law.

"The Niger junta has been depriving perceived political opponents of their nationality without meaningful due process, and contrary to Niger's obligations to prevent statelessness and protect fundamental rights," Allegrozzi said. "The junta should immediately revoke the decree and suspend the use of the easily abused terrorism database."

World.title: Djibouti: Djibouti Frees Top SA Investigative Journalist Micah Reddy
World.content:
South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists was detained on Saturday, but is now on his way back to South Africa.

Micah Reddy, the South African investigative journalist who was detained by government authorities in Djibouti on Saturday, 19 September, was released on Tuesday and is on his way home to South Africa, unharmed.

His family announced this on Tuesday following two days of anxiety after he and his local fixer Kooki Mahmoud disappeared from their hotel in Djibouti at about 1pm on Saturday. Reddy's family said in a statement that Mahmoud had also been released without charge.

"It is with immense relief and delight that we share the news that he is on his way back to South Africa, unharmed," the family said.

Reddy, a journalist and Africa Coordinator at the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), had been held in the custody of Djiboutian authorities "from 1pm on Saturday, 19 September 2026", the announcement added.

"Despite numerous efforts to establish his whereabouts and condition, no official information was provided until today," the family said.
