World.title: Sanctions showdown leaves a bad taste as Latvia cautions against 'normalising' Russia
World.content:
David vs Goliath: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs has criticised the EU for “cherry-picking” sanctions on Moscow in a move he says “normalises Russia”, after his small Baltic nation showed its teeth yesterday while opposing a push to remove two oligarchs from the EU’s blacklist.

 

Reminder: EU heavyweight France had stunned EU diplomats by pushing to remove Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the sanctions list as part of a prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan. Slovakia had also been lobbying to remove a second businessman, Mikhail Fridman, from the list.

Latvia fiercely opposed the move hours before a looming deadline on the sanctions’ renewal yesterday. The Baltic nation finally allowed both men to be delisted to avoid torpedoing the entire deal, which was needed to renew sanctions on some 2,600 individuals. My colleague Jorge Liboreiro has the details.

Speaking exclusively to my colleague Angela Skujins, Prime Minister Kulbergs said he had eventually dropped his opposition because "we all understood it is not worth risking" the whole EU sanctions package.

Sending the wrong message: “I’m worried about the playbook which it leaves,” Kulbergs cautioned, however, adding: “This is normalising Russia.” Watch.

Low energy: Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron has asked Brussels to take emergency steps to boost Europe’s diesel and jet fuel supply, according to a letter seen by Euronews’ energy reporter Marta Pacheco.

The communiqué comes as the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East threaten to further tighten global oil markets.

"In recent weeks, international supply has deteriorated once again, driven by the combined impact of the targeting of energy infrastructure — in Russia and the Middle East — and the recovery of consumption in Asia," reads the letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and sent on 18 September.

The EU executive in Brussels acknowledged yesterday it had received the letter, but stayed silent on which measures it would be tabling.

EU holds firm on Chinese power inverter phase-out: Meanwhile, the Commission will not extend its 1 November deadline for phasing out Chinese-made power inverters from EU-funded energy projects, despite calls from investors and the renewable energy industry for more time, my colleague Luca Bertuzzi writes this morning.

Industry groups and institutional investors had hoped Brussels would delay the deadline amid concerns over the availability and cost of alternatives. But EU officials told Euronews the Commission intends to stick to its timetable.

Today in New York: European Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica is set to announce the signing of two recovery projects for Gaza worth a total of $50 million (€43.7 million), my colleague Eleonora Vasques reports. The announcement will be made on the margins of the UN General Assembly.

UN agencies will implement the projects to provide essential services (water, sanitation and waste management) in the Strip. The projects are part of the “Team Gaza Initiative,” launched by the European Commission in July at the Palestine Donor Group meeting, which raised $1 billion (roughly €875 million) to support Gaza.

Greenland deal: Meanwhile in New York on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenland PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed a deal allowing the US to expand its military presence on Greenland through the modernisation and enlargement of its current Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of new defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.

‘Win-win-win’: The deal has been described as a win for all sides, and a crucial step in assuaging trans-Atlantic tensions that flared in the wake of Trump’s threats to annex the Arctic island. Nathan Rennolds has the details.

Morocco elects: Some 15.8 million registered voters are expected to head to the polls today to elect Morocco’s new parliament. This is the first political contest in the North African kingdom since locals protested against corruption in 2025.

What is on the ballot: Political commentators are watching to see how locals cast their ballots regarding issues such as the economy, the country’s plans to host the 2030 FIFA World Cup, and whether they will be swayed by July's 80,000-person mass border crossing into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, which saw over a hundred people lose their lives.

The vote comes a day after one of the EU’s most powerful parliamentarians, Manfred Weber from the centre-right European People’s Party, lashed out while visiting Ceuta, calling on the Moroccan government to take back all irregular migrants.

On Monday, Spain's Youth Minister Sira Rego said most underage migrants who entered Ceuta will not be returned. It’s estimated that of the 5,000–10,000 Moroccans whi remain in Ceuta, half are unaccompanied minors.

Exclusive: EU countries sound alarm over weapons brought back from Ukraine front line

Soldiers returning from the front line in Ukraine are bringing back weapons and military equipment, raising concerns that battlefield components could start circulating within the European Union, according to a confidential EU document seen by Euronews. The risk of firearms being diverted from the battlefield will be discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, as European authorities step up efforts to track weapons entering the bloc.

"Member states have reported weapon components and military equipment in the possession of returning combatants," reads the EU Council document, which focuses on the war in Ukraine's impact on EU internal security.

"While not necessarily connecting these individuals to organised smuggling activities, these detections demonstrate a potential risk of military components or other battlefield equipment being transported from Ukraine into the EU," the document continues.

Luca Bertuzzi has this exclusive piece of reporting.

More from our newsrooms

ECB calls for tougher EU crypto rules and wider ban on stablecoin interest. Europe's central banks want the EU's crypto rules tightened, calling for a wider ban on interest payments on stablecoins, new powers to curb tokens pegged to foreign currencies such as the US dollar, and EU-level supervision of crypto firms. Quirino Mealha and Eleonora Vasques have the latest.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham declines to rule out rejoining EU. The 2016 Brexit vote has proved tricky to shake off for many in the United Kingdom, including among the new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. According to UK media reports, he has declined to rule out including a pledge to rejoin the European Union in Labour's next election manifesto. Nathan Rennolds has the story.

Weber warns Morocco of 'obvious consequences' over Ceuta border crisis. European People’s Party (EPP) leader Manfred Weber warned that Morocco could face “obvious consequences” if the border with the Spanish exclave of Ceuta could not be stabilised, raising the prospect of further “uncontrolled situations” following the arrival of around 80,000 irregular migrants at the end of July. Vincenzo Genovese has the story.

We're also keeping an eye on

European Commissioner for Trade Maroš Šefčovič meets with US Ambassador to the European Union Andrew Puzder.

European Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica attends a briefing of the Board of Peace at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.

European Commission Executive Vice-President Roxana Mînzatu meets Acting US Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling.

EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas speaks at the UN Security Council meeting on Ukraine in New York City.

That’s it for today. Luca Bertuzzi, Jorge Liboreiro, Marta Pacheco and Eleonora Vasques contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: Eleven killed in South Africa as gunmen open fire on Durban homestead
World.content:
Eleven people, among them a pregnant woman, were shot dead late on Tuesday when armed men burst into a house in a township in Durban, South Africa, provincial officials said.

 

The victims had gathered at the homestead shortly before 11pm (local time) when the attackers entered and began shooting, according to Thamsanqa Ntuli, premier of KwaZulu-Natal, the province whose largest city is Durban.

Speaking to AFP on Wednesday, Ntuli said two people survived. Police have not yet identified a motive.

Ntuli said the killings had left residents "in profound shock and grief."

South African broadcaster eNCA reported that the gunmen herded everyone into a single room before opening fire, and torched a car belonging to one of the victims.

One resident told the channel he had grown up with some of those killed and had never seen anything like it in the area, likening the scene to something out of a film.

Mass shootings are a recurring feature of violent crime in South Africa, where both legally held and illegal guns are widespread. Attacks are frequently linked to gang feuds or to disputes between competing informal businesses.

The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with roughly 60 people killed every day in a population of about 62 million.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has called crime one of the gravest threats facing the nation, and in March soldiers were sent to violence hotspots nationwide to reinforce the police.

World.title: The Trump-Xi summit: Why Europe has so much at stake
World.content:
As Chinese President Xi Jinping lands in the US on Wednesday for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, Europeans will be watching closely for any decisions that could directly affect their economic interests.

 

Trump and Xi's second meeting in a year will cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths. This latest summit follows their crucial meeting in October 2025, where the two sides agreed on a trade truce after weeks of trade tensions.

The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June aimed at reducing its €1 billion-a-day trade deficit, setting a looming October deadline for tangible progress.

Since their China-US summit last year, the Iran war has erupted, triggering a surge in energy prices and ramping up pressure on the US President ahead of the November midterm elections. On China’s side, shipments to the US surged by 34.4% in a year, widening China's trade surplus to about $29.2 billion, according to Chinese data.

"Xi Jinping arrives in Washington with the upper hand, even on American soil," Alicia García Herrero, an expert at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, said.

Several issues on the table for Xi and Trump directly concern the EU. So what can Europeans expect from the US-China summit?

Tariff cuts

The trade truce, due to expire on 10 November, will be on the agenda, a year after it ended a trade war between the two with tit-for-tat tariffs exceeding 100%. For the Europeans, US tariffs on China are always a wrong signal, as they reroute Chinese exports to the EU market.

However, this week's summit might lead to stabilisation between Washington and Beijing.

According to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, China and the US will make “some ‌announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers.” A mutual tariff reduction covering $30 billion in goods is also expected.

“What we expect is for Trump to gain a sort of a win that he can sell for the midterm elections, and China to simply buy some more time to strengthen its industrial base,” Ivano di Carlo, an expert from the European Policy Centre (EPC), told Euronews.

Europe squeezed on rare earths

The trade truce also included exports of rare earths. During last year's trade war, Beijing had blocked global exports of the strategic materials, key for EU industry, for which it holds a monopoly of production and processing.

The issue was raised last week by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič during a video call with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. But Washington has far greater negotiating power than Brussels when it comes to securing access to the materials, García Herrero told Euronews.

“The US will negotiate for Europe and Europe will have to pay a price for that,” García Herrero said.

Europe non-existent on AI

The two powers are also expected to discuss artificial intelligence, amid growing calls for international safeguards. Two weeks ago, Jacob Coxon, who has worked as a researcher at both AI heavyweights OpenAI and Anthropic, said on X that both companies are “gambling with our lives” and that people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” raising global concerns around this technology.

Several incidents were also reported over the summer, including OpenAI agents hacking another AI company, Hugging Face’s platform.

Both China and the US have expressed concern about the risks surrounding AI development, but they are also locked in an intensifying technological competition. On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed an “AI hotline” proposal, which would be a “notification mechanism” between Washington and China to warn each other when an AI incident becomes serious enough to threaten national security.

“This AI dialogue that is going to become like a red button during the nuclear race is only shared by the US and China,” García Herrero said. “So it really leaves Europe as non-existent in terms of being a pole.”

According to the expert, the summit will “confirm the G20 nature of the world.”

World.title: Oil falls below $100 after Trump reports talks with Iran
World.content:
Oil prices fell on Wednesday after US President Donald Trump said American and Iranian representatives had held talks at the United Nations.

 

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at $98.41 a barrel in the morning in Europe. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate cost $95.21 a barrel for next month delivery. Brent has repeatedly risen above $100 since the Middle East war began in February.

The three-hour meeting was “very good” and “very productive”, Trump told reporters during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He said another meeting was planned soon.

His comments came hours after he told the UN he faced a “big decision” on whether to reach a deal with Iran or “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.

The US and Iran remain at an impasse. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, while the US has maintained a blockade of Iranian ports. Fighting involving Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has also disrupted energy exports through the Red Sea.

“The three-hour US-Iran meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant,” said Stephen Innes of Quintex Intel.

Prices also fell following a report that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations along its East–West Pipeline. The route allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia said this month that drones launched from Iraq had forced it to close the pipeline.

The kingdom hopes to resume exports later this week, Bloomberg reported, citing a source. Saudi Aramco has reportedly told Asian refiners that they may soon be able to collect crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. European refiners, however, have reportedly been told they will receive no Saudi crude under their October supply agreements.

Global stocks edge higher ahead of Trump–Xi meeting

European stock markets looked set to open higher on Wednesday. Futures for the Euro Stoxx 50 and Germany’s DAX rose 0.3%, while FTSE 100 futures gained 0.2% early in the European morning.

Asian shares mostly rose. South Korea’s Kospi gained 1.2%, with Samsung and SK Hynix both up more than 2%. Taiwan’s Taiex rose 0.9%, according to the Reuters report you supplied. The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.5%, its sixth consecutive daily rise. Japan’s stock market was closed for a holiday, although Nikkei futures traded higher.

On Wall Street, the Nasdaq rose 0.5% to a record close on Tuesday. The S&P 500 was little changed, while the Dow fell 0.4%.

In currency markets, the euro traded at $1.1429, near a two-month low, as investors considered the possibility of another US interest rate rise. The dollar also edged up against the yen to 157.60 yen.

Gold traded at $4,379 an ounce. US Treasury futures rose slightly as oil prices eased, keeping the yield on the 10-year government bond below 5%.

Investors were also looking ahead to a meeting on Thursday between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trade and competition over AI are expected to be on the agenda.

Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said the war in the Middle East could prove more consequential for markets, including whether the US could persuade China to use its influence with Iran.

World.title: India news: El Nino heat could kill 15,800 by February, report warns
World.content:
This year's powerful El Nino phenomenon, which is driving global heat to record levels and contributing to severe droughts, wildfires and water shortages, is likely to cause 15,800 deaths in India by the end of February, according to a research report released on Wednesday.

The warning, released by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab, said as many as 451,000 more deaths between June and February of next year could be attributed to El Nino, when compared to typical heat-related deaths in a year.

El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years, toward the end of the year. It comes in various strengths — depending on the prevailing conditions.

El Nino patterns are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases ofgreater than 3 degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.

The Climate Impact Lab report said the powerful heat this year was most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor. It projected that the Global South will see more heat-related deaths.

El Nino, regional wars fuel global food crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What could help prevent deaths?

Heat warnings, hydration outreach, cooling centers and a plan to cope with the heat are all ways governments can help protect people, the report said, adding that they should also expand hospital capacity and chalk out anticipatory financing.

New Delhi had several cooling stations across the city in the summer of 2026. However, not all cities and towns have the same resources Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.

But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans remains a challenge, he said.

"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari said.

World.title: Is Syria's 'new' economy for the rich only?
World.content:
The Syrian government says it is restructuring the economy and announces prosperity. But ordinary Syrians are not feeling it. In fact, they say their lives are getting worse. Who exactly is likely to benefit then?

Kanan Abdullah has been working as a driver in the Syrian capital Damascus for around 12 years but he, like many others in his trade, is now finding it difficult to make ends meet following recent fuel price rises in Syria.

"You're left with almost nothing at the end of the day" he told DW. "You have enough to buy another tank of gas but how are you supposed to buy food? Or what if you need money set aside to repair the car?" he complained.

His potential passengers feel the same way. "People are starting to worry about how they're going to get to work and get home because transport alone is costing them half their pay," added Kamar Kasoum, a local mother of three.

In mid-September, the Syrian government raised the price of all kinds of fuel, including petrol and diesel. Diesel saw the biggest hike, rising 40%. The energy ministry explained such changes were necessary because of higher global fuel costs — Syria remains dependent on energy imports — as well as local shortages.

In Damascus, local reporters say fares on public minibuses rose up to 70% almost immediately and taxi rides become 60% more expensive Image: Monsef Memari/Xinhua/picture alliance

Widest protests since dictatorship

The move triggered some of the most widespread protests Syria has seen since thedictatorial Assad regime was toppled in late 2024. While fuel prices are still comparable with other countries in the region, Syrians are struggling because of lower purchasing power, experts say. Demonstrators burned tires, blocked roads and called for the dismissal of politicians they held responsible.

The protests subsided as the Syrian government walked back some changes and announced plans to subsidize diesel for heating, agriculture and industry.

But higher fuel prices are only the latest to add inflationary pressure on ordinary Syrians. In its most recent bulletin on the consumer price index, the Syrian Center for Policy Research, says prices increased almost 25% between July 2025 and July 2026. Worryingly, the highest price increases — around 37% — were on "essential expenditure" such as housing, water, electricity and gas.

Protests against fuel price rises erupted in September: Experts say lifting subsidies without creating alternatives to help those most in need is what made locals so angry Image: Mahmoud Hassano/REUTERS

"There is no sensible correlation between the income an individual earns in Syria and the prices they're paying," Alaa Sndyan, an architect in Damascus, told DW. "People are starting to feel the pinch, they feel that prices have gotten way too high."

"And these protests and demonstrations didn't just come out of nowhere," Kamar Kasoum added. "We're at the point where we can't even say that we're just cutting back on non-priorities. It's like, let's just stick to eating and drinking. Nothing else."

Economic growth in Syria — but for whom?

All this is happening despite what appears to be a lot of good news about the Syrian economy. There are regular reports about billion-dollar, international investments and projects and, speaking at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai on Tuesday, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa predicted Syria's economy would be worth around $50 billion (approx. €44 billion) this year, up from around $20 billion in 2024.

But this much-celebrated prosperity somehow doesn't seem to be reaching ordinary Syrians, over two-thirds of whom still live in comparative poverty according to United Nations.

A new Syria for 'the rich'

Damascus architect Sndyan said it was hard to tell who's benefitting from economic development. "With a lot of the projects being announced now, we don't see anything happening on the ground, there's no impact on the real world," she argued. "And I always feel like these projects are aimed at a specific demographic: the affluent class. I am not sure these projects are actually for the people."

Sndyan added that she felt as if ordinary people who lost everything during Syria's civil war were being forgotten in the midst of various grand plans. She said she would also like to see more transparency and better communication from the government around its plans.

She is not the only one. There has been plenty of criticism about the direction of Syria's economic planning as well as concerns it may benefit the already-wealthy most.

More extreme anti-government activists have pointed to the luxury watches some Syrian politicians appear to be wearing, making accusations of "crony capitalism" and suggesting the government is diverting funds into the military in order to secure its own power. None of those accusations are verified.

But criticism has also comes from more moderate quarters. In an August story, Syrian outlet Al Jumhuriya looked into the billion-dollar real estate projects announced around the country. These are mostly comprised of gated communities and luxury apartments, it said. In a country with a major housing crisis, "who will actually be able to live in these projects?" the publication asked.

'Neo-liberal' policies not suitable

There's concern old patterns are being repeated. "As certain pre-existing forms of corruption and extraction change, new channels of privilege are emerging … albeit with new winners and losers," Syrian think tank Etana argued in an analysis this week .

Observers say the neo-liberal style reforms the Syrian government is currently committed to will only worsen this problem and, in the longer run, cause the same kinds of social problems that sparked Syria's revolution in 2011.

When the new Syrian government first took control in late 2024, ordinary Syrians were willing to give them a chance. But monthly polling by the magazine, Syria in Transition, indicates patience is wearing thin. By April this year, "the most serious deterioration was in attitudes toward the economy ... only 13% of respondents now believed the government was doing enough to tackle soaring energy and food prices while 66% said its efforts were insufficient," the magazine noted .

"The country's new leaders have undertaken a shock therapy program of economic liberalization without, it seems, fully accounting for the acute vulnerability and poverty of most Syrians," Sam Heller, an analyst with the New York-based think tank Century International, pointed out in Foreign Affairs magazine this week.

And that's not suitable, researcher Joseph Daher, an expert on Syria's political economy, argued in an analysis for the online bilingual outlet Syria Untold . "In countries emerging from conflict, 'success' cannot be measured solely by fiscal surpluses or price stability," he wrote. "True success is measured by the ability of fiscal policy to rebuild citizenship, justice, institutional capacity and public trust."

To do that, the Syrian government needs to change its policies, Karam Shaar, director of the Karam Shaar Advisory, a New Zealand-based consultancy for Syrian economic affairs, said during an online interview last week. Some of what the new authorities have done was necessary given the post-war situation, he conceded, but now more transparency, expertise and better governance was needed.

"I think they are they are starting to realize that [and] I continue to have a bit of hope that this will indeed happen," Shaar concluded.

World.title: South Africa: 11 killed in attack on homestead
World.content:
The motive for the shooting was not immediately clear.

Gunmen killed 11 people at a home in eastern South Africa, Kwa-Zulu Natal province's premier said on Wednesday.

Two people survived the attack.

The motive for the shooting was not immediately clear.

The shooting occurred at KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city.

"The victims, including a pregnant woman, were gathered at a house shortly before 11:00 pm [2100 UTC] when armed assailants reportedly entered the premises and opened fire," Kwa-Zulu Premier Thamsanqa Ntuli said.

"The incident has left the community in profound shock and grief," he said.

Police said that one of the victims died after being taken to hospital.

"Ten victims, including the woman, died at the scene and four were taken ​to hospital, were one of them succumbed to gunshot injuries," police said.

Some of the victims were known to police, according to the statement.

South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates.

More to come...

World.title: Sri Lanka: 15 men jailed for life in 2019 Easter bombings
World.content:
The 15 convicts have been given prison sentences of at least 200 years each, following a long trial in what was among Sri Lanka's deadliest attacks.

A court in Sri Lanka convicted 15 men over the deadly 2019 Easter bombings, sentencing them to 200 to 260 years in prison on Tuesday.

A three-judge bench of the High Court in Colombo found 14 of the defendants guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

The 15th accused was found guilty only of some charges.

The court also ordered the seizure of the convicts' property and assets.

Nine men were acquitted in the trial. Those convicted have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court.

On April 21, 2019, coordinated suicide blasts struck three churches and three luxury hotels, killing 279 people and injuring 574 more — making it among the worst attacks in Sri Lanka's history.

Investigators had blamed the attack on a local Islamist extremist group.

The 15 defendants were among a total of 25 individuals — all from Sri Lanka's minority Muslim community — accused of providing support to the suicide bombers.

Lengthy Sri Lanka Easter bombing trial

The trial lasted nearly five years with Sri Lankan authorities filing 23,270 charges in 2021 against the 25 suspects. One of the accused died in pretrial detention.

The case listed some 2,300 witnesses.

Mohamed Ibrahim Mohamed Naufer, an Islamic cleric and the alleged leader of the Easter Sunday bombings, was among those sentenced.

Prosecutors said he had radicalized the other defendants with his teachings. He was sentenced to 240 years in prison with hard labor.

'Intelligence failure'

Tuesday's verdict came as a separate probe looks into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state may have had links to those responsible for the blasts.

The country's former intelligence chief Suresh Salley was arrested over accusations that he had a role in masterminding the attacks, a charge he denies.

A parliamentary committee had earlier found that police and intelligence officials ignored foreign intelligence warnings of the attacks.

In July, a former police chief and a former senior official of the Defense Ministry were given the death sentence for failing to act despite prior intelligence warnings.

World.title: Trump signs 'tremendous' Greenland security deal
World.content:
Donald Trump strikes a security deal with Greenland and Denmark on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The deal comes after Trump repeatedly said the US should own the Arctic island.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland to strengthen Arctic and North Atlantic security.

Trump, Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen signed the deal on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.

The White House released the text of the deal shortly after that.

What's in the Greenland deal?

The deal, which the president first announced last week, bolsters US military and security presence on Greenland.

The US will reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and set up the other base on the eastern coast of the island in Mestersvig.

Trump said during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly that the US would "immediately begin the process of developing a significant military presence in appropriate locations and constructing two very important military bases."

He said the deal was "tremendous" for Europe and the US just before he signed it, adding, "And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible."

Under the agreement, the US will be "allowed to modernize and expand its activities" at the Space Force base.

The deal also reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Denmark and Greenland.

Trump has long said he wanted the US to take over Greenland

The agreement comes after months of pressure from Trump,who has long said he wants the US to control Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, a NATO ally.

Behind the scenes, American, Danish, and Greenlandic officials worked many months to address Trump's security concerns regarding the resource-rich island.

The dispute unsettled most Greenlanders and created tensions between the US, Denmark, and the European Union, which quickly increased security exercises and financial support for the Arctic island.

What did Trump really gain from the Greenland deal? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The race for Arctic

Greeland's future has come under the spotlight globally because of trade interests and expectations of future resource development. At least two-thirds of its territory lies within the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened new maritime routes.

Although the US played a prominent role in Greenland for decades, its military presence on the island has declined since 1945.

From having thousands of troops stationed across 17 bases and installations, only about 200 personnel remain today at Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland.

Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, described the agreement as "a win-win arrangement."

Denmark's parliament approved a bill last year to allow US military bases on Danish soil, widening a 2023 agreement made with the Biden administration that gave US troops broad access to air bases in Denmark.

US, Denmark and Greenland sign defense deal Image: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

Wide US mobility on Greenland

The agreement grants US military forces broad freedom of movement in Greenland and its territorial waters and restricts non-NATO countries from establishing military facilities in Greenland or maintaining a "permanent" military presence unless the signatories agree otherwise.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte welcomed the signing of the agreement, writing on X that "this agreement, together with NATO's growing role in securing this vital region, enhances our collective security and supports a safer and more stable future for all of us."

Editor's note: We join our media colleagues in objection to the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico. We are not going to use photos or video material produced by the White House and distributed through its official communication channels until further notice.

World.title: EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
World.content:
France and Luxembourg were behind the sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, a move that Kyiv labeled "shameful and unjustifiable."

The European Union on Tuesday reached a compromise to prolong sanctions for around 3,000 Russian individuals, entities and companies — but it also resulted in the lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.

It all comes after lengthy negotiations ahead of a Wednesday deadline to extend the sanctions, which required unanimity among EU countries to be approved.

"The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until 22 September 2029," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said.

"The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime," it added.

Previously, the sanctions were subject to six-month extensions, so Tuesday's agreement allows the EU to avoid another squabble over the sanctions for three years.

Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom Image: imago/ITAR-TASS

Ukraine denounced the EU's removal of oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman from its Russia sanctions list as "shameful and unjustifiable."

"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.

"Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor's entourage," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

Zelenskyy did say he was "grateful" to EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for "her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions list".

Kyiv has called on EU countries to impose "national" sanctions on the two oligarchs.

France and Luxembourg sought exemptions

France was one of the countries demanding the removal of Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov from the sanctions list.

Officials in Paris explained the decision as having to do with "national security" concerns. The French government has not provided any additional details.

According to AFP, diplomatic sources say the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan, whose regime is close to Usmanov.

Meanwhile, Fridman's sanctions exemption was put forth by Luxembourg.

Sources say the move comes as Fridman sues Luxembourg for €15 billion ($17 billion) over his frozen assets, due to EU sanctions.

Mikhail Fridman has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group Image: Mikhail Japaridze/TASS/imago images

Who are Usamov and Friedman?

Usmanov and Fridman are two of Russia's best-known oligarchs, and both have a net worth of $14 billion and 16 billion, respectively. They both are known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin.

The Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom. He currently owns the USM holding company, as well as MegaFon, one of Russia's main mobile phone operators.

For his part, Fridman, has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group, which includes Alfa Bank, Russia's largest and most important private commercial bank.

Fridman also co-founded investment firm LetterOne in Luxembourg and stepped down from its board of directors in 2022 after being targeted by European Union sanctions.

World.title: Amateur archeologist unearths Germany's largest trove of Roman coins
World.content:
What began as a routine search in a field near Wesseling led to the discovery of nearly 1,000 Roman silver coins, one of the most significant archaeological finds in Germany in recent years.

A massive trove of Roman silver coins dating back to the 2nd century AD have been discovered by an amateur archaeologist in Germany.

"It was clear to me that there was something significant here," said Oliver Riedl, describing the moment he found several coins near Wesseling, south of Cologne, a year ago.

After making the discovery, Riedl contacted the authorities to report the find and request assistance. A team of experts began excavations and uncovered a total of 934 Roman silver coins, also known as "denarii".

The hoard was put on display on Tuesday at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn, located in what was once the capital of West Germany.

According to the the local authority responsible for archaeological heritage preservation, this is the largest coin hoard from the era of Roman Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany.

Amateur archeologist Oliver Riedl contacted authorities after he unearthed the first few coins with his metal detector Image: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

A historic discovery

Regional archeological authorities believe the coins were most likely buried during the second quarter of the 2nd century AD.

"Of course, we can only speculate about the reasons, but it is highly likely that someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, banks did not exist at that time," said Erich Classen, the chief archaeologist of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Classen noted that there is no explanation as to why the coins were not discovered earlier, nor is it known who buried them. He added that "perhaps the owner died before being able to recover them or pass on knowledge of their location."

Coin hoards from the Roman period and other distant historical eras are not uncommon in the region. However, according to officials, few 2nd-century discoveries are as extensive as the one found in Wesseling. The institution also said that the current value of the collection is difficult to estimate. Nevertheless, thanks to extensive documentation preserved in written sources, there is a useful point of reference.

Germany displays largest Hadrian-era Roman coin hoard Image: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

At that time, an ordinary legionary earned about 300 denarii per year. However, approximately half of that amount was deducted to cover food and equipment costs," explained Rahel Otte, a researcher at the state's archaeological office.

"Therefore, a legionary would have had to save all of his disposable income for around six years to accumulate a treasure like the Wesseling hoard," she added.

The Cologne region remained under Roman control from approximately 39 BC to AD 459. The Romans established their presence in the area under the command of General Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa to secure the empire's frontier along the Rhine River. To that end, they founded a military outpost that later developed into Colonia Agrippina, present-day Cologne.

World.title: Military aircraft crashes near US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany
World.content:
The F-16 pilot was able to safely eject from the plane and was taken to receive medical care. The incident occurred near Spangdahlem Air Base in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate.

A fighter jet crashed near the US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany, on Tuesday.

The plane crash occurred at approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (12:30 UTC). The cause of the incident is currently under investigation.

The US military confirmed that the plane was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing and that its pilot was able to safely eject from the aircraft.

"The pilot ejected safely and is receiving medical care," the base said in a statement.

At least one person was injured, authorities said Image: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance

Local authorities in the remote Eifel region also confirmed that one person had been injured.

"Following a plane crash in the vicinity of US Air Base Spangdahlem, fire and emergency response teams from the Eifel District of Bitburg-Prüm were dispatched to the scene," the district said on its website.

"No comments can be made on the further details of the event from the side of the Eifel district at this time."

A NATO operations center

Spangdahlem Air Base is a NATO operations center that was built in the early 1950s. The US Air Force's 52nd Fighter Wing is garrisoned there. The base is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron comprising around 20 aircraft.

It is located north of the city of Trier in Rhineland-Palatinate, not far west of the border to Luxembourg.

The facility at Spangdahlem is considered one of the most important airfields for the US military in Germany, alongside Ramstein base, outside the city of Kaiserslautern.

Some 5,000 US military and civilian personnel-plus dependents are stationed at Spangdahlem, with around 700 to 800 Germans also employed at the facility.

World.title: Movimientos de subsaharianos hacia Marruecos alimentan la alerta por un nuevo salto masivo en Ceuta
World.content:
“Gran ataque 23 de septiembre” es el nombre de uno de los grupos de mensajería que los servicios de información e inteligencia están monitorizando esta semana, ante la amenaza de una nueva entrada masiva de inmigrantes en Ceuta y también en Melilla, coincidiendo con las elecciones en Marruecos este miércoles. Rabat ha blindado la frontera, por lo que distintas fuentes policiales dudan de que un episodio como el del 30 y 31 de julio, en el que unas 75.000 personas atravesaron El Tarajal, pueda volver a producirse. Pero movimientos de subsaharianos hacia el norte de África en los últimos días, que confirman fuentes de inteligencia, han alimentado la preocupación. La boya colocada por el Ministerio del Interior en el espigón para ejercer de barrera física pretende sortear los problemas judiciales de las devoluciones en caliente, pero distintas voces policiales reconocen que el control de la frontera depende esencialmente del reino alauí.

“Entrarán si quiere Marruecos que entren”, se resignaba este martes Félix, taxista de 44 años nativo de Ceuta. Rabea Abdeselam, de 43 años, también de origen ceutí, dudaba, en cambio, de la llegada de nadadores después de haber cruzado durante el día a Castillejos (Marruecos): “Han traído muchos policías y militares. Me han pedido documentación al volver. Está la cosa muy dura”.

En las últimas semanas, en redes sociales como Instagram o TikTok se ha extendido el hashtag haraga ―un término de origen árabe que quiere decir “los que queman” y que en el contexto migratorio se utiliza en referencia a “quemar” o saltarse los controles fronterizos― con fotografías de jóvenes que a finales de julio lograron entrar en España. Un contenido que cala en los que buscan emigrar del continente africano para buscar trabajo y mejores condiciones laborales en Europa, y en este contexto, fuentes de Inteligencia e Información explican que en las últimas semanas se vienen detectando “desplazamientos grandes” de subsaharianos “en trenes y autobuses” hacia Marruecos. Especialmente, explican, desde Sudán.

Dentro de esta corriente creciente, Ceuta se ha convertido en el objetivo principal, si bien Melilla, con unos servicios sociales mucho menos sobrecargados, también ha comenzado a estar en la conversación virtual, indican estas fuentes que conocen las labores de monitorización. “Dicen que Melilla es una mejor opción, sobre todo para ejecutar el salto en el momento de la oración [en referencia al momento del rezo musulmán]”, explican.

La coincidencia de estos llamamientos con las elecciones legislativas en Marruecos ha elevado una preocupación verbalizada, incluso, por el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, en su rueda de prensa de este lunes, en la que anunció un refuerzo de la seguridad en ambas ciudades autónomas. En total habrá 120 agentes durante las horas nocturnas y 90 en las diurnas, con un despliegue de tres pelotones de los Grupos de Reserva y Seguridad (GRS, aproximadamente 60 efectivos) para apoyar la dotación habitual destinada en la zona, como ha avanzado EL PAÍS.

La boya y la confianza en Marruecos

En Ceuta muchos vecinos parecen haberse resignado a que el agravamiento de este gran problema migratorio solo depende de Rabat. La sentencia del Tribunal Supremo, conocida el pasado 8 de julio, que prohíbe realizar devoluciones en caliente en la frontera si las entradas se producen a nado, fue una de las grandes dificultades de esta crisis. Los argumentos del fallo se extendieron como la pólvora y de forma tergiversada por las redes sociales de ciudadanos marroquíes, y la jurisprudencia provocó que ni una persona de las miles que llegaban por el mar pudiera ser retornada al país vecino de forma instantánea. Motivo por el que solo un día después de la entrada masiva, Interior decidió colocar una gran boya alargada en el Tarajal para ejercer de “barrera física”, de manera que si volvía a entrar algún migrante y, de acuerdo a la literalidad de la sentencia, estas devoluciones exprés sí pudieran producirse.

“La boya no es un medio disuasorio, es una herramienta jurídica”, indica un policía desplegado en Ceuta. La mañana de este martes, la prensa local advertía de que varios tramos del flotador habían quedado inutilizados, al quedar totalmente hundidos en el mar. Algo que este periódico ha podido comprobar a última hora de la tarde. Precisamente, el departamento de Marlaska anunció este martes que se habían iniciado los trámites para acometer la prolongación de hormigón y añadir un muro en el mar de 15 metros, con una inversión de unos siete millones de euros. Mientras eso llega, la queja de los policías y guardias civiles en el terreno más escuchada es que el control efectivo fronterizo está prácticamente en manos de Rabat. “Se parte de un hecho fáctico: la frontera no la custodiamos nosotros. No tenemos capacidad de repeler. Tienes que tener fe en Marruecos”, cuenta un alto cargo ceutí de la Policía.

Los distintos episodios migratorios en la frontera han ido modulando la capacidad de respuesta de las fuerzas de seguridad españolas, según reflejan estas fuentes que recuerdan, por ejemplo, la tragedia de febrero de 2014, por la que 16 guardias civiles utilizaron pelotas de goma y botes de humo y 15 inmigrantes que intentaban llegar a nado murieron en el mar. Un sargento, un teniente y 13 agentes de la benemérita terminaron procesados por un presunto delito de homicidio imprudente. Y en 2021, la justicia también censuró la actuación de la vicepresidenta del ejecutivo ceutí y la entonces delegada del Gobierno, que realizaron devoluciones en caliente de menores cuando la ley no lo permite. En opinión de algunos de los mandos policiales sobre el terreno la capacidad de “repeler” una entrada masiva en territorio español no depende entonces de la cantidad de agentes que haya desplegado, sino de la capacidad de disuasión anterior que tenga la gendarmería marroquí.

Las fuentes de inteligencia explican que del análisis de redes estos días no se ha detectado una estructura sólida que esté organizando un gran asalto, sino que puede tratarse de “intentos dispersos o en pequeños grupos”, aprovechando que las fuerzas de seguridad de Rabat estén empleadas en garantizar los comicios.

En cualquier caso, Marruecos ha garantizado al Gobierno que custodiará la frontera e impedirá cualquier salto. Así lo expuso, por ejemplo, el ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, que aseguró que está en constantes conversaciones con su homólogo marroquí, Naser Burita. Hasta tres ciudadanos ceutíes que este martes cruzaron a Marruecos y luego regresaron, en conversación con este periódico, aseguraron que existe un enorme despliegue policial mucho antes, incluso, de llegar a la zona fronteriza. También fuentes policiales que estos días han estado en contacto con el Centro Nacional de Inmigración y Fronteras (CENIF) han asegurado a EL PAÍS que se ha estado comprobando la zona con drones.

La preocupación, en cambio, no termina con las elecciones del país norteafricano porque las mentadas fuentes de inteligencia reflejan que los movimientos de personas del sur de África hacia arriba son indicativos de que la presión migratoria no cesará mientras siga el buen tiempo.

World.title: La buena cara de la industria cosmética española
World.content:
El sector del cuidado personal y la belleza, que aporta el 1% del PIB y emplea a 50.000 personas, se alza paulatinamente como una industria puntera en España y en el mundo. Sin embargo, su futuro pasa por superar tres grandes desafíos: hacer productos más sostenibles, combatir las falsificaciones y mantener las exportaciones en un clima internacional adverso

LICO Cosmetics Estefanía Ferrer Fundadora y directora ejecutiva Laboratorio de ingeniería cosmética nacido en Sevilla y concebido como una compañía nativa digital. Cantabria Labs Juan Matji Presidente Laboratorio farmacéutico español especializado en productos para el cuidado de la salud de la piel

La industria de la cosmética no tiene que maquillar sus cifras para demostrar su éxito. Así lo cree Óscar Mateo, director de Conocimiento y Estudios de Mercado de la Asociación Nacional de Perfumería y Cosmética (Stanpa). El informe más reciente de la asociación, que integra a más del 90% del sector, en torno a 300 empresas, asegura que en los últimos cinco años, el negocio ha crecido un 44% y ha duplicado sus exportaciones. Este es un ámbito económico amplio que aglutina la fabricación de productos para la higiene personal, el cuidado de la piel y el cabello, el maquillaje y hasta los perfumes. Precisamente estos últimos constituyen, en palabras de Mateo, el buque insignia del sector, gracias al peso de compañías españolas como Puig, cuya presencia trasciende nuestras fronteras.

El otro pilar es el cuidado de la piel, para el que la industria ha adoptado el nombre en inglés: skincare. Debe su crecimiento al interés cada vez mayor por mantener una piel sana y con buen aspecto. Lo dice Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, una compañía farmacéutica que fabrica productos, tanto cosméticos como medicamentos, para el cuidado de la piel. “Antiguamente las cremas eran para un cierto grupo de mujeres que contaban con recursos económicos, hoy se ha democratizado”, explica el empresario en un nuevo capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen, de Banco Sabadell.

El auge del sector también obliga a afrontar una nueva lista de desafíos que aparecen por el camino como poros abiertos. Entre ellos, destacan la búsqueda de fórmulas más sostenibles sin perder eficacia, la protección frente a las falsificaciones y la lucha contra la llamada quimicofobia, término con el que Estefanía Ferrer, ingeniera química y fundadora de LICO Cosmetics, describe la desconfianza que ciertos ingredientes generan en la población. Ferrer, cuya marca nació en el entorno digital, comparte conversación con Matji en este episodio del pódcast. La charla entre ambos empresarios sirve para conocer mejor sus historias y desgranar un negocio que enfrenta un futuro fresco y radiante.

“El ‘skincare’ está aquí para quedarse. Antiguamente era para un cierto grupo de mujeres con recursos económicos, pero hoy se ha democratizado” Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, sobre el ‘boom’ de la cosmética en España

Las fortalezas Una industria que avanza con paso firme y se expande por el mundo

Una industria en expansión. El sector de la cosmética y el cuidado personal avanza a un ritmo moderado, pero sostenido. Ha pasado de representar el 0,9% del PIB español al 1,03% en los últimos cuatro años. Entre las razones de su consolidación se encuentran el desarrollo de una cultura del cuidado de la piel y el cabello y el bienestar personal, con una mención especial a los cosméticos para el rostro y la fotoprotección solar, que empieza a consumirse de manera notable fuera del verano.

Potencia exportadora. España vende cada año más productos al extranjero y ya supera a manufacturas emblemáticas como el aceite de oliva, el vino y el calzado. Además, España es el segundo exportador mundial de perfumes, solo por detrás de Francia.

Con buena reputación. La industria española produce bajo uno de los marcos regulatorios más exigentes del mundo: el europeo. Además, trabaja constantemente para crear formulaciones más seguras. Para ello invierte de media el 3,4% en I+D+i. La media general de las empresas españolas de toda la economía es el 0,9%, de acuerdo con el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE). Esto permite adaptarse mejor a los cambios en el mercado. En los dos últimos años se ha reformulado uno de cada tres productos, de acuerdo con Stanpa.

Distribuida por el territorio. Aunque Cataluña, Madrid y la Comunidad Valenciana concentran gran parte de la producción, Stanpa destaca que existe bastante descentralización, como demuestran las empresas protagonistas del vídeo, con sede en Sevilla y Cantabria.

“España compite bien internacionalmente con el ‘skincare’. No tenemos nada que envidiar a los coreanos, que están tan de moda ahora” Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, acerca del buen estado de salud de la industria española

Los desafios Un sector que se esfuerza por garantizar la seguridad de sus productos y por reducir su impacto ambiental

Adaptarse a una regulación cada vez más compleja. Los productos y los procesos tienen que responder a nuevas exigencias europeas sobre ingredientes, seguridad, información al consumidor y trazabilidad.

El reto continuo de mejorar en sostenibilidad. Las empresas se enfrentan a varios desafíos para reducir su impacto en el medio ambiente.

Limitar el uso del plástico y mejorar las posibilidades de reciclaje de sus envases

Reducir el consumo del agua en la fabricación de sus productos, así como desarrollar metodologías para medir y reducir su huella hídrica

Encontrar ingredientes biodegradables que no impacten en la naturaleza, sin perder la eficacia

Mantener la competitividad internacional. Permanecer como el segundo exportador mundial de perfumes se transforma en un desafío en un escenario internacional complejo por las tensiones comerciales, los conflictos políticos y el aumento de los aranceles. En 2025, las exportaciones a Estados Unidos cayeron un 13% por el impacto de los aranceles, de acuerdo con Stanpa.

Combatir las falsificaciones. La compra de buena parte de los productos, como los perfumes o la cosmética de alta gama, resulta aspiracional y se enmarca en el lujo accesible. Por eso, son uno de los principales objetivos de los falsificadores. Y estas copias pueden no cumplir los requisitos europeos de seguridad y etiquetado.

Luchar contra la desinformación. El consumidor cada vez está más formado, aun así, se ha extendido a través de internet la idea de que cuantos menos productos químicos tenga una crema o un perfume, mejor será para la salud, un fenómeno que se conoce como quimiofobia, ya que se da por supuesto que los ingredientes químicos pueden ser perjudiciales para la salud. Pero hay que tener cuidado con esa información, resalta la fundadora de LICO Cosmetics. Los materiales que componen un cosmético siempre son químicos, tanto si proceden de una planta como si se sintetizan en un laboratorio. Y deben ser seguros para el consumo humano, algo que se encarga de garantizar el Comité Científico de Seguridad de los Consumidores (CCSC, por sus siglas en inglés).

World.title: Soy mayor de 65 años y voy a vender mi vivienda habitual. ¿Podría hacer una segunda venta más adelante y estaría exenta de tributación?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Tengo 66 años y voy a vender mi vivienda habitual, que tiene mayor valor que la que compro. Sé que puedo optar por varios modos de exención del incremento patrimonial. En el caso de que pasado unos años quisiera vender la casa, ¿podría volver a eximir plusvalías, siendo vivienda habitual y mayor de 65 años, pero siendo una segunda venta? A. Gómez

Respuesta. Está exenta de tributación en el IRPF la ganancia patrimonial obtenida por una persona mayor de 65 años como consecuencia de la transmisión de su vivienda habitual, sin que sea necesario reinvertir el importe obtenido en la adquisición de otra vivienda ni en ningún otro producto.

A estos efectos, se considera vivienda habitual aquella de la que el contribuyente sea pleno propietario y en la que haya residido de forma efectiva y continuada durante un plazo mínimo de tres años.

Por tanto, si se cumple este requisito, cualquier ganancia patrimonial obtenida con la venta de la vivienda habitual, con independencia de su importe, estará exenta de tributación en el IRPF, aunque no se reinvierta total o parcialmente el importe obtenido en otra vivienda habitual.

Asimismo, un mismo contribuyente mayor de 65 años puede beneficiarse de esta exención en más de una ocasión, siempre que cada una de las viviendas transmitidas tenga la consideración de vivienda habitual en el momento de la venta. Para ello, será necesario que haya residido en la nueva vivienda de manera efectiva y continuada durante un período mínimo de tres años.

En consecuencia, también podría aplicarse la exención a la ganancia patrimonial generada por la venta de una nueva vivienda habitual adquirida con posterioridad, aunque se trate de una segunda transmisión de vivienda habitual realizada por una persona mayor de 65 años.

No obstante, esta exención se refiere exclusivamente a la ganancia patrimonial en el IRPF. Es decir, no está exento del Impuesto sobre el Incremento de Valor de los Terrenos de Naturaleza Urbana (plusvalía municipal), que también se devenga con motivo de la venta y debe liquidarse ante el ayuntamiento correspondiente, aunque se trate de la vivienda habitual de una persona mayor de 65 años.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
