World.title: Heating Season Starts Across Czechia as Temperatures Fall
World.content:
District heating plants across the Czech Republic are beginning to supply heat as temperatures drop, with conditions for the start of the heating season now being met in much of the country.

Some plants have already begun providing additional heat during the colder morning and evening hours. The first systems to respond were mainly in mountainous parts of northern and western Czechia and in the Vysočina region.



Other heating plants are expected to gradually start operating in the coming days, depending on local temperatures and weather forecasts.

Since 2010, district heating systems have generally started supplying heat after September 20, although the exact timing varies considerably from year to year.

If temperatures rise again in late September or early October, heating can be suspended. Under the standard rules, heating is normally interrupted when the average outdoor temperature exceeds 13°C for two consecutive days and the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue to rise.

Last winter was colder than average

The previous heating season placed greater demands on heating systems than the years immediately before it.

According to figures from the Czech District Heating Association, the season was 4.9 percent colder than the previous year. It was also 3.2 percent colder than the average of the preceding 15 years.

The colder conditions translated into higher demand for heat, particularly during periods of sustained low temperatures.

Heating costs could increase next year

Households are not currently expected to face a direct increase resulting from a recent change in the interpretation of a fuel tax exemption, but some other users of district heating could see higher costs.

The issue concerns combined heat and power (CHP) generation. This year, the state changed how an existing fuel tax exemption is interpreted, limiting its application to the amount of heat supplied to households.

Heating companies say the change could increase annual heating bills for institutions such as hospitals and schools by tens or even hundreds of thousands of Czech crowns.

World.title: Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague’s Roxy Club
World.content:
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.

Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.



A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.

Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.

More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.

Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.

The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.

The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.

The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.

Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

World.title: Prague and the 15-Minute City? Only for One in Seven Residents
World.content:
In the first year of the Friendly City Index, Prague ranked second among Central and Eastern European metropolises.

Yet only 13.82% of residents can reach most daily destinations – work, schools, shops, or healthcare – within 15 minutes. The best metropolises in the region remain closer to “30-minute cities.”



Young Czechs are closest to the ideal: 34% of those aged 18–24 said they can reach everyday destinations within 15 minutes. Middle-aged people, especially 45–54, scored the worst at 14.7%.

Smaller Czech cities outperform Prague. Olomouc (36%), Ostrava (29.7%), and Brno (21.8%) all ranked better in their categories. Compact urban structures and shorter distances explain much of this advantage. Polish cities also dominated the rankings, including Krakow, Szczecin, and Lublin.

Among metropolises, Warsaw leads with 15.9%. In other categories: Krakow (30.3%), Split (44%), Rijeka (53.3%), and Zadar (53.6%). Riga ranked worst at 9.8%, while Zagreb scored only 20%.

The smaller the city, the better the accessibility

Around 10–15% in metropolises, 30% in large cities, 40%+ in medium-sized cities, and over 50% in small cities. Even cities with metro systems like Prague or Bucharest show little improvement, confirming that compactness and urban structure matter more than infrastructure alone.

Transport habits

In Central and Eastern Europe, 46% rely on cars and 27% on public transport. In Czechia, the split is nearly even: 42.6% drive, 42.4% use public transport. Among 18–24-year-olds, more than half (51.1%) rely on public transport. Alternative mobility options such as bikes, scooters, and carsharing remain marginal.

Urban planner Peter Bednár explains: “The point is not that all journeys must be short, but that most daily activities can be done without a car. Achieving this requires higher density and a mix of functions. Without enough services and destinations nearby, the most practical walk still leads to the parked car.”

About the index

The Friendly City Index is an international survey on quality of life and urban development. In 2025, it covered 54 cities in nine countries with 4,500 respondents, including 500 in Czechia. The study was carried out by Syno International in partnership with Bolt.

World.title: Where to See Prague’s Best Autumn Colors Without Leaving the City
World.content:
Autumn in Prague does not have to mean a crowded walk across Petřín or a stroll through Stromovka.

Beyond the city’s best-known parks, forests, valleys and protected natural areas offer quieter routes where the changing season can be enjoyed without leaving Prague.

Many of these places are also surprisingly easy to reach. A tram, bus or train can take you close to the starting point, making it possible to plan a two- or three-hour walk without a car or a full-day trip.



Vinoř Park and the Satalice Pheasantry

In northeastern Prague, a marked trail links Vinoř Park with the Satalice Pheasantry through a narrow wooded valley.

The landscape is shaped by the Vinořský Stream, sandstone formations and small springs. Along the route, walkers can also come across traces of the area’s history, including rock carvings, the remains of an old hillfort and the entrance to a water cave.

The area is especially attractive in autumn, when old oaks and other trees turn yellow and brown. A long avenue between Vinoř and Satalice adds another distinctive feature to the route.

The official educational trail is about 3.5 kilometers long and takes roughly two hours. It starts near the Malá Obůrka pond and finishes close to the Chapel of St. Anne in Satalice. From there, buses and trains provide connections back into Prague.

Hvězda offers more than its main avenue

Hvězda Game Reserve is one of Prague’s better-known green spaces, but many visitors stay on the central avenue leading from Vypich to the white Renaissance summer palace.

The quieter parts begin once you leave the main route and head into the surrounding woodland.

Oaks, beeches and hornbeams dominate the reserve. According to Prague’s records, more than half of its forest stands are over 150 years old. Several notable beech trees date from plantings carried out after 1763, including a tree recognized as the oldest and largest beech in Prague.

A loop through the reserve can lead from the summer palace toward the pond and Světlička wetland meadow before returning along one of the smaller paths.

Dalejské Valley offers a different side of Prague

Prokopské Valley is familiar to many Prague residents, but the landscape continues west toward Řeporyje in the quieter Dalejské Valley.

Here, limestone cliffs, former quarries, open slopes and the Dalejský Stream create a landscape that changes frequently along the trail.

One option is to follow the green-marked hiking route from Řeporyje toward Hlubočepy. Rather than forming one continuous wall of autumn foliage, the valley combines yellow trees with exposed rock and brownish grass-covered slopes.

The area forms part of the northeastern section of the Bohemian Karst and is recognized for its geological features. Prague’s Nature Portal recommends following the valley along the stream.

Hostivař Forest Park changes after summer

Hostivař is closely associated with its reservoir and summer swimming, but the area takes on a different character once the bathing season ends.

The woods surrounding the water offer numerous walking routes, with more than 35 kilometers of paths and trails running through the forest park.

A shorter walk can follow the reservoir, while longer routes continue through woodland and meadows and pass the animal enclosure near the gamekeeper’s lodge. The Botič Stream Basin educational trail also crosses the area.

Autumn brings changing colors to the oak and larch trees, while the reservoir provides views that are particularly noticeable on cooler mornings.

World.title: New Dog Playground Opens in Central Prague with Agility Course
World.content:
Prague 1 now has its first public dog playground, giving dog owners in the city center a dedicated space for exercise and training.

The new facility is located on Ludvík Svobody Embankment, next to the Ministry of Transport’s traffic playground and close to Lannov Park. It has been open to the public since September 16.



At the center of the site is an approximately 92-meter-long agility course. It includes a tunnel, slalom poles, an A-frame and several jumping obstacles. The playground is freely accessible and does not require prior booking.

“Space in the center of Prague is very limited, so we want to use every suitable location to serve local residents,” said Kateřina Klasnová, Prague 1’s deputy mayor responsible for the environment.

The playground is currently unfenced, meaning dogs can enter and leave the area freely.

Some dog owners raised concerns about the lack of a fence during the opening, and Prague 1 said it would consider adding one.

An information board at the site explains the operating rules and provides instructions for using the agility equipment. The playground also has a waste bin and two dispensers containing bags for dog owners to clean up after their pets.

Responsibility for the site lies with the Prague 1 Department of the Environment. Visitors can report damaged equipment or other defects directly to the municipal district.

World.title: Emeli Sandé to Bring Her Biggest Hits to Prague at O2 universum
World.content:
One of Britain’s most acclaimed contemporary singers, Emeli Sandé, returns to Prague on November 3 for a special live concert at O2 universum.

The singer-songwriter will perform her best-known hits alongside music from her latest album, How Were We to Know.

Tickets are available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

Select 2 tickets and enter promo code EXPATPRAGUE at checkout. You’ll only pay for 1 ticket. The offer is valid from 14 to 21 September 2026 for tickets in sectors 102-109, subject to availability.

Emeli Sandé’s biggest hits

Sandé became an international star with songs including Next to Me, Heaven, Read All About It, Clown and My Kind of Love, combining soul, pop and powerful vocals with deeply personal songwriting.

Her debut album, Our Version of Events, became one of the most successful British albums of its era and was the UK’s best-selling album of 2012. It also produced several of her biggest hits and established Sandé as one of the country’s leading vocalists.

She further cemented her place in British music history with performances at both the opening and closing ceremonies of the London 2012 Olympic Games.

In Prague, fans can expect a set spanning her career, including songs from her latest album, How Were We to Know. Released as part of a new chapter in her career, the album combines her distinctive soul influences with a contemporary pop sound.

ADONXS joins as special guest

Sandé will be joined by ADONXS, singer, songwriter and one of the newer names on the Czech and Slovak pop scene.

ADONXS represented the Czech Republic at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, where he performed his song Kiss Kiss Goodbye. He has also released tracks including Wasted and Perfume, while his latest single, Cherry on Your Cake, continues his development as a songwriter and performer.

His appearance at O2 universum will open the evening before Sandé takes the stage.

Emeli Sandé live at O2 universum

The Prague concert will bring together Sandé’s most recognisable songs with material from her more recent work, giving audiences the chance to hear her signature voice in a live setting.

With hits that have become familiar to audiences around the world, the concert offers a chance to revisit songs such as Next to Me, Heaven and Read All About It, while discovering the latest direction of her music.

World.title: EU Citizens Can Vote in Czechia’s October Elections: Here’s How
World.content:
EU citizens living in Czechia can vote in the country’s municipal elections this October, but those who are not already registered will need to take action before election day.

The elections will take place on October 9 and 10, with voters in Prague choosing representatives for both the Prague City Assembly and their local municipal district.

EU citizens aged 18 or over who have permanent or registered temporary residence in Czechia can vote in municipal elections. However, they must be registered in the relevant electoral register.

Registering to vote

The deadline for registration is October 7, but the civic initiative Volby pro všechny recommends registering as soon as possible.

Its EU Voter Registration Tool generates the necessary application form and explains how to submit it to the relevant municipal or district office.

Registering early also means voters should receive their ballot papers at home before election day, giving them time to understand the unfamiliar Czech voting system. Those who register closer to the deadline will receive their ballots at the polling station.

There is also an important option for those who miss the registration deadline. According to Volby pro všechny, EU citizens will have a special possibility this year to register directly at their polling station on election day, provided they bring the required identification and proof of residence.

Find your polling station

Voters cannot simply choose any polling station. Their home address determines where they can vote.

The Polling Station Finder allows residents to enter their address and find the correct polling place. It can also create a calendar reminder for election day.

Voters should bring a valid ID or passport and the relevant Czech residence document.

What will Prague residents vote for?

Prague voters will cast two votes: one for the Prague City Assembly, covering the capital as a whole, and one for the council of their municipal district.

For those unfamiliar with the division of responsibilities, Volby pro všechny has created a “Who Does What?” quiz explaining which level of local government deals with different issues.

The organization has also published an overview of political parties and groups and is preparing a quiz that will allow users to compare their answers on policy questions with the positions of Czech political parties.

A guide in 23 EU languages

Volby pro všechny has also prepared a seven-step checklist for EU citizens, available as a downloadable PDF in 23 EU languages.

For EU citizens who have never voted in Czechia before, the resources provide a straightforward way to check their registration, find their polling station and understand what to expect on election day.

World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Surprising choice by TimeOut: this Budapest neighbourhood is among the world’s coolest
World.content:
A perhaps unexpected corner of Budapest has been named among the world’s coolest neighbourhoods by Time Out. Rákóczi Square and its surrounding streets ranked 19th globally and seventh among European neighbourhoods in the magazine’s 2026 selection, putting a part of the Hungarian capital with a complicated past firmly on the international travel map.

The result may surprise visitors who associate Budapest’s fashionable districts primarily with the nightlife of District VII, the grand boulevards of Pest or the elegant streets around the Danube. Rákóczi Square, in District VIII, is a rather different proposition.

According to Time Out, the appeal lies partly in the neighbourhood’s mixture of local character, independent businesses, food, nightlife and changing public spaces. Around Rákóczi Square, century-old market culture now exists alongside new cafés, restaurants, pedestrianised streets and one of Budapest’s newest metro lines.

What exactly is the Rákóczi Square neighbourhood?

Rákóczi Square is not the name of an official Budapest district. The area highlighted by Time Out broadly covers the square itself and parts of the surrounding Csarnok neighbourhood in Józsefváros, Budapest’s eighth district.

At its centre stands the Rákóczi Square Market Hall, one of the city’s historic covered markets. Nearby streets such as Déri Miksa Street and Bacsó Béla Street have undergone major changes in recent years, helping to create a more pedestrian-friendly environment.

Photo: Alpár Kató / Daily News Hungary

Time Out also points to the area’s increasingly varied food scene. Traditional market stalls and inexpensive Hungarian eateries now sit alongside ramen restaurants, Korean food, Italian dishes, speciality cafés and modern bakeries.

Unlike Budapest’s established party district, however, Rákóczi Square has not become a single-purpose entertainment zone. Residential buildings, the market, small businesses and new hospitality venues continue to coexist.

If you missed it – Skip the tourist crowds: 7 secret thermal baths in Hungary most foreign visitors never discover

Rákóczi Square began as a livestock market

The history of Rákóczi Square stretches back to the late 18th century. Municipal documents show that the space had a commercial function from an early stage and was previously known as Borjúpiac, or Calf Market, because livestock trading took place there.

It received its present name in 1874, honouring Francis II Rákóczi, leader of the early 18th-century Hungarian uprising against Habsburg rule.

The neighbourhood changed dramatically as Budapest expanded in the late 19th century. One of the most important developments was the construction of the Rákóczi Square Market Hall, designed by István Rozinay and Pál Klunzinger.

According to the market hall’s historical overview, it opened in 1897 as Budapest’s second numbered market hall. Horse-drawn carts were originally able to enter the building to deliver goods.

The market later experienced periods of decline. Its closure was even discussed in the 1930s, while a serious fire damaged the building in 1988. Following restoration, it reopened in 1991.

A very different reputation in the 20th century

For decades, Rákóczi Square was known in Budapest for something other than food and architecture.

From the socialist era onwards, the square and nearby streets became strongly associated with street prostitution and the city’s underground economy. That chapter of the area’s history became widely known through director György Dobray’s 1988 documentary K – Film a prostituáltakról (Rákóczi tér).

The National Film Institute describes the film as a portrait of women working in what was then one of the best-known centres of Budapest’s sex trade.

This history matters because the neighbourhood’s transformation is not simply a case of a fashionable area becoming even more fashionable. Rákóczi Square spent decades carrying a distinctly rough reputation among Budapest residents.

Metro and public-space projects changed the area

One of the biggest physical changes came with the construction of Budapest Metro Line M4.

The square was comprehensively redesigned as part of the project, with new paving, landscaping, water features and public spaces surrounding the metro station. The refurbished square was largely completed by 2013.

Changes have since spread into neighbouring streets. Déri Miksa Street was redesigned to provide more greenery and space for pedestrians, while the section of Bacsó Béla Street closest to the square was transformed into a permanent pedestrian area in 2022.

These projects have helped shift the focus away from traffic and towards public life at street level.

What’s next? The Hungarian passport has never been so valuable: it’s among the world’s strongest travel documents

Why Rákóczi Square feels different from other parts of Budapest

What makes the area especially interesting is that the transformation remains incomplete.

The grand 19th-century market hall, ageing Budapest apartment blocks, memories of the socialist period, everyday market trade and contemporary cafés all occupy roughly the same few streets. The modern architecture of the M4 metro station adds yet another layer.

That makes Rákóczi Square less polished than some of Budapest’s better-known tourist districts, but arguably more revealing of how the city itself is changing.

Time Out’s ranking therefore says something broader about Budapest. International attention is increasingly moving beyond the Hungarian capital’s established landmarks and nightlife hubs towards neighbourhoods where everyday city life, history and urban renewal are still visibly mixed together.

World.title: How to find a job in Hungary in 2026: Salaries, job sites and what foreigners need to know
World.content:
Want to find a job in Hungary in 2026? International companies continue to recruit foreign-language speakers, particularly in Budapest, while engineering, technology, logistics, business services and tourism also provide opportunities. The less straightforward part is navigating Hungarian salaries, language requirements and – for non-EU citizens – an immigration system that has changed substantially in recent years.

Hungary employed around 112,900 foreign nationals in July 2026, 6,900 more than a year earlier, according to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH). At the same time, unemployment remained relatively low, although hiring conditions vary considerably between sectors and regions.

So where should foreigners look for work, which jobs can be found without speaking Hungarian, and what salary can applicants realistically expect?

Where to find a job in Hungary in 2026

For most applicants, the search starts online. Three platforms are particularly useful for people looking for jobs in Hungary: Profession.hu, CVonline.hu and LinkedIn.

Profession.hu

Profession.hu is Hungary’s largest and most established general job portal and should usually be the first stop for anyone searching across a broad range of industries.

It carries vacancies from major multinational companies as well as Hungarian employers, with positions ranging from administration and sales to engineering, finance, manufacturing and IT.

The site is mainly in Hungarian, but many s – particularly those from international employers – are published partly or entirely in English.

CVonline.hu

CVonline.hu is another major Hungarian recruitment platform, listing thousands of jobs across the country.

It can be particularly useful as a second search channel because not every employer advertises on the same platforms. Applicants can search by profession, location and employment type and upload a CV for recruiters to find.

LinkedIn Jobs

LinkedIn is especially important for foreign professionals and anyone looking for English-speaking employment in Hungary.

Multinational companies operating in Budapest frequently use LinkedIn to recruit for technology, finance, business services, sales, HR, marketing and management positions. It can also be more useful than Hungarian-language portals for applicants who do not yet speak Hungarian.

Rather than relying on one platform, jobseekers should monitor all three and set up alerts for relevant positions.

The EU’s EURES employment service also recommends using Hungary’s public employment services, private recruitment agencies, company career pages and professional networks. EURES notes that jobseekers cannot legally be charged for the services of employment agencies in Hungary.

A useful additional tactic is to identify major employers in your sector and check their own career pages regularly. Large international companies often advertise vacancies directly before – or instead of – placing them on general job portals.

If you missed it: Working in Hungary could become easier for non-EU professionals under new EU rules

Can you find a job in Hungary without speaking Hungarian?

Yes, particularly in Budapest, but it depends heavily on the profession.

The capital offers by far the widest selection of jobs where English is the main working language. Multinational business service centres regularly recruit employees in customer service, finance, accounting, procurement, IT, HR and sales.

Speaking another European language can be a major advantage. German, French, Dutch, Italian and Nordic languages are frequently sought by multinational employers serving international markets from Hungary.

Technology is another comparatively international sector. Software development, cybersecurity, data analysis, infrastructure and engineering positions are often available in English.

Outside multinational companies, however, Hungarian becomes significantly more important. Jobs involving local customers, public administration, healthcare, education or smaller Hungarian-owned businesses commonly require at least conversational Hungarian.

Which sectors offer the best opportunities in Hungary?

There is no single sector guaranteeing easy employment, but several areas regularly recruit skilled workers.

EURES identifies IT and new technologies, automotive manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, tourism, hospitality, transport and logistics among sectors with longer-term employment potential in Hungary.

Business service centres are particularly relevant for foreigners. Budapest has developed into a major Central European hub for shared-service and business-service operations, with international companies employing workers who communicate with customers or colleagues across Europe.

Engineering and manufacturing also remain important, particularly around major industrial centres such as Győr, Debrecen, Kecskemét and Szeged.

The labour market is not uniformly booming, however. Companies have become more cautious about recruitment following weaker economic growth, and demand varies considerably by profession. Specialised qualifications, technical expertise, digital skills and additional languages can therefore make a substantial difference.

How much can you earn in Hungary in 2026?

Hungarian wages remain considerably lower than those in Austria or Germany, although salaries at multinational companies and in highly skilled professions can be substantially above the national level.

According to the latest KSH earnings figures, the average gross monthly salary for full-time employees reached HUF 745,500 (around EUR 2,060) in July 2026. Average net earnings were HUF 523,300 (around EUR 1,450).

However, the median provides a more realistic picture of what a typical worker earns.

The gross median salary was HUF 618,200 (around EUR 1,710) per month, meaning half of full-time employees earned less than this amount. Median net earnings stood at HUF 437,900, or approximately EUR 1,210.

Hungary’s statutory monthly minimum wage in 2026 is HUF 322,800 (around EUR 890), while the guaranteed minimum for jobs requiring at least secondary-level qualifications or vocational training is HUF 373,200 (around EUR 1,030).

Applicants should always check whether a salary is quoted gross or net. Hungarian job s and employment contracts normally refer to gross salary, before tax and social contributions.

What’s next? New survey shows what Hungarians think about migration from poorer countries and guest workers

Budapest or elsewhere in Hungary?

For foreigners without Hungarian language skills, Budapest is generally the easiest place to start.

The capital contains the highest concentration of multinational headquarters, international business centres, financial institutions, technology companies and tourism-related employers.

However, opportunities outside Budapest should not be ignored.

Győr has a major automotive and manufacturing sector, Debrecen has attracted significant international investment in recent years, Kecskemét is another important automotive centre, and Szeged is developing rapidly as new large-scale investments arrive.

Foreigners with engineering or manufacturing experience may therefore find attractive opportunities outside Budapest, where living costs can also be lower.

Do EU citizens need a work permit in Hungary?

Citizens of EU and EEA countries have a comparatively straightforward route into the Hungarian labour market.

They generally do not need a Hungarian work permit to take employment in the country. However, those staying for more than 90 days must comply with Hungarian residence registration and address-registration requirements.

This means that a German, Italian, Polish or other EU citizen can usually apply for Hungarian jobs in much the same way as a Hungarian applicant, although administrative steps still follow after relocation.

What about non-EU citizens?

The situation is considerably more complicated for applicants from outside the EU and EEA.

Hungary operates several residence categories depending on nationality, qualifications and type of employment, including employment-purpose permits, the Hungarian Card, the EU Blue Card, National Card and permits connected with investment or intra-company transfers.

Rules for lower-skilled guest workers became substantially stricter in 2026.

Since 6 June 2026, new applications for Hungary’s guest-worker residence permit cannot currently be submitted, because the relevant government decree no longer designates countries whose nationals can submit new applications under that particular category.

A separate standard employment-purpose permit remains available to nationals of certain countries under specific conditions, while highly qualified employees may qualify through different routes.

Non-EU applicants should therefore establish which residence category applies to them before accepting a job offer or making relocation plans. Official information is available from Hungary’s National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing.

How should you apply for jobs in Hungary?

A one- or two-page CV is generally appropriate for professional vacancies.

For international companies, an English CV is normally sufficient if the  itself is in English. Applicants targeting Hungarian employers may benefit from preparing a Hungarian version as well.

Foreign applicants should clearly state their language skills and, where relevant, their existing right to work in Hungary. If employer-sponsored immigration paperwork will be required, it is better to clarify this early in the recruitment process.

Applications should also be tailored to the position. Sending hundreds of identical CVs is usually less effective than identifying suitable employers and adjusting the application to highlight relevant experience.

LinkedIn can be particularly useful here: following companies, recruiters and managers in your field can reveal vacancies before they reach the largest job portals.

Is it difficult to find a job in Hungary as a foreigner?

The answer depends largely on qualifications, languages and salary expectations.

Foreign professionals with sought-after technical skills, international business experience or multiple languages can have good prospects, particularly in Budapest. Applicants seeking entry-level English-only positions face stronger competition, while Hungarian language skills open up a considerably larger part of the labour market.

Anyone planning to find a job in Hungary in 2026 should therefore start with three questions: Is my profession in demand? Will a Hungarian salary cover the lifestyle I expect? And do I already have the legal right to work in the country?

Once those questions are answered, Profession.hu, CVonline.hu and LinkedIn provide three of the best places to begin the actual search.

Read here more about guest workers in Hungary

World.title: Wizz Air rethink could reshape ticket prices and routes across Europe
World.content:
Wizz Air is putting the brakes on one of the most ambitious growth plans in European aviation. The Hungarian-founded low-cost carrier has reduced its planned winter capacity, dramatically lowered its long-term fleet ambitions and is concentrating more heavily on Central and Eastern Europe – changes that could eventually affect both ticket prices and the routes available to passengers.

The shift does not mean that Wizz Air is shrinking. It still plans to carry substantially more passengers by the end of the decade. But the emphasis has clearly changed from expansion at almost any cost towards profitability, stronger existing markets and more careful decisions about where aircraft are deployed.

For passengers, the important question is what happens when one of Europe’s biggest low-cost airlines decides it no longer wants to grow quite so aggressively.

Wizz Air cuts winter capacity by 5%

The most immediate change concerns the coming winter.

Wizz Air announced on 17 September that it had reduced its planned capacity for the second half of its current financial year by 5%, citing geopolitical instability and volatile fuel prices. At the same time, the airline said stronger-than-expected summer revenues had allowed it to improve its near-term revenue outlook.

The wider aviation industry is facing a major increase in jet-fuel costs linked to the conflict involving Iran. Wizz Air is comparatively well protected in the short term: Reuters reported that around 80% of its fuel requirements over the next 12 months are hedged at prices significantly below current market levels.

Nevertheless, cutting planned capacity means fewer seats than the airline previously intended to put on sale.

That does not necessarily mean 5% of Wizz Air routes will disappear. Airlines can reduce capacity by cutting frequencies, operating fewer flights during weaker periods, postponing new routes or removing poorly performing services altogether. But it does mean Wizz Air will be more selective about where it flies.

Source: depositphotos.com

If you missed it: Wizz Air pays out EUR 184 million to passengers over two years – but many may have missed out on compensation

From Wizz 500 to a fleet of 335 aircraft

The longer-term change is even more significant.

Only a few years ago, Wizz Air’s highly ambitious “Wizz 500” strategy envisaged a fleet of 500 aircraft by 2030. Its 2024 annual report explicitly presented that target as a central part of the company’s growth strategy.

The new target is very different.

By financial year 2030, Wizz Air now plans to operate 335 aircraft, generate EUR 10 billion in annual revenue, carry 127 million passengers and achieve a 10% operating margin. CEO József Váradi said the airline would concentrate growth on its core markets, restore fleet productivity and mature its existing network.

In other words, the planned 2030 fleet is now roughly one-third smaller than envisioned under the original Wizz 500 strategy.

Reuters Breakingviews described the change as Wizz Air “clipping its wings” after several difficult years.

What went wrong at Wizz Air?

There was no single cause.

The airline was first hit by the pandemic, followed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and repeated disruption in Israel and the Middle East. Its attempted expansion further east also proved difficult.

In 2025, Wizz Air decided to close its Abu Dhabi operation after six years, citing geopolitical instability, airspace closures, restrictions on market access and operational difficulties in the region.

It subsequently closed its Vienna base in March 2026 after concluding that higher airport charges, taxes and ground-handling costs were no longer compatible with its ultra-low-cost model.

Perhaps the most damaging problem, however, came from the aircraft themselves.

Problems with Pratt & Whitney GTF engines forced dozens of Wizz Air aircraft out of service. In the financial year ending March 2025, operating profit dropped 62% to EUR 167.5 million, with 37 aircraft grounded because of engine-related maintenance problems.

Fuel has since become another major challenge. In the April–June 2026 quarter, Wizz Air reported an operating loss of EUR 183.3 million as higher fuel costs proved difficult to pass fully on to passengers accustomed to very low fares.

Could Wizz Air ticket prices rise?

This is where the new strategy becomes particularly relevant to passengers.

A slower expansion does not automatically mean higher fares. Wizz Air’s ultra-low-cost business model still depends on filling aircraft with price-sensitive travellers, and the airline competes aggressively with Ryanair and other carriers on many European routes.

However, less capacity can reduce downward pressure on ticket prices, particularly on routes where several low-cost carriers are simultaneously cutting planned flights.

Wizz Air has already said that it intends to increase revenue generated per available seat kilometre as its network matures. Its September update also improved the expected second-quarter revenue-per-seat performance from a decline to roughly flat year-on-year.

That suggests the company is increasingly focused not simply on carrying more passengers, but on earning more sustainably from the capacity it already operates.

For travellers, that could mean fewer extreme bargain fares on some routes or during busy periods. But competition, demand and fuel prices will remain crucial, so an across-the-board rise in Wizz Air ticket prices cannot be assumed.

Which Wizz Air routes could be affected?

The strategy gives a strong indication of where Wizz Air wants to concentrate its aircraft.

The company says it is refocusing on Central and Eastern Europe and selected growth markets. Its 2026 annual report states that aircraft have been reallocated towards cities including Budapest, Warsaw, Katowice, Bucharest, Sofia, Tirana, Chisinau and several other CEE bases.

That could make markets where Wizz Air already has substantial scale relatively well protected.

The withdrawal from Abu Dhabi and Vienna demonstrates the other side of the strategy: locations that are expensive, operationally difficult or insufficiently profitable are less likely to be maintained simply for the sake of network growth.

Passengers should therefore expect the airline to become more willing to move aircraft between bases, reduce weaker routes and concentrate flights where it believes it has a sustainable competitive advantage.

What does the rethink mean for Budapest?

For Hungarian passengers, there is an important distinction:

Wizz Air’s retreat from aggressive expansion does not currently look like a retreat from Hungary.

Quite the opposite.

Budapest is specifically among the airports receiving reallocated capacity under the airline’s strategy, while Central and Eastern Europe is now at the heart of the company’s renewed focus.

Wizz Air is therefore still likely to regard Budapest as one of its strategically important bases even as it becomes more selective elsewhere.

The bigger change is philosophical. The era in which Wizz Air’s overriding objective was simply to become dramatically larger appears to be ending.

The airline still intends to grow from its current fleet of roughly 270 aircraft to 335 by 2030 and carry 127 million passengers a year. But profitability, route quality and cost discipline now matter more than reaching an eye-catching aircraft target.

For European passengers, that could eventually mean a smaller range of marginal routes and fewer seats on weaker connections, while major Wizz Air markets receive more concentrated capacity. Whether it also means higher fares will depend on how much capacity rival airlines add – or remove – over the next few years.

The Wizz Air rethink is therefore not the end of its low-cost growth story. It is a significant change in how, and where, that growth will happen.

As we wrote earlier, Wizz Air restarts popular flights to multiple destinations from Budapest

World.title: Fuel prices in Hungary buck EU trend – but diesel is now climbing fast
World.content:
Fuel prices in Hungary stood out sharply from the rest of the European Union in August 2026, as petrol, diesel and lubricant costs surged across almost the entire bloc. While prices in the EU were 23.8% higher than a year earlier, Hungary recorded an increase of just 1.3% – the smallest among all 27 member states.

The Hungarian result is particularly striking because 18 EU countries recorded annual increases of more than 20%, according to Eurostat data reported by Anadolu Agency.

Bulgaria saw the steepest annual rise, at 34.5%, followed by Lithuania at 28.8%, Finland at 27.6%, Germany at 27.5% and France at 27.4%. At the other end of the ranking, Hungary’s 1.3% was followed by Sweden at 6.1% and Ireland at 11.7%.

However, the latest figures from Hungarian filling stations show why the Eurostat ranking does not necessarily mean motorists in Hungary are currently enjoying cheap fuel.

Fuel prices in Hungary have bucked the EU trend for months

August was not an isolated result.

In June, fuel and lubricant prices increased by only 2.3% year-on-year in Hungary, again the smallest rise anywhere in the EU. Across the bloc, the corresponding increase was 13.7%.

The difference became even more pronounced in July. EU prices were 16.9% higher than a year earlier, while Hungary was one of only two member states to record a decline, with prices edging down by 0.1%.

The August figures therefore extend a three-month pattern in which Hungary has remained at or very close to the bottom of the EU ranking for annual fuel-price growth.

Month-on-month movements in August also favoured Hungarian petrol users. Across the EU, diesel prices jumped 8.3% from July and petrol became 3.3% more expensive. Hungary, by contrast, recorded a 0.6% monthly decrease in petrol prices, according to the Eurostat figures reported by Anadolu.

But Hungarian motorists are now paying much more at the pump

The important distinction is that Eurostat’s figures compare August 2026 with August 2025. They do not show what has happened at Hungarian filling stations during September.

And the most recent picture is far less reassuring.

According to Hungarian fuel-price monitoring site Holtankoljak.hu, the nationwide average price on 22 September stood at HUF 636 (around EUR 1.76) per litre for 95-octane petrol and HUF 709 (around EUR 1.96) for diesel.

At the end of August, the site’s weekly figures showed petrol at around HUF 591 and diesel at HUF 677 per litre. This means prices have moved noticeably higher within a matter of weeks, with diesel remaining particularly expensive.

The figures underline an important caveat: recording the EU’s smallest annual price increase does not automatically mean Hungary has the cheapest fuel in the bloc.

Hungary introduces support over rising diesel prices

The increase in diesel prices has already prompted government intervention.

On 11 September, the Hungarian government said the retail price of diesel had risen by more than HUF 120 (around EUR 0.33) per litre since January. It subsequently announced financial support for certain private diesel-car owners and agricultural users.

Under the measure, people who owned a small or medium-powered diesel car of no more than 150 horsepower on 1 January 2026 will receive HUF 5,000 (around EUR 13.80) per month until the end of the year, for a total of HUF 20,000 (around EUR 55). The government said close to one million motorists could be covered by the scheme. Details: Hungary reveals new diesel subsidy details: Who gets EUR 55 and when will payments begin?

Agricultural users will meanwhile be able to reclaim the full excise duty included in diesel prices until the end of 2026.

Why are European fuel prices rising?

The pressure is not unique to Hungary.

The European Commission said earlier in September that continued instability in the Middle East and broader geopolitical uncertainty were creating significant volatility in crude oil and petroleum-product markets, particularly for diesel and jet fuel.

At the same time, the Commission stressed that there was no immediate oil supply problem in the EU, with demand being met through increased European refinery production, alternative imports and existing commercial and emergency stocks.

For Hungarian motorists, this creates a somewhat contradictory picture. Fuel prices in Hungary have increased far less over the past year than in almost any other EU country, and the country has repeatedly ranked at the favourable end of Eurostat’s comparisons.

But the rapid rise in diesel prices during recent weeks shows that Hungary is not insulated from the pressures affecting the wider European market. The next Eurostat figures will reveal whether Hungary can continue to buck the EU trend – or whether September’s increases mark the beginning of a very different picture.

World.title: 12 Michelin Key hotels in Hungary – what makes each one stand out?
World.content:
Hungary has secured 12 places in the 2026 Michelin Key hotel selection, with ten properties in Budapest and two beyond the capital. Two Budapest hotels received Two Michelin Keys, while another ten properties earned One Key, giving travellers an unusually varied collection ranging from grand Art Nouveau palaces to a tiny adults-only hotel by Lake Balaton.

All 12 Hungarian properties in this year’s selection were also recognised in 2025. The only hotel to disappear from last year’s 13-property Hungarian list is BOTANIQ Castle of Tura, whose business model has since changed.

What does a Michelin Key actually mean?

The Michelin Key is essentially the hotel counterpart of the restaurant world’s Michelin Star. Inspectors visit anonymously and consider five broad criteria: architecture and interior design, the quality and consistency of service, personality and character, value for money, and how significantly the property contributes to the experience of its destination.

One Key signifies what Michelin describes as a very special stay, Two Keys an exceptional stay, and Three Keys an extraordinary one. No Hungarian hotel currently holds the maximum Three-Key rating, but two have reached the second level.

Michelin Key hotels in Hungary with Two Keys

Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest – Two Michelin Keys

Few hotels are as closely tied to Budapest’s cityscape: the Four Seasons occupies the spectacular Gresham Palace, completed in 1906, directly opposite the Chain Bridge and looking towards Buda Castle. Its restored Art Nouveau architecture is combined with traditionally elegant rooms, while the top-floor spa includes an infinity pool overlooking the city. The combination of internationally recognisable architecture, one of Budapest’s most prestigious locations and a building that is itself a landmark makes the Gresham Palace much more than simply a luxury hotel.

Source: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest

Matild Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel – Two Michelin Keys

Matild Palace occupies one of the twin Belle Époque palaces commissioned by Archduchess Marie Clotilde near Elizabeth Bridge and has been transformed into a 130-room hotel without erasing the building’s historic identity. Guests find contemporary luxury inside, alongside Danube views, the Swan Spa, Spago by Wolfgang Puck and the rooftop bar The Duchess. It stands out for combining a genuine piece of Budapest architectural history with a distinctly modern hospitality concept rather than treating its historic shell merely as decoration.

Photo: Matild Palace

If you missed it: FirstMed and Daily News Hungary bring diplomats together for exclusive Budapest reception – photos, video

Eight One-Key hotels in Budapest

Anantara New York Palace Budapest – One Michelin Key

The defining feature of the Anantara is the legendary New York Café, which opened in 1894 and remains one of Budapest’s most elaborate historic interiors, with frescoes, chandeliers, gilding and monumental columns. The hotel continues that grand style in its rooms and suites and adds a 500-square-metre spa in the middle of the busy Grand Boulevard district. Few hotels allow guests to sleep in the same building as one of Budapest’s most famous cafés, making the property particularly strong for travellers interested in the city’s literary and architectural past.

Dorothea Hotel, Budapest, Autograph Collection – One Michelin Key

Opened in 2023, the Dorothea combines three buildings from different periods into a single 216-room hotel designed by Italian architect Piero Lissoni. Contemporary interiors contain references to Hungarian craftsmanship, while its large colonnaded atrium, garden restaurant and rooftop dining create very different spaces within the same property. What distinguishes the Dorothea is the way it uses several layers of Budapest architecture rather than relying on a single historic building or a purely contemporary design concept.

Hotel Clark Budapest – One Michelin Key

Hotel Clark sits in an almost impossible-to-beat location between the Chain Bridge and the Buda Castle funicular, with many rooms opening directly towards the Danube. Its interiors are contemporary and playful, while the Leo Rooftop has become known for its panoramic views over central Budapest. The hotel’s strongest characteristic is therefore its relationship with the city outside: some of Budapest’s most recognisable landmarks are effectively part of the view from the building.

Visual plan: Clark Ádám Square renovation. Source: budapest.hu

If you missed it: Inside Hotel Clark Budapest: Luxury, design and Danube views at the foot of the Chain Bridge

Kimpton BEM Budapest – One Michelin Key

One of the newest names on Budapest’s luxury-hotel scene, Kimpton BEM opened in 2024 inside a restored 19th-century palace on the Buda side of the Danube. Designer Marcel Wanders mixed the historic architecture with unusually bold contemporary interiors, incorporating references to Hungarian nature, Lake Balaton, mythology and animals, alongside the Agos restaurant and rooftop feNNen Skybar. Among the Michelin Key hotels in Hungary, it is particularly distinctive for rejecting restrained hotel minimalism in favour of theatrical colours, motifs and visual storytelling.

Kozmo Hotel Suites & Spa – One Michelin Key

The Kozmo occupies a protected building erected in 1910 that once housed what the hotel describes as the largest telecommunications centre in Central and Eastern Europe. Its monumental staircase, tower, high ceilings and historic architectural details have been retained, while contemporary art and large rooms and suites give the former institutional building an entirely different purpose. Its appeal lies in this unusual conversion: instead of a former palace or aristocratic residence, guests are staying inside a grand piece of Budapest’s early telecommunications history.

Párisi Udvar Hotel Budapest – One Michelin Key

Párisi Udvar is arguably the most visually extravagant property on the list, occupying a former shopping arcade whose architecture brings together Art Nouveau, Gothic, Moorish and Arabic influences. Its spectacular passage features details including Zsolnay ceramics, stained glass associated with Miksa Róth and a huge glass dome, while the guestrooms themselves adopt a more restrained contemporary style. What makes it exceptional as a hotel setting is that the lobby is not simply inspired by historic Budapest architecture: it is one of the city centre’s remarkable surviving architectural spaces.

Verno House – One Michelin Key

Verno House takes a smaller-scale approach, with 48 rooms in central Budapest near Szabadság Square and St Stephen’s Basilica. Rather than palace-like grandeur, its interiors use warm colours, rich textures and greenery to create the feeling of an urban retreat, complemented by an intimate spa and the Flava restaurant. That quieter, residential character gives Verno a different identity from Budapest’s monumental five-star hotels and makes it one of the more intimate properties in the Hungarian Michelin Key selection.

W Budapest – One Michelin Key

W Budapest occupies the historic Drechsler Palace on UNESCO-listed Andrássy Avenue, directly opposite the Hungarian State Opera House. Its design deliberately plays with contrasts – ballet and nightlife, historic architecture and modern luxury – with references to Hungarian culture, chess and even Harry Houdini appearing throughout the interiors. The result is one of the boldest reinterpretations of a Budapest landmark, with the former palace functioning not as a solemn heritage hotel but as an intentionally energetic contemporary space.

Two Michelin Key hotels in Hungary outside Budapest

The 2026 selection is heavily dominated by the capital, but its two non-Budapest hotels demonstrate that Michelin is also looking at smaller destinations. One is beside Lake Balaton, while the other forms part of a remarkable hospitality and gastronomic complex in Tata.

Hotel Petit Bois, Balatonfüred – One Michelin Key

Hotel Petit Bois is by far one of the smallest properties in the group, with just 13 rooms in the Lake Balaton resort town of Balatonfüred. The adults-only hotel combines Belle Époque elegance with contemporary technology and offers a rooftop restaurant, terrace and pool, while rooms look towards either its namesake park or the lake. Its scale is what makes it particularly interesting: Michelin recognition here is attached to a highly intimate boutique experience rather than the grand urban luxury offered by most of the Budapest hotels.

Platán Manor, Tata – One Michelin Key

Platán Manor stands immediately beside Tata Castle and offers just ten individually designed rooms overlooking the castle and its restored moat, with additional accommodation available nearby at Platán Street. Its unusual Mirror Spa has been constructed in the moat itself, while the wider Platán complex has a particularly strong culinary identity, including Platán Gourmet, which retained Two Michelin Stars in the 2025 restaurant guide. The combination of tiny scale, castle-side setting, destination gastronomy and spa facilities gives Platán an identity that no city-centre luxury hotel on the Hungarian list can really replicate.

Photo: Erika Gáncs

Budapest dominates, but the list is more varied than it first appears

The 12 Michelin Key hotels in Hungary reveal a clear strength in historic-building conversions: former palaces, a shopping arcade and even an early telecommunications centre have all become high-end hotels. Yet Michelin’s inclusion of the much smaller Petit Bois and Platán Manor shows that size, an international hotel brand and a Budapest address are not prerequisites for recognition.

The 2026 results also underline how closely Hungary’s luxury hospitality offer has become tied to architecture, history and gastronomy. For international visitors, that means the Michelin Key list can serve not only as a guide to where to sleep, but also as a compact introduction to some very different ways of experiencing Budapest, Lake Balaton and historic Tata.

World.title: Hungarian central bank makes a move towards the euro
World.content:
Hungary’s central bank has decided to lower its medium-term inflation target from 3 per cent to 2.5 per cent from 2028, a move that could support Hungary euro adoption by bringing domestic monetary policy closer to conditions prevailing in the euro area. However, several other economic, fiscal and legal requirements still need to be met before Hungary can introduce the common currency.

The Monetary Council of the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) decided after reviewing its inflation target that the new 2.5 per cent target will take effect on 1 January 2028, HVG reported.

The current target is 3 per cent, with a tolerance band of plus or minus one percentage point. According to the central bank, lowering the target brings Hungary closer to regional practice and to the European Central Bank’s 2 per cent inflation target.

The change will nevertheless begin influencing monetary policy before 2028 because central banks set interest rates based on their medium-term inflation outlook rather than current inflation alone.

Lower inflation target supports Hungary euro adoption

The MNB said Hungary’s economic convergence with the euro area and the decline in inflation expectations created room to lower the target. The central bank expects a lower-inflation environment to contribute to more predictable economic conditions and, over the longer term, lower nominal interest rates and financing costs.

It also explicitly linked the decision to Hungary’s preparations for joining the euro area.

MNB Governor Mihály Varga said earlier in September that euro adoption required a disciplined and coordinated strategy between monetary and fiscal policymakers. He said Hungary should introduce the euro in a way that allows the economy to continue converging both before and after joining the currency union.

The Hungarian government has meanwhile said it aims to meet the Maastricht criteria required for euro adoption around 2030. That does not amount to a formal date for replacing the forint with the euro: meeting the criteria would be a prerequisite for entering the final stages of the process.

If you missed it – Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%

What Hungary still has to do before introducing the euro

Lower inflation is only one element of euro-area accession.

EU countries seeking to adopt the single currency must meet convergence requirements covering price stability, sustainable public finances, long-term interest rates and exchange-rate stability. They must also participate in the Exchange Rate Mechanism, known as ERM II, for at least two years without severe exchange-rate tensions.

Hungary is not currently part of ERM II, and the European Commission states that the country has no formal target date for adopting the euro.

The Commission’s June 2026 Convergence Report also concluded that Hungary did not yet fulfil the conditions for joining the euro area. At the time of the assessment, Hungary failed the price-stability criterion, while Hungarian legislation, including rules governing the MNB, was not considered fully compatible with requirements for participation in the Eurosystem.

Inflation has since fallen, which helps explain why the MNB now sees scope for setting a lower target.

Public finances remain a major challenge

Fiscal policy remains another important part of the equation. Hungary is still subject to the EU’s excessive deficit procedure, although the procedure is currently held in abeyance following the Commission’s assessment of government measures.

The European Commission’s spring forecast projected Hungary’s general government deficit at 6.2 per cent of GDP in 2026 and 5.8 per cent in 2027. Public debt was forecast to rise from 74.6 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 75.1 per cent in 2026 and 76.8 per cent in 2027.

As a recent HVG analysis noted, euro preparations therefore require coordination between the government’s fiscal policy and the MNB’s monetary policy.

The reduction of the inflation target is a concrete change on the monetary side. For Hungary euro adoption to progress further, however, the country will also need sustainable public finances, exchange-rate stability, legal alignment and eventually entry into ERM II. The latest MNB decision therefore marks one step in a process that is likely to extend over several years.

What’s next? New analysis: Hungary’s government is full steam ahead with adopting the euro

Just in: interest rate decision – Monetary Council leaves base rate unchanged

The Monetary Council of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) left the 5.50 per cent base rate unchanged at its meeting on Tuesday, the central bank announced.

Source: MTI

Both ends of the interest rate corridor also remained unchanged: the overnight (O/N) deposit rate stands at 4.50 per cent, whilst the upper end of the corridor, the overnight (O/N) lending rate, stands at 6.50 per cent.

The decision was in line with analysts’ expectations.

The committee last cut the base rate in August, by a unanimous decision, by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent.

World.title: BREAKING! Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers
World.content:
Hungarian immunity rights have returned to the spotlight after prosecutors asked parliament to suspend the immunity of two former government ministers, while a separate request has also been filed concerning Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The three requests relate to separate criminal investigations and do not in themselves constitute findings of guilt.

According to 24.hu, prosecutors have requested the suspension of the parliamentary immunity of former culture and innovation minister Balázs Hankó, a Fidesz MP, and former national development minister Miklós Seszták, a KDNP MP. The authorities have also renewed proceedings concerning Magyar over an incident dating back to 2024.

Hungarian immunity rights and the investigation into Miklós Seszták

The most serious allegations outlined by prosecutors concern Seszták, who served as national development minister between 2014 and 2018.

According to the prosecution’s account cited by 24.hu, investigators suspect that Seszták and the former chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management company received more than HUF 11 billion (approximately EUR 30.4 million) in unlawful benefits between 2015 and 2018 from a representative of companies that had contractual links to the state-owned Volánbusz transport company.

Investigators also suspect that a representative of a construction group offered to return 10 percent of the value of certain contracts to Seszták through an intermediary in exchange for anticipated state orders. Prosecutors say the company group won several major state projects between 2015 and 2018 and allegedly provided more than HUF 1 billion, or around EUR 2.8 million, in unlawful benefits.

The broader Volán investigation is examining suspected losses of around HUF 10 billion (EUR 27.6 million) linked to allegedly overpriced bus purchases and other transactions. These remain allegations under investigation, and criminal liability can only be established by a final court judgment.

Prosecutors also seek to lift Balázs Hankó’s immunity

A separate request concerns Balázs Hankó and an investigation into the National Cultural Fund, known by its Hungarian abbreviation NKA.

Prosecutors suspect that a temporary NKA committee was used to distribute public funds for purposes that differed from those authorised by legislation and the body’s founding documents. According to investigators, some applications submitted under a funding scheme launched in July 2025 were approved without substantive assessment, with money allegedly used for election campaign-related expenses or personal purposes.

The case concerns funding decisions worth more than HUF 17 billion, equivalent to roughly EUR 46.9 million. Prosecutors believe Hankó’s alleged conduct could qualify as breach of trust causing particularly significant financial damage. Hankó and other people concerned by the investigation are entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán previously rejected the accusations surrounding the NKA case, describing the investigation as politically motivated and arguing that the fund’s decision-makers had merely distributed money allocated to Hungarian culture.

As we wrote earlier, Hungarian billionaire Jellinek and former state asset manager chief arrested

Péter Magyar’s immunity is also at issue

In an entirely separate case, prosecutors have once again sought the suspension of Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s parliamentary immunity over an alleged theft dating back to June 2024.

Authorities allege that during an altercation at a Budapest nightclub, Magyar took a man’s mobile phone after noticing that he was being filmed. The phone was later allegedly thrown into the Danube. Prosecutors first sought to have Magyar’s immunity lifted while he was serving as a Member of the European Parliament.

The European Parliament refused to waive his immunity in October 2025, citing concerns over possible political motivation behind the proceedings. The European Parliament stressed at the time that an immunity procedure was not a determination of criminal responsibility.

Magyar’s European Parliament mandate, and the immunity attached to it, ended on 8 May 2026. He became a member of Hungary’s National Assembly the following day and was elected prime minister on 9 May following TISZA’s victory in the April parliamentary election.

As a Hungarian MP, however, Magyar again enjoys parliamentary immunity. Prosecutors therefore need parliament’s consent before the criminal proceedings can continue against him.

Under Hungarian rules on parliamentary immunity, criminal proceedings against an MP generally cannot be initiated or continued without the prior consent of the National Assembly. Parliament will therefore have to decide separately whether the immunity of the politicians concerned should be suspended, making the requests the next major procedural step in all three cases.

World.title: In neighbouring countries: Austrian government agrees to extend mandatory military service
World.content:
The Austrian governing coalition has agreed on a new model to extend military service, Yannick Shetty, leader of the New Austria and Liberal Forum (NEOS), announced on Tuesday.

According to Anadolu, under the proposed reform, the current six-month basic training will be immediately followed by one month of active drills. Conscripts will then complete the remaining two months of reserve training at a later date.

Currently, military service in Austria is limited strictly to six months of basic training.

To pass the reform, the coalition requires a two-thirds majority in Parliament, meaning it must secure votes from the opposition.

The largest opposition party, the far-right Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ), is calling for an even longer extension of both military and civilian service. The Austrian Greens, on the other hand, remain opposed to the planned changes.

If you missed it – Hungarian Gripen crash: Swedish Saab offers support as investigation begins

Not just Austria

Austria is not the only country in Europe making changes to its conscription system in response to the war in Ukraine and perceived security threats from Russia.

Latvia reinstated mandatory military service in 2024 after a nearly two-decade hiatus. Croatia, following a 17-year hiatus, reintroduced mandatory two-month basic training for men starting in January 2026.

Denmark implemented a comprehensive reform starting in 2026. Military service will be drastically extended from four to eleven months.

Similarly, in Germany, which suspended a draft in 2011, a new model has emerged.

Under the new Military Service Act passed under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, conscription was not fully reinstated, but it was comprehensively reformed.

Starting in 2026, all 18-year-old men will be required to complete a digital questionnaire on physical fitness and military readiness.

Based on the responses, candidates will be invited to a physical examination in, with the goal of recruiting approximately 20,000 volunteers each year.

Hungary has no mandatory military service in peacetime

Unlike Austria, Hungary does not have mandatory military service in peacetime. Conscription was suspended in November 2004, when the last conscripts left the Hungarian Defence Forces, and the country switched to a professional, voluntary military system. Today, Hungarians can join the armed forces voluntarily as professional, contract or reserve personnel.

Hungary’s legal framework nevertheless retains the possibility of compulsory military service under exceptional circumstances. Under Hungarian law, citizens’ preparation for national defence is based on voluntary participation in peacetime, while military obligations may be activated under the special legal order applicable in wartime.
