World.title: As Geopolitical Competition Intensifies, the EU’s Balkans Policy Must Adapt
World.content:
With its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia’s aggression towards European security architecture has opened a new chapter in the history of geopolitics.

Given the changing role of the United States in international affairs, the diffusion of power through the rise of middle powers, and China’s assertiveness as a peer competitor, the contours of the international order will see increased volatility, competition and uncertainty.

In this multipolar, multi-ordered world, small actors such as the countries of the Western Balkans will pursue ad hoc alliances and engage in transactional foreign policy with multiple powers in parallel.

World.title: Albania ‘Not Ready for the Risks’ as AI Enters the Electoral Arena
World.content:
Artificial intelligence has already entered the electoral arena all around the world. From fake audio recordings of candidates to videos making politicians appear to utter words they never said, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly used to discredit political opponents, shape voters’ perceptions and influence their electoral behaviour.

Albania is no exception. From last year’s general elections to the marathon anti-government protests known as the “Flamingo Revolution”, AI has been widely used to produce online political content, often in harmful forms.

During the 2025 parliamentary polls, disinformation campaigns targeting political actors were orchestrated through anonymous pages and spread across digital platforms. During the ongoing “Flamingo Revolution” protests, BIRN has identified dozens of cases in which AI was used to disseminate false information, which was then amplified through anonymous social media pages and accounts.

World.title: Hungarians and Czechs Cool on Ukraine’s ‘Carpathian 8’ Ambitions
World.content:
More amenable partners

Poland, on the other hand, as Ukraine’s strongest ally in the region, was represented by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and showed the clearest interest in the C8 format.

For Poland, the appeal of the C8 appears to lie in the overlap between security and cross-border infrastructure. Projects presented at the summit included a 216-million-dollar industrial park and multimodal terminal on the Polish–Ukrainian border, designed to handle up to more than 2 million tonnes of cargo annually, as well as a 441-million-dollar plan by Ukrainian Railways to establish a low-cost passenger operator using European-gauge trains, with connections from Uzhhorod, Lviv and Kovel to EU cities including Warsaw.

Together with cooperation on missile defence and the longer-term reconstruction of Ukraine, these plans give Warsaw several concrete reasons to remain involved, say experts.

The summit also gave Warsaw and Kyiv an opportunity to inject new momentum into relations that have been strained in recent months. Tusk said he had come to demonstrate solidarity with Ukraine and discuss bilateral cooperation, including Poland’s participation in the European anti-ballistic missile initiative. After talks with Zelensky, the two leaders confirmed that Poland would join the coalition, and Tusk said Poland’s absence from the initiative when it was launched in Paris in July had been the result of “a certain misunderstanding”.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic – who will be the prime ministerial candidate for the ruling coalition in the snap election to be held on October 25 – made an appearance in person, which analysts say is in keeping with the strategy he has been following over the last few months that included a bilateral meeting with Zelensky in Belgrade and a multilateral forum in Kyiv.

“I assume it has something to do with the elections approaching in Serbia, as Vucic now needs to show his more pro-Western face to keep support coming from the EU. He will not communicate it much at home, but will use his presence vocally when talking to EU counterparts,” AMO’s Cermak told BIRN.

Indeed, Vucic suggested as much during the summit, when he presented the initiative as his personal commitment to Serbia: “I am doing all of this to further ensure stability and peace for our citizens and for Serbia.”

Vucic said that Serbia has traditionally relied on the countries of the former Yugoslavia and also looked toward the West: “We were wrong: I believe that expanding and strengthening our relations within the broader Carpathian region will mean a great deal for Serbia.”

By way of example, Vucic noted that the opening of the Belgrade–Budapest high-speed railway would further facilitate connectivity, while Serbia is also working to establish other better links with Romania, such as making progress in talks on the construction of the Timisoara–Belgrade motorway as well as connecting the two countries’ electricity transmission systems.

Vucic also noted how 50 per cent of Serbian exports now go to Romania, Hungary and the Czech Republic, while trade between Serbia and Ukraine has increased by 42 per cent (though he did not specify the period to which this increase referred). The Serbian Chamber of Commerce told the weekly Vreme in August that Serbian exports to Ukraine increased by 92.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, largely due to electricity exports.

Romania was represented by President Nicusor Dan at the summit, where he signed a memorandum of understanding with Ukraine aimed at improving connectivity between the two countries by opening 10 new border crossing points and also upgrading infrastructure.

Dan also said that protecting the rights of national minorities could be one of the priorities of the C8 initiative. “This format can make use of the linguistic and cultural wealth of the region, making the protection of the rights of national minorities a priority,” Dan said in his speech at the summit.

According to Dan, the C8 could also become an additional tool for the European integration of EU candidate countries.

World.title: Croatia Pushes for Stronger Frontex Role on Western Balkan Migrant Route
World.content:
Members of FRONTEX at a launch ceremony in Skopje, North Macedonia, April 2023. Photo: EPA-EFE/GEORGI LICOVSKI.

Croatia’s Interior Minister Davor Bozinovic said on Tuesday that his country advocates deploying the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, Frontex, in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, noting that more than 95 per cent of migrants using the so-called Western Balkan Route to enter Croatia come from that direction.

“Our goal, and the goal of the European Commission [in talks with Bosnia] was to resolve the status of Frontex there,” Bozinovic said, adding that Frontex is currently establishing some activities in the country, mainly along Bosnia’s eastern border.

“However, what interests us the most is the western border, where migrants mostly try to cross illegally into the territory of Croatia,” Bozinovic said. “That is one of the issues that I think we will discuss in the future,” he added.

Bozinovic said Frontex’s future mission was to strengthen the capacities of countries through which migrants travel to reach the European Union, and improve returns.

He said an organisation with such a large budget could play a much more effective role in returning migrants caught entering the EU irregularly to their countries of origin.

“Our three countries share a common goal of ensuring citizen safety, managing migration effectively, and further strengthening the [borderless] Schengen Area,” Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said, adding that cooperation had produced positive results, citing a 28-per-cent drop in irregular border crossings recorded in the first eight months of this year.

Bozinovic also noted a further decline in irregular migration along the Western Balkan route this year but warned that the route remained active and needed close monitoring.

“We will therefore continue with trilateral border patrols, as they have proven effective, particularly in the fight against migrant smugglers,” Bozinovic said.

He noted that 842 smugglers had been arrested this year and that prevention efforts had produced stronger results than in the previous period, with nearly 25 per cent more attempted entries into EU territory prevented than last year.

He was speaking at a meeting of the interior ministers of Italy, Croatia and Slovenia in Pordenone, Italy. The ministers confirmed their readiness to further improve cooperation through regular information sharing, joint operational activities and coordinated responses to security challenges.

“Today, there is no security challenge, especially for police forces, that does not have a cross-border dimension. The better we cooperate, the more successful we will be,” Slovenian Interior Minister Franci Matoz said.

World.title: Albania’s Intelligence Chief Suspended for Allegedly Aiding Crime Group
World.content:
The head of Albania’s State Intelligence Service, Vlora Hyseni. Photo: LSA.

Anti-corruption prosecutors on Tuesday placed Vlora Hyseni, head of Albania’s State Intelligence Service, SHISH, under house arrest and suspended her for allegedly revealing state secrets and assisting an offender.

The Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, has also questioned the former Chief of Police, Ilir Proda, it announced. Media reported that Hyseni is not currently in Albania.

SPAK added that a sector head of the Forensic Police and a businessman had been arrested in relation to the same case.

Hyseni is being investigated over a corruption scandal surrounding tenders of the national agency overseeing the development of state information systems, the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI.

Hyeni has headed the SHISH, the most important institution handling national security, since 2023, and her alleged involvement with the AKSHI corruption scandal potentially marks the most serious crisis over national security in the country’s history.

Hyseni was appointed head of SHISH after serving as Prime Minister’s Edi Rama national security adviser for about two years. She had earlier been deputy director of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency, KIA, but was dismissed from that post in June 2021 by Kosovo President Vjosa Osmani and Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

Her appointment as head of SHISH in 2023 was controversial because of her Kosovo citizenship and the unclear reason for her dismissal from Kosovo’s top security institution.

Meanwhile, former police chief Proda was seen at SPAK offices on Tuesday where, according to the media, he was questioned in relation to the AKSHI scandal and his house was searched.

AKSHI coordinates the development of state information systems and digitalisation procedures and administers the state public services portal, e-Albania.

The agency has managed a massive budget; some 19 of its procedures investigated by SPAK alone had an estimated total value of 5.9 billion lek, or about 59 million euros.

The SPAK investigation alleges that AKSHI’s director, Mirlinda Karcanaj, and her deputy, Hava Delibashi, placed many of these funds in the hands of a group linked to organised crime, pre-selected tender winners and ensured the diversion of tens of millions of euros into the accounts of IT businessman Ermal Beqiraj and Ergys Agasi.

Agasi is accused of forming a criminal group with Beqiraj to rig and extort tenders from the AKSHI, even using violence and hostage-taking.

Agasi was arrested in August 27 after being on the run for months. Beqiraj was arrested earlier in France on July 24 while flying a light aircraft through restricted airspace over a nuclear power plant.

Karcanaj, Delibashi and Agasi all deny charges while Beqiraj is still under arrest in France. SPAK alleges that he transferred a portion of his illicit proceeds to France, using the cash to purchase a château, two apartments and motor vehicles, while also depositing over 2 million euros in bank accounts.

The alleged involvement of top security officials in this scheme, providing criminals with information and assisting them, has left many in the country in shock.

“Whenever something happens, we say: ‘This is the end; nothing worse than this could possibly happen.’ But in this country, the problem is that even the end has no end,” Mentor Kikia, a journalist and analyst, wrote on Facebook.

The opposition has urged President Bajram Begaj to call an urgent meeting of the State Security Council.

Ruling Socialist Party MPs are urging caution. “We must await the final judicial verdict. Nothing is true until proven by the courts,” Blendi Cuci, a Socialist MP, told a meeting of parliament’s Committee on Internal Affairs and Defence, after opposition MPs asked for the issue to be urgently included in parliamentary sessions.

World.title: As Tech Giants Harvest Data, Montenegro Struggles to Track Them
World.content:
Mirko Radunovic from Podgorica planned to organise and monitor his gym training sessions by registering on a mobile fitness app.

Knowing the app's purpose, he did not find it off when it asked him to enter information about his age, health and exercise habits.

“I entered information about my age, health, nutrition and life habits, to create an appropriate training plan. After some time, I started receiving s for fitness equipment and supplements,” Radunovic told BIRN.

“When the app suggested that I add progress photos, I stopped using it. I removed it from my phone – but didn't ask for my data to be removed," he added.

World.title: Albania to Adopt EU Disability Access Standards – But Will They Be Enforced?
World.content:
Katerina Jaupaj understood from an early age that she could not take a step without thinking about the consequences. She was 18 months old and had only just started walking when she broke her leg for the first time.

Jaupaj was diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta, better known as brittle bone disease, a rare genetic disorder that affects the production of collagen and renders bones fragile. Those with the condition face a high risk of fractures, even from impacts or movements that would be considered ordinary for others.

The fear of injury followed Jaupaj throughout her childhood. While at school, she began using a wheelchair, but this only proved another source of anxiety.

World.title: ‘Our War is Being Judged’: In Kosovo, Outrage at Hague Verdict Simmers
World.content:
Thaci, Krasniqi, Veseli, and Selimi were sentenced to 25, 25, 18, and 13 years in prison respectively. They were found guilty of the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and two locations in Albania. They were found not guilty of crimes against humanity.

On Monday, the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK – the party widely seen as originating from the KLA, which has been led by both Thaci and Veseli in the past – announced it was initiating an attempt to change the law underpinning the court.

The PDK proposed that the trial proceedings to continue through to the conclusion of the appeals phase. However, if the case is sent for retrial, it should not start over in The Hague but instead in Kosovo.

In the case of a potential retrial, “new jurisdiction applies, and once the conditions are met, the case will be transferred to Kosovo for proceedings,” PDK leader Bedri Hamza told media on Monday.

He argued that the protests cannot be ignored, saying that “the parliament of Kosovo cannot act as if this matter does not affect the Republic of Kosovo”.

It’s not yet clear how much support the PDK proposal will get. But anger about the verdict is also shared by the ruling party, Vetevendosje. Prime Minister Albin Kurti, the leader of Vetevendosje, wrote on X on Monday that the court’s findings “were based on factual inaccuracies, historical misunderstandings, and legal errors. We expect these to be fully corrected on appeal.”

The Specialist Chambers were established under a law adopted in 2015 by the Kosovo Assembly, under pressure from Pristina’s Western allies. The court is part of Kosovo’s judicial system but located in The Netherlands and staffed by internationals as part of efforts to prevent witness-tampering during trials. Thaci was one of the politicians who supported the court’s establishment, saying it would prove the KLA’s war was just.

Kosovo’s former ombudsperson, Hilmi Jashari, told BIRN on Friday that a change of regulations on appointing and overseeing the judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers would be beneficial for a fair trial. But Jashari cautioned that demands to fully repeal the law on the court would not be a good way forward.

“I have heard recently that the only solution is to repeal the law [governing the Specialist Chambers]; then one hears suggestions that the president should pardon the convicted individuals, but practically speaking, embarking on such an undertaking is impossible from a legal and juridical standpoint,” Jashari told BIRN and Internews Kosova’s Kallxo Pernime TV programme on Friday.

Edward P. Joseph, a lecturer at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington DC, told Kallxo Pernime that the anger towards the court in Kosovo is understandable – particularly as the verdict comes soon after Bosnian Serb wartime general Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide, was buried with military honours in Belgrade.

“Consequently, this decision appears to Serbs in Belgrade as a form of vindication or absolution, while casting a shadow over the realities of the 1990s in Kosovo. That is why I find it very concerning,” Joseph said, claiming that Serbia and its supporters in Russia and China would exploit the verdict to spread their own narratives.

Serbia’s Interior Minister Ivica Dacic has welcomed the guilty verdict in exactly this way, saying it represents a “clear, though long-overdue, confirmation of what Serbia and the Serbian people have been saying loudly for more than a quarter of a century – that the so-called KLA was a criminal and terrorist organisation”.

Meanwhile on Monday evening in Pristina, protesters gathered again in the main square, determined that their message will be heard.

World.title: Croatia’s Končar Presents Hybrid Electro-Diesel Train at InnoTrans
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia’s well known Končar has presented its impressive hybrid electro-diesel train at InnoTrans in Berlin.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that Končar officially presented its latest step forward in Croatian industry in the field of urban mobility and infrastructure at the world’s largest transport technology fair, InnoTrans in Berlin. The train is an ultra-modern hybrid (bimodal) electro-diesel train intended for long-distance transport.

After it was put into regular service on the Zagreb – Split route a week earlier in cooperation with the customer HŽ Passenger Transport, the second train from this series has now also been presented to the international public. With the global premiere of its latest solution for more modern, more comfortable and more sustainable passenger transport, Končar has once again confirmed that the knowledge, competences and technological solutions developed in Croatia compete on equal terms with the biggest names in the European railway industry.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Among the most visited parts of the fair was the outdoor exhibition area with 3,500 metres of track, on which 130 exhibitors from 17 countries of the world exhibited a total of 113 vehicles, including the latest generations of trains, locomotives and vehicles with alternative propulsion systems.

Precisely in such an international environment Končar is presenting technological solutions developed and produced in Croatia for the 10th time, confirming its position among the relevant European manufacturers of modern rail vehicles and advanced solutions for sustainable urban mobility. After two years ago it was the only one at InnoTrans to present a battery train, which then also became the first such product in commercial use in Europe and one of the first such products in the whole world, Končar has also displayed its new bimodal electro-diesel train at one of the most attractive positions on the outdoor exhibition area of the fair – on 75-metre-long tracks.

At the same time, the latest solutions for railway infrastructure, electrification, urban mobility and traffic digitalisation were presented on the spacious indoor area, further emphasising the ability of the domestic company to independently develop and deliver integrated technological solutions for the transport systems of the future.

World.title: New Obligations for Traders in Croatia Soon, Fines Reach €30,000
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – New obligations are coming for traders and service providers in Croatia as of the first day of October, with fines reaching a staggering €30,000.

Fuels are more expensive across Croatia once again, and by expanding the so-called anchor prices, the government wants to increase transparency and prevent the spilling over of higher costs onto other products and services. Poslovni reports that whether the measure can help in the fight against inflation or will create an additional burden for entrepreneurs and craftsmen was discussed by guests on HRT’s Otvoreno.

price hikes will be more noticeable

Željko Krevzelj from the Ministry of the Economy said that the dual display of prices is part of the Government’s 11th package of measures, and the goal is to increase transparency and encourage consumers to monitor price changes more closely. “It’s an expansion of the measure that entered into force back on the 2nd of May 2025, while from the 10th of September, it was expanded to additional categories of products and services,” he explained. When it comes to the new products, he noted that the measure applies to products that existed up to the 10th of September and that the Ministry has sent additional clarifications on the application of anchor prices to economic associations.

“Fines for non-compliance with the measures are from three to 30,000 euros. The decisions enter into force on the 1st of October and we expect them to be applied,” Krevzelj said. According to the official government decisions, as of the 1st of October, alongside the current price of products and services, the price that was valid on the 10th of September 2026 must also be displayed. For the categories that were already covered by the earlier measure – food, drink, cosmetics, cleaning agents, toiletries and household products – the reference remains the price from the 2nd of May 2025.

The second new obligation relates to the publication of price lists on websites. Traders and service providers who have established websites will have to publish price lists there in XML or CSV format. Traders must update them once a day, no later than 08:00, while service providers must update them with every price change, also no later than 08:00 that same day. Published price lists must be available for 30 days.

where does inflation come into it?

Kristina Bakula from the Association Voice of Entrepreneurs assessed the expansion of the measure as extremely worrying. She warned that anchor prices have so far been applied by large systems that have their own IT departments, while now similar requirements are being placed in a short time on farmers, car mechanics, hairdressers and other small craftsmen.

“You’re talking about an anti-inflation package, and I am telling you that no additional cost falls under the fight against inflation. On the contrary, it encourages its growth,” Bakula said. She warned that additional costs for entrepreneurs have previously also been justified by transparency or the fight against inflation and that the new requirements could force some to hire an IT specialist to maintain websites and price lists.

“This isn’t the first situation in which additional costs for people are justified by ‘transparency’ or the fight against inflation. Let us remember that the problem of craftsmen where some craftsmen’s costs rose by 200 percent has not been extinguished. We have not solved that problem either, and you are pouring oil on the fire. People have to hire an IT specialist. Is a farmer supposed to become an IT specialist overnight? An inspector will come and say: ‘You have great tomatoes, but you have to refresh your price list if you have a website. You didn’t update it at eight in the morning.’”

Krevzelj replied that the measure applies to those who already have price lists and displayed products and that the Ministry is not imposing an obligation to publish prices where a price list on the website has not existed so far. Bakula then asked him whether that means that an entrepreneur who has services listed on the website but does not have a price list will not have to start publishing prices. “You’re loading us with new things that will achieve nothing,” Bakula said.

Krevzelj replied that the rules, instructions and clarifications are clear and announced new rulebooks that should further clarify the implementation of the measure.

some may close their online shops…

President of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts Dalibor Kratohvil said that those operating crafts are calling the Chamber and that nervousness has appeared among them because of the new rules and the short deadline for adaptation. HOK has therefore requested the withdrawal of the decision. As an example he cited the owner of a second-hand clothing shop who sells products for two, five or seven euros, and whose website is maintained by a neighbour who deals with IT and occasionally changes the prices.

“She’s worried about how she will manage everything. I’m afraid we are not going in a good direction,” Kratohvil said. He also warned that some craftsmen, because of the new obligations, are thinking about closing their web shops.

“Many have stated that they want to close their web shops, which is today a window to the world. People want to give up on those stories, and that is not desirable,” he emphasised. Kratohvil said that he does not agree with the Association Voice of Entrepreneurs on many issues and the manner of communication, but that craftsmen need to be enabled to work instead of being additionally burdened with administrative requirements. He added that HOK understands the Ministry’s intention, but considers that the existing Consumer Protection Act already prescribes how to deal with base prices. “We consider that this decision should be withdrawn,” Kratohvil concluded.

there’s a limit to how far the government can realistically go

Former Minister of the Economy Davor Štern warned that the discussion is taking place in a period of major disruptions on the world energy market. He noted that the price of diesel has risen 50 percent in the last six months, while the oil price is continuously oscillating. He said that he understands the positions of the Ministry, consumers, craftsmen and entrepreneurs and that a way needs to be found to prevent large jumps in fuel prices from being used for unjustified increases in other prices. One possibility, he said, would be the taxation of unjustified revenues and profits realised because of market disruptions. But he warned that even a tax on excess profit is not direct protection of consumers because that money ends up with the state.

“By displaying prices the consumer is still somewhat protected. That is good for consumers and the political environment,” Štern said. Speaking about the fuel price increase that has entered into force, he noted that a litre of diesel in Germany costs more than three euros. To the question of how the price in Croatia is still kept below two euros, he replied that the government has shown good will with its interventions, but that the possibilities of such a policy are not unlimited. “There is a limit to how far one can realistically go,” Štern concluded.

World.title: European Heat Dome at the End of September Will Also Affect Croatia
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Another European heat dome at the end of September will bring about unusual heat levels, and it will also affect Croatia.

Yet another unseasonably warm spell will hit a large part of Europe at the end of September, and unusually high temperatures could persist into early October. According to the forecast by Severe Weather Europe, a strong area of high pressure will develop over the continent that will draw very warm air northward from the Mediterranean and northern Africa. Index reports that in parts of western, central and northern Europe the air temperature aloft will be 8 to 12 degrees higher than the average for this time of year. At the surface temperatures in many areas will exceed 25 degrees, and in places even 30 degrees, which is very unusual for the end of September and the beginning of October.

high temperatures for croatia

Such a weather pattern is often called a heat dome. It is a large and long-lasting area of high pressure that keeps warm air over the same area. The air sinks towards the ground, heats further and makes the formation of clouds more difficult, so high temperatures can last for days, and sometimes even weeks. The heatwave is expected to gradually spread across the continent by the end of September, and stable and dry weather could continue into early October. For southern Europe and the Balkans warmer air is expected from Saturday and the beginning of next week.

Temperatures in northern Italy and the central part of the Balkans should reach between 28 and 30 degrees. The warming will also affect Croatia. According to the maps, on Sunday the 27th of September in Croatia, the highest daily temperatures are mostly expected between 22 and 26 degrees. By Tuesday the 29th of September it will warm further so temperatures in parts of the country will rise to around 27 degrees. The most pronounced deviation from usual temperatures is expected over the Po Valley and Tuscany in neighbouring Italy, the northern and central part of the Balkans and Greece.

heat across the iberian peninsula

The greatest heat during this week is expected on the Iberian Peninsula. In central and southern Spain and Portugal temperatures will exceed 35 degrees, and from Thursday to Saturday in places they could approach 40 degrees. It will also be very warm in France. In the central part of the country temperatures around 35 degrees are expected, while in the south they could reach approximately 36 degrees. In the north of France and in the Benelux countries, temperatures hovering at around 30 degrees are expected over the weekend. Warm air will then spread towards Germany, Poland and the Baltic countries. In western, central and northern Germany temperatures from Sunday to the beginning of next week could reach between 27 and 29 degrees, and in places approach 30.

heavy rain for northwestern europe

In England, the warming will be shorter, with temperatures mostly between 25 and 28 degrees. In Ireland and Scotland it will be significantly cooler, with temperatures mostly around 15 degrees. While a large part of the continent will be under the influence of warm and dry air, western Ireland, Scotland and southwestern Norway can expect very moist air from the Atlantic. By the beginning of October more than 150 millimetres of rain could fall locally there. Forecasts show that the warm period could continue into early October. Then the area of high pressure would expand further towards the north and east of Europe, and the largest deviations from usual temperatures could appear in Sweden and Finland.

World.title: HRejting: Croatians Fear Corruption and Inflation the Most
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – The latest HRejting poll has revealed that Croatians still fear corruption and inflation more than climate change or wars.

Corruption and the complete non-functioning of the rule of law are the greatest threat for the citizens of Croatia, according to a new HRejting survey. Index reports that the poll was conducted for HRT by the agency Promocija plus between the 15th and the 18th of September on a sample of 1,000 respondents. The maximum sampling error is +/- 3.04 percent, at a 95 percent confidence level.

what do croatians fear the most?

Respondents were asked 21 questions about the threats they fear the most. As many as 73.4 percent of respondents listed corruption and the non-functioning of the rule of law as one of the greatest. Immediately behind that are inflation and the rise in the cost of living, followed by ecological incidents and pollution.

69 percent of citizens fear serious illnesses, while almost 64 percent fear poverty. Immediately behind is the fear of a rise in crime. A decline in the quality of public healthcare worries 62 percent of those surveyed, followed by alienation among people and the mass departure of young people. Around 56 percent of citizens fear climate change and natural disasters. Around 53 percent of respondents fear political instability. A slightly smaller percentage worries about the loss of personal freedoms, cyber attacks and the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence. Mass migrations and demographic collapse are seen as a threat by around 52 percent of those polled. At the bottom of the list of threats are terrorism, job loss and technological lagging. The fewest respondents, 39 percent, fear war and military conflict in the region.

most expect a less secure future for croatia

The survey also covered the question of Croatia’s security in the next ten years. More than half of the respondents, precisely 51.6 percent, believe that life in the country will be significantly less secure. That the security situation will remain roughly the same is thought by 29 percent of those polled. Only 10 percent expect that Croatia will be significantly more secure, while 8.5 percent did not know how to assess the future state.

World.title: New Law for Foreign Workers in Croatia Faces Criticism
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – A new law facing foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027 is already causing a stir and facing criticism from migration experts.

You go to another country, get a job, learn around thirty basic phrases of its language and that is, according to the law, enough to be considered “integrated.” Most would argue that this statement is so ridiculous that it’s difficult to quantify. Poslovni reports that the aforementioned notion is all that will be required of foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027. They will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at level A1.1 in order to extend their residence and work permit. Apparently, that’s “integration”.

Is basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is very clearly “no.” The data that his institute collects shows that Croatia is only beginning to scratch the surface of a problem that, as the number of foreign workers grows, will become ever more complex. Balabanić views the obligation to pass A1.1 Croatian simultaneously as an integration measure and as an administrative condition, but emphasises that its meaning should primarily be integrative.

“Knowledge of the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first preconditions for beginning to feel part of society. Nevertheless, such a low level of language knowledge by itself does not resolve questions of the legal security of foreign workers nor their finding their way in Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can actually exercise them,” Balabanić highlighted.

croatia’s responsibility as a state

Precisely for that reason, while the worker hasn’t mastered Croatian, information about residence, work, the healthcare system and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and that, Balabanić emphasises, in one place, and not scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mainly comes down to the relationship between the worker and the employer, the social dimension is equally important, and that, according to his words, cannot be one-way. Foreign workers need to get to know the norms and values of the society they are coming into, but the domestic population must also accept that Croatia is becoming culturally more diverse.

How weak that readiness is at this moment is shown by a study by the Institute for Migration Research from November 2025, conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and as a family member only a negligible number of respondents. “That’s why I would say that Croatia is still in an early phase of the integration of foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, available information, social contacts and the readiness of the domestic population to accept new fellow citizens we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić said. When it comes to the financing of integration, Balabanić clearly emphasises that the largest part of the cost should be borne by the state.

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily because of the needs of the domestic labour market and the shortage of labour in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest part of the responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

That, he emphasises, does not mean that the responsibility must be exclusively state. Local self-government has an important role because integration takes place in concrete communities – the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as the needs of those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, but Balabanić warns that it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, since they already bear significant costs of employing foreign workers. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have the obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the law.

the so-called information vacuum

Precisely there Balabanić sees the real danger that integration becomes something that the state formally requires of the foreign worker, while at the same time not providing them with the tools to fulfil that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration exclusively their personal problem,” he said. When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the everyday life of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out only one. The language barrier, inadequate accommodation, violation of labour rights, difficult access to healthcare and social isolation, he says, are intertwined – but the common denominator of most of these problems is the chronic lack of available and reliable information.

Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding regulatorily to the new situation; amendments to laws and regulations are being adopted, but the open question remains how many of them the administration manages to implement in practice. Tightened criteria for employers, for example, were supposed to regulate the market, but at the same time increased the administrative burden, so some workers waited months for the extension of their permit. A particular problem is the healthcare system – according to another study by the Institute from November 2025, conducted on 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously complicates regular health care.

Language remains an obstacle even when workers themselves try to find information, because the official websites of institutions are very often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of that many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, sometimes the only, source of information becomes the employer or the employment agency. “A series of entirely practical questions, from whether the employer can keep the passport, whether they have the right to unemployment benefit, whom to turn to if their rights are violated – for a large number of workers remain without a reliable answer. Croatia today does not primarily lack regulations. It lacks a system that will enable the foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” Balabanić highlighted.

financial burden

Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers in whom several unfavourable circumstances overlap – those who went into debt in order to reach Croatia at all through long chains of intermediaries, and therefore more readily accept poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer on whom they depend for salary, accommodation and information about their own rights. The education of children is for now not among the most pronounced problems, since a large part of labour migrants still live in Croatia without family, but with the growth in the number of those who stay long-term and bring families, that topic, Balabanić estimates, will become increasingly important.

World.title: Croatia in Top 20 Countries With Highest Quality of Life – But It Doesn’t Mean What You Think
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia has entered into the top 20 countries with the highest quality of life, but it certainly doesn’t mean what you think it means…

The new ranking by World Population Review brings quite a surprise, and that’s that Croatia has placed 20th among countries with the highest quality of life. However, what’s odd to note is that behind this attractive ranking lies a methodology that is important to explain. Poslovni reports that Croatia has surprisingly found itself among the 20 best-placed countries in the world according to the quality of life ranking published by World Population Review. With an index of 181.7 points Croatia occupies 20th place, immediately behind Slovenia, which is 19th with 182.4 points.

the ranking leaves you scratching your head…

Particularly interesting is the fact that according to this ranking numerous developed countries remain behind Croatia. Lithuania is 21st, the United Kingdom 22nd, Czechia 23rd, Belgium 26th, Canada 27th, Ireland 28th, France 29th, Portugal 31st, while Italy is only in 40th place.

At the very top is Luxembourg with 218.2 points. It is followed by the Netherlands (216.5), Denmark (215.1), and a major surprise is Oman, which with the same result as Denmark occupies fourth place. They are followed by Switzerland, Finland, Norway, Iceland, Austria and Germany. Australia is 11th, New Zealand 12th, Sweden 13th, the USA 14th, and among the top 20 are also Estonia, Qatar, Japan, Spain, Slovenia and Croatia.

this ranking isn’t what you might think it is

Nevertheless, it is necessary to emphasise that this is not an official international ranking of the “standard of living” in the classical economic sense. World Population Review for this ranking uses Numbeo’s Quality of Life Index, which attempts to encompass everyday quality of life through eight areas: purchasing power, safety, healthcare, cost of living, the ratio of property prices to income, time spent in traffic, pollution and climate conditions. It is precisely the last items that help explain why Croatia stands so high. For example, Numbeo’s data for Croatia show high scores for safety and very favourable climate conditions as well as a relatively low level of pollution.

World.title: Croatia Among EU Countries With Lowest Share of Insured Climate Losses
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia is exceptionally vulnerable to climate events, yet it is remains among the EU countries with the lowest share of insured climate losses.

Even before the catastrophic fire in Omiš, Croatia already had a 75 percent larger burned area in 2026 than in the comparable period back in 2025. Poslovni reports that the European Commission estimates that today. only around 25 percent of catastrophic losses across Europe are covered by private insurance, which is why national budgets too often become the “insurer of last resort.”

the number of fires in croatia increased

The number of fires in Croatia rose by 7.62 percent, while the burned area rose by 75.06 percent compared to the same period last year. That difference says more about climate risk than any single image of a burning hill; an individual event today simply carries greater damage than a few years ago. Recent fires near Omiš, on Pelješac and Brač further confirmed this. The Omiš fire affected more than 1,000 hectares and led to the evacuation of around a thousand people. By mid-September, around 668,000 hectares had burned in fires across the European Union, almost twice the twenty-year average for the same part of the year, although less than the record 2025. The figures from across Europe warn that this season was not an exception but a continuation of a trend that Croatian companies, banks and insurers still need to take more seriously. Behind the scenes of burning hills lies the statistics about money, about premiums, damages and about who ultimately pays the bill when one decides to gamble with climate risk.

“Climate risk is increasingly becoming everyday life and the question is whether we have an idea of how much it can cost us. Companies that today assess their exposure only through last year’s damage are building a false sense of security,” believes Jasminka Horvat Martinović, President of the Management Board of Marsh Croatia, warning that this is a major trap of the moment in which a large part of the Croatian business sector finds itself.

A Reuters analysis, based on data from the European Environment Agency, shows the scale of the problem at the level of the entire Union: climate disasters and extreme weather conditions cost the European Union around €822 billion in the period from 1980 to 2024, and as much as a quarter of that amount occurred in the last four years. According to the latest EEA data, less than 20 percent of total losses in that period were covered by private insurance. For Croatia the gap is even larger: less than three percent of total economic losses linked to weather and climate extremes were insured.

unsurprisingly, croatia isn’t doing anywhere near enough

Croatia is thus among the European countries with the lowest share of insured climate losses. The floods in Spain in 2024 imply reconstruction costs of around 0.7 percent of GDP in the period 2024–2026, which is approximately €11 billion, while the German floods of 2021 cost the state treasury around €30 billion because insurance covered only a smaller part of the damage.

“The problem is no longer in the cost that disasters bring but in the fact that they are becoming regular. As long as they are treated as one-off budget burdens, the system does not adapt. The result is that an ever larger part of the bill ends up with taxpayers,” emphasises Horvat Martinović.

Some countries have already gone a step further than considering new models. Portugal in April, after major floods at the beginning of 2026, announced a fund for natural disasters and earthquakes and a system of compulsory insurance of housing and business infrastructure, with a public assistance mechanism for lower-income households. In Greece, from 1 June 2025, insurance against forest fire, flood and earthquake has been compulsory for companies with annual turnover greater than €500,000, with coverage of at least 70 percent of the value of the assets covered.

In the meantime a new step has also been taken at the level of the European Union. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 16 September announced the establishment of the Climate Insurance Alliance with the aim of reducing the large gap in insurance against climate disasters. The Commission estimates that today only around 25 percent of catastrophic losses in Europe are covered by private insurance, which is why national budgets too often become the “insurer of last resort.” The new initiative should include insurers, investors, risk modelling experts, public institutions and policyholders and encourage solutions such as group and parametric insurance.

croatia’s fire risk is enormous

That European statistic primarily reflects floods and storms, but the same pattern of underinsurance also applies to fires, and the Croatian 2026 season shows this on its own local example.

According to data from the State Firefighting Operational Centre 193 of the Croatian Firefighting Association, in the period from 1 January to 10 August 2026, 29,358 firefighting interventions were recorded in Croatia, of which 8,832 were fires. Of that, 5,575 open-space fires and 3,897 vegetation fires were recorded, and 9,646 hectares were burned. Compared to the same period in 2025, the number of open-space fires rose by 12.99 percent, the number of vegetation fires by 23.40 percent, and the burned area by 75.06 percent. What makes that statistic particularly relevant for the business community is the relationship between the two figures. On the day of that cut-off the total number of fires rose by 7.62 percent, and the burned area by 75 percent. The risk, therefore, does not grow so much by frequency as by consequence. An individual event today carries a significantly greater loss than a few years ago. The Omiš fire shows this precisely; it was not the largest by area – the Split one from 2017 was four to five times larger. In addition, fires are no longer exclusively a coastal story. The risk, in other words, is moving from a seasonal to a permanent category.

The Croatian business sector mostly reacts to risk after it materialises, instead of structuring it in advance. “A strategic approach is important, and that means recognising the risk before it becomes damage,” emphasises Horvat Martinović, adding that companies should carry out in-depth analysis of exposure to climate risks, scenario models and adapted insurance solutions, from parametric covers, where the payout is activated automatically on the basis of pre-defined parameters such as the amount of precipitation or wind speed, to solutions for critical infrastructure and renewable energy sources. For example, in the energy sector, better mapping and prevention can reduce risk by 20 to 30 percent.

In the meantime newer data from the Croatian insurance market are also available. In the first seven months of 2026 the total collected premium rose by 6.9 percent to €1.3 billion, while the non-life insurance premium rose by 7.3 percent. Insurance against fire and elemental damage accounted for 9.5 percent of the non-life insurance premium. At the same time the amount of settled claims in non-life insurance rose by 15.9 percent, and 9.7 percent of that amount related to fires and elemental damage.

croatian companies need to ask themselves some serious questions

The growth in the number of policies on the Croatian market looks like a sign of maturity. But if a large part of property still remains uninsured or underinsured, that growth only means that the bills tomorrow will be larger than today. What distinguishes companies that survive a major loss is a pre-set risk management strategy, not the policy itself.

Croatian companies, Horvat Martinović believes, need to ask themselves the practical question of whether their risk assessment has been made on the basis of what happened last year, or on the basis of what is already now visible as coming. Climate risk is entering insurance prices, property values and public budgets ever more strongly; waiting for the next major event to show where the system is vulnerable, concludes Horvat Martinović, is becoming an ever more expensive strategy.

World.title: Dismissal of Plenković Sought Following Hazardous Waste Scandal
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – SDP is seeking the dismissal of PM Andrej Plenković following the hazardous waste scandal in Lika.

By the end of this week, SDP will officially submit to parliamentary procedure a proposal for a vote of no confidence in the Government of Andrej Plenković. Index reports that it will do so over the case of illegally dumped hazardous waste in Gospić and other parts of Croatia. 55 signatures of MPs were already collected for the initiative a month ago, but SDP will submit only 30, the minimum required. The proposal has been signed by all opposition parties except DOMiNO and the Croatian Sovereignists.

The reason for submitting only part of the signatures is a provision of the parliamentary Rules of Procedure according to which an MP can support only one such proposal within a period of six months. SDP is thus leaving open the possibility that some MPs, before the expiry of that deadline, support a new request for the dismissal of the Government or one of its members, reports Novi list.

an october vote

After Speaker of Parliament Gordan Jandroković receives the proposal and places it on the agenda, the Government has eight days to respond, and the vote must be held within 30 days. This means that MPs should declare themselves on confidence in the Government during October. The parliamentary majority currently has 79 MPs, so according to the present balance of forces there are not enough votes to pass a vote of no confidence. In the proposal SDP explains in eight points why it considers Plenković’s government politically responsible for the illegal accumulation of 37,000 tonnes of waste in Gospić, but also for cases of environmental pollution in other parts of Croatia.

sdp: the government shaped this system for years

SDP’s fundamental thesis is that long-term changes to regulations and the weakening of control mechanisms opened the space for illegal waste dumping. SDP claims that responsibility reaches the Prime Minister because his Government “for years shaped the regulations, organised supervision and chose the people at the head of key institutions.”

They also state that part of the powers for acting in such cases belonged to the Government and its president. They particularly single out suspicions linked to former Chief State Inspector Andrija Mikulić, who was appointed by Plenković’s government. “Were individual failures of supervision the result of deliberate favouritism, did those who were supposed to prevent the illegalities by their actions enable their continuation,” SDP asks in the proposal.

the pm is being accused of downplaying the issue

In the request SDP also deals with what it calls the Prime Minister’s downplaying of the seriousness of the problem of illegally buried waste in Gospić. “A stronger reaction by the Government followed only with the growth of public pressure and protests,” they claim.

In the final part of the request they state that political responsibility must lead to a change in the waste management system and that citizens have the right to effective remediation and the accountability of those who managed the system for years. An additional political dimension is given to the case by the statement of Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Ivan Anušić, who last weekend recalled that as early as 2023, after the fire at Drava International, he called out the State Inspectorate. Anušić said at the time that the Inspectorate had to control the quantities and type of waste and the method of its disposal. “Unfortunately, three years later we see where we are when it comes to those who ran the Inspectorate and when we talk about Gospić, but also about scandals linked to waste,” Anušić said.

Back in July 2024, the Croatian Government gave Mikulić a second term as Chief State Inspector. Anušić was already a member of the government at that time.

World.title: Al Zaidi joins Trump-led multilateral Middle East summit in New York
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi participated in a high-level multilateral summit convened by U.S. President Donald Trump in New York on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, gathering regional heads of state and delegation chiefs on the sidelines of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly to address escalating security fractures and regional stability.

According to an official statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Media Office, the multilateral summit brought together delegation leaders from 12 key nations: the United States, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, and Turkey.

The extensive convening represents one of the broadest multilateral diplomatic assemblies centered on Middle Eastern security architectures since the outbreak of recent regional confrontations.

Discussions during the closed-door proceedings centered on pressing regional and international security files, focusing on practical mechanisms to defuse active conflict zones and re-establish baseline regional stability.

Participating leaders evaluated joint measures to secure vital international trade corridors, safeguard vulnerable maritime and overland supply chains, and shield regional economies from ongoing geopolitical volatility to ensure uninterrupted development and commercial flow across the Middle East.

World.title: Iraq, Syria to deepen ties as Al-Zaidi meets Al-Sharaa in New York
World.content:
New York (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq and Syria stepped up ties under Damascus’ new leadership on Tuesday, with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi meeting Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa in New York amid rising regional economic and security concerns.

The meeting, which took place on the margins of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, discussed bilateral cooperation as well as attempts to lessen regional tensions, according to the Iraqi Prime Minister’s office.

The talks are vital for Baghdad because Iraq desires greater economic ties with Syria as well as alternate trade and energy channels at a time when fighting with Iran has hindered shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the primary outlet for Iraqi petroleum exports.

Iraq has already begun to search for methods to send additional oil north via Turkey, as the strait’s interruption highlights the hazards of depending largely on southern export facilities.

Baghdad has begun shipping some southern oil to Kirkuk as part of a plan to boost exports via Turkey’s Ceyhan Port.

Syria might become another significant Western outlet.

Baghdad and Damascus have been exploring new energy and transportation linkages, including ambitions to ultimately connect Iraqi oil to Mediterranean and European markets.

The Al-Zaidi-Al-Sharaa summit also signals a significant change in the relationship between Baghdad and Damascus after the demise of Bashar al-Assad’s administration and the steep reduction in Iranian influence in Syria.

The relationship is especially significant for Iraq given Al-Sharaa’s own history.

Before seizing power in Damascus, Assad participated in the Iraqi resistance during the 2003 US-led invasion and was held by US troops in Iraq for many years.

He then returned to Syria and created the al-Qaeda-affiliated Nusra Front, before leaving al-Qaeda to manage Hayat Tahrir al-Sham.

Despite this history, Baghdad has now appointed Al-Sharaa as Syria’s president, highlighting the strategic necessity of preserving working ties between two nations with a long border and important interests in security, commerce, energy, and regional transit.

The meeting took place at the UN General Assembly, where diplomacy is dominated by the ongoing struggle between the United States and Iran.

Iraq has worked to avoid getting drawn further into the conflict while developing ties with Gulf neighbors, Turkey, the United States, and Syria.

U.S. Ambassador to Turkey and Special Envoy to Iraq and Syria Tom Barrack, who has played an important diplomatic role in regional affairs, welcomed the meeting, posting on X that Iraq and Syria were moving toward greater cooperation, stability, and economic ties.

Al-Zaidi and Al-Sharaa also attended a larger summit in New York hosted by US President Donald Trump, which included presidents and senior officials from the GCC, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, and Turkey. The talks focused on regional security, global commerce, and supply chains, as Middle Eastern crises continue to affect energy markets.

Baghdad’s improved links with Damascus might serve both economic and geopolitical purposes, such as creating new westward routes, increasing cross-border security, and mending ties with a Syria that is no longer controlled by Iran as it was under Assad.

World.title: Iraq pushes oil expansion in New York talks with ExxonMobil, HKN Energy
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq is pushing up attempts to enhance oil output and attract more US energy investment, with Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi meeting separately with ExxonMobil and HKN Energy executives in New York during his visit to the United Nations General Assembly.

Al-Zaidi met with ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods and his group to explore prospective collaboration in oil exploration and producing sectors.

The negotiations centered on raising crude production and enhancing the use of Iraq’s oil resources, with Baghdad hoping for increased participation from foreign energy corporations that can contribute investment, technology, and technical experience to the industry.

In a separate meeting, Al-Zaidi met with HKN Energy Chairman Ross Perot and company officials, pushing the US oil and gas producer to expedite work on its projects and contractual obligations in Iraq.

Al-Zaidi called for more action on projects aimed at increasing oil output and said that his administration will seek to overcome barriers that may cause delays in execution.

According to the Prime Minister’s office, HKN has shown a willingness to extend working hours and speed up project implementation.

The Iraqi leader also said that the government is arranging a Baghdad Energy Conference to promote new exploration blocks as investment prospects for foreign oil and gas businesses.

The ExxonMobil and HKN talks highlight Baghdad’s larger drive to attract more foreign investments into its energy sector, increase production capacity, and establish commercial connections with big US businesses.

The energy drive coincides with a broader diplomatic agenda in New York. Al-Zaidi is attending the UN General Assembly and has participated in talks with US President Donald Trump and leaders from the GCC and other Middle Eastern countries, including Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan, as regional governments confront the ongoing US-Iran conflict and its economic and security consequences.

The diplomatic consultations come at a critical moment for Baghdad, which wants to avoid being dragged further into the regional conflict while preserving ties with Washington, Tehran, and Arab neighbors.

Al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States comes just before the U.S.-led coalition mission in Iraq ends on September 30, as Baghdad attempts to change its ties with Washington toward investment, energy, and wider economic cooperation.

The discussions with ExxonMobil and HKN centered on oil development, with Iraq seeking investment and technology from US corporations as it attempts to raise output and pursue new exploration options.

World.title: With reconstruction stalled, Palestinians in Gaza shelter in buildings at risk of collapse
World.content:
Gaza City – In her Gaza City apartment, Heba Arafat walks uphill across a living room slanted at a steep angle after Israeli airstrikes caused the building’s foundations to collapse, leaving the entire structure tilted.

Like thousands of people in Gaza, Arafat chose to risk living in an apartment building damaged during nearly three years of war between Israel and Hamas, with countless Israeli airstrikes on the Palestinian territory.

“We were forced to live here because we had nowhere else to go. All of our homes were destroyed, our land was razed and we have nothing left,” said Arafat, 47.

According to the UN, 84 percent of all structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed by October 2025, and Gaza’s civil defence says 2,000 buildings across the territory are at risk of collapse.

Last week, 21 people including 12 children died in Gaza City after a six-storey building that local authorities said had been hit repeatedly by Israeli airstrikes collapsed. Israel denied having struck the building.

Arafat lives with her six daughters and husband in their old apartment building in Gaza City’s Al-Shati Refugee Camp, which they left at the height of the war that began in October 2023 with Hamas’s massive attack on Israel.

The family returned after an October 2025 ceasefire, which has reduced but not ended Israeli strikes. They found that their four-storey building, in which 30 people now live, had collapsed inward at the ground floor, the result, she said, of an Israeli ground operation in the area.

Like most buildings in Gaza City, the windows were blown away by blasts, with makeshift bedsheets spread across the frames providing little privacy.

As she spoke, Arafat illustrated her building’s slant by leaving a water bottle sideways on the floor, only for it to quickly roll away to the other end of the room.

While no territory-wide estimate exists, Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN humanitarian coordinator for the Palestinian territories, said last week that people across Gaza were living in “hundreds of damaged and unsafe shelters”.

– ‘Where can we go?’ –

“Where can we go? Even though this house is dangerous,” Arafat said. “We have been terrified ever since we heard about houses collapsing. The danger has become even greater” than we thought.

Gaza City municipal staff patrol the streets to identify buildings at risk of collapse and mark them with stencils.

“These homes pose a genuine threat to the lives of the displaced persons sheltering inside them, as well as to residents in the vicinity and those in nearby displacement camps,” said Hosni Muhanna, a Gaza City spokesman.

But Muhanna knows that people are likely to remain in these buildings for lack of better options.

“Thousands of displaced people are forced to seek shelter in these dilapidated buildings which are on the verge of collapse to escape the hardships of displacement camps that offer no protection against the summer heat or winter cold.”

Most residents of Gaza were displaced at least once during the war, and many of them remain in enormous camps for the displaced, in tents provided by humanitarian organisations or in improvised shelters.

– Stalled reconstruction-

With diseases such as the skin infection impetigo rampaging through certain camps due to the lack of waste disposal and general overcrowding, many Gaza residents have found it safer to take the risks of moving into the damaged buildings.

And with Gaza’s economy in tatters, many remain dependent on aid, which Israel has allowed into Gaza with restrictions since the declaration of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025.

But Israel has kept carrying out airstrikes, and has restricted the entry of a range of equipment that it says could also have military use, but which Gazans and international NGOs say are needed for the territory’s vast reconstruction needs.

These can include large machinery needed to clear rubble from the site of destroyed buildings, or spare parts and lubricants needed to keep other tools running, UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric said in August.

With the ceasefire process stalled for months, reconstruction efforts planned under the ceasefire have yet to begin.

According to a joint assessment published by the United Nations, World Bank and European Union in April, Gaza will require $71.4 billion in recovery and reconstruction spending over the next decade.

“We’re afraid a wall or the roof might fall on us, so we huddle together, afraid that one of us might get hurt,” Arafat said.

World.title: Oil prices fall after Trump hails ‘good’ talks with Iran
World.content:
Hong Kong – Oil prices fell on Wednesday after President Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had met for “very good” talks at the United Nations.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, and main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, dipped to $98.91 and $89.93 per barrel respectively in early Asian trade — well below the symbolic $100 mark they have smashed repeatedly since the Middle Eat war broke out in February.

The three-hour meeting was “very good”, “very productive” and “they have another one scheduled in the very near future”, Trump told reporters as he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Trump’s announcement came just hours after he delivered a bellicose address to the UN in which he said he faced a “big decision” on whether to make a deal with Iran or “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.

Nearly seven months after US-Israeli strikes on Tehran triggered the conflict, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and the United States persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

A parallel conflict between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has enveloped the kingdom, squeezing energy exports from the Red Sea.

“The three-hour US-Iran meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant,” said Stephen Innes at Quintex Intel.

Trump has pledged that oil would come down “as soon as” the United States wins the war.

The dip in oil prices came as the world’s biggest crude exporter Saudi Arabia reportedly rebooted operations along its East-West Pipeline — a crucial oil export route shut down by the conflict rocking the Middle East.

Riyadh said this month that drones launched from Iraq had forced the closure of the pipeline, which it had increasingly used to bypass the lockdown of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran.

The kingdom is aiming to resume exports later this week, Bloomberg quoted a source as saying.

But while Saudi oil giant Aramco reportedly told Asian refiners they could soon pick up crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the firm told their European counterparts will not be allocated oil in October, Bloomberg said.

– AI buzz –

Asian markets were mixed, with Taiwan’s Taiex index — home to chipmaking titan TSMC — up 0.8 percent following a renewed burst of confidence in artificial intelligence.

Anthropic and OpenAI released new, cheaper AI models within hours of each other on Tuesday, days after the heads of both companies called for a slowdown in the development of the powerful technology.

Anthropic’s release comes a few weeks before its expected stock market debut. OpenAI has delayed its IPO plans until next year.

Facebook owner Meta kicked off the AI buzz at the start of the week, surging 11 percent after its free AI agent Muse — which can book travel, send emails and make purchases — topped download charts.

Traders are also looking to Washington ahead of a summit on Thursday between Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping that is expected to focus on trade between the world’s two biggest economies.

A simmering US-China trade war is a key concern, as both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year but have yet to secure a lasting agreement.

“But the higher impact issue will be the war in the Middle East and any support the US can extract from China to use its leverage to sway the Iranians,” said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

“Another high-powered issue will be artificial intelligence and the arms race evolving between the two economic and strategic competitors, following recent warnings from US tech leaders that the technology poses existential risks without stronger guardrails.”
