Childhood obesity is likewise on the rise, a trend that Desnacido primarily attributes to growing sedentary habits, or having little to no physical activity.

Now a health advocate who has lost over 20 kg, Comboy said its chronic nature can put children at greater risk later on: “Simula pagkabata pa lang, ‘pag hindi talaga siya naagapan, kalalakihan nila ’yung obesity.” (If the condition isn't addressed early on — starting in childhood — they will grow up with obesity.)

Factors affecting obesity prevalence

What is driving the increase? Desnacido pointed to several contributing factors.

Obesity prevalence by place of residence in the Philippines This chart visualizes the obesity prevalence between urban and rural residents in the Philippines. Select an age group below to highlight specific data. 60 45 30 15 0 0 Category - Age

She explained that urban areas offer "greater convenience," enabling residents to easily order meals online or rely on ride-hailing apps instead of walking. Regions with larger urban populations tended to have higher obesity prevalence, based on the FNRI rates.

While convenience opens healthier options, people still opt for unhealthy food, or in some cases, eat too much. This is evident in the proliferation of fast food chains and the eat-all-you-can culture.

From Comboy’s experience, Filipinos would mostly reach for salty or sweet foods. “So sa tingin ko talaga, may kakulangan sa pagpili ng pagkain. Kasi bakit ’yung iba…nagiging healthy pa rin?”

(I really think there’s a shortcoming in food choices. Because why is it that some people still manage to stay healthy?)

Comboy also said that social media increasingly influences unhealthy food consumption, as food bloggers and celebrities participate in mukbang (eating broadcast) videos and promote many dining establishments.

Ultimately, the risk of overweight and obesity further skyrockets when people do not burn off their calories after eating, Desnacido added.

The percentage of adults and older persons insufficiently physically active slightly decreased in 2025, while it increased among adolescents.

Insufficiently physically active Filipinos through the years This is the percentage of individuals classified as insufficiently physically active across different age groups from 2018 to 2025.

Physical inactivity is defined as engaging in less than 60 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity physical activity per day among adolescents aged 10–17, or failing to meet the adult recommendations of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week.

Despite slight changes this year compared to 2023, the trend remained constant across all age groups since 2018. There have been no significant shifts since the FNRI started tracking physical inactivity.

Desnacido said that without physical activity, fat accumulates in the body and increases the risk of obesity.

Comboy also noticed that children and adults spend excessive hours on digital devices rather than staying active. He then urged parents to guide their children toward better nutrition and healthier diet habits.

The wealthier, the riskier

Another factor in obesity prevalence is access. FNRI data revealed that as people gain more means to buy food, obesity risk increases.

The prevalence distribution across wealth statuses in the survey demonstrated that obesity rates increase alongside growing financial capacity.

Obesity prevalence by wealth quintile in the Philippines This chart visualizes the obesity prevalence across Philippine wealth quintiles. Select an age group below to highlight specific data. 60 45 30 15 0 0 Category - Age

Richer families have more purchasing power that grants them access to unhealthy foods.

“They have a greater quantity and wider variety of foods to buy,” Desnacido said.

“Kaya ng mayayaman na bumili ng masustansyang pagkain, pero sila rin ang kayang bumili ng mga pagkain na mahal [at] unhealthy,” she added. (The wealthy can afford to buy nutritious food, but they are also the ones who can afford to buy expensive, unhealthy food.)

More vulnerable Filipinos

If the trend continues, the Philippines could face a substantial increase in noncommunicable diseases.

“More obesity-related illnesses can mean higher healthcare costs, reduced productivity, disability, [and] premature mortality,” Desnacido said.

In the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition from 2023-2028, the Philippines aims to reduce obesity and overweight prevalence per age group per year:

Children under five (0-59 months old): Reduce from 3.9% (2021-2022) by 1.9% per year

School-age children (5-10 years old): Reduce from 14% (2021-2022) by 2.2 percentage points per year

Adolescents (10-19 years old): Reduce from 13% (2021-2022) by 2.133 percentage points per year

Adults (20 years old and above): Reduce from 38.6% (2018-2019) by 3.4 percentage points per year

By 2025, no age bracket had reached its target, though children under five remained nearest to theirs.

Comboy, also an auditor of the Obesity Philippines Association, called for more active action from the government and health sector. “Mas okay talaga ’yung prevention kaysa d’on sa nagre-react na… Bigyan [sana] nila ng magandang program din ang obesity. Kasi chronic disease na rin siya eh.”

(Prevention is truly better than just reacting to the problem. They really ought to implement a good program for obesity, too, since it is a chronic disease.)

Desnacido emphasized that the Philippines needs “bold commitments” to mitigate obesity risks through a multisectoral strategy encompassing environment, transportation, economy, and health awareness.

She encouraged the public to follow the Pinggang Pinoy (Filipino plate) guide, a food plate model designed to determine proper food portions per meal per age group, along with regular exercise, to achieve a balanced diet.

“There should be variety; there should also be moderation,” said Desnacido. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Video of Marcos saying Romualdez’s arrest is ‘staged’ is AI-generated
World.content:
An AI detection tool flagged the clip's audio as 98.6% likely to be synthetic

Claim: A video shows President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. privately telling his cousin, former House speaker Martin Romualdez, that his arrest is only for show, and that he would be acquitted as long as he stays silent.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The clip was posted on Facebook by the page “Jz Plays” as part of a series labeled “Cousins Forever Series.” Its caption reads, “BBM vs. Romualdez palabas” (BBM vs Romualdez, a show), with the hashtags #bbm #PBBM #BongbongMarcos.

In the clip, Romualdez is shown asking, “Insan, ano ‘to? Bakit pinapaaresto mo ako?” (Cousin, what is this? Why are you having me arrested?)

Marcos replies, “Palabas lang ‘yan insan, parang ‘yung ginawa namin kay Bonoan. Hospital arrest lang naman ‘yan, pero ang ending niyan, abswelto ka pa rin, basta wag ka lang magsasalita, ha?”

(That’s just a show, cousin, like what we did with [former public works secretary Manuel] Bonoan. It’s only a hospital arrest, but in the end, you’ll still be acquitted, just don’t talk, okay?)

Romualdez responds, “Ayos, ang galing mo talaga insan!” (Great, you’re really something, cousin!) Both men then laugh.

The same clip was reposted by another user, seemingly as a reaction to the conversation, with the caption, “Ito talaga ang totoong nangyayari, kahit itaga niyo sa bato (This is really what’s happening, mark my words).”

As of writing, the two posts have garnered more than 160,000 views and 4,000 reactions combined.

The facts: AI detection tool Hive Moderation revealed that the clip has a 89.5% likelihood of being AI-generated, and specifically flagged the speech as 98.6% likely to be synthetic. The posts featuring the clip does not label or disclose that it was AI-generated or digitally altered.

No such exchange has also been documented anywhere, with no Palace recording, press statement, or news report confirming that this supposed conversation took place.

Amid claims that Romualdez’s arrest was staged or involved particular instructions, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla has said that Marcos gave no instructions on how Romualdez’s case should be handled, even offering to show his own phone records to prove no conversations took place.

Marcos himself later rejected suggestions that the arrest was staged, calling that framing “just another attack” rather than a genuine comment on the proceedings.

Romualdez’s arrest: The video plays into the public falling-out between the two, once close political allies, now divided by the flood control corruption scandal.

While confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center, Romualdez was arrested on September 7 under a warrant issued by anti-graft court Sandiganbayan tied to a P7.44-billion plunder case over alleged flood control kickbacks.

He has denied all allegations against him, saying in a statement that he wants due process to run its course and the evidence to speak for itself, while maintaining that he broke no laws.

Earlier, he rebuked the executive branch over the 2025 budget scandal. In a video statement in April, Romualdez seemingly alluded to the President when he said that if corruption were to occur, it does not happen at the level of legislative approval alone but also at the level of execution, when the national budget is executed and projects implemented. (READ: Swipe at Marcos? Romualdez blames executive for budget corruption scandal)

On September 14, Romualdez was moved to the New Quezon City Jail after doctors cleared him for transfer. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges against him. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Banks Dominate First Fintech Wave, But Infrastructure is Driving Next
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s largest banks have come to dominate one of Central Asia’s most digital consumer finance markets, leaving less room for independent fintech startups and pushing the sector’s next phase of growth toward open banking, embedded finance and shared financial infrastructure, according to a new industry report.

Fintech in Kazakhstan 2026 was presented at the Central Asia Fintech Summit in Almaty. The report was developed by RISE Research & Advisory, in partnership with Tarlan Payments, BCC Hub, and Fintech Center, with the support of the National Bank of Kazakhstan. This is the third annual national study of Kazakhstan’s fintech market.

According to the report, Kazakhstan’s fintech market has become increasingly concentrated around its largest banks, with five banks accounting for 69% of sector assets. Three super-apps have also emerged as the main platforms for everyday financial services.

Their apps now integrate payments, lending, e-commerce, travel, transport, government services and other everyday functions into a single ecosystem. Banks are extending the same model to small businesses, where, according to the report, they address 16 of 19 core needs, spanning from company registration and account opening to payments, credit, payroll and accounting.

Experts said that dominance has left limited space for independent consumer-facing fintech firms, pushing startups toward open banking, embedded finance and other infrastructure-driven business models.

Kazakhstan’s fintech startups raised around $72 million in venture capital between 2021 and 2025, but funding has fallen sharply since its peak at $32 million in 2023.

Investment dropped to $19 million in 2024 and just $8 million last year, with most deals still concentrated at the pre-seed and seed stages. Capital is also shifting away from consumer-facing models towards B2B and financial infrastructure businesses.

Changing market architecture

The report also highlights substantial changes in how the market is regulated. Kazakhstan is reshaping the architecture of its financial market, combining regulatory reforms with shared digital infrastructure designed to connect banks, fintech firms and consumers more closely.

A unified QR payment system, phone-number transfers, the digital tenge, Digital ID and the National Anti-Fraud Center are creating new opportunities for the sector.

According to the experts, the changes could lower barriers to market entry for fintech companies, while also bringing them under stricter compliance and regulatory requirements.

“Over the past year, Kazakhstan has undertaken its most sweeping overhaul of financial regulation in three decades. The changes include a new banking law, a Digital Code and an artificial intelligence law, alongside the rollout of a unified interbank QR payment system, transfers by phone number, the full circulation of the digital tenge, and a nationwide regulatory framework for digital assets operating alongside the jurisdiction of the Astana International Financial Centre,” said National Bank Deputy Governor Binur Zhalenov.

“Kazakhstan has become the only jurisdiction in the region to operate a full stack of digital financial infrastructure, including a central bank digital currency, instant payments, open banking and a regulated digital asset market, within a single regulatory framework,” said Zhalenov.

The shift is also visible in consumer behavior. Kazakhstan has become a predominantly cashless payments market, with non-cash transactions accounting for 88% of payments in 2026, up from 67% in 2019. Within that market, QR payments are gaining ground rapidly. Their share of cashless transactions doubled from 14% in 2023 to 28% in 2025, while QR turnover reached around $17 billion in the first five months of 2026.

On July 19, unified interbank QR and phone-number transfer systems came into effect across retail banks.

Kazakhstan is also building open-API infrastructure to allow banks and technology companies to exchange data more easily. According to the study, this will change the basis of competition. With payment rails becoming more standardized, proprietary payment systems offer less differentiation, putting greater emphasis on product quality, customer experience, data capabilities and value-added services.

“The ability to interact seamlessly between systems should not be a competitive advantage. Customers should be able to transfer money and pay for purchases regardless of which bank they use. Financial institutions, meanwhile, should compete where value is actually created: in customer experience, products, pricing and innovation,” said National Payment Corporation CEO Zhanar Samayeva.

“The same principle applies to trust. As financial services become instantaneous, increasingly data-driven and interconnected, security issues can no longer be addressed only at the level of individual institutions. Fraud prevention, digital identification, cybersecurity and operational resilience should increasingly operate at the level of the entire ecosystem,” she explained.

Banking-as-a-Service

The study points to Banking-as-a-Service as a distinct segment of Kazakhstan’s fintech market. Banking-as-a-Service, or BaaS, allows fintech companies and other businesses to offer financial products using the licensed infrastructure of a partner bank, rather than building a banking operation from scratch.

At least four banks now give external companies access to licensed banking infrastructure, processing and related services, allowing fintech firms and non-financial platforms to launch financial products through a partner bank.

“One of the more visible trends in recent years has been the growth of digital neobanks built on Banking-as-a-Service. Three years ago, such services were offered by perhaps one bank. Today, there are four or five banks providing their licence, processing and infrastructure, allowing fintech companies to create their own digital products, including niche banks,” said Assem Bolatzhan, CEO of Women in Tech Kazakhstan.

“This model is becoming increasingly popular. It works well at scale, for example in Southeast Asia and Korea. Kazakhstan’s market is smaller, but the direction remains promising,” she added.

Dynamic digital assets market

Kazakhstan’s digital asset market is also moving from regulatory experimentation toward a more established part of the financial system. Platforms licensed by the Astana International Financial Centre processed $10.6 billion in digital asset transactions in 2025, while the number of regulated providers has surpassed 50.

As national rules develop alongside the AIFC regime, stablecoins, tokenized real-world assets and crypto payments are beginning to move beyond regulatory sandboxes into commercial use. The next major area of growth could be tokenization, which may give Kazakh assets access to broader pools of global capital.

At a Sept. 15 meeting, the Kazakh government adopted a 65-measure plan to expand Kazakhstan’s regulated digital asset market and announced first tokenization projects.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Auction Rights to 56 Hydrocarbon Subsoil Blocks
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry will hold an electronic auction for the right to use 56 hydrocarbon subsoil blocks, with most lots offered for exploration and production as the country seeks to attract investment into its oil and gas resource base.

The auction is scheduled for Dec. 25 on the e-Qazyna platform. Applications to participate will be accepted through Nov. 18, inclusive.

Most blocks are intended for geological exploration and subsequent hydrocarbon production, while four lots are designated specifically for production, Kazinform reported on Sept. 21.

Most blocks are located in Kazakhstan’s western regions, including the Aktobe, Atyrau, West Kazakhstan and Mangystau Regions. The Western Ulytau block spans the Kostanai and Ulytau Regions.

Block sizes vary considerably. The Tyubedzhik (Karakum) block in the Mangystau Region covers 58.95 square kilometers, while Ustyurt Block 4, also in the Mangystau Region, spans 4,058.53 square kilometers. The Karasu block, located in the Atyrau and Aktobe Regions, covers 2,339.49 square kilometers.

The upcoming auction forms part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to expand geological exploration and attract investment into the country’s subsoil sector. Kazakhstan has been increasingly digitizing the process, with electronic auctions and access to geological information available through the e-Qazyna infrastructure. The electronic auction process has been fully automated since 2020, while a unified digital platform launched in 2025 further expanded online access to subsoil-use services.

In March, Kazakhstan also signed a long-term geological exploration agreement with Shell Kazakhstan covering the Zhanaturmys field in the Aktobe Region, highlighting continued efforts to expand the country’s hydrocarbon resource base.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UK Seek to Deepen Trade Through Higher-Value Exports and Mineral Processing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Kingdom are seeking to build on rapidly growing bilateral trade by expanding Kazakh exports beyond raw materials and deepening cooperation in mineral processing and higher-value production.

The push reflects a broader shift in the bilateral relationship. As outlined in a recent analysis for The Astana Times, the entry into force of the UK-Kazakhstan Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (SPCA) in July has created a wider institutional framework for cooperation in critical minerals, trade, logistics, education and technology.

The agreement points to a gradual shift from a relationship centered largely on resource extraction toward one focused on processing, technology, investment and higher-value production. Recent developments, including a $107 million agreement on rhenium recycling and Kazakhstan’s first multimodal fertilizer shipment to the UK via the Middle Corridor, illustrate how that shift is beginning to translate into practical projects.

Minister of Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev discussed the priorities with the UK Government’s Trade Envoy to Azerbaijan and Central Asia, Lord John Alderdice, focusing on trade diversification, industrial cooperation, investment, and scientific and educational ties.

Trade between Kazakhstan and the UK reached $1.63 billion in 2025, up 83.7% from 2024. In January-July, turnover reached $1.25 billion, up 68.5% from the same period the previous year, reported the ministry’s press service on Sept. 22.

Despite the strong growth, Kazakhstan is seeking to diversify its trade structure. Current exports to the UK are dominated by silver, crude oil, copper and copper cathodes.

“It is important for us to move from the achieved growth to deeper and more diversified trade. First and foremost, we are interested in expanding the export of Kazakh products to the British market beyond raw materials,” Shakkaliyev said.

To support this effort, Shakkaliyev proposed organizing a trade and economic mission for British importers and retail chain representatives to visit Kazakhstan and establish direct contacts with domestic producers. The officials also discussed British requirements for product quality, certification, packaging and standards.

Critical minerals emerged as another key area, with the officials highlighting opportunities to move beyond extraction toward processing and the production of higher value-added products.

Lord Alderdice said British companies and universities could work with Kazakhstan not only in resource extraction but also in developing processing capacity.

“Kazakhstan has significant natural resources, but it is especially important that you set the task not to limit yourselves to their extraction, but to create added value and develop processing. It is precisely here that we see great opportunities for cooperation,” he said.

The meeting also covered prospects for British investment in manufacturing, energy, logistics and high-tech industries, alongside efforts to strengthen direct links between companies.

The officials also discussed standardization and export readiness as part of efforts to help Kazakh producers enter the British market. Kazakhstan expressed interest in exchanging expertise with the British Institute of Export and International Trade and expanding cooperation between KazStandard and the British Standards Institution (BSI).

The officials also considered preparations for carbon-related trade requirements, including the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as well as cooperation between universities and research institutions in mining, mineral processing and the nuclear industry.

Following the meeting, Shakkaliyev and Lord Alderdice confirmed their interest in developing specific trade, investment, industrial and research projects and expanding direct contacts between businesses and relevant organizations in Kazakhstan and the UK.

World.title: Kazakhstan Hotels Receive MICHELIN Keys for First Time
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has been included in the MICHELIN Guide’s global hotel selection for the first time, with five hotels receiving the prestigious One MICHELIN Key distinction and nine others entering the guide’s recommended hotel selection.

The MICHELIN Guide has unveiled its MICHELIN Key Selection 2026, a global selection of outstanding hotels assessed through independent and anonymous inspections. Kazakhstan’s inclusion marks the country’s debut in the MICHELIN Guide’s hotel geography.

Five Kazakh hotels received the One MICHELIN Key distinction: The Veil Hotel, The St. Regis Astana and The Ritz-Carlton in Astana, as well as The Ritz-Carlton and Tenir Eco Hotel in Almaty, reported Kazakh Tourism on Sept. 22.

The MICHELIN Guide also included nine more hotels in its recommended selection. They are Sheraton Astana Hotel, Swissôtel Wellness Resort Alatau Almaty, Qazaq Auyl Eco Hotel, Qazaq Garden, Donatello Premium Almaty, Radisson Blu Hotel Almaty Airport, Zvezdnaya Eco-Hotel, YURTA Boutique Hotel and Medina Palace Hotel.

The MICHELIN Guide highlighted Kazakhstan’s growing appeal as an international tourism destination, placing the country among destinations that offer travelers experiences beyond established global tourism routes.

“The first MICHELIN Key is a celebration. It is also an invitation for travelers to look beyond the world’s most established destinations,” the MICHELIN Guide said, highlighting the diversity of experiences identified by its inspectors, from remote safari destinations to architectural landmarks in Kazakhstan’s capital.

The inclusion of Kazakh hotels followed strategic initiatives by Kazakh Tourism to develop tourism infrastructure and raise hospitality standards.

Kazakh Tourism Chairman Talgat Gazizov said the recognition could help strengthen the country’s position in the international premium tourism market.

“Having Kazakhstan appear on the global MICHELIN map is a significant recognition of the quality of service and authenticity offered by domestic hotels. The presence of 14 properties in the international selection confirms the competitiveness of Kazakhstan’s hospitality sector and provides a strong multiplier effect for tourism infrastructure development. Our key task is to translate this international recognition into sustainable growth in inbound tourism and strengthen Kazakhstan’s image as a key destination in Central Asia,” Gazizov said.

The MICHELIN Key was introduced in 2024 as a hotel distinction based on a methodology comparable to the rigorous standards that the MICHELIN Guide has applied to restaurants since 1900.

Anonymous inspectors assess hotels against five universal criteria: their ability to provide guests with a destination experience; the quality of architecture and interior design; consistency of service and comfort; the consistency between price and the experience offered; and the property’s individuality and authenticity.

The One MICHELIN Key distinction is awarded to hotels with a distinct character that provide a level of hospitality above the standard expected within their category.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Digital Road Safety Measures as Astana Traffic Grows
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding artificial intelligence, automated traffic enforcement and average-speed monitoring as road safety indicators improve, while rapidly growing vehicle numbers are driving the development of smart transport systems in Astana.

Road safety indicators improve

At a Sept. 22 government meeting, Minister of Internal Affairs Yerzhan Sadenov reported a 5% decline in road accidents nationwide, a 15% decrease in fatalities and a 6% reduction in injuries following measures to strengthen road safety.

On national roads, Transport Minister Nurlan Sauranbayev reported that from January to August, accidents fell by 10%, fatalities by 14% and injuries by 11%.

The authorities are expanding digital enforcement. The number of automated traffic-violation detection systems has increased from 28,000 to 32,000. The TOR platform brings together the Internal Affairs Ministry’s relevant digital services, while artificial intelligence monitors vehicles, identifies drivers who have been behind the wheel for more than eight hours, and helps locate stolen vehicles.

Average-speed monitoring is another key measure. The system currently operates on 12 sections covering 2,800 kilometers. Another 16 sections, covering an additional 2,800 kilometers, are planned by the end of the year, bringing total coverage to 5,600 kilometers across 28 sections.

Astana manages growing traffic

The capital is facing increasing pressure on its road network. Astana currently has 471,000 registered vehicles, compared with 420,000 in 2024 and 446,000 in 2025. The number increases by 25,000- 30,000 vehicles annually.

In addition, around 150,000 vehicles enter and leave the city every day, reflecting the scale of commuter traffic.

To manage these flows, Astana is implementing a comprehensive transport development program supported by an Intelligent Transport System (ITS). Some 80% of the city’s traffic-light facilities – 664 out of 847 – have been adapted to the system, with another 79 planned for adaptation this year.

AI supports the Smart City

As part of Astana’s Smart City project, more than 1,200 traffic-violation detection complexes operate in the capital, and more than 60,000 cameras are integrated into the city’s Situation Center.

The number of violations that can be detected automatically has increased from four to 15, while 35 types of AI-based video analytics have been introduced. Detection of the new violation types began in April.

These technologies are being developed alongside infrastructure measures to improve traffic flow and road safety.

Public transport expansion

Astana is also expanding public transport in response to growing mobility demand. Dedicated Bus Lanes now extend for 146 kilometers, 6.6% more than a year earlier.

The city’s bus fleet has increased by 60% over the past several years, from 1,200 to 1,900 vehicles. The city purchased another 80 buses this year, with 350 more planned for 2027.

The Tarlan Astana light rail transit (LRT) system will be integrated with bus routes and transport hubs as it develops. The city expects public transport users to reach 60% by 2030.

The city is also implementing new road infrastructure projects to redistribute traffic and improve connectivity across the capital.

World.title: Astana and Almaty Enter Global Top 300 Cities, Stand Out for Human Capital
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana and Almaty have placed among the world’s 300 highest-ranked cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index by Oxford Economics, with both Kazakhstan’s major urban centers showing their strongest performance in human capital. Almaty ranked 265th globally and Astana 281st among 1,000 cities assessed by the international economic research firm.

Kazakhstan’s cities in the global ranking

Almaty ranked higher overall at 265th, while Astana placed 281st. The index evaluates cities across five categories: Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment and Governance.

Almaty’s strongest result came in Human Capital, where it ranked 66th globally. Astana also entered the global top 100 in the category, ranking 98th.

The two cities’ category profiles show different strengths. Almaty ranked 288th in Economics and 269th in Quality of Life, while Astana ranked 264th and 360th, respectively. In Environment, Almaty was 845th and Astana 630th. Both received the same Governance rank of 622nd.

Oxford Economics defines Human Capital through indicators including population growth, age profile, universities, corporate headquarters, educational attainment and the share of foreign-born residents.

Human capital as a source of growth

The report emphasizes the relationship between human capital and economic development. According to Oxford Economics, cities that move into higher-value sectors can attract and retain skilled workers, while strong industries encourage investment in education and skills.

“The end result is an increase in the stock of human capital, which further incentivises investment, accelerating economic growth further still,” the report said.

This dynamic is increasingly important as the global urban economy changes. Oxford Economics notes that many cities in Asia and the Middle East are gaining ground by expanding labor markets and moving into technology, advanced manufacturing and financial and business services.

The report also identifies Astana as a Regional Leader, an archetype comprising important cities that are significant within their regions and tend to outperform their respective countries on indicators such as economic growth and income per person.

A changing global urban landscape

The 2026 index places New York first, followed by London and Paris. Seattle, San Francisco, Dublin, Boston, San Jose, Tokyo and Zurich complete the top 10. The report says North American and European cities still dominate the top positions, but the global economic landscape is becoming increasingly multipolar.

Asia is central to this shift. Oxford Economics expects cities across Asia Pacific and the Middle East to record significant gains in the coming years as economic growth improves living standards and quality of life.

For Kazakhstan, the results put Almaty and Astana firmly within the global top 300, while their relatively strong human capital rankings highlight the role of education, skills, labor markets and demographic factors in their position among the world’s major urban economies.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Joins Kazakhstan’s Reading Nation Marathon
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen has joined the nationwide Reading Nation marathon in its Parasat category, a non-competitive initiative that promotes reading through the personal example of public figures. Unlike participants in the competitive stages, those in Parasat do not compete for cash prizes; the category focuses instead on promoting a culture of reading through personal example.

The marathon’s competitive stages offer substantial cash prizes: regional winners receive 600,000 tenge (US$1,337) for first place, 450,000 tenge (US$1,000) for second and 300,000 tenge (US$668) for third, while the 10 top readers selected at the national final will each receive 10 million tenge (US$22,293), bringing the total value of the main national prizes to 100 million tenge (US$222,937).

Dimash chooses Karipbek Kuyukov’s story

For the marathon, Qudaibergen selected the autobiography of Kazakh artist and anti-nuclear movement activist Karipbek Kuyukov, “Life Without Hands”, which recounts the artist’s life and his work despite being born without arms as a result of the effects of nuclear testing in the Semipalatinsk region, reported the Ministry of Culture and Information on Sept. 21.

Qudaibergen said he had met Kuyukov personally in Karagandy before a Miner’s Day concert.

“His life journey, unyielding perseverance in the face of hardship and strength of spirit made a particular impression on me,” he said.

The Reading Nation marathon runs from September to April 2027. It includes Kazakh and Russian-language leagues and seven areas involving schoolchildren, students, teachers, families, civil servants and other participants.

National focus on reading

The initiative follows a presidential decree signed in May on measures to develop reading culture and form a “reading nation.” The document sets reading promotion as a priority in culture, education and innovation policy and envisages measures to expand access to books and modernize the country’s literary and library infrastructure.

The campaign comes amid broader discussion about reading and foundational skills in the digital and AI era. Kazakhstan’s latest PISA results showed that 15-year-old students performed below the OECD average in reading, mathematics and science.

Against this backdrop, the government is also preparing measures to promote reading through new library formats, wider access to literature and a national concept for developing reading culture in the AI era.

World.title: Who Will Pay for Processing Kazakhstan’s Copper?
World.content:
The new methodology for calculating copper concentrate processing tariffs raises a broader question: how competitive and predictable will Kazakhstan’s copper value chain be for international business?

Kazakhstan is seeking to develop domestic processing and create more value within the country. This is particularly important for copper, as the country has a significant resource base while the metal is becoming increasingly important for global industry, energy and technology.

Against this backdrop, the Ministry of Industry and Construction has proposed a new methodology for calculating the tariff for processing copper concentrate. The aim is to establish a unified and transparent mechanism for determining the cost of processing raw materials at copper smelting facilities in Kazakhstan.

Under the proposed approach, the tariff would be based on processing costs, a normative profit margin and investment components, including investment in new copper smelting capacity.

For the domestic market, this is primarily a question of tariff regulation. For international businesses, however, the issue is broader: how will the economics of Kazakhstan’s copper value chain be structured, and how competitive will these conditions be compared with the global market?

Global market, global benchmarks

Copper concentrate processing is part of an established international supply chain. Smelters and concentrate producers operate in a market where processing economics depend not only on domestic costs, but also on global supply and demand.

One of the key market benchmarks is the Treatment Charge (TC). When concentrate is abundant and smelting capacity is relatively limited, treatment charges tend to be higher. When concentrate becomes scarce, smelters compete for feedstock and TC declines.

In some market conditions, treatment charges can reach zero or even become negative.

This does not necessarily mean that smelting is uneconomic. Rather, it reflects the broader revenue structure of copper processing.

One concentrate, multiple sources of value

A copper smelter generates economic value from more than the treatment charge itself.

Copper and other metals, including precious metals, are recovered from the concentrate. Sulphur contained in the feedstock can be used to produce sulphuric acid, which also has an independent market value.

As a result, an international processor assesses the overall economics of the operation rather than simply the cost of the processing service. This includes the value and composition of the concentrate, recoverable metals, prices for final products, potential revenues from sulphuric acid and production costs.

This is why a zero or negative TC does not automatically indicate that processing is loss-making. Under certain market conditions, a smelter may accept concentrate without a treatment charge in order to maintain capacity utilisation and generate value from the metals and by-products recovered during processing.

What does this mean for Kazakhstan?

The proposed Kazakh methodology is primarily cost-based, taking into account processing expenses, a normative profit margin and investment costs.

This raises an important question: how does the calculation account for the revenue side of the business, including the economic value of additional metals and sulphuric acid?

For domestic regulation, this is a question of tariff design. For international investors, it is also a question of competitiveness and comparability.

A copper concentrate producer does not assess processing costs in isolation. The economics of the entire chain matter: mining, transportation, processing, financing and the sale of copper and associated products.

A change in the economics of one stage can therefore influence the attractiveness of the entire project.

From raw materials to global value chains

This issue is particularly relevant as Kazakhstan seeks to move from the export of raw materials towards higher-value production.

Developing domestic copper processing is consistent with this objective and could also strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in emerging international supply chains for critical minerals.

For investors, however, the equation goes beyond the availability of mineral resources or processing capacity. It includes the long-term predictability of regulations, logistics and processing costs, access to infrastructure, export opportunities and the overall stability of a project’s economic model.

At the July 2026 meeting of the Council of Foreign Investors, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev again identified critical minerals and the production of higher value-added products as promising areas for investment.

Asian Development Bank Vice-President Fatima Yasmin, in turn, noted that global capital is becoming more selective, with investors paying particular attention to predictable rules, transparent procedures and projects that can be clearly assessed from a financing perspective.

More than a tariff

The discussion around the methodology therefore goes beyond the relationship between a concentrate producer and a smelter.

If Kazakhstan wants to attract international capital into deeper copper processing, investors need to understand how the economics of each stage of the value chain are determined.

Can the new methodology support the development of domestic processing while maintaining the competitiveness of Kazakhstan’s copper industry?

Will the resulting tariff remain comparable with international commercial conditions?

How will foreign companies factor it into long-term investment decisions?

And how will the new regulatory framework fit into Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to create a more predictable investment environment?

These questions matter because a country’s competitiveness is not determined by a single tariff or incentive. It is shaped by the overall investment and operating environment.

For Kazakhstan, the debate therefore goes beyond the price of processing copper concentrate. Ultimately, it is about the country’s position in the global copper value chain — whether Kazakhstan remains primarily a supplier of raw materials, becomes a processor, or develops into a fully-fledged participant in international value chains, creating greater value through processing, technology and industrial capabilities.

World.title: Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Race time is set, but getting home is anyone’s guess
World.content:
Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix

Sports journalist Anar Khanlarov left his home in Sumgayit half an hour earlier than usual on 21 September to make it to Baku in time for a TV programme. But even that was not enough.

He planned to take the metro from 20 January station to Nizami, then a bus to 28 May, followed by bus No 5 towards State Flag Square. As the İdman TV studio was undergoing renovation, filming was taking place at the Rowing Federation building on the boulevard.

His bus became stuck in traffic near Winter Park. Khanlarov continued on foot towards the Puppet Theatre, hoping to catch another bus from there or, failing that, take a taxi. When he reached the theatre at 20:40, he found that the road towards Bayil was closed. The programme began at 21:00, but Khanlarov did not reach the filming location until 21:25, alternating between walking and running. By then he was sweating heavily, and the production team decided he was not in a suitable condition to appear on air. As a result, Khanlarov did not take part in the programme at all that day.

The main events of the Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix will take place on 24–26 September. But even before the racing begins, road closures and changes to bus routes have brought life in the city to a standstill.

26 bus routes changed, leaving passengers with no real alternative

According to a plan by the Azerbaijan Land Transport Agency (AYNA), 26 bus routes have been changed between 21 and 26 September.

Route No 5, which Khanlarov had planned to take, is among those affected. On one section, the bus runs between Nariman Narimanov metro station and Suleyman Rahimov Street, while on another it runs along a route covering the Salyan Highway, Bibi-Heybat Mosque and the Baku Funicular. Under the new arrangements, it is no longer possible to use the bus to travel from the city centre to Bayil via the usual route. Some stops on this and other routes are inside the restricted race zone. There is no alternative public transport available.

The changes have also affected people travelling into the city from the suburbs. Buses No 149 and 149E from the settlement of Sahil and No 195E from Alat now run only as far as the Lokbatan transport hub near the Bina shopping centre. Passengers travelling to the city centre have to change to another form of transport. Bus No 125 reaches the centre via the ring road through Badamdar.

The transit corridors announced by the organisers are also not an alternative for bus passengers. On 21–22 September, they are open from 07:00 to 09:00 and from 18:00 to 20:00. However, these arrangements do not apply to public transport. Except in emergencies, picking up and dropping off passengers is also prohibited within the transit corridors. By the time Khanlarov reached the Puppet Theatre at 20:40, he says, the evening transit window had already closed.

‘We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes’

Former transport officials have also complained about the traffic jams. Mais Aghayev, former head of the Baku Transport Agency’s press service, wrote on Facebook:

“We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes on the stretch from the Mikayil Aliyev roundabout towards Heydar Aliyev Avenue.”

The congestion has also been acknowledged by the authorities. On the evening of 22 September, the Intelligent Transport Management Centre reported traffic jams on 28 May Street, as well as on the section of Shamsi Badalbeyli Street running from Winter Park towards the Central Bank. These streets are also part of the routes affected by AYNA’s changes to bus services.

Seven schools and universities switch to remote learning

Measures related to the race are not limited to changes to transport. According to the Baku City Education Department, seven schools are holding classes online from 22 to 26 September: Public Schools No 6, 7, 8 and 23, Classical Gymnasium No 160, Lyceum No 132–134 and the Ilyas Efendiyev Elite Gymnasium.

Under an order issued by the Ministry of Science and Education, universities in Baku have also switched to remote learning from 23 to 25 September. The ministry says the measure is intended to ensure continuity of the education process.

The move may reduce the number of daily journeys to schools and universities. However, remote learning creates additional difficulties for working parents: who will look after younger children, and how will families ensure they have the devices and internet access needed for online classes? The switch to remote learning does not mean parents no longer have to go to work. So while it may ease pressure on the transport system, it does not necessarily ease the everyday burden on families.

No indication of how much longer journeys will take

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative party, linked the problem to Baku’s fragmented system of governance in a Facebook post on 14 September. In his view, the key factors are the availability of public transport and journey times. He also argues that any changes to working hours should take into account the school schedules of employees’ children.

Economist Akif Nasirli told Radio Azadliq that the race should be held outside the city centre. In his view, the economic benefits of the event should not be used to justify restrictions on residents’ freedom of movement:

“People have the right to move freely in their own country, in their own capital.”

AYNA’s traffic management plan for the race, published on 19 September, lists alternative streets that drivers can use. However, it provides no information on actual bus frequencies along the altered routes, how much additional time journeys will take, or how much time passengers may lose when changing between separate sections of disrupted routes.

For residents, it is not enough simply to know which street a bus will take. They need to know when to leave home, where they will have to change and whether they can get to work on time. Without this information, the burden of adapting to the route changes — and the consequences of any resulting delays — falls on passengers themselves.

World.title: Why Georgia closed 10 schools days into new academic year
World.content:
School closure in Georgia

Ten state schools in Georgia were closed during the first three days of the new academic year. Some of the buildings are due to be demolished and rebuilt, while others will undergo repairs.

The decision followed assessments by the National Forensics Bureau, which found that the school buildings were in a state of disrepair and unsafe for use.

One of the schools is in Tbilisi, while the others are located in different regions across the country.

For the first week after the closures, the schools switched to remote learning. During this period, the Education Ministry and school administrations are expected to urgently find alternative premises.

All 10 schools are likely to be temporarily accommodated in neighbouring schools, with classes held in two or three shifts and lesson times shortened. If any of the alternative schools are too far away, school buses will be provided.

More than 4,000 pupils and around 400 teachers are now waiting for the ministry to decide where they will be relocated and which shifts they will study and work in.

his is not unprecedented. In recent years, thousands of pupils across Georgia have been studying in temporary, “borrowed” premises, while schools that were demolished have yet to be rebuilt.

How events unfolded and what the decisions were based on

The closure of all 10 schools followed the same pattern. The start of the new academic year on 15 September was celebrated as usual, with balloons, flags and flowers in school courtyards and classrooms.

Three days later, on the evening of 17 September, parents received messages informing them that the schools were being closed.

Number of pupils and teachers at the closed schools. Source: JAMnews, based on data from the official schools portal.

In all 10 cases, the decisions to close the schools were based on assessments by the National Forensics Bureau dated 10 September 2026. The education minister says the ministry did not receive the documents until 17 September, explaining why the closures were announced at such short notice.

Some parents do not believe that the school buildings are unsafe. They suspect that some of the decisions may be linked to corrupt deals and investors’ interests.

JAMnews examined publicly available documents relating to all 10 schools, including decisions by the Authorisation Council, expert assessments, public procurement records, renovation plans and municipal reports.

We sought answers to several questions: Why were these schools allowed to begin the academic year as normal on 15 September if their buildings had to be vacated just days later? When did the responsible authorities learn about the condition of the schools? And if the buildings were already destined for demolition, why was money allocated for their renovation year after year?

Renovating schools only to abandon them

The documents examined by JAMnews show that concerns about the poor condition of some of the schools had been known for years. In other cases, however, there had previously appeared to be no need even for repairs, let alone demolition.

Some of the schools underwent minor renovation work in recent years, with substantial sums spent on the projects.

For example, according to public procurement records, Public School No 16 in Kutaisi underwent various repairs in 2015, 2017 and 2022. The largest amount was spent in 2015 — around 190,000 lari [about $70,300].

The Kutaisi school made its most recent purchase just three weeks before the start of the current academic year. On 24 August, the administration signed a 2,500-lari [about $925] contract for maintenance of the school grounds, including mowing and removing grass.

Public School No 16 in Kutaisi. The start of the academic year was celebrated with invited entertainers. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

The public school in the village of Misaktsieli underwent major renovations in 2008, while its heating system was completely upgraded last winter.

This is also confirmed by the Mtskheta municipality’s 2025 budget. According to the document, several schools were due to undergo renovation work funded through a targeted transfer from the state budget. The school in Misaktsieli was among them.

The Misaktsieli school continued to spend money on various works and services in 2026. Its most recent contract, signed on 4 September, was worth 12,515 lari [about $4,635] and covered the removal of flooring, plumbing work and the subsequent installation of granite flooring.

The school in the village of Abranlo, in the Kvemo Kartli region, is the smallest of the schools closed in recent days, with around 80 pupils. It too has undergone renovation work in recent years.

Mariko Tsikoridze, a project co-ordinator for CENN in Kvemo Kartli, says three sanitation and hygiene projects were carried out at the school before 2019. Toilets were built, washbasins renovated, and an illegal rubbish dump created by local residents in the school grounds was cleared.

“We brought in six truckloads of soil and built a sports ground. The local authorities were also actively involved at the time,” Tsikoridze says.

The school is now due to be demolished. Its headteacher, Mikheil Jakeli, wrote on social media that, according to the National Forensics Bureau’s assessment, constructing a new building would be preferable to repairing the existing one, prompting the ministry to decide on demolition.

Problems left unaddressed

For some of the schools, JAMnews was unable to find any relevant records in the public procurement system. However, municipal reports and local media articles show that concerns about the condition of these schools had been raised for years.

For example, parents of pupils at Public School No 5 in Khashuri were calling for repairs as early as January 2023, complaining about damaged walls, floors and doors, as well as loose stair railings.

First day of the new academic year at Public School No 5 in Khashuri. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

In municipal reports from the Imereti region, Public School No 2 in Tskaltubo had for years been listed as a building in need of renovation.

Available records for 2022-2026 contain no evidence of major renovation work at the school. However, according to Info Imereti, minor repairs were carried out, including in the summer of 2026.

“There is an assessment stating that the building is not cost-effective to repair. It would therefore be better to construct a new one rather than renovate it,” Mamuka Chkhetiani, head of the Tskaltubo education resource centre, told Kutaisi Post.

Officials knew as early as 2022-2023 that Public School No 3 in Senaki was in a state of disrepair. In 2022, the school’s headteacher, Marine Naneishvili, told Etaloni that the building was due to be demolished.

The Finance Ministry’s 2023 review of investment projects listed the “Construction of Public School No 3 in Senaki”as a separate project, with 12.696m lari [about $4.7m] allocated for it. It is unclear what became of the project.

Public School No 3 in Senaki. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

Reaction at schools

Members of the school communities at two of the 10 schools — in Tbilisi and Misaktsieli — responded to the authorities’ decision with protests, which are still continuing. At the other schools, discontent has largely been confined to social media, where parents have complained about the disruption to both their children’s plans and their own.

“We are in shock” is the most common reaction beneath posts announcing each new school closure.

Two of the three schools closed in the Kakheti region — Public School No 3 in Gurjaani and the school in the village of Velistsikhe — are in Gurjaani municipality. More than 500 children attend the Velistsikhe school, while School No 3 has 148 pupils.

“Congratulations to the school community of Velistsikhe Public School — pupils, parents, teachers and everyone interested in improving our school,” headteacher Nona Menabdishvili wrote on social media alongside the news of its closure.

The post attracted numerous comments, many of them essentially asking: “What is there to celebrate?” Others shared stories of schools elsewhere that have remained closed for years.

Unlike Menabdishvili, Mikheil Jakeli, headteacher of the school in Abranlo, expressed no enthusiasm about the Education Ministry’s decision.

He has appealed to the ministry to allow pupils to complete the current academic year in the old building, subject to appropriate safety measures, “to avoid moving the children elsewhere just days after the start of classes and causing them unnecessary stress”.

‘From positive assessment to demolition’ – story of School No 21

The largest of the 10 schools to be closed is Public School No 21 in Tbilisi, formerly Gymnasium No 6. News of its closure was also the first to emerge.

It is one of the capital’s most prestigious schools. Because of its emphasis on German-language teaching, it is often referred to as the “German school”.

According to a National Forensics Bureau assessment dated 10 September 2026, several problems were identified in the school building, including a risk of plaster falling from the façade, a faulty drainage system, cracks in some areas and damage to reinforced concrete blocks.

The assessment also identified seismic vulnerability as a separate problem, citing the absence of an earthquake-resistant reinforcement belt on the roof parapet and other failures to comply with current seismic standards.

Protest outside Public School No 21 on 18 September 2026. “Don’t demolish the Sixth,” reads an improvised protest banner.

However, the same school had previously received a very different assessment from the same National Forensics Bureau on 15 November 2023, when it underwent authorisation. The assessment said the building required repairs, but gave it an overall “positive” evaluation, and the school was authorised to operate until 2032.

In April 2026, the Authorisation Council carried out scheduled monitoring of the school and, citing the positive assessment, said the building required repairs and gave the school until 2028 to address the problems.

In other words, as recently as spring 2026, official documents still listed School No 21 as requiring repairs rather than demolition.

However, by the time the Authorisation Council made that assessment, a new examination of the school building was already under way.

The Municipal Development Fund had requested the examination on 16 September 2025. An expert inspected the building on 10 December, and nine months later, on 10 September 2026, issued a new assessment.

The building was initially classified as Category III based on the extent of the damage. However, following Georgian government decree No 161 of 22 April 2026, which sets out criteria for assessing whether buildings are fit for use, the damage was subsequently classified as Category IV because of seismic safety concerns.

How could the school have deteriorated so severely in three years that it now needs to be demolished? This is the question being asked by parents. Many suspect corruption. The school is located in a prestigious tourist area, prompting speculation that a private investor may be interested in the site.

Parents fear that the school will be demolished and never rebuilt. They are demanding an independent assessment and say they will not allow the building to be torn down. They also oppose both online learning and the relocation of pupils to other schools.

If we don’t act now, we will lose our school’ – story of Misaktsieli village school

Protest outside the school in Misaktsieli, 18 September 2026.

Irine Kalandadze’s child started first grade this year. He had barely had time to settle into school when his parents were told it was closing:

“He had only been at school for three days and was eagerly looking forward to the next one — he liked it so much. Then suddenly we were told the school was closing. I can’t explain this to my child, and it is very painful for me too. This is precisely the stage when children need to develop a love of school, and now we don’t even know where or how he will study.”

The school in Misaktsieli serves five villages in Mtskheta municipality and has more than 500 pupils.

Parents say lessons will be held online for the first week after the closure, after which the children will be transferred to the school in the village of Tsilkani. But that school has capacity for only 300 pupils, meaning classes will have to be held in several shifts.

Parents do not know for certain whether the Misaktsieli school is due to be demolished or is being closed for repairs. On 18 September, residents gathered in the school grounds and demanded an explanation from the headteacher, who told them that he had not yet seen the expert assessment himself.

Villagers fear there may also be business interests behind the decision: the school is in a popular tourist area, occupies a large site and is surrounded by numerous commercial properties.

“We all want our children to study in a modern school. It’s just that we have seen many examples of how school renovation projects have ended,” Irine says.

Parents are demanding that, if the school needs repairs, the work be postponed until spring. If the building is to be demolished, they want construction of a new school to begin simultaneously on vacant land nearby, with the existing building demolished only once its replacement is ready.

“If we don’t act now, we will lose our school,” Irine says.

The protest is continuing, and parents say they have no intention of backing down.

Not an exception, but a wider trend

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, there are 2,086 state schools in the country.

In 2022, the Education Ministry launched a large-scale reconstruction programme that was intended to cover 800 schools.

Since then, hundreds of schools have closed across Georgia. Two years ago, in 2024, the fact-checking platform FactCheck reported that 21,203 pupils had been relocated to alternative premises.

Based on publicly available data, the number is likely still in the tens of thousands. The Municipal Development Fund, which oversees school reconstruction, regularly publishes updates on the completion or launch of work at schools across Georgia.

For example, in August 2026, the fund announced tenders for the reconstruction of 11 schools. None of the 10 schools closed in recent days appears on that list, suggesting that the overall number of schools currently not operating in their own buildings is considerably higher.

On 18 September, as thousands of teachers, pupils and parents were reeling from the news that their schools were being closed, government officials were holding a high-profile ceremony to reopen the renovated Public Schools No 4 and No 5 in Batumi.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze and other senior officials at the opening of two schools in Batumi. Photo: Municipal Development Fund.

What is actually happening?

Education experts say the situation illustrates systemic problems and a lack of a consistent strategy and long-term vision in the education system.

Education expert Revaz Abkhazava lists the problems created by what he describes as a poorly planned intervention — the reconstruction of schools:

It has disrupted the education process;

It has upended established routines for parents and children, including attendance at after-school clubs and additional classes;

It has shown a complete disregard for teachers’ needs, with low salaries forcing many to work at several schools at the same time;

It has imposed additional costs on the state for transporting pupils to other schools.

“The education system is extremely complex. It consists of many interconnected components. If you fail to see it as a whole, you get what we are seeing now. A single decision does not simply create one problem — it can push the entire system to the brink of collapse.”

Abkhazava says such decisions are the result of experienced and qualified professionals with institutional knowledge being pushed out of the education system.

“School reconstruction is a technical task. It does not require any special expertise. Education management professionals could have resolved this issue very easily.”

The expert also points to problems in communication between state institutions. The process, he says, was not managed in a way that would have ensured the assessments were ready at least a month before the start of the academic year.

Revaz Abkhazava believes the root of these problems lies in the politicisation of Georgia’s education system. He says education should not serve any political party and that safeguards are needed to ensure this, including an education council and teachers’ associations. He also argues that the ministry’s strategy should not change every time a new minister takes office.

“The education system should be as decentralised as possible. The ministry should employ professionals with knowledge and experience in education management and education policy.

“The ministry should focus on evaluation, analysis and research, and make decisions based on them. It should support educational institutions, while those institutions should have the autonomy to make decisions on matters that concern them,” the expert concludes.

World.title: Armenian orphanage worker brutally assaults disabled resident
World.content:
Armenian orphanage worker assaults disabled child

A care worker at the Kharberd specialised orphanage in Armenia brutally assaulted a disabled child who is unable to walk or speak.

The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, which oversees the institution, confirmed the incident and said it had taken place several weeks ago. The care worker was immediately dismissed and is now under house arrest.

“A disabled child was beaten with a mop in a place where they were supposed to receive care and support. In reality, this is the kind of care the child needs to be protected from,” said Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda.

Rights activist questions purpose of such institutions

“If we do not want violence, these institutions should not exist at all. Family-based upbringing and alternative forms of care are possible for all children if the state makes the necessary effort and allocates the necessary resources. The state’s obligations do not begin after a disabled child has been beaten, nor do they end with the dismissal of the alleged abuser or their placement under house arrest,” Hovsepyan said.

Until such institutions cease to exist, however, he says the state is obliged to establish a system that:

“prevents violence and identifies signs of it in a timely manner;

provides safe mechanisms enabling all children to report abuse;

guarantees a proper investigation and the child’s swift recovery.”

Details of the incident

Local media have established further details about what happened at the orphanage. The incident is now known to have taken place on 13 August.

The child who was assaulted has cerebral palsy and is unable to walk independently or speak.

The care worker who assaulted the child had worked at the orphanage since September 2012.

“In room D-1 of the orphanage, the care worker initially struck the resident, F.M., several times. After he fell to the floor, she picked up a floor mop and continued striking him on his lower back, spine and left shoulder blade. As a result, F.M. suffered severe physical pain and emotional distress,” journalists reported.

Child’s condition described as satisfactory

Nver Kostanyan, spokesman for the minister of labour and social affairs, wrote on social media that the orphanage administration had “identified the incident” and immediately reported it to law enforcement:

“The care worker has been dismissed, while it is for law enforcement agencies to determine whether criminal charges are warranted. The child is in good health and continues to receive care at the specialised orphanage.”

Kostanyan said such incidents were a “red line” for the ministry:

“Any instance of violence is unacceptable and will be subject to an appropriate criminal-law assessment.”

Expert opinion

Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda, warns that disabled children often avoid speaking about abuse they have experienced.

“There are many reasons. Among other things, they think they will not be believed, because what they say is often called into question,” he wrote on Facebook.

Hovsepyan stressed that the public only learnt about the abuse at the orphanage after it was reported by the media. The rights activist believes such cases should be closely scrutinised by state bodies, particularly now that there is no mechanism for public oversight.

A group of civil society experts previously operated at the initiative of the Labour Ministry, carrying out regular monitoring of care centres for children and elderly people.

“The monitoring group was disbanded about three years ago. Easily. But its work is not being resumed with the same ease,” Hovsepyan said.

Hovsepyan himself was a member of the group. He recalls that in 2021 it visited the Kharberd specialised orphanage and documented a case of discrimination against a minor in its care:

“At the same orphanage, staff wore gloves when touching a teenager living with HIV who had recently been transferred there. Separate dishes were used for him. His clothes were washed separately. Other children were told to stay away from him. And yet the world has long known that HIV is not transmitted through this kind of contact.”

The orphanage staff themselves told the experts about this because they believed they were ‘doing everything right’.

Following the recent violent assault, Hovsepyan says he is not convinced that conditions at the specialised institution have improved:

“I am also not sure whether all new employees receive the necessary training before they start working with children. Nor am I sure that the state is taking steps to ensure that children are in safe hands.”

World.title: A pair of porcupines, Khrashuna and Khramuna, at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Tbilisi Zoo is home to two Indian porcupines, a female and a male named Khrashuna and Khramuna. Their keepers chose the names for a reason: the porcupines make funny “crunching” sounds when they eat. Khrashuna is the bolder of the two, while Khramuna is more cautious.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: ALL VIDEO

______________________________________________________________________________

Contrary to popular belief, porcupines have nothing in common with either badgers or hedgehogs. Badgers are carnivores, hedgehogs are insectivores, while porcupines are rodents.

Their most distinctive feature is their long, thick quills, which they mainly use for defence. When threatened, their first response is to flee rather than attack. And no, porcupines do not shoot their quills — that is simply a myth. When they sense danger, they

Alongside their varied diet, Khrashuna and Khramuna always have branches in their enclosure. They gnaw on the wood, which helps keep their teeth strong.

Porcupines are nocturnal animals. During the day, especially in summer, they prefer to stay in their shelter. They become active in the evening and start looking for food. That is why visitors who come to their enclosure during the day may see nothing more than a nose or head poking out of the burrow.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Porcupines at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: European Court of Human Rights to review case of Georgian activist Irakli Miladze
World.content:
The Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has accepted the case of Georgian activist Irakli Miladze. The case concerns freedom of expression online and administrative proceedings brought against the activist.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) asked the court to refer Miladze’s case to the Grand Chamber in August 2026.

According to GYLA chair Tamar Oniani, this means that until the Grand Chamber delivers its judgment, Georgia’s city and appeals courts cannot cite the case as a precedent when restricting freedom of expression on social media.

Irakli Miladze case

In 2022, authorities fined activist Irakli Miladze for using profanity in a video in which he criticised Tbilisi’s transport policy. He directed some of the offensive language at the city mayor, municipal officials and police officers.

Authorities brought the case under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which covers petty hooliganism, including the use of obscene language in public places. Tbilisi City Court ordered Miladze to pay 2,000 lari [~$740], but the Court of Appeal reduced the fine to 500 lari [~$185].

On 19 May 2026, the ECHR’s Fourth Section ruled on the case and found that the authorities had not violated Miladze’s freedom of expression, which Article 10 of the Convention protects.

Irakli Miladze

The court found that Miladze’s statements did not form part of a public debate and therefore did not warrant the same level of protection for freedom of expression as statements on matters of political or public interest.

The court also considered the size of the fine and its consequences, noting that the sanction did not prevent Miladze from continuing his civic and political activities. At the same time, the court confirmed that the concept of a “public space” also covers online platforms when they are widely accessible to the public.

The case will now be reconsidered, but this does not mean that the Grand Chamber has already found that Miladze’s rights were violated. In its final judgment, it may uphold the previous ruling or take a different position.

The key question will be whether Miladze’s statements on TikTok were protected by freedom of expression and whether imposing an administrative fine on him was justified.

According to GYLA, the significance of referring the case to the Grand Chamber is further underscored by the fact that, after the May 2026 ruling, the Interior Ministry established a so-called “censorship department”. GYLA says its activities are linked to administrative cases brought against citizens over opinions they post on social media.

Irakli Miladze case

World.title: ‘One cashbox’ for two parties: Transparency International Georgia study
World.content:
According to a study by Transparency International Georgia (TI), a significant share of the funding for the pro-government and anti-Western People’s Power party comes from people who have previously funded, or continue to fund, the ruling Georgian Dream party.

The study found that, as of August 2026, 28 people had donated a total of 861,750 lari [~$320,000] to People’s Power, which split from Georgian Dream in 2022. Of these, 21 had previously donated 1,969,169 lari [~$730,000] to Georgian Dream. Another three continue to fund both parties.

TI says these financial links indicate that People’s Power is not independent of the political and business circles surrounding Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili.

The study highlights a group of businesspeople and companies linked to Ivanishvili’s circle. According to the organisation, members of this group donated a total of 381,000 lari [~$141,000] to People’s Power between 2024 and 2026.

One of them is Archil Mamatashvili, CEO of JSC Cartu Insurance Company and a member of the supervisory board of Ivanishvili-linked Artu Holding. In 2025–2026, Mamatashvili donated 70,000 lari [~$26,000] to People’s Power. He had previously donated 55,600 lari [~$20,600] to Georgian Dream.

According to the study, Cartu Insurance Company received government and municipal procurement contracts worth around 3.5 million lari [~$1.3 million]. Other company representatives — Alla Kakhniаuri, Kakha Kobiashvili, Zaza Verdzеuli, Givi Lebanidze and Zurab Chachkhiani — donated a total of around 1 million lari [~$370,000] to Georgian Dream.

Another major donor to People’s Power is Giorgi Damenia, a business partner of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s brother, Alexander Ivanishvili, in the company Tornado+. In 2025–2026, he donated 120,000 lari [~$44,400] to the party. Damenia had previously donated 170,000 lari [~$63,000] to Georgian Dream, while Tornado+ itself donated 85,000 lari [~$31,500] to Ivanishvili’s party between 2016 and 2018.

Another member of Ivanishvili’s business circle is Irakli Bekaури, CEO of Bolero & Company, owned by Vakhtang Karichashvili. Karichashvili, who holds Georgian and Russian citizenship, has been described as a business partner of Ivanishvili’s cousin, Ucha Mamatshvili. According to the study, his companies rank among Georgia’s largest wine exporters to Russia. Between 2014 and 2024, his companies received 56 million lari [~$20.7 million] in subsidies from Georgia’s Agriculture Ministry.

In 2026, Bekauri donated 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power. He had previously donated 327,000 lari [~$121,000] to Georgian Dream.

Among people linked to Bekauri and Karichashvili is Levan Getsadze. Public Registry records list him at various times as a representative of companies linked to Ucha Mamatshvili’s business partners. Getsadze donated 13,000 lari [~$4,800] to People’s Power, which the study says was his first political donation.

For many years, Getsadze owned Trezor, a company founded in 2019 that operated a medical laboratory in Tbilisi. Soon after its establishment, the company began taking part in public procurement and has since received contracts worth around 3.2 million lari [~$1.19 million]. The laboratory is now owned by the US company Quest Biosciences LLC.

The study also links another major People’s Power donor, David Balanchivadze, to Ucha Mamatshvili’s business circle. In 2016–2017, the investigative journalism studio Monitor linked Balanchivadze’s appointment as executive director of RMG GOLD to Mamatshvili’s interests.

Balanchivadze began making political donations to Georgian Dream in 2016. According to the study, he donated a total of 532,000 lari [~$197,000] to the party. In 2026, he donated 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power.

Among the donors to People’s Power is Giorgi Meskhi, who served as director of the state-owned company Sakspetstrans from 2017 to 2020. In 2024, he donated 58,000 lari [~$21,500] to the party.

While running the state-owned company, Meskhi founded the construction company Hiteco Group with his business partner Giorgi Khujadze. Meskhi now owns 100% of the company and serves as its director. Hiteco Group is building a multi-storey hotel in Tbilisi. Meskhi also owns a 33% stake in Gonio Group.
