World.title: Azerbaijan to establish laboratory meeting international standards for mining and metallurgical industry
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. The establishment of a laboratory compliant with international standards is planned as part of the development of Azerbaijan’s mining (metal ores) and metallurgical industry.

This is outlined in the "State program on the development of the mining (metal ores) and metallurgical industry for 2027–2030," approved by the President ofthe Republic of AzerbaijanIlham Aliyev.

In accordance with item 8.1.7 of the State Program’s action plan, work will be undertaken to establish a laboratory compliant with international standards for the mining (metal ores) and metallurgical industries.

According to the document, the current situation regarding the establishment of the laboratory will be assessed between 2027 and 2030—taking international best practices in the field into account—and a feasibility study for the laboratory's creation will be prepared.

The Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources (MENR), the Ministry of Economy, the Azerbaijan Investment and Business Development Agency (AIBDA), and AzerGold CJSC will participate in the implementation of this measure.

The state program also envisages establishing the necessary material and technical infrastructure to ensure the laboratory operates in compliance with international standards. Furthermore, plans are in place to secure accreditation for the laboratory.

The document notes that, alongside the laboratory's establishment, the provision of laboratory analysis and related services in the relevant sector will be ensured.

Thus, the new laboratory is expected to enable the analysis of materials and metal ores used in the mining and metallurgical industries in accordance with international standards. The laboratory's operations are intended to facilitate both the enhancement of the quality of industrial analyses and the more systematic provision of relevant services.

The state program specifically stipulates that measures to establish the laboratory be implemented with due regard for international best practices. To this end, the plan involves an initial assessment of the current situation and the determination of the economic and technical rationale for the laboratory's establishment, followed by the provision of the necessary material and technical infrastructure and the completion of the accreditation process.

World.title: Azerbaijan to bring gold and copper deposits in Nakhchivan into production
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. Gold and copper deposits in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of Azerbaijan will be brought into production.

This is outlined in the "State program on the development of the mining (metal ores) and metallurgical industry for 2027–2030," approved by the President ofthe Republic of AzerbaijanIlham Aliyev.

The decree noted that the feasibility study (FS) for the Ortakand gold deposit will be finalized and a final investment decision will be made. Construction of a processing plant for the Ortakand gold deposit is planned to begin, while preliminary assessments will be carried out for other priority deposits.

Production at the Ortakand deposit will then begin, and final investment decisions will be made on bringing other priority deposits into operation.

The main implementing agency for the process is AzerGold CJSC. Other implementing agencies are the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources and the Ministry of Economy.

Chairman of the Board of AzerGold CJSC, Zakir Ibrahimov, said at a meeting chaired by President Ilham Aliyev on September 22 dedicated to the draft state program for the development of the mining and metallurgical industry that initial production at the Ortakand gold deposit in Nakhchivan is planned for 2029. The gold resources amount to 246,000 ounces, with an economic value of 1.8 billion manat ($1.06 billion). The required investment is 255 million manat ($150 million), and the project is also planned to be financed through AzerGold's internal revenues and borrowed funds.

World.title: Elders call for royal commission into Pilbara child protection crisis
World.content:
Aboriginal elders are calling for a royal commission into Western Australia's child protection agency and the minister's resignation amid concerns about the living conditions of some Indigenous children in the Pilbara.

Two government ministers and their advisors today flew to South Hedland, 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, for meetings spurred by reporting in The Australian newspaper claiming more than a dozen children were living unsupervised at a home in town.

The government has disputed that reporting, but admits an investigation into what had happened took too long.

Linda Doogiebee-Dridi (Milbugana) has called for WA's child protection minister to resign. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Nyamal elder Linda Doogiebee-Dridi (Milbugana) accused WA's child protection agency of being negligent in their care of children in the town, and claimed the state government had continuously failed to engage with elders.

'Blatant disrespect'

Ms Doogiebee-Dridi said she was aware of the issues at the home in question in Frisby Court, but felt as though community elders had been left in the dark about what was being done to help the children.

She said Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski, who also visited town last week after the report was published, disrespected some elders by not meeting with them.

Jessica Stojkovski arrived in Port Hedland for another meeting with elders. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

"This is our country, we were born here, grew up here, but we are not invited to sit at the table and have conversation," she said.

"The minister, who blatantly disrespected us … it does create frustration and anger."

Doris Eaton (right) is a Nyamal and Pitjikarli elder also attending today's meetings with the national commissioner. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Aside from calling for Ms Stojkovski's resignation, Ms Doogiebee-Dridi said she felt strongly that a royal commission needed to happen so there was "a focal point for us to have a voice".

"We co-design a kind of footprint to go forward with, to ensure our young people are getting education and learning," she said.

Commissioner lands in Port Hedland

The National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, Sue-Anne Hunter, also flew to the port town today for talks with locals.

Ms Hunter's commission is an independent body, tasked with advocating for the wellbeing and rights of young First Nations people, with the ability to launch formal inquiries.

The National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, Sue-Anne Hunter (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

She said she planned to convene a roundtable on child safety in Perth later this week after consulting with Pilbara residents "with direct knowledge and experience" of the issues facing Aboriginal children.

Ms Doogiebee-Dridi said she was optimistic about the meeting, which was being billed as a "culturally safe forum" that would also address the "systemic issues" plaguing communities.

"I'm hoping she'll listen about the issues happening in our community. We've only just started collectively grouping together," she said.

Local elders says not enough resources are being invested in South Hedland. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Minister will not resign

The issue has engulfed all sides of politics in WA, with Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas also flying to South Hedland on Tuesday evening, accusing Labor of trivialising and playing down the seriousness of the problem.

"We are dealing with children's lives here," he said.

"If [the minister] is not capable of dealing with it without the bureaucratic mumbo-jumbo which she trotted out over the last week or so, then the premier should put a senior minister in who can do the job."

Kariyarra elder Patricia Mason talking with National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Shadow Minister for Child Protection, Nick Goiran, called for the reinstatement of a standalone child protection body.

"If you have a standalone department for child protection, you've got a director-general who's got one job to do and that is to keep children safe," he said.

Speaking in South Hedland today about the Frisby Court issues, Minister for the Pilbara Amber-Jade Sanderson said it was clear there had been "missed opportunities for escalation of acute cases".

WA Ministers Amber-Jade Sanderson and Jessica Stojkovski arrive in Port Hedland. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

She announced a child health safety leadership group, bringing together government, non-government and local council representatives, will meet weekly.

Ms Stojkovski said there were also plans to expand the opening of the town's night space to seven nights a week.

She said she would not resign.

"I want to see that where we see a problem, that we can fix it, and that's what I am dedicating myself to," she said.

Ms Stojkovski confirmed the investigation into the Frisby Court home was closed and the family had been removed.

It is alleged more than a dozen children were living unsupervised in a home in Frisby Court in South Hedland. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

"My understanding is that they are getting all of the supports that they need to keep those children safe," she said.

In regard to the criticism that the child protection minister did not meet with elders, she said she met with some last week, but committed to returning so she could meet with more.

"Admittedly, it was a short trip last week because we had parliamentary duties, but at that time I committed to coming back, which is what I have done today," she said.

Clean-up crews were clearing the South Hedland home of debris, with the WA government denying it was to sanitise the view for the commissioner. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

While the minister would not say which elders she met with last week, she did speak with Dorothy Papertalk, who lived on Frisby Court.

An onslaught of tradesmen have attended the home and done repairs since the issue first came to light last weekend, which Ms Stojkovski denied was tied to cleaning up the street for the commissioner's visit.

World.title: Canberrans told to direct anger at Trump over nation's most costly fuel
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The ACT's chief minister says Canberrans should be "rightly angry" about high fuel prices in the territory but says that anger should first be aimed at United States President Donald Trump.

Canberra is currently the most expensive capital city in the country for both petrol and diesel.

The ACT Legislative Assembly has now supported a move to hold an inquiry into the capital's high fuel prices, with a particular focus on examining why ACT motorists pay more for fuel than people just over the border in New South Wales.

Oil prices have dropped but Australian motorists should remain wary The global benchmark for oil prices has fallen by more than $2 a barrel, but what does this mean for Australians at the bowser?

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said there were several factors that resulted in the ACT's high fuel prices, including transport costs to get fuel from Sydney, a lack of retail competition and less fuel being sold due to a rise in hybrid and electric vehicles.

"Cars and trucks are more fuel efficient now than they were 25 years ago," Mr Barr said.

"All of the fixed infrastructure costs associated with a petrol and diesel distribution network are now being spread across fewer litres of sale."

However, Mr Barr said "international factors" were clearly to blame for the current cost increases for fuel.

"People would rightly be angry, and they should be angry firstly with Donald Trump and what appears to be a pointless and unwinnable war that he has started," he said.

'Canberra tax' is culprit: opposition

Opposition leader Mark Parton, who initiated the call for the fuel price inquiry, said Mr Barr was "deflecting" by talking about the US President.

"It doesn't explain the price differential between here and 10 kilometres that way," the Canberra Liberals leader said.

"Donald Trump has got nothing to do with that; he hasn't given some blessing [to] Queanbeyan, Jerrabomberra, Goulburn and Braidwood."

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton has accused the ACT chief minister of "deflecting" when it comes to Canberra's high fuel costs. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Mr Parton said he also "didn't buy" the argument around less fuel being sold in the ACT leading to high prices, instead blaming the "high cost of doing business" in the territory.

"This is the most expensive place in Australia to sell anything," he said.

"It's not fair for regular people in Canberra that they have to pay this 'Canberra tax' whenever they go to the petrol bowser."

Calls for portable rental-bond scheme

ACT Greens housing spokesperson Rebecca Vassarotti wants a portable rental-bond scheme. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Cost-of-living relief dominated debate in the Legislative Assembly on Wednesday, with the ACT Greens moving a motion to call on the ACT government to set up a portable rental-bond scheme.

ACT Greens housing spokesperson Rebecca Vassarotti said the scheme would mean Canberra renters moving house would no longer have to find thousands of dollars while waiting for a previous bond to be returned.

"We are in a cost-of-living crisis, we are in a housing crisis and we know renters are really at the front-end," she said.

"What we are really focused on is providing a mechanism to take a little bit of pressure off renters and ensuring that they are not having to front up extra thousands of dollars if they don't need to."

ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne says portable rental-bond schemes are costly. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne said the government has had conversations with New South Wales and Victoria, which both established similar schemes.

"All the schemes have had significant start-up fixed costs as well as significant ongoing costs," she told the Legislative Assembly.

" We all agree with the objective of portable rental-bond schemes, but it is not as simple as the government holding on to a bond and moving it into the next residential tenancy agreement. "

Meanwhile, the government is hoping to pass the budget this week, spruiking its housing crisis support fund.

"Building more homes is critical, but we also know that many low-income Canberrans need financial support right now," Housing Minister Suzanne Orr said.

"The Housing Crisis Support Fund will help renters who are experiencing financial hardship, providing them with support to remain in their homes," she said.

World.title: SA greyhound racing allowed to continue, with independent watchdog
World.content:
South Australia's greyhound racing will be allowed to continue — with a new independent watchdog — after a report was handed down into its two-year reform period.

The state's greyhound racing industry was given a two-year deadline to implement dozens of recommendations to improve its practices, following an independent inquiry sparked by ABC reporting.

The independent inquiry, led by former Victorian police commissioner Graham Ashton, delivered 87 recommendations in 2023.

Sal Perna, Victoria's former racing integrity commissioner, was appointed in 2024 to monitor the implementations of the recommendations and handed his final 172-page report to the government on Wednesday.

Mr Perna made two key recommendations: that racing continue in South Australia and that there was a need for greater oversight of animal welfare and integrity issues.

Sal Perna says he believes the remaining five recommendations can be accomplished "in the near future". (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

South Australia had until now been the only state without an integrity oversight body.

"The reforms that have been made in greyhound racing in South Australia are significant — there's been changes to administration, to operation, to integrity, to race day and a lot of them have been focused on the welfare part, which is probably the most critical," Mr Perna said.

Mr Perna said Greyhound Racing SA has responded to 73 of the 78 recommendations that they were responsible for.

"The other five are still a work in progress but we think [they] can be accomplished in the near future," he said.

"They've spent a lot of money — millions — in accomplishing the recommendations that were required and I think they're in a much better position."

The state government said it would implement legislation next year to support the creation of an integrity body.

"We will be engaging with all interested parties, not just greyhound racing, but of course the RSPCA and other welfare groups," sport and racing minister Rhiannon Pearce said.

Greyhound Racing SA chief executive Brenton Scott welcomed the government's announcement, describing it as a positive outcome for the greyhound industry that provided certainty on its future.

"I believe we've got the strongest possible welfare and integrity framework that can be put in place to ensure a sustainable and ethical industry going forward," he said.

Mr Scott said all of the recommendations regarding racing safety had been implemented, and there were "still minor amounts of work required" for full implementation on the five remaining recommendations.

Elle Trahair says she is concerned about the length of time it will take to implement the integrity body. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

But Coalition for the Protection of Greyhounds spokeswoman Elle Trahair said some of the five outstanding recommendations related to how dogs were trained and lived; areas she said were where the "biggest welfare harms occur".

"Injuries, over-breeding [and] the way greyhounds are housed and kept are the biggest welfare issues affecting the industry and its ongoing social license, and they remain outstanding," she said.

She also criticised the time it would take to implement the independent watchdog.

"This policy response from the government with no clear timeframes does not meet that community expectation and is not good enough," she said.

Greens MLC Melanie Selwood opposed the announcement and said her party would "continue to stand with the community in demanding an end to greyhound racing in South Australia".

Mr Scott said greyhound racing in South Australia had been "completely transparent" during the past two years.

"Moreover, we expect to be held to account and the implementation of the racing integrity body will ensure that accountability is enhanced and we will be judged by our performance," he said.

World.title: Firearms businesses struggling under Minns government's gun laws
World.content:
Firearms dealers have tearfully described losing retirement nest eggs and being forced to sell their home, blaming the Minns government's post-Bondi gun laws.

Taylah Malloy and her mother Sarah Turner were among families who rallied at parliament on Wednesday, as six crossbenchers work to block Labor's buyback regulations and repeal new limits on ownership.

Ms Turner says the business they have "nothing to retire on". (Supplied)

Ms Malloy said her parents' business, Arms & Ammo, in the Newcastle suburb of Beresfield, was meant to fund their retirement but had become worthless since the changes.

"Imagine if your parents, their super just blew up in their faces, and they ended up with nothing," Ms Malloy said.

The massacre of 15 people at a Jewish celebration in December prompted the NSW parliament to pass Australia's strictest gun laws.

Most licence holders were banned from owning more than four firearms and certain types now require stricter licences.

Buyback offer 'a drop in the ocean'

As part of the state's buyback scheme due to begin in November, dealers have been offered grants of up to $25,000.

Ms Malloy said her parents' business had lost more than $800,000 in firearms trade alone, and described $25,000 as a "drop in the ocean".

"There are people that are losing that amount per day within their businesses," she said.

Ms Turner said her business had stock it could no longer sell because of the lower caps on ownership.

"It's like being in quicksand," Ms Turner said.

Ms Malloy's parents have a business based at Beresfield in Newcastle. (Supplied)

The dealership could not recoup the costs of the firearms through the buyback scheme, she said, as it applies only to individual licence holders.

Ms Turner broke down as she described how the family and clay target shooters and hunters had lost everything they built.

"We put our life into our business, and it's just been taken away," she said.

"We've got nothing to retire on."

Zac and Courtney Kirwan said they were preparing to shut their firearms, hunting and outdoors store at Castle Hill in Sydney's north-west after trade plunged 80 per cent.

"It's just like turning off a tap," Mr Kirwan said.

Part of Mr Kirwan's store in north-west Sydney. (Supplied: Zac Kirwan)

He said the business, Badlands, supported the couple and their two young daughters, and employed five people.

Now the family has had to sell a house and move back in with their parents.

"We're basically losing everything. We have to find new jobs," Mr Kirwan said.

"I think sometimes people don't realise, well the government doesn't realise how much damage they can do to personal lives with the stroke of a pen," he said.

Mr Kirwan is expecting to close the firearms, hunting and outdoors store he runs with his wife in Sydney's north-west. (ABC News: Alex Lewis)

Mr Kirwan described the $25,000 grant proposed as a "spit in the face", saying their business was "probably over $1 million down".

"It's literally crushed us, and we've done nothing wrong."

The premier's office has been approached for comment.

In question time, Attorney General Michael Daley said it was "inarguable" there were "too many guns in our society".

"We've seen a spate of gangland shootings," Mr Daley said.

Upon announcing the buyback scheme in August, NSW Premier Chris Minns said: "This is a big undertaking, but the principle behind it is simple: fewer dangerous guns in our community means a safer New South Wales."

Mr Daley says there are "too many guns in our society". (ABC News: Nick Dole )

Disallowance motions to freeze buyback regulations

While the state Liberals supported the reforms passed on Christmas Eve, the party has pledged to remove the caps and freeze the buyback.

Last week, the opposition backed an attempt by independent Barwon MP Roy Butler to stop the buyback regulations by voting in favour of a disallowance motion.

Another disallowance motion is set to be moved by the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party (SFF) next month in the upper house, where the numbers are much tighter.

The NSW Liberals have pledged to remove the caps and freeze the buyback. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

SFF MLC Mark Banasiak said stopping the regulations could come to a single vote.

"I'm never confident, but I'm working my backside off to make sure we get this done," Mr Banasiak said.

"Regardless of what you think about firearms, these are small business owners, and this government is deliberately and wilfully destroying their business."

World.title: Snowtown murderer moves to pre-release centre after being granted parole
World.content:
Snowtown killer James Spyridon Vlassakis is today being transferred to the Adelaide Pre-release Centre, marking the first step towards his release into the community.

The decision to release Vlassakis — following the completion of his non-parole period — was upheld earlier this month after the South Australian government attempted to block it.

The 46-year-old will live in the pre-release centre, at Yatala in Adelaide's northern suburbs, for up to 12 months while the Parole Board monitors his progress and decides what his conditions will be once he is released into the community.

He had been residing at a South Australian prison.

Vlassakis was the youngest of the four perpetrators involved in the so-called "bodies in the barrels" serial killings between 1992 and 1999.

A court sketch of Snowtown killer James Vlassakis from May 2026. (Supplied)

He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 26 years after pleading guilty to his involvement in the murders of Fred Brooks, Gary O'Dwyer, David Johnson and his half-brother Troy Youde.

Vlassakis was a key prosecution witness and played a part in securing convictions against John Bunting and Robert Wagner who were jailed for 11 and 10 murders respectively after they were found guilty at trial.

Ronald Lane, the nephew of Snowtown victim Barry Lane, also known as Vanessa Lane, said he thought Vlassakis's sentence was "very soft".

"I just think the laws need to be look into and changed so that nobody else has to go through the same sort of thing that myself and my family have gone through," he said.

Vlassakis was not involved in the murder of Mr Lane in October 1997.

World.title: Australian rock legend Angry Anderson dies, aged 79
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Rock singer, actor, youth advocate and charity ambassador Angry Anderson has died.

Anderson's family and band mates announced in a statement today that the 79-year-old had died on Monday, surrounded by loved ones in Australia.

"Angry was a devoted father, and much-loved bandmate, friend, and member of the wider music and entertainment community," the statement said.

" His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas. "

It comes after Anderson suffered a cardiac arrest in August while on tour with his band.

Anderson was admitted to a German hospital during the European leg of Rose Tattoo's 50th anniversary tour, prompting the band to cancel a concert on August 9.

The next day, it announced it could not go ahead with the rest of the European tour.

Angry Anderson performing with Rose Tattoo in recent years. (Facebook: Rose Tattoo)

Rose Tattoo was due to return for another Australian leg of the tour in September.

As well as achieving international acclaim with the band, Anderson had a successful solo career, with his hit Suddenly finding chart success in Australia, the UK, Ireland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

He had multiple television and movie roles, was well known for his charity work and later courted controversy for anti-Islam views.

Rose Tattoo in 2026. (Facebook: Gary 'Angry' Anderson — Official)

Painful childhood reflected in music

Gary Anderson was born in Melbourne on August 5, 1947, and grew up in what was then the working class suburb of Coburg.

His mother had moved to Australia from Mauritius when she was 19 and pregnant with him.

Angry Anderson and his mother. (Supplied)

Anderson told a 2009 episode of the ABC's Talking Heads that when he got his first tattoo, his mother tried to scrub it off his skin.

"She looked at me, tears brimming in her eyes, that look that no man wants to see in his mother's eyes because you realise you've broken her heart," he said.

Angry Anderson says he broke his mother's heart when he got his first tattoo. (Supplied)

Anderson said he had a difficult relationship with his father.

"I don't remember laughter in our house," he said.

"I can't remember his touch, I can't remember his smell, I don't remember him touching me apart from when he hit me.

Angry Anderson says he cannot remember his father showing him affection. (Supplied)

"He had many demons to fight and I inherited a lot of those from him."

Anderson said he struggled to fit in at tech school.

He said it was expected that he would become a fitter and turner but, instead, he loved English and reading books.

And as the other teenagers shot up in height, Anderson remained 156 centimetres tall, making him a target for bullies.

He revealed he struggled with the idea that he may have been a "bad seed" and was destined for a life of crime and dysfunction.

He said music became the outlet for his angst and aggression, which had earned him the nickname Angry Ant.

Anderson's first band Buster Brown formed in 1973 and released one album through Mushroom Records.

It disbanded in 1975.

Angry Anderson performing with Buster Brown in the early 1970s. (ABC: Talking Heads)

The banned blues band

Anderson has been with Rose Tattoo since it formed in 1976.

They described themselves as standing out "from the mass of bands in satin pants like a raw steak in a vegetarian restaurant".

After spending two years on the pub circuit, they released their first album in 1987.

In a 2001 interview for the ABC's Australian rock history series Long Way to the Top, Anderson said Rose Tattoo was initially miscategorised as a punk band.

He also said they did not initially aim for the rock 'n' roll genre.

"We were a blues band," Anderson said.

"We just liked to play some things really, really fast and very loud."

Rose Tattoo formed in 1976 and achieved international success. (Facebook: Rose Tattoo)

He described their style as "totally aggressive, take no prisoners, spare no one, have no mercy-type music".

"The more out of control we became, the bigger crowds we'd pull, and that feeds the beast," he said.

Over the decades, Rose Tattoo released eight albums with hits including Bad Boy for Love, Rock 'n' Roll Outlaw, Nice Boys and We Can't Be Beaten.

Angry Anderson fist bumps a fan while on stage with Rose Tattoo in The Netherlands in July. (Facebook: Rose Tattoo)

It was inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) Hall of Fame in 2006.

ARIA described the band as redefining hard rock with "a gritty, slide guitar-heavy sound" and outlaw image that made them icons of the pub rock era.

But the success was not without early controversy.

In its early days, Rose Tattoo was banned from ABC's Countdown for life after Anderson and guitarist Mick Cocks swapped chewing gum — hands free — mid-performance.

An ABC executive thought the two men were kissing.

Anderson said several radio networks then refused to play their songs.

"We just rolled around on the floor in hysterics because we thought it was the funniest thing going," he said.

From rock 'n' roll to fatherhood

In 1982, Anderson met Lindy Michael who gave birth to their first child, Roxanne, a year later while Rose Tattoo was on tour with Aerosmith.

Lindy Michael and Angry Anderson (pictured with daughter Roxanne) married in 1986. (Supplied)

Anderson said his daughter was two weeks old before he met her.

"The first time I actually looked into those eyes, that was it," he said.

" I went from being this wild, out-of-control rock dog to being a sort of 'I want to paint the front fence'. "

The couple also had three sons before they separated.

Anderson said he made sure all his children received hugs and affection from him.

He became emotional while telling Talking Heads host Peter Thompson about his 18-year-old son getting out the car and, in front of his workmates, leaning in through the window to tell his father he loved him and to kiss him goodbye.

Angry Anderson says he was determined to show his love to his children. (Supplied)

Tragically, in 2018, one of the couple's sons, Liam, was killed by a friend during a drug-fuelled hallucination in Sydney.

Matthew Flame was found not guilty of murder, but guilty of manslaughter and was sentenced to eight years in jail.

Anderson told Flame's trial that Liam's death had left him "condemned to a life of sadness".

Suddenly a writer of love songs

In 1986, while Rose Tattoo was on a break, Anderson turned his attention to writing a solo album.

One of the songs he came up with, along with co-writers Andy Cichon and Kevin Beamish, was Suddenly, which became one of his biggest hits.

He said he had never written a love song before.

"Why shouldn't anyone know how I feel about not just my daughter but the women in my life," he told Talking Heads.

Tens of millions of people tuned in to watch Scott and Charlene's wedding on Neighbours, which featured Angry Anderson's solo hit Suddenly. (AAP/Network 10)

It featured as the wedding song on the Neighbours episode where Scott and Charlene, played by Jason Donovan and Kylie Minogue, get married.

The 1987 episode is described by the Australian Film and Sound Archive as "the royal wedding of Australian soap, an event almost as important in the 1980s as the Charles and Di nuptials".

The organisation said the episode was watched by more than 20 million people across Australia and Britain.

Angry Anderson performs Bound for Glory at the 1991 AFL Grand Final. (Supplied)

Other solo hits followed for Anderson, including Bound for Glory, which earned him a pre-game performance at the 1991 AFL Grand Final.

From stage to screen

Becoming a family man started to tame Anderson and he found his fame taking him in a new direction.

He had roles in a number of Australian television comedy shows and a part in the Mad Max film Beyond Thunderdome, which starred Tina Turner.

A scene from Mad Max: Beyond Thunderdome, starring Tina Turner. (Supplied: IMDb)

He had already begun social outreach work when he landed a regular youth affairs segment on Ray Martin's Midday program on the Nine Network.

"I didn't act or look like a typical reporter on a TV show," Anderson said.

"I just let it roll."

One of his first stories was about child sexual abuse, where he not only talked to survivors but went inside a prison and spoke to convicted paedophiles about their rehabilitation.

Anderson was not afraid to allow a segment to go to air showing him crying while listening to a prisoner talking about the harm he had caused to his victim.

Anderson later revealed on the program that he had been abused as a child.

When Ray Martin left Midday for A Current Affair, he took Anderson with him.

They created a new series which involved him completing challenges for charities, such as building respite accommodation for people affected by HIV/AIDS, creating a playground for children with disabilities and helping drought-stricken farmers.

Ray Martin kickstarted Angry Anderson's television career with a spot focusing on youth affairs on Midday in the 1980s. (Supplied)

Anderson also took several tilts at politics, unsuccessfully running for the National Party in the 2013 federal and 2015 NSW state elections, expressing controversial views about Islamic immigration during the federal campaign.

During an appearance on the SBS documentary series Go Back To Where You Came From in 2012, Anderson was critical of Australia's refugee policy and advocated sending back asylum seekers who arrived by boat.

After the show, however, he admitted that his perspective had softened.

In 2016 he ran for the NSW senate with the Australian Liberty Alliance, an anti-Islam minor party.

Anderson has also been connected to numerous children's hospitals, the Starlight Children's Foundation, youth cancer support services Canteen and Camp Quality and the Make-A-Wish Foundation.

He has worked with drug rehabilitation programs, the Salvation Army's youth homelessness service and was the face of a national campaign to raise awareness about prostate cancer after the death of Rose Tattoo guitarist Peter Wells.

He was made a Member of the Order of Australia for his role as a youth advocate in 1993.

"I wear the medal proudly," he said, becoming emotional during the segment on Talking Heads.

World.title: Less tax for many investors after CGT, negative gearing changes, study finds
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The federal government has been accused of causing a property downturn and "breaking promises" in relation to the housing tax changes announced in the May budget.

Property investors have been some of the most vocal critics, but others say changes to Australia's negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT) rules are long overdue and are an attempt to give first-home buyers a more "level playing field".

Researchers from the e61 Institute have weighed into this debate by analysing data on 920,000 housing investments between 2008 and 2025 and calculating how the tax changes would have affected them.

Their conclusion is that the impact of the policy changes on investors is "softer than what might be expected from commentary around the reforms".

Essentially, the 50 per cent discount on the CGT introduced by the Howard government in 1999 will be replaced by a return to the inflation-based deduction that existed prior to that.

A minimum tax rate of 30 per cent will also be applied to capital gains to reduce incentives for asset owners to shift the timing of sales to periods when they have low taxable incomes.

Negative gearing will only be available on new builds, although owners of properties purchased before 7:30pm on budget night (May 12, 2026) will still be deduct their property investment losses from their wider income.

The changes will take effect from July 1, next year.

Some investors could pay less tax

About 53 per cent of housing investors will pay more tax overall under these changes and 43 per cent will pay less, according to the research.

Here's how the budget's tax changes will affect you Answers to all your questions about the federal budget's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax.

In regard to the CGT changes, this policy would result in lower tax on 54 per cent of investments, while 42 per cent would have to pay more tax after selling their properties, the authors of the e61 report found.

However, they arrived at a different result in relation to how the new negative gearing rules would affect investments.

They argued it would lower rental income tax for 28 per cent of investors, while 49 per cent would have to pay more.

"The new way of taxing CGT is likely to raise more revenue for the budget bottom line, mainly coming from high-return investments," e61 Institute senior research economist and report co-author Elyse Dwyer said.

"It ties the tax bill more closely to the actual size of an investor's gain, so small and negative returns are taxed more lightly and large real gains are taxed more heavily.

"That also brings down the overall riskiness of housing as an investment, because large positive and large negative returns get pulled closer to the middle."

The e61 analysis also found that investors who were highly leveraged or had "little other taxable income", such as retirees, were most likely to pay higher taxes under the changes.

Mixed reactions to property tax overhaul

During his budget announcement, Treasurer Jim Chalmers estimated the CGT and negative gearing reforms would result in an extra 75,000 people owning homes over the next decade.

Economists defend capital gains changes at inquiry Economists have offered qualified support for the government's plans on day one of a Senate inquiry.

Treasury forecast there would be about 35,000 fewer homes built, but other taxpayer-funded measures would boost overall supply by about 30,000.

It also estimated the drop in investor demand would see house prices rise by 2 per cent less than they otherwise would over the next few years.

However, the confluence of the tax changes with rising interest rates and increased economic uncertainty has caused many forecasters to be downbeat about the likely path of housing values.

Jim Chalmers says about 75,000 people will own a home as a result of the tax changes over the next decade. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham recently forecast house prices could fall by as much as 13 per cent from peak to trough and many other analysts have also tipped double-digit declines.

Construction lobby groups have also been critical of the government's housing tax changes.

The Master Builders Association argued they would result in 8,700 fewer homes being built over the next four years, which would be a dent to the government's aim to build 1.2 million homes over a five-year period.

The Real Estate Institute was even more pessimistic, estimating 25,000 fewer homes being built over five years.

Angus Taylor says the changes will be scrapped if the Coalition comes into power. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The changes have also been described by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor as an assault on aspiration. He pledged to repeal them if the Coalition wins the next election.

But Grattan Institute chief executive Aruna Sathanapally said the changes would shift the composition of the housing market in favour of owner-occupiers.

Independent economist Saul Eslake has objected to the 30 per cent minimum CGT, but says the overall proposal will improve equity in the tax system by bringing the tax treatment of investment income closer to the tax treatment of wage income.

Peter Varela from ANU's Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, which often collaborates with Treasury, said Australia's arrangements for taxing investment income were "a mess" and that this was "a step in the right direction".

World.title: Katherine promised new $13.3m levee after town's worst flood in 28 years
World.content:
Months on from the worst flooding Katherine has seen in almost three decades, the regional Northern Territory town has been promised a new multi-million-dollar levee.

The Katherine River recorded its highest flood peak since 1998 in March this year, with authorities at the time describing the Top End's extreme weather as "back-to-back, compounding, concurrent, consecutive events within a four-month period", including two tropical cyclones in a single wet season.

In a statement released today, the NT government announced $13.3 million had been earmarked for the construction of a 3-kilometre long flood levee in Katherine South.

In early March, workers in Katherine could be seen installing metal rails across several roads to establish the levee. (ABC News: James Elton)

With funds drawn from the NT's $100m Flood Recovery Fund, established during the March floods, a spokesperson for the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government said the new levee would help protect "an additional 210 homes and businesses" in Katherine South.

"Once complete, the combined function of the Katherine north and south levees will provide greater flood protection for Katherine residents, mitigating flood impacts up to a one in 20-year flood event," they said.

Trent de With, a local volunteer who has supported Katherine's flood recovery efforts, said the levee would be "very advantageous to the people who live on that side of town".

Trent de With was among the army of local volunteers who stepped in to support flood-affected homes and businesses in Katherine earlier this year. (ABC News: James Elton)

Mr de With said after the March floods, stagnant water sat in some Katherine South streets "for the longest period out of anywhere".

"And they weren't directly in the line of fire, it was just back-feeding from the other creeks," he said.

The plan features a wall levee and earth embankments. (Supplied: NT government)

The government says the Katherine South levee will extend "from the western side of the Katherine Country Club in Pearce Street, to the southern tip of Katherine South on the Victoria Highway".

The levee is expected to feature new 1.6-metre high dirt embankments and a 1.5-metre tall levee wall, plus road raising works on Murphy Street, Murray Street and Bicentennial Road.

It is not yet clear how long the southern levee will take to deliver, or when construction will begin.

NT funds bolster federal commitment

Katherine Town Council Mayor Joanna Holden said locals were feeling positive about today's announcement.

The NT government has committed millions of dollars to expand Katherine's flood mitigation strategy, months on from the town's worst flooding in almost three decades. (ABC News: James Elton)

Cr Holden said the federal government had previously promised $9.1m, but the extra NT government funding could help deliver "a better outcome" for Katherine than initially expected.

"So it's not a new project, but it's fantastic that the NT government are now contributing out of that $100 million [fund]," she said.

The mayor said while "the council at this stage hasn't been engaged in a great deal of the planning", she wanted to ensure the project did not come at a cost to ratepayers or local infrastructure.

Joanna Holden has welcomed the $13.3 million NT government commitment, hoping it can save Katherine South from future floods. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Cr Holden said the new levee could potentially divert more water to the Katherine showgrounds, where there were buildings and "a lot of electrical outlets", so the council was keen to weigh in on the plan.

"This year, the water remained there for a significant period of time after the flooding and that obviously in itself — having water sitting there — creates more issues," she said.

" We had at least one saltwater crocodile on the showgrounds this year, so we're probably wanting to know if that levee bank's going to keep them back where they belong as well. "

Floodwater overwhelmed the local levee and spilled into Katherine's CBD in early March. (ABC News: James Elton)

River, drains front of mind

Mr de With said he hoped the new infrastructure would push future floodwater further back from residential streets.

He said the existing northern flood levee diverted water around the town and "allows it to pretty much flow straight into the southern side" of Katherine.

"All it does is move the problem from one place to another, at the moment," he said.

Loading...

In welcoming the new levee, Mr de With explained local stormwater drains — particularly around Tindal Street — would need to also be investigated as they often fill with floodwater, which inundates lower-lying roads along the river.

"Even the one in the main street, there's a drain directly connected to the river," he said.

"That was one of the reasons that the main street started to flood early on, was because of the back-feeding [and] coming back from the river."

World.title: The $16b Aussie tech firm in a slanging match over its China links
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesFintech The $16b Aussie tech firm in a slanging match over its China links Kishor Napier-Raman September 23, 2026 — 5:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jack Zhang, the co-founder and chief executive of Australian-born payments company Airwallex, once claimed to have worked 100 hours a week for the past 20 years. These days, some of that time appears to be dedicated to playing keyboard warrior, with Zhang embroiled in increasingly intemperate online sparring over the company’s links to China. The source of Zhang’s online animus is Keith Rabois, the Trump-aligned Silicon Valley venture capitalist who has repeatedly accused Airwallex of being vulnerable to legal obligations to assist with Chinese Communist Party espionage upon request, on the basis that it could be compelled to hand American users’ data to Beijing. Airwallex co-founder Jack Zhang has been sparring online over the company’s China links. Mia McDonald This week, Zhang accused Rabois (who is on the board of rival payments start-up Ramp) of “unhinged conspiratorial rants” on X. Rabois rather ominously warned that Zhang would be “pleading the fifth soon”, in a reference to the constitutional provision that protects people from self-incrimination. The Airwallex boss then responded with a Mad Men meme. So far, so silly. But Rabois’ claims clearly continue to get under Airwallex’s skin.



Airwallex, which was founded 11 years ago in a Melbourne cafe, but is now domiciled in the Cayman Islands, has been a runaway Australian fintech success story, most recently soaring to a $16 billion valuation and becoming the country’s second-most valuable start-up after Canva. But it has never quite been able to run away from a series of damaging headlines. Related Article Exclusive

Fintech Airwallex hires influencers to praise CEO’s ‘thought leadership’ Local outlets, including this masthead, have reported on a relentless, aggressive workplace culture at the company. Airwallex has attempted to shrug this off as the teething problems associated with a high-growth start-up, and the disconnect between its founders, a bunch of ambitious type A strivers like Zhang (who insists that burnout is not in his vocabulary), and less motivated staff. But the past 12 months have brought more serious allegations. In January, weeks after Rabois made his claims about Chinese espionage, the financial crimes regulator AUSTRAC ordered an external audit of Airwallex’s anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing program, at the company’s expense, putting plans for a 2026 NASDAQ listing on ice. The probe is ongoing, and there has been no mention of China by AUSTRAC.



In the US, Rabois’ concerns about China have also made it all the way to Capitol Hill, where a Republican-controlled congressional committee warned Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that the company’s links to China could compromise sensitive American data. In June, Republican senator Tom Cotton said that while Airwallex “markets itself as an Australian company, its ties to communist China run deep”. Zhang responded by framing these criticisms as blinded by bias against his own country of origin. “I was born in China. I cannot change that fact, nor would I seek to,” he wrote in a recent letter to the congressional committee. “I am a proud Australian citizen. I arrived in Melbourne as an immigrant at 15 with little English and no safety net, and Australia gave me the education, the opportunity and the freedom to build something.” Through all this, however, the company has at times come across as impossibly thin-skinned. In January this year, it threatened litigation against media outlets including this masthead if they refused to remove critical articles about the company that quoted leaked internal documents, including some concerning its work culture. This masthead also revealed that it was seeking to hire influencers to praise Zhang’s “thought leadership”. Since then, Airwallex has embarked on a less clunky image-laundering blitz. Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg was drafted onto its newly formed economic advisory council along with ex-US senator Roy Blunt in May. Last year, the company forged a partnership with English Premier League football champions Arsenal, and in July, revealed an  directed by Spike Lee and featuring club legend Thierry Henry.



Airwallex is plotting a major expansion into the United States and has beefed up its lobbying muscle there. Rachael Horwitz, a Silicon Valley veteran, with senior positions and Google, Meta and Andreessen Horowitz, was drafted in as senior vice president global communications and corporate affairs. Samantha Vinograd, a former Biden administration counter-terrorism advisor and national security pundit on CBS, has started running corporate affairs. Former Bloomberg and Politico White House reporter Jennifer Epstein is head of editorial and economic impact communications. Meanwhile, according to the Financial Times, it has been moving staff who do not work in China-facing roles out of that country in response to those security concerns. While these fears might have delayed a planned IPO until next year, they have not stopped the company from continuing to secure more funding from investors who believe in its product, sending its valuation ever higher. Despite that valuation, and all its on-paper success, Airwallex remains acutely sensitive to criticism of its operations in China. Jack Zhang is no Don Draper, and he clearly thinks about Keith Rabois quite a bit. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Lachie Neale arrives in Melbourne with a grand final suspension hanging over his head
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL grand final Lachie Neale arrives in Melbourne with a grand final suspension hanging over his head Hannah Kennelly Updated September 23, 2026 — 5:14pm ,first published 10:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lachie Neale and his teammates arrived in Melbourne on Wednesday to a mixture of Lions faithful, and media waiting to hear just what he’d say about the one-match ban set to rule him out of Saturday’s grand final against his former club, Fremantle. The Lions confirmed earlier in the day that they would appeal the decision handed down by the AFL tribunal on Tuesday night in a last-ditch bid to free the superstar onballer to play. Lachie Neale at Melbourne Airport. Getty Images Neale, coach Chris Fagan, and the rest of the Lions arrived shortly before 4pm to a sea of people. While Fagan greeted fans warmly, and Will Ashcroft and Hugh McCluggage posed for photos, the man of the moment, Neale, approached the cameras with his head down and face partially concealed by a yellow Bears cap. He gave a brief statement to reporters, confirming the club’s appeal.



“The club and myself have decided to appeal the tribunal’s decision, obviously very hopeful that that’s successful, but regardless of the result I will be here to support the boys and the club this week,” he said. Loading “It’s a big week for the club.” His statement lasted just 15 seconds, and he did not take any questions from media. It’s the second year in a row that Neale’s availability to play in the league’s biggest game will go down to the wire, after he overcame a calf injury last year to be subbed on at half-time and have a telling impact against Geelong.



Neale’s fate this time around rests in the hand of the AFL appeals board, led by chairman Richard Loveridge. The appeals board has the power to overturn the tribunal’s decision and will sit on Thursday afternoon at 4pm local time. Lachie Neale copped an initial one-game ban for the gut punch. The suspension was upheld. Fox Footy, Getty On Tuesday night, Neale unsuccessfully contested the one-match ban imposed on him for striking Jack Ginnivan during the preliminary final clash against Hawthorn. Not even Neale’s record of avoiding suspension in 320 AFL matches for the Lions and Dockers saved him from losing his shot at the Lions’ hat-trick of premierships. The tribunal was highly critical of Neale, saying he gave “inconsistent” evidence about his clash with Ginnivan, as the Lions desperately tried to have the impact downgraded from medium to low, allowing Neale to be fined instead and to be able to face Fremantle at the MCG.



Neale’s long-time teammate Dayne Zorko sat next to him on the plane and spoke with media at the airport, noting he was disappointed for his teammate, but said the Lions would remain focused. View post on X “Obviously, it’s a lot,” Zorko said when asked how Neale was doing. “He seems to be fine… he’s just taking it in his stride.” When asked what his view was on the incident and the debate surrounding it, Zorko replied, “You don’t want my opinion, mate”.



When asked if the penalty was worth a match ban, Zokro replied: “No”. “He’s [Neale] got an impeccable record, you’d like to think that would hold a fair bit of weight, maybe it doesn’t,” he added. Neale’s father Robbie spoke with ABC Adelaide on Wednesday morning and said his son would not want to be a distraction for the team. “So I think he’ll be in two minds this morning as to the way forward. I’m sure he’ll get the right advice,” he said.



“To me, it’s just plain wrong, so I hope they do appeal it. Loading “The last thing Lachie wanted this week was a headline. It’s just so disappointing,” he added. Neale’s case tested the AFL’s crackdown on gut punches and whether a player should be granted leniency after 15 AFL seasons without a suspension. However, former Fremantle captain David Mundy said on Wednesday the tribunal had been right to suspend Neale.



“It’s, obviously, a horrible outcome for Lachie and his prospects this weekend. But I think the AFL has been very clear in its mandate to try and stamp out that sort of action and behaviour,” he said. Editor's pick Opinion

AFL grand final Not all games are equal. This radical idea for grand final punishments proves it Michael Gleeson Sports columnist “I am very confident we’ll be talking about it again after Thursday night’s appeal [should it go ahead], but I think the messaging from the AFL and his tribunal have been very clear.” The Lions’ opponents on Saturday, the Dockers, are the club Neale started his career at. And it’s widely accepted that he is poised to join a third club, Collingwood, in the weeks ahead, meaning if the ban is upheld by the appeals board, he will have played his last game in Lions colours. World.title: Rock legend Angry Anderson dies at age 79
World.content:
Updated CultureMusicVale Rock legend Angry Anderson dies at age 79 Nell Geraets Updated September 23, 2026 — 5:13pm ,first published 4:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian music legend Angry Anderson, one of the country’s most influential rock stars, has died at the age of 79. The Rose Tattoo frontman’s death was confirmed in a statement shared by his bandmates and family on Wednesday. He founded the group in 1976 and served as its lead vocalist until shortly before his death. Rose Tattoo vocalist Angry Anderson has died at the age of 79. Lisa Maree Williams/Getty Images “It is with great sadness we announce the passing of Gary ‘Angry’ Anderson on the eve of Monday 21 September 2026, surrounded by his loved ones here in Australia,” the statement read. “Angry was a devoted father, and much-loved bandmate, friend, and member of the wider music and entertainment community. His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas.”



Anderson suffered a cardiac arrest in late August and was admitted to a hospital to undergo treatment. On August 10, the band announced the cancellation of the European leg of its One Last Ride tour after Anderson was hospitalised due to a “medical issue”. It was set to be the band’s final tour before stepping away after more than five decades of performing live. The band had begun its European tour in July, and had nine more shows to go before announcing the cancellation. Rose Tattoo were scheduled to return to Australia this month to perform several farewell gigs across Melbourne, Sydney, Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane. The veteran rocker was born Gary Stephen Anderson in Melbourne in 1947. Beginning in the Australian pub circuit, his music career picked up major steam when Rose Tattoo released its self-titled debut album in 1978. The record was well received both at home and abroad, climbing to the top of UK heavy metal charts.



Angry Anderson with his Jesus Christ Superstar co-stars Anthony Warlow, John Farnham and John Stevenson in 1992. Robert Pearce/Fairfax Media Anderson’s solo single, Suddenly, released in 1987, became a huge success after it was played during the wedding of Scott and Charlene (played by Jason Donovan and Kylie Minogue) on the TV soap Neighbours. The track shot to No.2 on the Australian charts at the time, and No.3 on the UK singles chart. David Campbell, son of Jimmy Barnes and co-host of Nine’s Today Extra, paid tribute to the veteran rocker who sang at his wedding to Lisa Hewitt in 2008. “I got to share many a stage and sporting field with Angry Anderson,” Campbell wrote. “He was a great frontman with a wicked sense of humour and a huge heart. His generosity went above and beyond when he performed our bridal dance with his hit ballad, Suddenly. I can never repay him for that memory. My condolences to his family and the members and crew of Rose Tattoo.”



Rose Tattoo released a slew of other well-known tracks with Anderson as lead vocalist, including Bad Boy for Love (1977), Rock ‘N’ Roll Outlaw (1978) and We Can’t Be Beaten (1982). In 1978, the band released the song Nice Boys, which American rockers Guns N’ Roses famously went on to cover on their 1986 EP Live ?!*@ Like a Suicide (and again on their 1988 EP G N’ R Lies). Related Article Updated

Australian music Rock legend Angry Anderson suffers a cardiac arrest Rose Tattoo disbanded in 1987, though briefly reassembled in 1993 to open for Guns N’ Roses. In 1998, they officially regrouped and began touring again. Rose Tattoo was later inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2006. Beyond his music career, Anderson also appeared onscreen, most notably as Ironbar in Mad Max: Beyond Thunderdome (1985), and on stage as King Herod in the 1992 Australian arena concert Jesus Christ Superstar. He also became a prominent advocate for prostate cancer research after some of his bandmates died from the disease, including the group’s founding guitarist, Pete Wells. And in 1993, Anderson was made a Member of the Order of Australia for his role as a youth advocate.



Loading In the statement on Wednesday, the rocker’s family and bandmates asked for privacy and thanked fans for their support. “We kindly ask that their wishes are respected as they come to terms with this devastating loss and take time they need to grieve. We thank everyone for their prayers and messages of love and continued support,” it read. “Stay young, grow strong.” More to come The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaKourakis royal commission Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build Chip Le Grand September 23, 2026 — 5:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Kourakis royal commission has started at the top. At its first public hearing, convened just one month after receiving its letters patent, it published in full cabinet-in-confidence documents that show Jacinta Allan knew more than three years ago there was big trouble on the Big Build. This was a ballsy opening from an inquiry intent on sending a message that it is not mucking about. Government ministers, senior bureaucrats, contractors, union bosses and the crooks who grew fat off publicly funded major projects have been put on notice that the royal commission is determined to clean up Victoria’s answer to the Augean stables. Commissioner Chris Kourakis during the opening hearing of the royal commission on Wednesday. Joe Armao Just as importantly, Commissioner Chris Kourakis has signalled his willingness to stand back and interrogate some bigger, long-overdue questions about how we got here. In laying down ethical markers early in his inquiry, Kourakis reminded us of some basic principles of how major projects paid for with public money should be commissioned, designed, managed and safeguarded.



The first of these is that governments, before committing billions of taxpayer dollars to build anything, must with due diligence and care choose the right projects for the right reasons. Related Article Kourakis royal commission Seven construction giants singled out in royal commission; Bombshell Allan briefing flagged “Governments must select and design infrastructure projects around the socioeconomic needs of the Victorian public, and not party political interests,” the commissioner said. Is this how the government conceived of the Suburban Rail Loop, supersized its wildly popular level crossing removal program, or settled on the route for the future airport rail link? If the royal commission is not satisfied, the original sin of Labor’s $150 billion infrastructure program will be laid bare – pork barrelling on a previously unimagined scale. Another principle articulated by Kourakis is that once a project is committed to, responsibility lies with the elected government and its public agencies to competently manage contracts and minimise risks.



When things go wrong – such as bikies and recently paroled criminals worming their way onto building sites – it is up to senior bureaucrats to promptly raise the alarm with responsible ministers, who in turn need to show the leadership required to stop the rot. It is here that the documents obtained by the royal commission relating to Allan’s knowledge of and response to evidence of criminal activity on Big Build sites in June 2023 inform a fascinating case study. The cabinet-in-confidence documents detail concerns held by the Major Transport Infrastructure Authority, a government agency responsible for big rail and road projects, about organised crime figures turning up at Big Build sites and potentially standing over contractors. Putting aside the question of whether the former premier was truthful to The Age two months ago when we questioned her about one of these briefing notes, an issue for the royal commission is what she did at the time.



She wrote the next day to then-police chief Shane Patton to pass on the intel. Was this enough? What other steps did Allan, MTIA boss Kevin Devlin and other government officials take to protect the integrity of the Big Build and contractors already confronting a skewed industrial landscape? As counsel assisting the commission Chris Young, KC, noted, this was a time when the North East Link, the West Gate Tunnel, the Metro Tunnel and level crossing removal projects were all under construction. The CFMEU, a union that had previously shown itself to be unconstrained by the law, was in a position of immense leverage. And thanks to the newly elected Albanese government, the Australian Building and Construction Commission – the federal watchdog – was about to be put down. Commissioner Kourakis also provided some opening observations about the responsibility of union officials, noting the special privileges and powers they have under our industrial relations system. “It is an especially egregious breach of trust to abuse those privileges and powers for personal gain, and there can be no tolerance at all for the carpetbaggers who corrupt an industry through extortion and bribery, whatever euphemisms they may employ to hide what they really do,” he said.



According to information already provided to the commission, the CFMEU in Victoria long ago ceased behaving like a union. “It has been alleged that the bosses of the CFMEU used their own power to line their own pockets and to enrich organised crime figures who infiltrated the union, rather than for the benefit of their members,” said counsel assisting, Chris Carr, SC. Multiple subcontractors involved in the Big Build are alleged to have had Mick Gatto on their payroll. Justin McManus This allegedly involved a CFMEU-backed shakedown in which subcontractors paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to Mick Gatto and other organised crime figures to secure union-endorsed enterprise bargaining agreements – the Big Build’s version of a golden ticket. “These are grave allegations,” Carr said. “Their accuracy will need to be carefully assessed. If they are true, it suggests that the CFMEU operated as a facilitator for organised crime, and that the Big Build involved an enormous transfer of wealth from taxpayers to organised crime.” Thanks to the dogged reporting of Nick McKenzie and other journalists, these allegations are not new to readers of The Age. And they might not be the worst of it.

The Parenthood chief executive Georgie Dent used a speech at the National Press Club on Wednesday to campaign for more equitable parental leave legislation as the country’s birth rate falls, which would bring Australia in line with other OECD countries.

The Parenthood chief executive Georgie Dent discussed the urgent need for reforms to help support Australians to afford the family sizes they desired. Alex Ellinghausen

World.title: ‘Someone knows what happened to Gus’: Four-year-old’s parents make desperate plea
World.content:
NationalCrime ‘Someone knows what happened to Gus’: Four-year-old’s parents make desperate plea Riley Walter September 23, 2026 — 5:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On his family’s sheep station in South Australia’s remote Mid North region, August Lamont was growing into a sweet and curious boy. The four-year-old, also known as Gus, loved music, stories and playing in nature. At Oak Park, about 350 kilometres north-east of Adelaide, Gus was growing up in the same rugged environment his mother, Jessica Murray, cherished as a child. As he explored the world around him, Gus’ parents envisioned a bright future for their oldest son. Instead, they have spent almost a year desperately searching for answers as they reconcile a life without Gus, who vanished from his family’s sprawling station on September 27 last year. The South Australia government has offered a $1 million reward to find Gus Lamont, who disappeared from his family’s sheep station in September last year. SA Police “During the time that Gus has been missing, he should have celebrated his fifth birthday, and his little brother’s first birthday with us,” Jessica Murray said in a pre-recorded statement played by SA Police on Wednesday. “One of the most heartbreaking things is that Gus and his little brother will not grow up together and spend their lives together. Gus was adored by his little brother.” “We miss Gus more than we can describe,” his father Joshua Lamont said. “We are desperate to have him return home to us, and we are desperate for answers. We believe that someone knows something. Someone knows what happened to Gus and may even know where he is.”



After an unprecedented search to find the four-year-old, in which search parties scoured hundreds of square kilometres, the South Australian government on Wednesday offered a $1 million reward for information in a desperate bid to solve a mystery that has garnered national attention. Related Article Crime Gus vanished in the South Australian outback. Police have focused their attention close to home Detectives are working under Task Force Horizon, the large-scale operation launched to find Gus. According to Gus’ family, the boy was last seen playing in the dirt near the Oak Park homestead. Initially, investigators were told Gus’ family believed he had wandered off and was feared to be lost somewhere on the property. In the months since, detectives have ruled out the theory, alongside the possibility that Gus was abducted from Oak Park, which is 45 kilometres from the nearest main road. “The focus of Task Force Horizon remains on the third scenario, and that is that someone known to Gus has been involved in his disappearance,” Detective Superintendent Darren Fielke, the officer in charge of SA Police’s Major Crime Investigation Branch, said on Wednesday.



Police in February declared Gus’ disappearance a major crime. One of Gus’ grandparents remains a suspect, Fielke said. Josie Murray has publicly identified herself as the suspect during several media interviews. No charges have been laid, and his parents are not suspects. World.title: The $16b Aussie tech firm in a slanging match over its China links
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesFintech The $16b Aussie tech firm in a slanging match over its China links Kishor Napier-Raman September 23, 2026 — 5:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jack Zhang, the co-founder and chief executive of Australian-born payments company Airwallex, once claimed to have worked 100 hours a week for the past 20 years. These days, some of that time appears to be dedicated to playing keyboard warrior, with Zhang embroiled in increasingly intemperate online sparring over the company’s links to China. The source of Zhang’s online animus is Keith Rabois, the Trump-aligned Silicon Valley venture capitalist who has repeatedly accused Airwallex of being vulnerable to legal obligations to assist with Chinese Communist Party espionage upon request, on the basis that it could be compelled to hand American users’ data to Beijing. Airwallex co-founder Jack Zhang has been sparring online over the company’s China links. Mia McDonald This week, Zhang accused Rabois (who is on the board of rival payments start-up Ramp) of “unhinged conspiratorial rants” on X. Rabois rather ominously warned that Zhang would be “pleading the fifth soon”, in a reference to the constitutional provision that protects people from self-incrimination. The Airwallex boss then responded with a Mad Men meme. So far, so silly. But Rabois’ claims clearly continue to get under Airwallex’s skin.



Airwallex, which was founded 11 years ago in a Melbourne cafe, but is now domiciled in the Cayman Islands, has been a runaway Australian fintech success story, most recently soaring to a $16 billion valuation and becoming the country’s second-most valuable start-up after Canva. But it has never quite been able to run away from a series of damaging headlines. Related Article Exclusive

Fintech Airwallex hires influencers to praise CEO’s ‘thought leadership’ Local outlets, including this masthead, have reported on a relentless, aggressive workplace culture at the company. Airwallex has attempted to shrug this off as the teething problems associated with a high-growth start-up, and the disconnect between its founders, a bunch of ambitious type A strivers like Zhang (who insists that burnout is not in his vocabulary), and less motivated staff. But the past 12 months have brought more serious allegations. In January, weeks after Rabois made his claims about Chinese espionage, the financial crimes regulator AUSTRAC ordered an external audit of Airwallex’s anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing program, at the company’s expense, putting plans for a 2026 NASDAQ listing on ice. The probe is ongoing, and there has been no mention of China by AUSTRAC.



In the US, Rabois’ concerns about China have also made it all the way to Capitol Hill, where a Republican-controlled congressional committee warned Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that the company’s links to China could compromise sensitive American data. In June, Republican senator Tom Cotton said that while Airwallex “markets itself as an Australian company, its ties to communist China run deep”. Zhang responded by framing these criticisms as blinded by bias against his own country of origin. “I was born in China. I cannot change that fact, nor would I seek to,” he wrote in a recent letter to the congressional committee. “I am a proud Australian citizen. I arrived in Melbourne as an immigrant at 15 with little English and no safety net, and Australia gave me the education, the opportunity and the freedom to build something.” Through all this, however, the company has at times come across as impossibly thin-skinned. In January this year, it threatened litigation against media outlets including this masthead if they refused to remove critical articles about the company that quoted leaked internal documents, including some concerning its work culture. This masthead also revealed that it was seeking to hire influencers to praise Zhang’s “thought leadership”. Since then, Airwallex has embarked on a less clunky image-laundering blitz. Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg was drafted onto its newly formed economic advisory council along with ex-US senator Roy Blunt in May. Last year, the company forged a partnership with English Premier League football champions Arsenal, and in July, revealed an  directed by Spike Lee and featuring club legend Thierry Henry.



Airwallex is plotting a major expansion into the United States and has beefed up its lobbying muscle there. Rachael Horwitz, a Silicon Valley veteran, with senior positions and Google, Meta and Andreessen Horowitz, was drafted in as senior vice president global communications and corporate affairs. Samantha Vinograd, a former Biden administration counter-terrorism advisor and national security pundit on CBS, has started running corporate affairs. Former Bloomberg and Politico White House reporter Jennifer Epstein is head of editorial and economic impact communications. Meanwhile, according to the Financial Times, it has been moving staff who do not work in China-facing roles out of that country in response to those security concerns. While these fears might have delayed a planned IPO until next year, they have not stopped the company from continuing to secure more funding from investors who believe in its product, sending its valuation ever higher. Despite that valuation, and all its on-paper success, Airwallex remains acutely sensitive to criticism of its operations in China. Jack Zhang is no Don Draper, and he clearly thinks about Keith Rabois quite a bit. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
