A boil water notice for the Mangaore community after two dead rats were found in a reservoir supplying drinking water to the area.

The Horowhenua District Council said the rats were found during a routine monitoring using an underwater drone.

It said it carried out monthly inspections of its reservoirs, with the last testing on September 13. There was no indication of how long the two rats had been in the reservoir.

The council said about 30 to 40 properties may be affected.

The affected reservoir has been taken offline and an existing alternative reservoir is now supplying the local network.

Chief executive Monique Davidson said the council acted quickly after the rodents were discovered and is working with Taumata Arowai, the Water Services Authority.

"Our teams today have been flushing the main water network, draining any potentially contaminated water from the network, reducing the risk to having a minimal impact, however, caution still applies and that is why we've issued the boil water notice," she said.

The affected reservoir will be drained, cleaned and disinfected before being refilled.

"We understand this news may be unsettling for our Mangaore residents, and we want to ensure the community are well informed about the status of their drinking water."

The council said thorough water quality testing would be carried out before the reservoir was returned to service.

The work was expected to be completed by tomorrow afternoon.

Until the notice is lifted, residents are advised to boil water for drinking, preparing food, brushing teeth, washing fruit and vegetables, making ice and preparing infant formula.

World.title: 'NZers do not care about this topic' - PM on new Nicky Hager book
World.content:
The prime minister and deputy prime minister are dismissing claims in a new book that argues the Taxpayers' Union used anti-Māori racism as a political tool - especially during its Stop Three Waters campaign.

Christopher Luxon says New Zealanders "do not care" while David Seymour says Hager "does this every three years, and most of New Zealand wonders what the fuss is about".

Meanwhile, the Greens are pulling out of all debates being hosted by the Taxpayers Union as a result of the book.

Hager's book Dirty Work - launched on Tuesday night - argues the Taxpayers' Union (TU) helped shift the 2023 election campaign to the right. He claims both Seymour and Luxon pivoted toward the anti-Māori rhetoric to gain votes.

In the book, Hager said Seymour initially had no interest in "Māori bashing", noting that in 2017 and 2020 campaign materials, the ACT party had no focus on Māori issues.

Hager then pointed out that in 2022 Seymour started to assemble "his own race-based policies".

"If TU could play the race card and get away with it, and be rewarded with money pouring in from angry and fearful supporters, ACT wanted to get in on it too."

Hager also described Luxon changing his tune over time, where initially Luxon would not be drawn on race when it came to Three Waters.

Speaking on a TU podcast, Luxon corrected a claim from Williams that iwi would be getting 50 percent governance of the country's water. "They're not actually governors," he told Williams.

Later he changed his language, Hager claimed, and declared that National would scrap Three Waters plus other "iwi related policies".

Hager quoted a source saying Seymour and Luxon "knew what they were doing... They were jumping aboard because there was power and there were votes there".

Asked about the book at Parliament on Wednesday, Luxon said he did not have much to do with the TPU. "They're no fan of the National Party."

Asked if he agreed that the TPU engaged in race baiting policies, Luxon said:

"Can I be really honest with you? I do not care about some leftwing journalist Nicky Hager and I also don't care about the Taxpayers' Union.

"What I do care about is what people out there care about, which is actually getting the show on the road, and actually getting an Indian FTA in place, making sure we get resource management laws in place is a good thing."

He also said he was "pretty unhappy" about a campaign the TPU ran, which took a swipe at Nicola Willis.

Willis told reporters the organisation had a right to exist in free democracy.

"Their members choose to contribute their money to them and their campaigns. I find some of their campaigns distasteful, but that's a matter for them, not for me."

Luxon was quoted in the book as thanking the TPU and its members "for all the work you do".

"I really enjoy what you guys do."

Asked if Luxon stood by those comments, he said: "I do not care and New Zealanders do not care about this topic."

Seymour was also asked about the book, and said he would love to answer but did not want to reward "bad behaviour".

It was put to him that Hager claimed that once Seymour engaged in race based politics around iwi ownership of water assets, the ACT Party's polling went up.

Seymour said his Maiden Statement included comments around his opposition to the Treaty being used to divide Māori and non-Māori ancestors.

"It's there in black in white in 2014."

He credited a rise in the polls in his own performance improving, the euthanasia legislation, standing up for licensed firearm owners, opposing through Covid and building a strong organisation.

"This guy should get another job than political commentator because he's missed quite a lot in that story."

Hager canvassed that history in his book, saying: "Seymour had proven in his first six years in Parliament, from 2014 to 2020, that he could be successful without stooping to race politics."

Asked specifically about the Three Waters campaign, Seymour said he opposed the government's policy that "vital Three Waters infrastructure should be co-governed and people should be put in charge of it based on their race".

In regards to his policies and election materials changing, Seymour referenced the Labour government's Māori health authority, Three Waters with co-governance, and the He Puapua report.

"If you want to know what changed in that period, the government of the day made it an issue by dividing New Zealanders by race as official policy."

Seymour rejected the claim he pivoted to race-based policies because there were votes in it.

Further questions saw Seymour issue an expletive: "Holy sh*t, you guys.

"This is the end of a three year term, we've done spectacular things for New Zealand, we have saved money, we have cut red tape.

"People are worried about the cost of living, they're worried about how we're gonna be safer in this country - happy to talk about any of that," said Seymour.

He then dismissed those asking about the book as "obsessed with one guy and a book" that he claimed was "filled with factual inaccuracies quoting disgruntled former staff members of an organisation they've got nothing to do with."

Meanwhile, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters told reporters he checked the index of the book, and did not see his name "so I just moved on".

"The trouble with publishing is too many people with half a mind to write a book do so," he added.

Green co-leader Chloe Swarbrick said the party was pulling out of all debates being hosted by the Taxpayers Union as a result of the book, and called on other party leaders to do the same.

"Anything that legitimises the Taxpayers' Union and the kinds of tactics that they are using to undermine our democracy, it's just cooked," she said.

"If the National and ACT Party do not want to be associated with it, then they need to withdraw themselves."

The Greens had been set to take part in electorate debates in Auckland Central and Mount Albert, and had already taken part in a Wellington Bays debate.

Asked what about the book had prompted the change of heart, she said it was the "fulsome nature of it all".

"The fact that now we have in such black and white detail the connection between the tactics that are deployed, the intention, the agenda... it really is just the straw that broke the camel's back."

World.title: Fonterra to report full-year earnings a year on from sale of brands business
World.content:
Dairy giant Fonterra reports its full-year earnings on Thursday morning, with all eyes on how the company has performed after selling its brands business.

Fonterra sold the Mainland group businesses to French dairy giant Lactalis for $4.2 billion last year.

The rationale was that the co-operative was better placed to focus on its ingredients business and sales to business customers.

Earlier this month the company said it expected its 2026 full-year underlying earnings to be at the top end of its previously announced range of 60-70 cents per share.

In a May earnings update, Fonterra said a disciplined focus on strategy had driven total group year-to-date operating profit of $1.8b, up from $1.7b a year earlier.

Former chief executive Miles Hurrell said last year the co-op was targeting earnings to be back at current levels within three years, offsetting the earnings impact of divesting the consumer and associated businesses.

The result on Thursday is the first delivered by new chief executive Richard Allen, after company updated its milk price forecast last week.

The new forecast midpoint has lifted from $9.25 per kgMS to $9.50 per kgMS, with the forecast range lifted and narrowed from $8.00-$10.50 per kgMS to $8.50-$10.50 per kgMS.

World.title: More than 50 businesses sign letter calling out politicians' 'anti-business rhetoric'
World.content:
Audio player for " More than 50 business leaders sign open letter to politicians " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1539313%2Fmore-than-50-businesses-sign-letter-calling-out-politicians-anti-business-rhetoric

More than 50 business leaders sign open letter to politicians Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A business leader says many in the business sector were reluctant to stand up to politicians and policies they disagreed with due to "fear of retribution".

An open letter calling on politicians to uphold private property and contract rights has been signed by more than 50 business leaders.

It comes off the back of proposals to sell off or separate supermarket assets, and buy back the Australian-owned BNZ.

Businesses across the construction, grocery, property, banking and investment sectors have signed the open letter.

New Zealand Initiative executive director Oliver Hartwich who wrote the letter, told Checkpoint he had significant support from the businesses he spoke with but some expressed fear in signing the letter.

"I've heard that from several members, really, that they thought the moment you stand up for business, and the moment you stand up to politicians, there's a fear of being singled out."

He said this was not a single-party issue and many businesses did not want to stand up to politicians that may be their next regulator or minister.

"There seems to be a problem, actually, in the communications between business and politics... in this small market of ours, there is always a problem with being singled out in the end."

The letter expressed deep concerns about "anti-business rhetoric" by politicians and are asking for some of these policies to be withdrawn.

"It's the same political leaders who are telling us, for example, that the cost of living is too high, supermarkets' prices are too high, and something needs to be done. So they're basically blaming the supermarkets for exploiting customers."

Hartwich said the election campaign should be focused on "decent ideas" and not just what "polls well".

"We should make sure that new players can enter into the New Zealand retail market."

World.title: 'The worst I've ever seen it' -  firefighters' union demands inquiry into FENZ management
World.content:
A firefighters' union is demanding an inquiry into the management of fire and emergency services, saying there is a risk to public safety.

New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union (NZFPU) members handed over a petition with more than 50,000 signatures to government at Parliament this afternoon.

The NZFPU went on strike for an hour today - the 64th strike since industrial action started two years ago.

Audio player for " Firefighters union calls for inquiry into management of FENZ " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1539072%2Fthe-worst-i-ve-ever-seen-it-firefighters-union-demands-inquiry-into-fenz-management

Firefighters union calls for inquiry into management of FENZ Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden declared last week she had no confidence in the Fire and Emergency (FENZ) chief executive, with a damning select committee report revealing organisational failings.

Union secretary Kurt Walsh was a volunteer for eight years before becoming a career firefighter a decade ago.

"It's the worst I've ever seen it," he said.

President Joe Stanley said his biggest concern was the risk to the public.

"We've already started to see it now, we've seen fire trucks deployed to emergencies that can't make it there and other trucks have to come.

"What I'm most scared of is that someone will ring 111 one day and we won't be able to make it."

The petition revealed several areas of cross-party consensus.

Green MP Chloe Swarbrick described the state of the emergency services through an anecdote of her time working with crews at Auckland's Pitt Street station.

"In the mess hall, there is a photo of when the Queen came to visit decades ago and all of our fire trucks are lined up.

"There were more operational heavy aerials then than there are now."

The Green Party said it supported a review and wanted to put FENZ into the Minister of Emergency Response Management's portfolio.

Labour has also committed to a full review into FENZ funding if elected.

Internal affairs spokesperson Lemauga Lydia Sosene thanked firefighters and pledged her party's support to them.

"Labour will commit to also extending the presumptive cover of ACC to our firefighters who do not have to prove that their work related injuries and illnesses have come from firefighting."

National announced its own three-point plan earlier in the day to make FENZ a government agency, provide extra health support for volunteers, and get fire trucks into service.

National's emergency management spokesperson Mark Mitchell said the plan would not require extra funding.

"The reset has got no fiscal cost to it. Everything will be delivered within baselines for FENZ," he said.

MP Tim Costley said FENZ's problems stemmed from operational issues rather than financial ones, but Stanley disagreed.

"It's both a funding issue and a mismanagement issue," he said.

"The mismanagement is there is a significant amount of money that goes to Fire and Emergency New Zealand every year. It's been used inappropriately and not focused solely on delivering what our communities need, which is someone to turn up when they ring 111."

He added that many call outs to emergencies were not funded through the insurance levies that support FENZ.

However, ACT's Brooke van Velden questioned using insurance levies to fund emergency services.

"I personally don't believe that it's appropriate so I'd like to ask the National Party, will they find up to $850 million extra in potentially new taxation or if not, where else will they get that money from?"

Meanwhile, the government has also confirmed it is not getting directly involved in Fire and Emergency's proposed restructure.

The restructure has proposed to cut 140 positions and make changes to 700 roles in FENZ's most sweeping changes since it was set up in 2017.

Launched last November, it has been on hold amid the ongoing industrial strife.

Asked by RNZ if he would dump the restructure, Mitchell said FENZ was responsible for operational decisions such as that.

"Fire and Emergency are responsible for making operational decisions, and like any other government agency, this would continue to be the case.

"If National is re-elected, we would restore accountability by making FENZ a departmental agency, offer more support to volunteers, and ensure the frontline have the equipment and training they need. The Government's expectation would be to ensure clear accountability on FENZ to deliver for firefighters and communities," said Mitchell in a statement.

World.title: 'Damaging stereotype' of Pasifika in AI-generated Voyager ad
World.content:
An  by Voyager Broadband that depicts two brown men attacking a Pākehā counterpart after their internet lags out while watching a UFC match has been criticised as 'lacking cultural due diligence'.

The AI-generated , which appeared on YouTube ads, has been taken down after questions were raised with the company last week over what kind of prompts were used in the ad.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405449973112

In the ad, the two brown men are depicted making animalistic noises prior to the attack on the white man, who is hospitalised as a result.

In a statement to RNZ Pacific, a spokesperson for Voyager Broadband said the  was created as part of a marketing activity and was intended to be humorous.

"The  was created using AI generated video as part of our marketing activity," spokesperson said.

"The concept was intended to depict three mates watching UFC together, with the humour coming from the stream cutting out and their exaggerated reaction. There was no racial intent behind the concept or the portrayal of the characters."

The spokesperon said that Voyager was now reviewing the prompts and instructions used to generate the video "so we can understand how they contributed to the final content".

Leon Bristow, founder of BEINGS.co and former Young New Zealander of the Year finalist. Kiwibank New Zealander of the Year Awards

However, Leon Bristow, the founder of BEINGS.co, a directory that connects advertising agencies with diverse talent, and a former Young New Zealander of the Year finalist, said such s reflect a "huge lack of Māori and Pasifika representation."

"Aside from it being AI, on the surface it might seem harmless but clearly there's been a lack of cultural due diligence," Bristow said.

"The intention may have been to show the frustration of bad internet, but when the people acting violently, accompanied by animalistic sounds, are Māori/Pasifika attacking a white man, it portrays a damaging stereotype our communities continue to face."

Harmful stereotypes

For decades, Māori and Pacific communities have been subject to misrepresentation in advertising, often through the repetition of harmful stereotypes.

In 2023, the Department of Corrections came under fire for two television ads that the Advertising Standards Authority went on to uphold complaints against Corrections over.

The 'harmful' recruitment ads reinforced stereotypes of Māori as criminals and Pākehā as Corrections staff.

Bristow explained that advertising in Aotearoa has suffered from a significant lack of Māori and Pasifika representation "to better inform mass media, and the messages communicated; messages that play an important role in shaping our culture."

"This [Voyagers] ad reinforces why we need better equity, diversity, inclusion and belonging, so that we don't risk sending the wrong narratives, again," Bristow said.

New 'lens'

Following questions from media about what prompt was used to generate the ad, Voyager's spokesperson explained the company had looked at the issue with a new perspective.

"Having considered the  through that lens, we could see how aspects of the content could be interpreted differently from what was intended. We removed it immediately.the spokesperson said.

"The portrayal does not reflect how Voyager wants to represent people or communities in our advertising, and we regret that the  was published."

Bristow said it would be interesting to see what kind of prompt had been used to generate the  in the first place.

World.title: The NRL finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object
World.content:
If we're ever going to solve that old question about unstoppable forces and immovable objects, the best way might be letting Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew run straight into each other.

The Penrith and Newcastle wingers will go head-to-head in Sunday's preliminary final with collisions that promise to rock the foundations of Stadium Australia.

Between them they boast a little over 200kg of prime Samoan beef, forged by pumping ludicrous amounts of steel in one case and fuelled by a truly startling quantity of Coke Zero in the other.

With a grand final berth on the line they will do what they do best: taking the ball and smashing into each other and anything else that gets in their way.

To'o has long been counted as one of the NRL's top wingers. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

They'll do it returning kicks, they'll do it early in sets, they'll do it close to the line to try and barge in and score and they'll do it over and over again until one of them is grand final bound.

Nobody can do all those things, grand finals included, like To'o, which is why he's the best winger of his time, but having played against Marzhew since the two's junior days he'll readily admit to taking some inspiration from the Knights wrecking machine.

"He's someone I like to base my game on, he's really strong and a big part of their team. I'm honoured to battle it out with my uso Greg," said To'o.

"It's our job to put our body on the front line and get the set started. It doesn't matter if it's one person in front of you, or two or three or four or five, just go as hard as you can."

Marzhew has enjoyed one of the best years of his career in 2026. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Likewise, Marzhew has looked to To'o plenty of times before and this season has the Panthers legend covered for tries (24 to 16), line breaks (27 to 21) and tackle busts (124 to 112), although To'o has him beat for average run metres (194 per game to 188)

Marzhew's form has earned him Newcastle's player's player award and he believes the challenge of taking on players like To'o has brought out the best in him.

"Penrith are one of my favourite teams to play against, they have so many representative players and I'm getting to go up against one of the best wingers to ever do it," said Marzhew

"I pride myself on that kind of stuff [big carries]. I try to excel with it because it's what the boys expect of me, if the crowd gets on top that's the cherry on top."

Fighting against greater numbers and winning is To'o's specialty. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's been doing it for so long now it's hard to imagine a time when To'o didn't relish the contact but he did have to learn to love it.

"When I was a bit younger, I was a bit shorter than I am now, I wouldn't say I was scared but there was that feeling that I might get knocked around," said To'o.

"I don't know if that counts as scared, I guess it pretty much does.

"It wasn't until my old man said, 'You're running it straight and getting knocked down or you're coming off and going home.'

"So I decided I'd run it straight. That was probably under-13s, I just dialled in and decided."

For Marzhew, who's got about 10kg on To'o, the issue was much simpler — there's never been any fear because he has always felt made for this

"Nah, that's the job description [running into people]," said Marzhew.

"That's what I signed up for."

The duo have plenty in common aside from their belief that the best way to solve a rugby league problem is to run right through it.

Both can really put on the dancing shoes — To'o's been hitting a little samba-type number after scoring recently, most notable after wrapping up Penrith's qualifying final over the Roosters with a late intercept try following one of his best games of the season.

"It's a Brazilian dance on TikTok, all the kids in my family, my nieces and nephews are always doing it," said To'o.

"My son does the dance and a Spider-man celebration as well, so I just wanted to honour all the kids.

"Now it's become a thing, I'll see kids down at the shops and they'll ask me to do it.

"But Greg's got me. He's built different. I've seen his moves, he's got the hips for it."

To'o's not kidding — Marzhew was a champion breakdancer in his youth, twice travelling to the United States to represent Australia in the world championships.

He says he's too big to move like he used to but the popping and locking and clean backflip he landed at the NRL's fan fest before the season opener in Las Vegas says otherwise.

But Marzhew needs just one try to equal Dom Young's record for most four-pointers in a season for the Knights and he'll likely have to go over To'o to do it, so the dancing will have to wait.

Marzhew and the Knights will be out to defy the odds yet again. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

"I'll let him take it, my mind is on something else — maybe after the game," said Marzhew.

"No dance, but I'd love to equal the record and share it with my brother, Dom Young, on the other wing."

If Penrith win, it will mark To'o's sixth grand final appearance while Marzhew is after his first.

A crowd of over 50,000 is expected, with a horde of Knights fans expected on hand for the club's first preliminary final since 2013.

The support comes as no shock to Marzhew, who has loved the city ever since arriving from Gold Coast in 2023, and he's ready to run into, over or through anything that gets in the way of Newcastle premiership dream.

"It's not a surprise, I wouldn't expect it but I love it and to play for them in this situation is an honour," said Marzhew.

"It's always a privilege to play in any game for Newcastle. I love playing for this town. It was home right from that first year."

World.title: Umpire felt 'threatened' by player, fan abuse after unruly AFL finale
World.content:
A 34-year-old Seaford man is expected to be charged for allegedly throwing a plate of food at a woman and child during last week's AFL preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane.

He is expected to be charged on summons with aggravated unlawful assault and discharge a missile.

AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

Police have interviewed the man and another 56-year-old Tullamarine man, who was identified after allegedly throwing a bottle onto the MCG's field of play at the conclusion of the match.

The Tullamarine man has been fined $418 under the Major Events Act.

He is the second man to be fined after security detained a 40-year-old Croydon man for throwing a bottle onto the field of play, before he was spoken to by police.

Bottles and cans were thrown onto the field after the game, including some aimed at the umpires as they walked off the MCG after a holding-the-ball decision by field umpire Hayden Meyer against Jarman Impey that gave Brisbane a go-ahead goal with 18 seconds remaining.

Umpire says he felt 'threatened' by Hawks duo

Sicily and Barrass (number 37) were seen having words with Meyer (left) immediately following the final siren. (AFL)

Meyer, who will officiate in this weekend's AFL grand final, was confronted by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass in the aftermath of his decision.

He said he had received an apology from Barrass but was still waiting to hear from Sicily.

"The abuse that came my way, I felt threatened," Meyer told reporters on Wednesday.

"I expressed exactly that [to the AFL] — the language, and the way that those two players, James [Sicily] and Tom [Barrass], came at me, I felt threatened and intimidated in that situation.

"So I spoke to [umpires boss] Steve McBurney the day after and gave my view of the situation, and how I felt and what occurred, and he then transferred that to Swanny [AFL football boss Greg Swann] and the MRO to eventually come up with a decision around the fines.

"[Barrass] was very apologetic and very sincere in his apology. I accepted his apology and thanked him for taking the time out of his day to give me a call."

Meyer says Sicily (pictured) is yet to apologise for abusing him on the final siren. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Meyer refused to make a call on whether the Hawks pair, who were fined over their actions, should be suspended instead.

"That's out of my control, that's not my decision … I suppose what I take from it is that it's not a great look for junior umpires and kids that are sitting on the couch that we want to recruit into umpiring," he said.

"They see that after the game on the weekend and, if I'm sitting on the couch, I'd be like, 'Do I really want to go to my local umpiring community group and sign up to be an umpire?'

" That was the big disappointing thing for me, that we struggle with umpiring recruitment in local communities, and that doesn't help. "

Despite the protestations from Hawthorn fans, Impey admitted the umpires made the right call.

"It was the right decision," he told the Kick It Forward podcast at the Brownlow Medal on Monday night.

"Naturally, when you think there are 30-40 seconds to go, you try and hold it in go from there, but credit to Hayden.

"I hope there was no hate message towards him, so sending love to him."

Jarman Impey (left) admitted the umpires had made the right call in penalising him for holding the ball in the final seconds. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

Ahead of this weekend's grand final, Meyer pleaded for fans to not "cross the line" again.

"I've never experienced bottles being thrown at me post-game. It was pretty scary, to be honest, and I hope it never happens again in any game, any sport," he said.

"[To fans attending the grand final], I would say be passionate, cheer for your team, but respect others, respect the people you're sitting next to, respect the umpires — have fun, but don't cross the line."

Police are continuing to make enquiries regarding the fan behaviour during and after the match.

World.title: Neale breaks silence on grand final ban as Lions downplay appeal impact
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Lachie Neale says he will remain in Melbourne to support Brisbane in Saturday's AFL grand final even if he is not successful with his appeals board hearing.

An appeals board hearing is the final avenue available for Neale, who unsuccessfully challenged the ban at a tribunal hearing last night.

The Lions announced this afternoon they would appeal the tribunal's decision.

Neale's dad 'worried for him' if ban keeps him from playing grand final Lachie Neale's father says the family is "worried" about the star Lion missing the AFL grand final at the end of a tumultuous year.

Neale has travelled to Melbourne with the Lions squad. The appeals board hearing will be held tomorrow, beginning at 4pm, AEST.

"Obviously, as you guys will be aware, the club and myself have decided to appeal the decision," Neale told reporters at Melbourne Airport.

"Obviously very hopeful that that's successful, but regardless of the result, I will be here to support the boys and the club this week. It's a big week for the club."

Neale did not take any questions from reporters and departed after giving a brief statement.

Brisbane veteran Dayne Zorko said the lead-up to this year's grand final was "not too dissimilar" to last year', when Neale was under an injury cloud.

There were doubts over Neale's availability in the lead-up to last year's grand final against Geelong due to a calf injury. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"There was a lot of scrutiny last year about whether he'd play or he wouldn't [and] in '24 he had a broken foot, so we're used to it," he said.

"He [Neale] seems to be fine. He wants to play and he's just taking it in his stride.

"You work so hard to get to this position, so he is disappointed, but we'll appeal it and go from there.

"We've had this stuff in the past. It's water under a bridge for us. We just keep going forward with our process and worry about what we can control.

"[Neale has an] impeccable record, you'd like to think that would carry a bit of weight [at the tribunal]. Maybe it doesn't.

"We can't get too carried away about it just being a Lachie Neale team. We're the Brisbane Lions, we've got a lot of players on our list.

"We played a few finals last year without him, as well. We'll just let that run its course. We're not going to get distracted by that, it's not our business to get distracted by it.

"We'd love for him to be out there, we hope he's out there, but if he's not, the next man up mentality is going to come into play."

Brisbane has brought an extended squad down to Melbourne ahead of the grand final.

No decision has been made yet on who will replace Neale if his suspension is upheld.

To succeed at the appeals board hearing, the Lions will have to prove the tribunal finding was either an error of law, an unreasonable decision, a manifestly excessive classification, or a manifestly excessive sanction.

They face Fremantle in Saturday's grand final at the MCG, chasing a third successive premiership.

Neale was suspended after the tribunal rejected his "inconsistent" evidence in a landmark case.

Why Neale's grand final ban was upheld The tribunal says it had reason not to overturn Lachie Neale's appeal. Now the AFL world waits to hear whether the Lions will launch an appeal.

He was found guilty of striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The two-time premiership captain argued his action was not a strike, but a body-check.

After a dramatic four-and-a-half-hour hearing, the tribunal upheld the charge and dismissed pleas for a downgrade due to exceptional and compelling circumstances.

The off-the-ball blow on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

Neale argued contact was made with his shoulder and chest and was not a strike.

He said Ginnivan "might have taken a bit of a dive to get a free kick".

"My shoulder made contact with his body and shoulder first and my arm wrapped around Jack," he said.

"But I didn't feel like I was striking him at all. It was more a bump or body-check."

The Lions will roll the dice on Lachie Neale's ban at an appeals board hearing. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

But tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC dismissed Neale's version of events.

"We find that this was a forceful blow delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand," Gleeson said.

"When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts.

"We are comfortably satisfied that this is what occurred. We find that this is what Neale intended.

"We have listened carefully to Mr Neale's evidence but we find it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video and, to that extent, we do not accept it."

ABC/AAP

World.title: Neale's dad 'worried for him' if ban keeps him from playing grand final
World.content:
Lachie Neale's father says the family is "worried" about the star Lion missing the AFL grand final at the end of a tumultuous year.

Neale copped a one-game suspension for striking Jack Ginnivan during the Lions' stunning preliminary final victory at the MCG on Saturday night, but the club has confirmed it will appeal against the decision.

Before the appeal was revealed, Robbie Neale told ABC Radio Adelaide in the lead-up to Saturday's decider against Fremantle that he felt the suspension was "just plain wrong".

"[He's played] 320 games, never been suspended," he said.

Why Neale's grand final ban was upheld The tribunal says it had reason not to overturn Lachie Neale's appeal. Now the AFL world waits to hear whether the Lions will launch an appeal.

"I just think to miss the grand final for this, it just … I've followed footy for a long time [and] it just doesn't add up to me."

Before the appeal was confirmed, Robbie said Lachie would have been torn on whether to appeal and prolong the process in grand final week.

"Lachie won't want the distraction for the team," he said.

Neale was also the centre of attention leading up to last year's grand final win over Geelong as he raced the clock to recover from a calf injury.

Neale was under an injury cloud heading into last year's decider. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

He ultimately played only the second half, kicking a crucial long-range goal in the third quarter.

"This one [the suspension], we're worried for him, because I know this means everything to him to play in this grand final," Robbie said.

"Easy to say that he's already played in a few, but they've got a chance to create history here."

The two-time Brownlow medallist has been in the headlines a lot this year, including giving up the captaincy before the season following a widely publicised marriage breakdown.

He was permitted to leave the team at the end of the season and went into Collingwood for a medical ahead of a reported move to the Magpies next year.

"The last thing Lachie wanted this week was another headline. It's just so disappointing," Robbie Neale said.

Robbie Neale said there had been "fabricated garbage" around his son, particularly regarding the Collingwood visit during the season.

"He does even amaze me in terms of how he's been able to compartmentalise and just focus on his job and play footy," he said.

"And he's had a pretty good year."

World.title: 'Flying mullet' Browning announces athletics retirement
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Two-time Olympian Rohan Browning has reflected on the moment that changed his life, as he announced his retirement from athletics.

Browning finishes his career as the fourth-fastest Australian over 100 metres, having run a personal best of 10.01 seconds at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

Sporting a distinctive hairstyle which earned the nickname 'Flying mullet', Browning recorded the time in the heats to qualify for the semifinals in his Olympic debut.

"That was a moment that changed my life," Browning said in an Australian Athletics statement.

"It gave me a really healthy dose of self-belief because it had been a quiet period for Australian men's sprinting.

Bizarre end to Australia's athletics campaign A hilariously understated celebration marked the end of an enthralling athletics campaign in Glasgow, and the beginning of Australian track and field being taken seriously around the world.

"There weren't many role models on the scene, and I feel like I had to forge that path myself."

A four-time national champion, Browning was content to call time on his career following Australia's shock victory in the men's 4x100m relay at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

The 28-year-old joined Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi and Calab Law in winning Australia's first gold medal in the event since 1974.

"I really wanted to go out on a high note, and after winning the gold medal at the Commonwealth Games in the relay, it was only going to go downhill from there," Browning said.

"The athlete in me still thinks that I could get back, run personal bests and compete at the highest level, but no athlete is ever going to be truly satisfied.

Rohan Browning (left) helped Australia win a drought-breaking relay gold at the Commonwealth Games. (Getty images: Ian MacNicol)

"The thing that I'm actually proudest of is that I made every team from my debut in 2017 to my retirement in 2026."

Australian Athletics chief executive Simon Hollingsworth said Browning did himself proud during his career.

"Rohan has been a fantastic athlete and ambassador for our sport," Hollingsworth said.

"His 2021 Tokyo performance inspired Australians and the generation of sprinters who followed.

"To go out with a superb relay run for gold in Glasgow is a fitting finale."

Although Browning was unable to dip under 10 seconds legally, he did run a wind-assisted PB of 9.89 in Austria earlier this year.

Browning also competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

He ran at five World Athletics Championships, with his best finish in the 100m being a semifinal appearance at the 2023 edition in Budapest.

World.title: Mary Fowler's Man City score controversial goal with flare burning on pitch
World.content:
Mary Fowler's Manchester City have started their Women's Champions League campaign with a controversial draw against Bayern Munich, scoring a crucial goal with a flare burning among the players.

The reigning English champions came back from 2-0 down to equalise after Fowler's injection in the 63rd minute.

But it was City's first goal from Beth Mead that had Bayern players fuming.

In the final seconds of the first half, Kerstin Casparij broke down the right wing and was pursued by Franziska Kett towards the edge of the 18-yard box, where a flare was sending purple smoke billowing.

Bayern goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic waved her arms in an apparent attempt to get the attention of officials as the play unfolded, but Casparij seemed unfazed by the nearby flare as she outpaced Kett and whipped a cross into the box, where Bunny Shaw's shot was blocked, and Mead cleaned up the scraps to make it 2-1 heading into the break.

As City celebrated, Mahmutovic and Kett started to complain before their teammates joined in, with referee Olatz Rivera Olmedo immediately removing the projectile from the pitch.

Discussions continued as the ball returned to halfway for the kick-off before VAR confirmed the goal would stand, giving City crucial momentum heading into half-time, leading to an improved second-half performance and ultimately an 86th-minute equaliser by Carlotta Wamser.

Elsewhere on the first matchday of the tournament, Arsenal's trio of Australians — Steph Catley, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Caitlin Foord — all started as the 2025 winners began the quest to regain their continental crown against Danish part-timers HB Køge.

The Gunners won 1-0, but needed an injury-time penalty from Mariona Caldentay that bank worker Alberte Vingum almost saved.

"It was a pretty crazy last five minutes, but that's football," Catley said.

"They defended great; we tried so many avenues to goal.

"Credit to the girls, they kept trying, and Mariona was very calm in that moment."

And in Monza, veteran Matildas defender Aiva Luik played the 90 minutes as Hacken went down 1-0 to Internazionale, becoming the oldest group stage/league phase player at 41, according to UEFA.

Capped 45 times by Australia, Luik is at her 16th club in her 10th country during her 26-year career.

"I still feel young. The secret is coffee and chocolate," she said.

Inter, making its competition debut, scored in the fifth minute through Haley Bugej from a corner but couldn't find a second, with the Swedes more dangerous on the break.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC with wires

World.title: Banned Swans to make first public appearance since Pullman Hotel scandal
World.content:
Sydney's five suspended players will make their return to the club this week and will address the Swans' playing group "at some point".

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are expected to return to club this week for their exit meetings.

Exit meetings are carried out with all players on a senior list at the end of each season to discuss their future with the club.

Swans coach Dean Cox arrived at the club's Moore Park base early today, before Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich briefly spoke to media.

"Look, it's a natural thing that the players will come into the club over the next period," Pavlich said.

"Don't know exactly when that'll be, given that the season's now finished and player exit meetings are occurring.

"And the players at some point will have a chat to the broader group and the club, but yeah, there's no timeline."

Swans coach Dean Cox arrives at the club's headquarters ahead of player exit meetings. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

The five have not been at the club since August after they were stood down for breaching club standards following a post-match party at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate from a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid, and there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Pavlich would not be drawn on the specifics surrounding the five's return.

Asked what he would want the five to say in their address, Pavlich said: "I want them to be themselves.

"I want them to come in and do what we'd normally do at the end of a season, which is, yeah, player exit meetings.

"If they've got something to say to their player group, if they've got something to say to the club, then we'll hear them out then."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Tones And I breaks silence on NRL grand final pre-match fiasco
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

On Tuesday, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys told ABC Sport the NRL's plans to have Tones And I perform before next month's showpiece event would be cancelled.

The NRL will use the money set aside for pre-match entertainment to contribute to children playing rugby league.

But Tones And I's management said no deal had been signed or confirmed in writing.

Via a statement sent to ABC Sport, her management representative Regan Lethbridge said "prior commitments" were a sticking point.

"Tones was recently approached to perform the pre-show at the NRL grand final," the statement read.

"An offer was presented to Tones via management on September 5.

NRL grand final loses pre-match act The NRL grand final is set to go ahead without pre-match entertainment after negotiations with Australian artist Tones and I collapsed.

"Tones had a prior commitment with Macklemore in America and explored all avenues to make it work.

"Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing.

"Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer.

"We wish the NRL nothing but the very best for their event."

The Sydney Morning Herald reported the issue centred the NRL's insistence Tones And I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

But neither Tones And I nor V'Landys has cited the set list as the issue at play.

Tones And I has previously said she loathed the hit song, which enjoyed significant commercial success when released in 2019.

Macklemore found himself at the centre of his own live upheaval after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's The Loop Tour, over pro-Palestinian comments.

'A different direction'

V'landys said he wished Tones And I well.

"I'm a fan of Tones And I," he told ABC Sport on Tuesday.

"She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction."

V'landys said the cost of putting on any artist for a grand final performance was about a million dollars.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

Peter V’landys said money set aside for pre-match entertainment would be invested in junior rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

To have no pre-game show would be a stunning break from tradition.

The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year.

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones And I broke down.

"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to … play rugby league," he said.

" We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act. "

State governments across the country are bidding for the grand final hosting rights.

New South Wales holds the rights, but it is unclear whether the state minister for sport, Steve Kamper, or Premier Chris Minns were consulted.

Neither provided comment in response to questions.

New South Wales Rugby League chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

Tech.title: OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again
Tech.content:
After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward.

On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community.

The nine-member group is stacked with who researchers described to The Verge as celebrities in the field, drawn from institutions including Stanford, Harvard, Oxford, and Cambridge, with multiple Fields Medals and MacArthur “genius grants” among them. It will be hosted by Princeton, New Jersey’s Institute for Advanced Study (IAS), one of the world’s most revered centers of mathematical research and the former intellectual home of figures including Albert Einstein, John von Neumann, and J. Robert Oppenheimer.

“The other fundamental fact is that our overarching aim is to represent as well as we possibly can the interests of the mathematical community.”

OpenAI said the group, called the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), will operate independently, with the freedom to offer advice the company has not requested, publicly comment on its impact on mathematics, and make its advice public, though it did not provide details on what this may entail. It appears that the group will be granted early access to OpenAI’s research in order to fulfill its task. Members will not be paid by OpenAI and the group can change its membership as it sees fit, OpenAI said. “Its value depends on its members being able to exercise their own judgement and challenge ours,” the company said. “The group will advise on the review and communication of emerging results: they will help OpenAI assess their significance, advise on how to coordinate their dissemination, and advise on academic and professional standards of mathematical research. It will also advise on how our tools can support mathematical research and learning.”

For all the emphasis on independence, it remains unclear how much influence the group will actually have or why it was formed in the first place. Simon Machado, a researcher at ETH Zurich in Switzerland, said the whole thing seemed “shrouded in mystery” and he questioned how the nine members were selected. The group’s bare-bones website says it “came together after OpenAI approached some of its members about establishing an external advisory board,” but that, following discussions with the company, the mathematicians decided to launch an independent group instead and invite others to join. It’s not clear which members were initially approached by OpenAI or how the remaining members were selected.

In a blog post published Tuesday, advisory group member Martin Hairer elaborated on the group’s origins and the thinking behind it, responding to what he called a “torrent of misinformation” surrounding its formation. “It is obvious that AI has already had a profound impact on mathematical research and raises numerous questions of correct attribution of ideas, priority, human understanding of ideas, etc.,” he wrote, adding that there is no sense in the community “taking a hard ‘ostrich’ approach of simply ignoring the AI labs and refusing to talk to them on principle.”

While acknowledging that the group was formed in response to an approach from OpenAI, Hairer stressed that not all of its members had been contacted by the company and that the resulting organization is “genuinely independent of OpenAI and any other of the so-called ‘frontier’ AI labs.” Beyond “obvious confidentiality requirements,” he said members have not signed any restrictive agreements governing what they can say publicly, adding that they receive no financial compensation and are relying on the IAS for technical support.

“The other fundamental fact is that our overarching aim is to represent as well as we possibly can the interests of the mathematical community,” wrote Hairer, a professor of mathematics at Imperial College London and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL). While noting that the group is hardly a representative sample of the community, he said he is “absolutely certain that all nine of us take this extremely seriously and are acting in good faith.”

However the members were selected, the group currently comprises an elite cadre of academic mathematicians. The small size raises further questions about whether the group has the breadth of expertise required to evaluate everything coming its way, given the highly specialized skills and knowledge required to operate at the frontiers of mathematics.

Francesco Fournier-Facio, an incoming mathematics professor at Heriot-Watt University in Scotland, described himself as pretty “ambivalent” about the panel, saying that greater engagement with mathematicians “can only make things better.” But he questioned whether this group fully reflects the community whose work and livelihoods are being upended by OpenAI’s quest to rack up mathematical trophies. “It feels like an ivory tower,” he told The Verge.

Machado similarly questioned whether the group’s members fully understand, or can speak to, the concerns of the broader mathematical community when it comes to AI. “They’re amazing mathematicians, but I don’t know if they are the people I want to represent me in more political questions,” he said. For mathematicians in their and similarly elite positions, Machado said, “I think that the reality they are facing is very different from the reality that most mathematicians are facing right now.”

Whether the group can earn mathematicians’ trust will ultimately determine how effective it will be at containing the fallout from OpenAI’s recent parade of missteps in announcing results and, more importantly, soften the blow for whatever the company is planning to announce next. In his blog, Hairer said members would “be very naïve to believe that the AI labs won’t try to spin whatever we say in a way that suits their PR machine, which dwarfs anything we could possibly come up with.”

Nevertheless, Hairer argued it would be hypocritical not to engage now that OpenAI appears to be making an effort, particularly after so many criticized the company’s conduct and poor communications. The group has yet to settle on the advice it intends to provide, he said, but there is a clear problem it is responding to: “It is a fact that AI companies have in recent months been producing some high profile mathematical results and that their publication and dissemination has been falling far short of acceptable mathematical practice, whichever way that is defined.”

“We are currently facing the very specific challenge of advising OpenAI on how to coordinate the release of a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model.”

For now, Hairer said the group is gathering input through conversations with colleagues, a public feedback form, and discussion on Proofs and Prompts, a blog that has emerged as a key forum for mathematicians reckoning with AI’s impact on the field.

But the group’s biggest challenge likely lies ahead. When announcing the advisory group, OpenAI casually dropped the news that its new, unreleased model — the same that resolved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem — has now “resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.” It has previously said it is closing in on another Millennium Prize problem. On its website, the group said dealing with this logjam is its first priority: “We are currently facing the very specific challenge of advising OpenAI on how to coordinate the release of a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model.”

In part, the new effort at engaging mathematicians is an acknowledgement of the monumental PR disaster its attempt was, in which the company found itself fending off accusations of scooping researchers, failing to credit the human work its models built upon, and even stealing from those using its models. Those controversies led many mathematicians to wonder if the company understood — or even respected — the discipline and community it had barreled into.

After the last few months and with so much having been written about what mathematicians want, Kevin Buzzard, a mathematics professor at Imperial College London, wondered why OpenAI felt like it needed such an elite body to understand what the community wants. “It wasn’t proofs of hard theorems, it was better understanding of our subject,” he said. “It’s not entirely clear to me that you need a committee of brilliant people to hammer the point home.”

Tech.title: Paramount will need to release way more movies to make this merger work
Tech.content:
Now that Paramount has reached a settlement with the 12 states that were suing to block its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), the studio is even closer to becoming one of the world’s biggest production houses. In addition to spending at least $300 million more on film and TV projects produced in the US, Paramount says that it will release a minimum of 30 movies annually after it absorbs WBD. On paper, these goals make it sound like Paramount is trying to ensure that the entertainment industry won’t be harmed by its WBD acquisition. But when you look at the studios’ recent output, it seems very much like Paramount CEO David Ellison is making promises to the public that he might not be able to keep.

In a statement about the settlement, California Attorney General Rob Bonta stressed that the settlement was designed to maintain consistent film output and domestic production while “protecting the livelihoods of workers above and below the line.” (Of course, any redundancies caused by a merger of this scale will likely lead to layoffs, which makes Bonta’s claim that the settlement “protects workers, jobs, and Hollywood” questionable in the first place.) In a statement of their own, Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) president Sean Astin and chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree-Ireland thanked Bonta and noted that the settlement represents “the lowest standards that our employers must meet.”

Though the acquisition — which has not yet officially been finalized — would permanently fuse Paramount and WBD, the settlement only requires the newly merged company to adhere to a few rules for just five years. In the first two years, Paramount/WBD has to either put out 30 films annually or pay $30 million per film into healthcare and retirement funds managed by Hollywood’s biggest unions. During the following three years, the merged studio would need to release 32 films annually, and if it fails to meet any of these requirements during this five-year period, it will be forced to sell off its 49 percent stake in Miramax Studios to one of its competitors.

In terms of overall output, these proposed goals would be a step up for both Paramount and WBD as separate corporate entities. Over the past six years (including projects slated to debut later in 2026), Paramount has released an average of 15 films annually while WBD has averaged 17. Assuming that the newly merged studio will stick to Paramount and WBD’s previously announced release slates for 2027 and 2028, it would need to put more than a few new projects on the board in order to avoid multimillion dollar penalties. But that probably isn’t all that much of a concern to Paramount because the settlement doesn’t require the new company to produce the projects necessary to hit its annual movie quota.

Paramount/WBD could fulfill its obligations by distributing films that it acquires from other production houses. These films would carry the Paramount/WBD branding, but they would be the products of labor carried out by teams with no direct connection to the studio. Paramount/WBD could also flood the zone with completely new, original films it greenlights and finances itself. But many of those movies could feel less ambitious because the settlement only requires that 20 percent of them have production budgets over $50 million.

Paramount appears to have convinced Bonta and his fellow attorneys general that absorbing WBD will give it the ability to basically double its usual output. But that logic presumes every single aspect of both studios’ production pipelines will continue to operate normally once Paramount and WBD become one. Though Paramount/WBD could ramp internal production up, what feels much more likely to happen is the studio doing the bare minimum to abide by the settlement’s terms. Everything about this settlement makes it seem like Ellison is playing a long game, and after those guardrails disappear in five years, Paramount/WBD will be in an even stronger position to shape the broader entertainment landscape.

Tech.title: Rabbit’s new AI agent doesn’t need an R1 to run
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rabbit, the company behind the underwhelming R1 device, is rolling out a standalone AI agent that you don’t need its hardware to use, as reported earlier by Wired. The startup says its new OS3 “agentic operating system” runs in the cloud but operates locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices.

According to Rabbit, you can add up to five devices to one account, along with your preferred AI models. OS3 will automatically determine the devices, files, apps, and AI models it needs to complete a task. You can also access OS3 through its dedicated desktop site, a paired messaging app like Telegram or iMessage, as well as on Rabbit’s R1 device.

Though Rabbit founder Jesse Lyu tells Wired that the startup has stopped manufacturing R1 devices, it isn’t giving up on AI hardware entirely. It’s instead focusing on a new vibe-coding “cyberdeck” that will run OS3 when it launches within “months,” Wired reports.

Rabbit claims its OS3 system won’t store, copy, use, or sell your data. It notes that it will still keep your chats and memories stemming from them on its servers. Other AI providers linked to OS3 will also handle your data under their own privacy rules.

Tech.title: Saudi Arabia’s new Exobot EVs make the Cybertruck look normal
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is mostly known for its global dominance over petroleum production and oil reserves — not necessarily cars and auto manufacturing, and certainly not electric vehicle production. So it was a little surprising on Monday when a Saudi startup called Ceer unveiled a pair of hyper-angular, spaceship-like EVs, with plans to launch an additional five models by 2030.

The Exobot (yes, that’s the real name) sedan and SUV are expected to go on sale in Saudi Arabia starting in 2027. The ultra-futuristic designs scream Tron, Blade Runner, and every other sci-fi movie you’ve seen — and then some. The gullwing doors are ripped straight from the Tesla Model X (which, of course, was ripped straight from the DeLorean and a range of other rare production cars). Wild and wedge-shaped, the Exobots seemed built explicitly to draw attention. Which, in an attention-based economy, is probably the right strategy.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

The sedan Exobot has low-slung, supercar proportions with a steeply raked windshield that flows seamlessly into the hood. The front fascia features a razor-thin, full-width LED light bar nestled under a sharp, forward-jutting nose, giving it a mean, visor-like glare. The two-tone bodywork and ample windshield immediately had me thinking about the Ferrari Luce, the polarizing electric supercar released earlier this year.

The SUV boasts a blocky, military-meets-cyberpunk stance with high ground clearance and aggressive angles. The whole thing looks thick and armor-plated, with a flat roofline and a distinctive, tactical presence. I wouldn’t be surprised to see this thing bouncing along the Moon’s surface someday. Both were designed by Rob Melville, McLaren’s former design director. But according to Autocar, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had final say on the design.

Previous Next













1 / 8

Ceer is hoping to take advantage of all the upheaval in the global car market, driven largely by the flood of Chinese electric vehicle exports in Asia, Europe, and South America. The US appears on its way to becoming an automotive backwater, with its ahistorical embrace of internal combustion engines and steep tariffs designed to keep Chinese EVs at bay. Why not release a pair of bombastic Batmobiles as a way to distract from the originating country’s extreme oil dependency?

Ceer didn’t exactly emerge from nothing. Rather, it’s a joint venture between Saudi Arabia’s PIF sovereign wealth fund and Foxconn, the Taiwanese company most known for manufacturing the iPhone for Apple. The company will be funded by the kingdom’s vast oil wealth, but with the purpose of building a lineup of vehicles that run on electricity.

Even though it’s distinctly a project built to jump-start the kingdom’s auto industry, Ceer needed to venture outside its borders when hiring for its top roles. Jim DeLuca spent 37 at General Motors, ending up as executive VP for global manufacturing, before joining Ceer as CEO.

“We ⁠wanted to make sure the world could see what Saudi Arabia is capable of,” DeLuca told Reuters.

The kingdom has had mixed luck when it comes to automotive projects. There were plans to build a Jaguar-Land Rover factory there over a decade ago, but to no avail. Toyota declined a deal with the Saudis in 2019. The Public Investment Fund owns a controlling stake in California-based Lucid Motors, which is now building a manufacturing facility in King Abdullah Economic City.

Ceer is taking a diversified approach to its vehicle lineup. While the first models will be electric, subsequent vehicles will be hybrid and combustion-engine, depending on market demands.

That said, starting a car company from scratch is daunting. Just ask Fisker, Lordstown, or Arrival — all of which went bankrupt. Even Lucid, with its support from PIF, is still struggling. We’ll have to see whether Ceer can buck that trend.

Tech.title: Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 comes in an Extreme version too
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Qualcomm has announced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, this year joined by the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 too. The company describes both new phone chips as flagships, and the spec differences are relatively minor, mostly limited to improved AI processing, video capture, and gaming performance on the Extreme model.

Both Gen 6 chips are built on a 2nm process, and share much in common, including their modems, display specs, security features, GPS, and memory and storage support. Qualcomm no longer publishes detailed breakdowns of the cores across its silicon, but the CPU details given are identical, with two big cores at up to 5GHz and six performance cores running at up to 4GHz. Despite that, the Extreme is described as having slightly superior performance across its CPU, GPU, and NPU.

Some differences are more clear-cut. The 8 Elite Extreme is capable of driving superior video capture, including 8K at 60fps, 4K at 240fps, and support for the Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec. A larger shared memory pool for the NPU should drive faster and more efficient AI performance on the Extreme chip too, while AI-dedicated matrix cores in the GPU (plus more memory) should boost gaming performance slightly when using AI features.

Image: Qualcomm

With core performance seemingly similar, the jump up to the Extreme chip is relatively minor, so it will be interesting to see which chips manufacturers use for which phones. Motorola is the first to jump on board, confirming that its newly announced Signature 27 flagship will use the Extreme chip. Qualcomm has announced that the two chips will also be adopted by Vivo, Xiaomi, Oppo, Honor, iQoo, Nubia, OnePlus, Redmi, Redmagic, and ZTE.

The two 8 Elite Gen 6 chips are Qualcomm’s first 2nm silicon, joining Apple’s A20 Pro and MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro in bringing the new silicon scale to smartphones.

Tech.title: Apple clarifies that Texture and Grain controls are exclusive to the latest iPhones’ cameras
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s new texture and grain controls for stylizing photos will be more limited on older phones than initially expected.

A confusingly worded press release from Apple indicated that the new features, announced alongside the iPhone 18 and 18 Pro earlier this month, would be “available” on older devices like the iPhone 16 and iPhone Air that “support the latest generation of Photographic Styles.”

But it turns out that “available” didn’t mean that older iPhone models would have full access to those new features.

Making texture adjustments to enhance or smooth a subject’s skin and adding film grain will only be an option when those phones are being used to edit shots taken with the latest iPhone models. Apple has since updated recent press releases to state that those controls will only be available for “photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and the Ultra Wide, Main, and Center Stage cameras on iPhone Duo.”

The original version of a September 11th release, which was issued the day before the latest versions of the iPhone and Apple Watches became available for preorder, is still available in its original form on other websites with a footnote specifying that the new “texture and grain controls in Photographic Styles will be available on iOS 27 on iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.”

This limited compatibility was corroborated by a Reddit user who was able to make adjustments to texture and grain on their iPhone 16 Pro Max, but only while editing sample photos taken on an iPhone 18 Pro by photographer Austin Mann who made them available for download on his website. I also had access to those new Photographic Styles controls when editing Mann’s samples on my own iPhone 16 Pro running iOS 27, but they were not available on photos I captured myself.

The Verge has reached out to Apple for clarification on how the feature is supposed to work on older phones but did not immediately get a response.
